_note: One mystery a week for thirty-six weeks at every grade that has been written. Each case is a short story, a question, the suspects with what the text says about each, and the teacher answer with its proof quotes. A mystery is a claim-and-evidence task in disguise, which is why it sits beside the writing step and uses the same frame. Built by scripts/merge-mysteries.mjs from scripts/mysteries/g<N>.json; do not edit by hand.

debate.story: On Monday morning, Ms. Park opened the library and gasped. Books were all over the floor. A trail of sawdust led from the shelf to the class pet cage. The cage door stood open and Nibbles the hamster was gone. Coach Dan came in at eight to borrow a whistle from the desk. Leo was out sick on Friday, but his library key is still missing. Behind the beanbag was a nest of torn paper.
debate.question: Who made the mess? Pick one and show the words that prove it.

suspects.why: a sawdust trail, an open cage and a nest of torn paper
in at eight to borrow a whistle from the desk
out sick Friday, with his library key still missing

evidence: “A trail of sawdust led from the shelf to the class pet cage.”
“Behind the beanbag was a nest of torn paper.”
arguments.against: “Coach Dan came in at eight to borrow a whistle from the desk.”

evidence: “Coach Dan came in at eight to borrow a whistle from the desk.”
arguments.against: “The cage door stood open and Nibbles the hamster was gone.”

evidence: “Leo was out sick on Friday, but his library key is still missing.”
arguments.against: “A trail of sawdust led from the shelf to the class pet cage.”

debate.note: Nobody has an alibi any more, so the children have to weigh evidence instead of crossing names off. The sawdust and the nest are the strongest words on the page and they point one way. A missing key and an early visit are both reasons to wonder, and neither explains torn paper behind a beanbag.

debate.question: Where are the pencils going? Pick one answer and quote the story.

suspects.why: flies out when her cage is open, and fifteen on the cabinet
sits beside the cup and was back from the nurse by ten
took a handful to the office with nobody counting

evidence: “Mr. Ortiz found fifteen pencils in a pile on top of the cabinet.”
arguments.against: “Nina sits beside the pencil cup and was back from the nurse by ten.”

evidence: “Nina sits beside the pencil cup and was back from the nurse by ten.”
arguments.against: “The class parrot Kiwi flies out when her cage door is left open.”

evidence: “Mr. Ortiz took a handful of pencils to the office on Tuesday.”
“Nobody counted them before he left.”
arguments.against: “Mr. Ortiz found fifteen pencils in a pile on top of the cabinet.”

debate.note: Fifteen pencils on a cabinet is the best evidence in the story, and a parrot is the only suspect who could get them up there. The teacher is the fun answer and the class should be allowed to make it, as long as they notice it does not explain the pile.

cases.title: The Apple Orchard Mix-Up
cases.story: The class went on a field trip to Red Barn Orchard. Each student picked a bag of apples. On the bus, Mia saw that her bag of red apples was now full of green ones! Her seat partner, Jack, had a bag of red apples and a big grin. Mr. Stone, the bus driver, had both hands on the wheel the whole ride. The farmer had stayed back at the orchard. Jack laughed. "I traded bags when you were looking out the window. I love red apples!"
cases.question: Who switched Mia’s apples?

suspects.why: bag of red apples, big grin, he said he traded
both hands on the wheel the whole ride
stayed back at the orchard

cases.answer: Jack switched Mia’s apples.
proof: "Her seat partner, Jack, had a bag of red apples and a big grin."
"I traded bags when you were looking out the window."
clears: Mr. Stone: "…had both hands on the wheel the whole ride."
Farmer: "The farmer had stayed back at the orchard."
cases.explain: This shows Jack had Mia’s red apples because he said he traded bags. Because of this, Jack is the one who switched them.

debate.story: The class picked apples at Red Barn Orchard. On the bus, Mia's bag of red apples was full of green ones. Her seat partner Jack had red apples and a big grin. Mr. Stone stopped the bus twice and walked down the aisle. The farmer loaded every bag into the luggage hold himself. Mia set her bag down by the gate while she tied her shoe.
debate.question: How did Mia end up with green apples? Make the case for one answer.

suspects.why: red apples in his bag and a big grin beside her
stopped the bus twice and walked down the aisle
loaded every bag into the hold himself

evidence: “Her seat partner Jack had red apples and a big grin.”
arguments.against: “The farmer loaded every bag into the luggage hold himself.”

evidence: “Mr. Stone stopped the bus twice and walked down the aisle.”
arguments.against: “Her seat partner Jack had red apples and a big grin.”

evidence: “The farmer loaded every bag into the luggage hold himself.”
“Mia set her bag down by the gate while she tied her shoe.”
arguments.against: “On the bus, Mia's bag of red apples was full of green ones.”

debate.note: A grin is not evidence and the class should be pushed on that. Jack having red apples is evidence, but so does everybody who picked red ones. The bag set down by the gate is the quiet sentence that lets this be an accident, and the best answers find it.

cases.title: The Case of the Flat Tire
cases.story: After school, Jada found her bike tire flat. She looked closely and saw a sharp thumbtack stuck in the rubber. A row of thumbtacks had fallen out of the art room box onto the sidewalk. Her friend Theo rode a scooter and never touched the bike rack. The crossing guard, Mr. Hill, stood at the corner all afternoon. "My tire ran over a tack!" Jada said. "It was an accident, not a person."
cases.question: What caused Jada’s flat tire?

suspects.why: tack stuck in the tire, tacks on the sidewalk
rode a scooter, never touched the rack
at the corner all afternoon

cases.answer: A fallen thumbtack caused the flat tire.
proof: "…saw a sharp thumbtack stuck in the rubber."
"A row of thumbtacks had fallen out of the art room box onto the sidewalk."
clears: Theo: "…rode a scooter and never touched the bike rack."
Mr. Hill: "…stood at the corner all afternoon."
cases.explain: This shows the tack popped the tire because it was stuck right in the rubber. Because of this, a fallen thumbtack caused the flat.

debate.story: After school, Jada found her bike tire flat. A sharp thumbtack was stuck in the rubber. Tacks had spilled from the art room box onto the sidewalk. The art room door is next to the bike rack. Theo parked his scooter against Jada's bike at lunchtime. Mr. Hill moved three bikes out of the gateway that afternoon. Nobody saw the tire before three o'clock.
debate.question: What made the tire flat? Choose one answer and back it up.

suspects.why: a tack in the rubber, spilled from the art room box
parked his scooter against her bike at lunchtime
moved three bikes out of the gateway that afternoon

evidence: “A sharp thumbtack was stuck in the rubber.”
“Tacks had spilled from the art room box onto the sidewalk.”
arguments.against: “Theo parked his scooter against Jada's bike at lunchtime.”

evidence: “Theo parked his scooter against Jada's bike at lunchtime.”
arguments.against: “A sharp thumbtack was stuck in the rubber.”

evidence: “Mr. Hill moved three bikes out of the gateway that afternoon.”
“Nobody saw the tire before three o'clock.”
arguments.against: “The art room door is next to the bike rack.”

debate.note: There is a tack in the tire and nobody disputes it, so the real question is how it got there. Rolling over one is an accident; being pushed onto one is not. Ask what would be different about the tack's position in each case, and listen for children who want to go and look.

cases.title: The Mystery of the Cloudy Tank
cases.story: On Monday, the class fish tank was cloudy and green. Goldie the fish was hiding behind a plant. Over the weekend, the tank had been sitting in bright sunlight by the window. The fish food can was full, so nobody overfed Goldie. The filter was unplugged because a cord had been bumped during cleaning. "No sun and a working filter will fix it," said Mr. Diaz.
cases.question: Why did the fish tank get cloudy?

suspects.why: bright sun, filter unplugged
food can was full
just hiding behind a plant

cases.answer: Sunlight and an unplugged filter made the tank cloudy.
proof: "…the tank had been sitting in bright sunlight by the window."
"The filter was unplugged because a cord had been bumped during cleaning."
clears: Too much food: "The fish food can was full, so nobody overfed Goldie."
cases.explain: This shows the water could not stay clean because the filter was off and sunlight helps algae grow. Because of this, the tank turned cloudy and green.

debate.story: On Monday the class fish tank was cloudy and green. All weekend it sat in bright sunlight by the window. The filter was unplugged when a cord got bumped during cleaning. The food can was refilled on Friday and nobody wrote down how much went in. Two helpers cleaned the tank on Friday and changed half the water. New water can cloud a tank for days.
debate.question: Why did the tank go cloudy? Pick one answer and prove it.

suspects.why: bright sun all weekend and a filter left unplugged
a can refilled Friday with nobody writing down how much
half the water changed on Friday by two helpers

evidence: “All weekend it sat in bright sunlight by the window.”
“The filter was unplugged when a cord got bumped during cleaning.”
arguments.against: “Two helpers cleaned the tank on Friday and changed half the water.”

evidence: “The food can was refilled on Friday and nobody wrote down how much went in.”
arguments.against: “All weekend it sat in bright sunlight by the window.”

evidence: “Two helpers cleaned the tank on Friday and changed half the water.”
“New water can cloud a tank for days.”
arguments.against: “The filter was unplugged when a cord got bumped during cleaning.”

debate.note: Everything in this case happened on Friday, so the day cannot choose between them. A full food can no longer proves nobody overfed, because nobody knows what went in. The cleaning is the answer children rarely reach, and the sentence about new water is there for them to find.

cases.title: The Midnight Noise
cases.story: Every night at midnight, the Garcias heard a loud tap-tap-tap on the roof. Lucia thought it was a ghost. Her dad climbed up in the morning and found acorns all over the roof. A big oak tree hung right over the house. In the corner of the roof sat a squirrel’s nest full of acorns. The neighbors were asleep and their lights were off by 10:00. "It’s not a ghost," Dad said. "It’s a busy squirrel!"
cases.question: What is making the noise on the roof?

suspects.why: acorns on the roof, nest full of acorns
no clues point to a ghost
asleep with lights off by 10:00

cases.answer: A squirrel is making the noise.
proof: "…found acorns all over the roof."
"…sat a squirrel’s nest full of acorns."
clears: Neighbors: "The neighbors were asleep and their lights were off by 10:00."
cases.explain: This shows a squirrel is on the roof because its nest and acorns are right there. Because of this, the tapping is a squirrel, not a ghost.

debate.story: Every night at midnight the Garcias heard a loud tap-tap-tap on the roof. Dad climbed up and found acorns all over the shingles. A big oak hangs right over the house. A squirrel's nest sits in the roof corner. On windy nights the oak branches scrape the roof above Lucia's room. The neighbours' porch light switches off at midnight with a loud clunk. The sound comes at the same minute every night.
debate.question: What is making the noise? Choose one and show the words.

suspects.why: acorns on the shingles and a nest in the roof corner
branches that scrape the roof on windy nights
a porch light that clunks off at midnight

evidence: “Dad climbed up and found acorns all over the shingles.”
“A squirrel's nest sits in the roof corner.”
arguments.against: “The sound comes at the same minute every night.”

evidence: “On windy nights the oak branches scrape the roof above Lucia's room.”
arguments.against: “Dad climbed up and found acorns all over the shingles.”

evidence: “The neighbours' porch light switches off at midnight with a loud clunk.”
“The sound comes at the same minute every night.”
arguments.against: “A big oak hangs right over the house.”

debate.note: The same minute every night is the hardest fact here, and it fits a switch far better than an animal or the weather. Squirrels do not keep to a clock. Children who notice that are using a word they would normally read straight past.

cases.title: The Scattered Leaf Pile
cases.story: On Saturday, Dad and Lila raked a giant pile of leaves in the front yard. They went inside for lunch. When they came back, the leaves were spread all over the street! The trees across the street were bending back and forth. The weather report on the radio said wind gusts of 30 miles per hour. Their dog, Pepper, had been napping inside by the heater. The neighbor kids were away at a soccer game. "The wind wins this time," Dad sighed.
cases.question: What scattered the leaf pile?

suspects.why: trees bending, 30 mph gusts
napping inside by the heater
away at a soccer game

cases.answer: The strong wind scattered the leaves.
proof: "The trees across the street were bending back and forth."
"The weather report on the radio said wind gusts of 30 miles per hour."
clears: Pepper: "…had been napping inside by the heater."
Neighbor kids: "The neighbor kids were away at a soccer game."
cases.explain: This shows the wind was very strong because the trees were bending and gusts were 30 miles per hour. Because of this, the wind scattered the pile.

debate.story: On Saturday, Dad and Lila raked a giant pile of leaves. They went inside for lunch and came back to leaves all over the street. The trees across the road were bending back and forth. The radio said gusts of thirty miles an hour. Pepper got out through the side gate at noon and came back muddy. The neighbour kids walked home past the yard after their soccer game.
debate.question: What scattered the leaves? Pick one answer and quote the story.

suspects.why: trees bending and gusts of thirty miles an hour
out through the side gate at noon, and back muddy
walked home past the yard after their game

evidence: “The trees across the road were bending back and forth.”
“The radio said gusts of thirty miles an hour.”
arguments.against: “Pepper got out through the side gate at noon and came back muddy.”

evidence: “Pepper got out through the side gate at noon and came back muddy.”
arguments.against: “The radio said gusts of thirty miles an hour.”

evidence: “The neighbour kids walked home past the yard after their soccer game.”
arguments.against: “The trees across the road were bending back and forth.”

debate.note: Leaves all over the street is a wide mess, and that is the detail to lean on. A dog scatters a pile where it jumps in; wind takes it down the road. Ask where each suspect would have left the leaves, and the shape of the mess starts doing the work.

cases.title: The Case of the Chewed Pumpkin
cases.story: The Lopez family carved a jack-o’-lantern and set it on the porch. In the morning, big chunks were missing from the top! Small hand-shaped prints were in the dirt by the steps. The trash can lid was knocked over, and food was spread on the driveway. Little Rosa had been asleep upstairs all night. The cat, Shadow, was locked inside. That night, Mr. Lopez saw a masked raccoon munching on the pumpkin. "Happy Halloween, raccoon!" he laughed.
cases.question: Who chewed the pumpkin?

suspects.why: hand-shaped prints, trash knocked over, seen munching
asleep upstairs all night
locked inside

cases.answer: A raccoon chewed the pumpkin.
proof: "Small hand-shaped prints were in the dirt by the steps."
"That night, Mr. Lopez saw a masked raccoon munching on the pumpkin."
clears: Rosa: "Little Rosa had been asleep upstairs all night."
Shadow: "The cat, Shadow, was locked inside."
cases.explain: This shows a raccoon was at the porch because raccoons have hand-shaped paws and one was seen eating it. Because of this, a raccoon chewed the pumpkin.

debate.story: The Lopez family carved a jack-o'-lantern and set it on the porch. By morning big chunks were missing from the top. Small hand-shaped prints were in the dirt by the steps. The trash can lid was knocked over and food was spread on the driveway. Rosa's muddy slippers were by the back door in the morning. Shadow the cat got out through the kitchen window on Tuesday night.
debate.question: Who chewed the pumpkin? Make the case for one answer.

suspects.why: hand-shaped prints, a knocked lid and food on the drive
muddy slippers by the back door in the morning
out through the kitchen window on Tuesday night

evidence: “Small hand-shaped prints were in the dirt by the steps.”
“The trash can lid was knocked over and food was spread on the driveway.”
arguments.against: “Rosa's muddy slippers were by the back door in the morning.”

evidence: “Rosa's muddy slippers were by the back door in the morning.”
arguments.against: “Small hand-shaped prints were in the dirt by the steps.”

evidence: “Shadow the cat got out through the kitchen window on Tuesday night.”
arguments.against: “The trash can lid was knocked over and food was spread on the driveway.”

debate.note: Muddy slippers put Rosa outside and they do not put her on the porch roof or in the bin. Hand-shaped prints are the strongest words in the case and children should be asked whose hands are that small. A cat out at night still cannot tip a bin.

cases.title: The Muddy Footprints
cases.story: After recess, muddy footprints went across the clean classroom floor. They were small and round, with four toes. They led to the reading corner. There, curled up on the beanbag, was Daisy, the school therapy dog, who had come in from the wet playground. Every student had wiped their shoes on the mat. Mrs. Moore had boots on, but her prints were big and flat. "Daisy, you need a towel!" the class giggled.
cases.question: Who made the muddy footprints?

suspects.why: small round prints with four toes, on the beanbag
wiped their shoes on the mat
her prints were big and flat

cases.answer: Daisy the dog made the muddy footprints.
proof: "They were small and round, with four toes."
"…curled up on the beanbag, was Daisy… who had come in from the wet playground."
clears: Students: "Every student had wiped their shoes on the mat."
Mrs. Moore: "…her prints were big and flat."
cases.explain: This shows the prints came from a dog because people do not have round prints with four toes. Because of this, Daisy made the mess.

debate.story: After recess, muddy footprints crossed the clean classroom floor. They were small and round, with four toes. Daisy the therapy dog was curled on the beanbag at the end of the trail. The mat by the door was soaked and had been walked round by some children. Mrs. Moore wears boots with a round heel the size of a fist. The prints are about three inches across.
debate.question: Who left the muddy prints? Pick one and prove it from the story.

suspects.why: small round prints with four toes, ending at her beanbag
a soaked mat that some children walked around
boots with a round heel the size of a fist

evidence: “Daisy the therapy dog was curled on the beanbag at the end of the trail.”
“They were small and round, with four toes.”
arguments.against: “Mrs. Moore wears boots with a round heel the size of a fist.”

evidence: “The mat by the door was soaked and had been walked round by some children.”
arguments.against: “They were small and round, with four toes.”

evidence: “Mrs. Moore wears boots with a round heel the size of a fist.”
“The prints are about three inches across.”
arguments.against: “Daisy the therapy dog was curled on the beanbag at the end of the trail.”

debate.note: Four toes is the word that decides this and it takes one careful reader to find it. Mrs. Moore's heel is round too, which is why the story gives her a size. Ask what three inches across looks like, and let somebody measure it on the desk.

cases.title: The Lost Backpack
cases.story: When Eli got home, he could not find his green backpack. He remembered wearing it at the bus stop. On the bus, he took it off to show his friend a toy. The next morning, the bus driver, Ms. Joy, held up a green backpack. "I found this under seat 7 last night," she said. Eli always sits in seat 7. His mom had checked the whole house, and his little sister said she never saw it.
cases.question: Where did Eli leave his backpack?

suspects.why: took it off on the bus, found under his seat
mom checked the whole house
she never saw it

cases.answer: Eli left his backpack on the bus.
proof: "On the bus, he took it off to show his friend a toy."
"Eli always sits in seat 7."
clears: Home: "His mom had checked the whole house…"
Sister: "…his little sister said she never saw it."
cases.explain: This shows Eli left it on the bus because he took it off there and it was found under his seat. Because of this, the backpack was on the bus all night.

debate.story: When Eli got home he could not find his green backpack. He took it off on the bus to show his friend a toy. Ms. Joy found a green backpack under seat seven that night. Three children in Eli's class have green backpacks. His mother looked in his room but not in the hall closet. His little sister was carrying a green bag at breakfast.
debate.question: Where is Eli's backpack? Choose one answer and back it up.

suspects.why: taken off on the bus, and a green one under seat seven
a room searched, but not the hall closet
carrying a green bag at breakfast

evidence: “He took it off on the bus to show his friend a toy.”
“Ms. Joy found a green backpack under seat seven that night.”
arguments.against: “Three children in Eli's class have green backpacks.”

evidence: “His mother looked in his room but not in the hall closet.”
arguments.against: “He took it off on the bus to show his friend a toy.”

evidence: “His little sister was carrying a green bag at breakfast.”
arguments.against: “Ms. Joy found a green backpack under seat seven that night.”

debate.note: Three green backpacks in one class is the sentence that breaks the easy answer. A green bag under seat seven is a green bag, not his green bag. Ask the children what Eli could check to be sure, and look for the ones who say his name inside it.

cases.title: The Lost Soccer Trophy
cases.story: The Tigers won the big soccer game, and their shiny trophy sat in the trophy case. The next day, it was gone! A muddy cleat print was on the floor by the case. Coach Kim wears sneakers, not cleats. The janitor, Mr. Lee, had just mopped the hall and his shoes were clean. Sam, the team captain, still had mud on his cleats from practice. At lunch, Sam held up the trophy. "I was taking it to show my grandpa at the nursing home!" he said. "I forgot to ask first."
cases.question: Who took the trophy?

suspects.why: mud on his cleats
wears sneakers
shoes were clean

cases.answer: Sam took the trophy.
proof: "Sam, the team captain, still had mud on his cleats from practice."
"A muddy cleat print was on the floor by the case."
clears: Coach Kim: "…wears sneakers, not cleats."
Mr. Lee: "…his shoes were clean."
cases.explain: This shows Sam was by the case because the muddy cleat print matches his cleats. Because of this, Sam is the one who took the trophy.

debate.story: The Tigers' trophy sat in the case and the next day it was gone. A muddy cleat print was on the floor by the case. Sam still had mud on his cleats from practice. Coach Kim keeps the case key on her whistle cord. Mr. Lee mopped the hall at six and props the case open to dust it. The print points away from the case, toward the gym.
debate.question: Who took the trophy? Pick one answer and show the words.

suspects.why: mud still on his cleats from practice
the case key on her whistle cord
mopping at six and propping the case open to dust

evidence: “Sam still had mud on his cleats from practice.”
“A muddy cleat print was on the floor by the case.”
arguments.against: “Coach Kim keeps the case key on her whistle cord.”

evidence: “Coach Kim keeps the case key on her whistle cord.”
arguments.against: “Sam still had mud on his cleats from practice.”

evidence: “Mr. Lee mopped the hall at six and props the case open to dust it.”
“The print points away from the case, toward the gym.”
arguments.against: “A muddy cleat print was on the floor by the case.”

debate.note: The whole team wears cleats and the whole team had just been at practice, so a cleat print narrows this less than it seems. The direction of the print is the detail worth chasing. Who keeps a key matters too, and the class should notice that a locked case needs one.

cases.title: The Thanksgiving Pie Puzzle
cases.story: On Thanksgiving morning, Grandma set a pumpkin pie on the porch to cool. An hour later, one big slice was gone! There were tiny footprints with three toes in the flour on the steps. Feathers were stuck to the edge of the plate. Cousin Ella was inside helping set the table the whole time. Uncle Ray was in the yard raking leaves, and his hands were covered in dirt, not flour. Out by the fence, a wild turkey was pecking at orange crumbs. "Well," Grandma laughed, "someone else is thankful for pie!"
cases.question: Who ate the slice of pie?

suspects.why: three-toed prints, feathers, orange crumbs
inside setting the table the whole time
raking leaves, dirt on his hands, not flour

cases.answer: The wild turkey ate the slice of pie.
proof: "There were tiny footprints with three toes in the flour on the steps."
"Feathers were stuck to the edge of the plate."
"Out by the fence, a wild turkey was pecking at orange crumbs."
clears: Cousin Ella: "…was inside helping set the table the whole time."
Uncle Ray: "…his hands were covered in dirt, not flour."
cases.explain: This shows a turkey was at the pie because turkeys have three toes and leave feathers. Because of this, the wild turkey ate the slice.

debate.story: Grandma set a pumpkin pie on the porch to cool. An hour later one big slice was gone. Tiny three-toed prints crossed the flour on the steps. Feathers were stuck to the edge of the plate. A wild turkey was pecking by the fence all morning. Ella came out twice for napkins from the porch cupboard. Uncle Ray leaned his rake against the porch rail at ten.
debate.question: Who took the slice of pie? Make the case for one answer.

suspects.why: three-toed prints, feathers, and a turkey by the fence
out twice for napkins from the porch cupboard
a rake leaned against the porch rail at ten

evidence: “Tiny three-toed prints crossed the flour on the steps.”
“A wild turkey was pecking by the fence all morning.”
arguments.against: “Ella came out twice for napkins from the porch cupboard.”

evidence: “Ella came out twice for napkins from the porch cupboard.”
arguments.against: “Feathers were stuck to the edge of the plate.”

evidence: “Uncle Ray leaned his rake against the porch rail at ten.”
arguments.against: “Tiny three-toed prints crossed the flour on the steps.”

debate.note: Feathers on the plate are hard to explain away and the class should start there. Being on the porch is not the same as taking pie, which is the difference between Ella and the turkey. One big slice is also worth noticing: a bird pecks rather than slices.

cases.title: The Missing Birthday Cupcakes
cases.story: It was Maya’s birthday, and her dad baked 12 cupcakes. He put them on the counter to cool. When Maya came home, only 9 were left! Her little brother Ben had pink frosting on his chin. The dog, Rocket, was asleep in the yard and had been outside all day. Grandma was at the store and came home after Maya. Maya smiled at Ben. "I think someone couldn’t wait for the party!"
cases.question: Who ate the missing cupcakes?

suspects.why: pink frosting on his chin
outside all day
at the store, came home after Maya

cases.answer: Ben ate the missing cupcakes.
proof: "Her little brother Ben had pink frosting on his chin."
clears: Rocket: "…had been outside all day."
Grandma: "…was at the store and came home after Maya."
cases.explain: This shows Ben ate a cupcake because the frosting on his chin matches the cupcakes. Because of this, Ben is the one who ate them.

debate.story: Maya's dad baked twelve cupcakes and left them on the counter to cool. When Maya came home, nine were left. Ben had pink frosting on his chin. Rocket came in through the dog flap twice that afternoon. The counter is low enough for a dog to reach the near end. Grandma came home early and set her shopping bags down on the counter. Nobody counted the cupcakes after they came out of the tin.
debate.question: Where did three cupcakes go? Choose one answer and prove it.

suspects.why: pink frosting on his chin
in through the dog flap twice, and a low counter
home early, with shopping set on the counter

evidence: “Ben had pink frosting on his chin.”
arguments.against: “Rocket came in through the dog flap twice that afternoon.”

evidence: “Rocket came in through the dog flap twice that afternoon.”
“The counter is low enough for a dog to reach the near end.”
arguments.against: “Ben had pink frosting on his chin.”

evidence: “Grandma came home early and set her shopping bags down on the counter. Nobody counted the cupcakes after they came out of the tin.”
arguments.against: “The counter is low enough for a dog to reach the near end.”

debate.note: Frosting on a chin proves Ben ate frosting. It does not prove he ate three cupcakes, and that gap is the whole lesson. The dog flap and the low counter are two sentences that work together, and children who use both are building a real case.

cases.title: The Missing Mitten
cases.story: After recess, Ava had only one red mitten. She looked in her pockets and her cubby. Then she heard a tiny meow from the lost-and-found box. Inside was the school cat, Marshmallow, curled up on her red mitten! Red fuzz was stuck to his white fur. Ava’s friend Grace had blue mittens on both hands. The recess aide, Mr. Ray, had been watching the swings. "Marshmallow, you made a bed!" Ava giggled.
cases.question: Who took Ava’s mitten?

suspects.why: curled up on the mitten, red fuzz on his fur
blue mittens on both hands
watching the swings

cases.answer: Marshmallow the cat took the mitten.
proof: "Inside was the school cat, Marshmallow, curled up on her red mitten!"
"Red fuzz was stuck to his white fur."
clears: Grace: "Ava’s friend Grace had blue mittens on both hands."
Mr. Ray: "…had been watching the swings."
cases.explain: This shows the cat had the mitten because he was lying on it with red fuzz on his fur. Because of this, Marshmallow took Ava’s mitten.

debate.story: After recess Ava had only one red mitten. Marshmallow the school cat was curled in the lost-and-found box on something red. Red fuzz was stuck to his white fur. Grace borrowed Ava's spare mitten on Tuesday and has not given it back. Mr. Ray gathers everything left on the field into the box each day. Ava took her mittens off at the swings and left them on the bar.
debate.question: Where is the mitten? Pick one answer and quote the story.

suspects.why: curled on something red, with red fuzz on his fur
borrowed a spare on Tuesday and never gave it back
gathers everything left on the field into the box

evidence: “Marshmallow the school cat was curled in the lost-and-found box on something red.”
“Red fuzz was stuck to his white fur.”
arguments.against: “Mr. Ray gathers everything left on the field into the box each day.”

evidence: “Grace borrowed Ava's spare mitten on Tuesday and has not given it back.”
arguments.against: “Red fuzz was stuck to his white fur.”

evidence: “Mr. Ray gathers everything left on the field into the box each day.”
“Ava took her mittens off at the swings and left them on the bar.”
arguments.against: “Marshmallow the school cat was curled in the lost-and-found box on something red.”

debate.note: The mitten is probably in the box, and the argument is about how it got there. A cat dragging it and an aide collecting it end in the same place, which is a good thing for children to notice. Taking the mittens off at the swings is the sentence that makes the aide's answer work.

cases.title: The Gingerbread House Mystery
cases.story: The class made a gingerbread house for the winter party. On Friday morning, the candy roof was missing three gumdrops! Small brown droppings were on the shelf next to the house. A tiny hole had been chewed in the back wall. The custodian, Ms. Ruiz, had locked the room at 4:00. All the students had gone home on the bus. That afternoon, Mr. Kent set a humane trap and caught a little gray mouse with sugar on its whiskers. "Our mystery guest likes candy!" said the class.
cases.question: Who ate the gumdrops?

suspects.why: droppings, chewed hole, sugar on its whiskers
locked the room at 4:00
had all gone home on the bus

cases.answer: A little mouse ate the gumdrops.
proof: "Small brown droppings were on the shelf next to the house."
"A tiny hole had been chewed in the back wall."
"…caught a little gray mouse with sugar on its whiskers."
clears: Ms. Ruiz: "…had locked the room at 4:00."
Students: "All the students had gone home on the bus."
cases.explain: This shows a mouse got into the house because mice chew small holes and leave droppings. Because of this, the mouse ate the gumdrops.

debate.story: The class gingerbread house lost three gumdrops from its roof overnight. Small brown droppings sat on the shelf beside it. A tiny hole was chewed in the back wall. Ms. Ruiz dusted that shelf on Thursday and moved the house twice. Two students stayed late on Thursday to finish their reading. The gumdrops that went were the three nearest the edge. Nobody heard anything in the night.
debate.question: Who took the gumdrops? Choose one and show the words.

suspects.why: droppings on the shelf and a hole chewed in the back
dusted that shelf and moved the house twice
two who stayed late on Thursday to finish reading

evidence: “Small brown droppings sat on the shelf beside it.”
“A tiny hole was chewed in the back wall.”
arguments.against: “Ms. Ruiz dusted that shelf on Thursday and moved the house twice.”

evidence: “Ms. Ruiz dusted that shelf on Thursday and moved the house twice.”
arguments.against: “A tiny hole was chewed in the back wall.”

evidence: “Two students stayed late on Thursday to finish their reading.”
“The gumdrops that went were the three nearest the edge.”
arguments.against: “Small brown droppings sat on the shelf beside it.”

debate.note: A chewed hole is the one piece of evidence a person cannot easily have made, and it should anchor the argument. The three nearest the edge is the detail that keeps the children in the case, because it is what a hand in a hurry would take.

cases.title: The Dark Holiday Lights
cases.story: The Kims put lights on their tree every December. One night, the lights would not turn on! Dad checked every bulb, and none were broken. Then June found the plug lying on the floor next to the vacuum cleaner. Mom had vacuumed under the tree that afternoon. The cat had been sleeping in June’s room all day. Mom smiled. "Oops! I must have pulled the plug with the vacuum."
cases.question: Why did the lights go out?

suspects.why: plug on the floor by the vacuum, Mom vacuumed there
sleeping in June’s room all day
none were broken

cases.answer: The vacuum pulled out the plug.
proof: "Then June found the plug lying on the floor next to the vacuum cleaner."
"Mom had vacuumed under the tree that afternoon."
clears: Cat: "The cat had been sleeping in June’s room all day."
Bulbs: "Dad checked every bulb, and none were broken."
cases.explain: This shows the plug came out while Mom cleaned because it was next to the vacuum. Because of this, the lights had no power.

debate.story: The Kims' tree lights would not come on. June found the plug lying on the floor by the vacuum cleaner. Mum vacuumed under the tree that afternoon. The cat sleeps under the tree every evening and knocked an ornament down on Tuesday. Dad checked the first ten bulbs and stopped. The string has eighty bulbs on it. Nothing smelled burnt and no bulb looked black inside.
debate.question: Why will the lights not come on? Pick one answer and back it up.

suspects.why: a plug on the floor by the vacuum, used under the tree
sleeps under the tree and knocked an ornament down
only the first ten bulbs checked out of eighty

evidence: “June found the plug lying on the floor by the vacuum cleaner.”
“Mum vacuumed under the tree that afternoon.”
arguments.against: “The cat sleeps under the tree every evening and knocked an ornament down on Tuesday.”

evidence: “The cat sleeps under the tree every evening and knocked an ornament down on Tuesday.”
arguments.against: “Mum vacuumed under the tree that afternoon.”

evidence: “Dad checked the first ten bulbs and stopped.”
“The string has eighty bulbs on it.”
arguments.against: “June found the plug lying on the floor by the vacuum cleaner.”

debate.note: Ten bulbs out of eighty is the number to stop on, because checking an eighth of something is not checking it. The plug on the floor is still the simplest answer, and the vacuum and the cat are two ways it could have got there. Nothing in the case chooses between them.

cases.title: The Clock That Stopped
cases.story: When the class came back from winter break, the wall clock said 2:15. But it was only 8:30 in the morning! The clock hands were not moving at all. Mr. Park climbed up and opened the back. The battery was old and covered in white crust. Nobody had been in the room over break because the doors were locked. He put in a new battery, and the clock started ticking right away.
cases.question: Why did the clock stop?

suspects.why: old battery with crust, worked with a new one
the room was locked over break
no clues point to a ghost

cases.answer: The clock stopped because the battery died.
proof: "The battery was old and covered in white crust."
"He put in a new battery, and the clock started ticking right away."
clears: Student: "Nobody had been in the room over break because the doors were locked."
cases.explain: This shows the battery was the problem because the clock worked as soon as it had a new one. Because of this, a dead battery stopped the clock.

debate.story: After winter break the wall clock said 2:15 when it was half past eight. The hands were not moving at all. The battery was old and crusted white. The caretaker was in the room twice over break to fix a window. A power cut hit the school at 2:15 on the second day of break. Battery clocks do not stop in a power cut.
debate.question: Why did the clock stop? Choose one answer and prove it.

suspects.why: an old battery crusted white, with the hands still
in the room twice over break to fix a window
a cut at 2:15 on the second day of break

evidence: “The battery was old and crusted white.”
“The hands were not moving at all.”
arguments.against: “A power cut hit the school at 2:15 on the second day of break.”

evidence: “The caretaker was in the room twice over break to fix a window.”
arguments.against: “The battery was old and crusted white.”

evidence: “A power cut hit the school at 2:15 on the second day of break.”
arguments.against: “Battery clocks do not stop in a power cut.”

debate.note: The power cut at exactly 2:15 is the kind of coincidence that feels like proof, and the next sentence takes it away. That pair is the whole case. A crusted battery can also stop at any time, including 2:15, and children should be asked whether a matching time is really evidence.

cases.title: The Melting Snowman
cases.story: The class built a giant snowman at recess. After lunch, he was only half as big! His carrot nose was on the ground. Some kids thought a dog knocked him over, but there were no paw prints in the snow. The sun was shining bright, and the snow around him was wet and slushy. The thermometer by the door said 45 degrees. "Our snowman is melting!" said Ava.
cases.question: What happened to the snowman?

suspects.why: bright sun, wet slushy snow, 45 degrees
no paw prints
everyone was at lunch

cases.answer: The warm sun melted the snowman.
proof: "The sun was shining bright, and the snow around him was wet and slushy."
"The thermometer by the door said 45 degrees."
clears: Dog: "…there were no paw prints in the snow."
cases.explain: This shows it was too warm for snow because 45 degrees is above freezing. Because of this, the sun melted the snowman. (Science link: matter changes from solid to liquid.)

debate.story: The class built a giant snowman at recess. After lunch he was half the size. His carrot nose lay on the ground. The sun was bright and the snow around him was wet and slushy. The thermometer by the door said forty-five degrees. A dog ran across the yard at lunchtime and the snow is too soft to hold a print. Two children came out early and were seen near the snowman.
debate.question: What happened to the snowman? Pick one and quote the story.

suspects.why: bright sun, slushy snow and forty-five degrees
across the yard at lunchtime, on snow too soft for prints
two out early and seen near the snowman

evidence: “The sun was bright and the snow around him was wet and slushy.”
“The thermometer by the door said forty-five degrees.”
arguments.against: “Two children came out early and were seen near the snowman.”

evidence: “A dog ran across the yard at lunchtime and the snow is too soft to hold a print.”
arguments.against: “The thermometer by the door said forty-five degrees.”

evidence: “Two children came out early and were seen near the snowman.”
“His carrot nose lay on the ground.”
arguments.against: “The sun was bright and the snow around him was wet and slushy.”

debate.note: No paw prints used to clear the dog and now the story says the snow is too soft to hold one. Missing evidence is not the same as evidence of nothing, and that is a big idea for eight-year-olds. Half the size, evenly, is what melting looks like; a push leaves a side knocked in.

cases.title: The Broken Bird Feeder
cases.story: The class hung a bird feeder outside the window. On Monday, it was on the ground, and all the seeds were gone! There were big hoof prints in the snow under the tree. The branch it hung from was low, and bark was rubbed off the trunk. Small birds can not knock down a heavy feeder. The custodian, Mr. Bell, had not been outside all weekend. On Tuesday, the class saw a deer stretching its neck to lick the new feeder.
cases.question: Who knocked down the bird feeder?

suspects.why: hoof prints, rubbed bark, seen at the feeder
too small to knock down a heavy feeder
not outside all weekend

cases.answer: A deer knocked down the bird feeder.
proof: "There were big hoof prints in the snow under the tree."
"On Tuesday, the class saw a deer stretching its neck to lick the new feeder."
clears: Birds: "Small birds can not knock down a heavy feeder."
Mr. Bell: "…had not been outside all weekend."
cases.explain: This shows a deer was at the feeder because deer have hooves and one was seen licking it. Because of this, a deer knocked it down.

debate.story: On Monday the bird feeder lay on the ground with every seed gone. Big hoof prints were in the snow under the tree. Bark was rubbed off the trunk at shoulder height. The branch it hung from is thin and bent low with the weight. Mr. Bell cleared snow from that path on Sunday with a shovel. Forty starlings came to the feeder on Saturday.
debate.question: What brought the feeder down? Make the case for one answer.

suspects.why: hoof prints and bark rubbed off at shoulder height
forty of them at the feeder on Saturday
clearing snow from that path on Sunday with a shovel

evidence: “Big hoof prints were in the snow under the tree.”
“Bark was rubbed off the trunk at shoulder height.”
arguments.against: “Mr. Bell cleared snow from that path on Sunday with a shovel.”

evidence: “Forty starlings came to the feeder on Saturday.”
“The branch it hung from is thin and bent low with the weight.”
arguments.against: “Big hoof prints were in the snow under the tree.”

evidence: “Mr. Bell cleared snow from that path on Sunday with a shovel.”
arguments.against: “Bark was rubbed off the trunk at shoulder height.”

debate.note: One small bird cannot pull a feeder down and forty of them on a thin branch is a different question. That is a sentence the old case did not let anybody ask. The rubbed bark is still the best evidence, and children should say what height shoulder height means for a deer.

cases.title: The Missing Marshmallows
cases.story: On a snowy day, Grandpa made hot cocoa for Nora and her little brother, Max. He set out a bowl of marshmallows. When Nora came back from washing her hands, the bowl was empty! Max had white sugar powder on his fingers and a puffy cheek. Grandpa had been at the stove stirring the pot. The dog was outside playing in the snow. Max giggled, and a marshmallow fell out of his mouth.
cases.question: Who ate the marshmallows?

suspects.why: sugar on his fingers, puffy cheek, one fell out
at the stove stirring the pot
outside playing in the snow

cases.answer: Max ate the marshmallows.
proof: "Max had white sugar powder on his fingers and a puffy cheek."
"Max giggled, and a marshmallow fell out of his mouth."
clears: Grandpa: "Grandpa had been at the stove stirring the pot."
Dog: "The dog was outside playing in the snow."
cases.explain: This shows Max ate them because a marshmallow fell out of his mouth. Because of this, Max is the marshmallow thief.

debate.story: Grandpa made cocoa and set out a bowl of marshmallows. When Nora came back from washing her hands the bowl was empty. Max had white powder on his fingers and a puffy cheek. Grandpa put a handful into each mug before he stirred. The dog came in from the snow and was shut in the kitchen for ten minutes. The bowl was on the low shelf by the door.
debate.question: Who emptied the bowl? Choose one answer and show the words.

suspects.why: white powder on his fingers and a puffy cheek
a handful into each mug before he stirred
shut in the kitchen ten minutes, with the bowl on a low shelf

evidence: “Max had white powder on his fingers and a puffy cheek.”
arguments.against: “Grandpa put a handful into each mug before he stirred.”

evidence: “Grandpa put a handful into each mug before he stirred.”
arguments.against: “Max had white powder on his fingers and a puffy cheek.”

evidence: “The dog came in from the snow and was shut in the kitchen for ten minutes.”
“The bowl was on the low shelf by the door.”
arguments.against: “When Nora came back from washing her hands the bowl was empty.”

debate.note: Empty is the word to push on. Grandpa took handfuls for the mugs, which may be most of the bowl, and Max may only have taken the last few. Two suspects can share one bowl, and a class that reaches that answer has done better than one that picks a single name.

cases.title: The Vanished Valentines
cases.story: For the Valentine’s party, each student had a paper bag mailbox by the open window. After lunch, five valentines were missing from Kai’s bag! Ms. Rose found pink cards stuck in the bushes outside the window. The flag on the pole was flapping hard in the wind. Kai’s bag was the closest one to the window. All the students were at lunch, and the door was locked. "The wind delivered them outside!" said Ms. Rose.
cases.question: What happened to Kai’s valentines?

suspects.why: open window, cards in the bushes, flag flapping
everyone was at lunch, door locked
she found the cards

cases.answer: The wind blew the valentines out the window.
proof: "Ms. Rose found pink cards stuck in the bushes outside the window."
"Kai’s bag was the closest one to the window."
clears: Classmates: "All the students were at lunch, and the door was locked."
cases.explain: This shows the wind took the cards because they ended up in the bushes right outside the open window. Because of this, the wind made the valentines vanish.

debate.story: Five valentines were missing from Kai's paper bag after lunch. Ms. Rose found pink cards in the bushes under the open window. The flag on the pole was flapping hard. Kai's bag is the closest one to the window. Two children came back early from lunch for their coats. Ms. Rose tidied the bags into a neat row before lunch. Nobody counted the cards that morning.
debate.question: Where did the valentines go? Pick one answer and prove it.

suspects.why: an open window, cards in the bushes and a flapping flag
two back early from lunch for their coats
tidied the bags into a neat row before lunch

evidence: “Ms. Rose found pink cards in the bushes under the open window.”
“The flag on the pole was flapping hard.”
arguments.against: “Two children came back early from lunch for their coats.”

evidence: “Two children came back early from lunch for their coats.”
arguments.against: “The flag on the pole was flapping hard.”

evidence: “Ms. Rose tidied the bags into a neat row before lunch.”
“Nobody counted the cards that morning.”
arguments.against: “Kai's bag is the closest one to the window.”

debate.note: Cards in the bushes under the window is strong and it is not the whole story, because five went and the case never says how many were found. Nobody counted them that morning either. Ask how we would know five are missing at all, and watch a good argument start.

cases.title: The Volcano That Would Not Erupt
cases.story: At the science fair, Ben’s volcano was supposed to fizz and bubble. He poured in the vinegar, but nothing happened! His sister, Ruby, looked at the box of baking soda. It was full of white powder, but the label said Powdered Sugar. Ben had grabbed the wrong box from the kitchen. The judge, Ms. Lane, had not touched the table. Ruby ran home and brought the real baking soda. Fizz! The volcano erupted all over the table.
cases.question: Why didn’t the volcano erupt?

suspects.why: label said Powdered Sugar, worked with real baking soda
had not touched the table
it fizzed once the right powder was added

cases.answer: Ben used powdered sugar instead of baking soda.
proof: "It was full of white powder, but the label said Powdered Sugar."
"Ben had grabbed the wrong box from the kitchen."
clears: Ms. Lane: "The judge, Ms. Lane, had not touched the table."
cases.explain: This shows the powder was wrong because only baking soda makes vinegar fizz. Because of this, the volcano would not erupt until Ruby brought the real one.

debate.story: At the science fair, Ben's volcano was supposed to fizz and bubble. He poured in the vinegar and nothing happened. Ruby looked at the box of baking soda. It was full of white powder, but the label said Powdered Sugar. The vinegar bottle had stood open on the kitchen shelf since last summer. Ms. Lane moved the table an hour before, and the cone leaned over. A leaning cone spills instead of fizzing upward.
debate.question: Why did the volcano not erupt? Pick one answer and prove it.

suspects.why: a box labelled Powdered Sugar, full of white powder
moved the table an hour before, leaving the cone leaning
a bottle left open on the shelf since last summer

evidence: “It was full of white powder, but the label said Powdered Sugar.”
arguments.against: “The vinegar bottle had stood open on the kitchen shelf since last summer.”

evidence: “Ms. Lane moved the table an hour before, and the cone leaned over.”
“A leaning cone spills instead of fizzing upward.”
arguments.against: “It was full of white powder, but the label said Powdered Sugar.”

evidence: “The vinegar bottle had stood open on the kitchen shelf since last summer.”
arguments.against: “He poured in the vinegar and nothing happened.”

debate.note: The label is the loudest clue and it is worth asking what a label proves. A box can be refilled. Nothing happened at all is the phrase to lean on, because a leaning cone would still have fizzed somewhere, and old vinegar would still have made a little gas.

cases.title: The Missing Play Crown
cases.story: The night before the school play, the king’s gold crown went missing! The costume box had glitter spilled all over it. A trail of gold glitter led down the hall to the art room. In the art room, Zoe was painting a castle backdrop, and her hands were covered in gold glitter. She held up the crown. "It needed more sparkle!" she said. Mr. Fox, the director, had been on stage the whole time. Kenji, who plays the king, was at home practicing his lines.
cases.question: Who took the crown?

suspects.why: glitter trail to the art room, glitter on her hands
on stage the whole time
at home practicing

cases.answer: Zoe took the crown to add more sparkle.
proof: "A trail of gold glitter led down the hall to the art room."
"…her hands were covered in gold glitter."
clears: Mr. Fox: "…had been on stage the whole time."
Kenji: "…was at home practicing his lines."
cases.explain: This shows Zoe had the crown because the glitter trail ended right where she was working. Because of this, Zoe is the one who took it.

debate.story: The night before the play, the king's gold crown went missing. The costume box had glitter spilled all over it. A trail of gold glitter led down the hall to the art room. Zoe was in the art room painting a castle, with glitter on her hands. Mr. Fox carried the costume box to the stage before rehearsal. Kenji took his crown home on Tuesday to practise wearing it.
debate.question: Where is the crown? Choose one answer and show the words.

suspects.why: a glitter trail to the art room, and glitter on her hands
carried the costume box to the stage before rehearsal
took his crown home on Tuesday to practise wearing it

evidence: “A trail of gold glitter led down the hall to the art room.”
“Zoe was in the art room painting a castle, with glitter on her hands.”
arguments.against: “Mr. Fox carried the costume box to the stage before rehearsal.”

evidence: “Mr. Fox carried the costume box to the stage before rehearsal.”
arguments.against: “A trail of gold glitter led down the hall to the art room.”

evidence: “Kenji took his crown home on Tuesday to practise wearing it.”
arguments.against: “The costume box had glitter spilled all over it.”

debate.note: Gold glitter is everywhere in this case, which makes it weaker evidence than it looks: a box covered in it marks whoever touches it. Kenji taking the crown home is the plainest answer and the easiest to check, and children should notice nobody has asked him.

cases.title: The Silent Piano Key
cases.story: In music class, one piano key would not make a sound. Mrs. Song pressed it again and again. Then she opened the top of the piano. Inside, a striped sock was stuck on the strings! The sock had a name tag that said Theo. Theo had taken off his wet socks after recess and laid them on top of the piano to dry. The window was closed, and the room was quiet. Theo turned red. "I think my sock slipped in!"
cases.question: Why was the piano key silent?

suspects.why: sock with his name tag stuck on the strings
the window was closed
it worked once the sock was out

cases.answer: Theo’s sock fell into the piano.
proof: "Inside, a striped sock was stuck on the strings!"
"Theo had taken off his wet socks after recess and laid them on top of the piano to dry."
clears: Wind: "The window was closed, and the room was quiet."
cases.explain: This shows the sock blocked the strings because it was stuck right inside with Theo’s name on it. Because of this, the key could not make a sound.

debate.story: In music class one piano key would not make a sound. Mrs. Song opened the top and found a striped sock stuck on the strings. The sock had a name tag that said Theo. Theo laid his wet socks on top of the piano after recess. The window above the piano was open all morning. The felt under that key is worn through to the wood. A worn key can stick without anything inside the piano.
debate.question: Why is the key silent? Pick one and quote the story.

suspects.why: a sock with his name tag, laid on the piano to dry
open above the piano all morning
worn through to the wood under that key

evidence: “The sock had a name tag that said Theo.”
“Theo laid his wet socks on top of the piano after recess.”
arguments.against: “The felt under that key is worn through to the wood.”

evidence: “The window above the piano was open all morning.”
arguments.against: “The sock had a name tag that said Theo.”

evidence: “The felt under that key is worn through to the wood.”
“A worn key can stick without anything inside the piano.”
arguments.against: “Mrs. Song opened the top and found a striped sock stuck on the strings.”

debate.note: A sock on the strings is real and the worn felt is real, and both can stop a key. The test is free and the class can say it: take the sock out and press the key again. Children who propose that have done the most useful thing in the lesson.

cases.title: The Stuck Kite
cases.story: On a windy March day, Zara flew her new rainbow kite at the park. Suddenly, the string went slack and the kite disappeared! Zara looked up and saw a rainbow tail hanging from the top of a tall oak tree. The broken string was tangled in the branches. Her brother, Sam, was on the swings far away. Nobody else at the park had a kite. "The wind pushed it right into the tree," Zara sighed.
cases.question: Where did Zara’s kite go?

suspects.why: rainbow tail in the tree, string tangled in branches
he was on the swings far away
nobody else had a kite

cases.answer: The kite got stuck in the oak tree.
proof: "Zara looked up and saw a rainbow tail hanging from the top of a tall oak tree."
"The broken string was tangled in the branches."
clears: Sam: "Her brother, Sam, was on the swings far away."
Others: "Nobody else at the park had a kite."
cases.explain: This shows the kite is in the tree because its tail and string are tangled in the branches. Because of this, the wind blew the kite into the oak tree.

debate.story: On a windy March day, Zara flew her rainbow kite at the park. The string went slack and the kite disappeared. A rainbow tail now hangs from the top of a tall oak. The broken string is tangled in the branches. Sam was on the swings under that same oak. The string had a knot in it that Zara tied herself last week. A knotted string snaps at the knot when the wind pulls hard.
debate.question: Why did the kite come down? Make the case for one answer.

suspects.why: a rainbow tail in the oak and string tangled in the branches
on the swings under that same oak
a knot she tied last week, where a string snaps

evidence: “A rainbow tail now hangs from the top of a tall oak.”
“The broken string is tangled in the branches.”
arguments.against: “The string had a knot in it that Zara tied herself last week.”

evidence: “Sam was on the swings under that same oak.”
arguments.against: “A rainbow tail now hangs from the top of a tall oak.”

evidence: “The string had a knot in it that Zara tied herself last week.”
“A knotted string snaps at the knot when the wind pulls hard.”
arguments.against: “The broken string is tangled in the branches.”

debate.note: Everybody can see where the kite is, so the real question is why the string broke. The knot is the only answer that explains a break rather than a tangle. Ask where the broken end is, and whether anybody has looked at it.

cases.title: The Green Footprints
cases.story: On St. Patrick’s Day, green footprints went across the hallway! They started at the art room door. Inside, a can of green paint was tipped over on the floor. Leo’s sneakers had wet green paint on the bottoms. The art teacher, Ms. Fern, had stepped out to make copies. The class leprechaun trap was still set and empty. Leo looked at his shoes. "Uh-oh. I think I’m the leprechaun!"
cases.question: Who made the green footprints?

suspects.why: wet green paint on his sneakers
the trap was still set and empty
had stepped out to make copies

cases.answer: Leo made the green footprints.
proof: "Inside, a can of green paint was tipped over on the floor."
"Leo’s sneakers had wet green paint on the bottoms."
clears: Leprechaun: "The class leprechaun trap was still set and empty."
Ms. Fern: "…had stepped out to make copies."
cases.explain: This shows Leo stepped in the paint because the green paint on his shoes matches the footprints. Because of this, Leo made the footprints.

debate.story: On St. Patrick's Day, green footprints went across the hallway. They started at the art room door. Inside, a can of green paint was tipped over on the floor. Leo's sneakers had wet green paint on the bottoms. Ms. Fern carried the paint can to the sink before she went for copies. The leprechaun trap by the door has a green smear on its lid.
debate.question: Who made the green footprints? Choose one and back it up.

suspects.why: wet green paint on the bottoms of his sneakers
a green smear on the lid of the trap
carried the paint can to the sink before leaving

evidence: “Leo's sneakers had wet green paint on the bottoms.”
arguments.against: “Ms. Fern carried the paint can to the sink before she went for copies.”

evidence: “The leprechaun trap by the door has a green smear on its lid.”
arguments.against: “Inside, a can of green paint was tipped over on the floor.”

evidence: “Ms. Fern carried the paint can to the sink before she went for copies.”
“They started at the art room door.”
arguments.against: “Leo's sneakers had wet green paint on the bottoms.”

debate.note: Paint on Leo's shoes proves Leo stepped in paint. It does not prove he tipped the can, and it does not prove the prints in the hall are his. Ask whether anybody has matched the prints to his sneakers, because the case never says they did.

cases.title: The Puddle in the Hall
cases.story: During a big spring storm, a puddle appeared in the middle of the hallway. Kids thought someone spilled a drink. Mr. Diaz looked up and saw a brown water stain on the ceiling tile. Every few seconds, a drop of water fell from it. The water fountain was at the other end of the hall and was dry. No cups or bottles were anywhere near the puddle. "The roof has a leak!" said Mr. Diaz.
cases.question: What made the puddle?

suspects.why: water stain on the ceiling, drops falling
no cups or bottles nearby
at the other end of the hall and dry

cases.answer: A leaky roof made the puddle.
proof: "Mr. Diaz looked up and saw a brown water stain on the ceiling tile."
"Every few seconds, a drop of water fell from it."
clears: Drink: "No cups or bottles were anywhere near the puddle."
Fountain: "The water fountain was at the other end of the hall and was dry."
cases.explain: This shows the water came from the ceiling because drops were falling from the stain. Because of this, the roof leak made the puddle.

debate.story: During a spring storm a puddle appeared in the middle of the hallway. Mr. Diaz looked up and saw a brown stain on the ceiling tile. Every few seconds a drop of water fell from it. The water fountain at the end of the hall was leaking at its pipe on Monday. A leak can run along a floor and gather in a low spot. Three children came in soaked and shook out their coats right there.
debate.question: Where did the puddle come from? Pick one answer and prove it.

suspects.why: a brown ceiling stain with a drop falling every few seconds
three children shaking out soaked coats right there
a fountain pipe that was leaking on Monday

evidence: “Mr. Diaz looked up and saw a brown stain on the ceiling tile.”
“Every few seconds a drop of water fell from it.”
arguments.against: “Three children came in soaked and shook out their coats right there.”

evidence: “Three children came in soaked and shook out their coats right there.”
arguments.against: “Every few seconds a drop of water fell from it.”

evidence: “The water fountain at the end of the hall was leaking at its pipe on Monday.”
“A leak can run along a floor and gather in a low spot.”
arguments.against: “Mr. Diaz looked up and saw a brown stain on the ceiling tile.”

debate.note: A drop falling every few seconds is the strongest sentence in the case, because it is still happening while everybody watches. Shaken coats stop. Ask what the puddle will look like in an hour under each answer, and the class has designed a test without being told to.

cases.title: Who Ate the Garden?
cases.story: Mrs. Gray’s class planted lettuce in the school garden. On Friday, the lettuce had big bites taken out of it! There were long, thin tracks in the dirt. A rabbit hole was under the fence. The birds only sat on the roof and ate seeds from the feeder. The class turtle, Speedy, was inside his tank all week. The next morning, the class saw a fluffy white rabbit nibbling a leaf. "Mystery solved!" said Mrs. Gray.
cases.question: Who ate the lettuce?

suspects.why: tracks, hole under the fence, seen nibbling
ate seeds from the feeder
inside his tank all week

cases.answer: A rabbit ate the lettuce.
proof: "A rabbit hole was under the fence."
"…the class saw a fluffy white rabbit nibbling a leaf."
clears: Birds: "…ate seeds from the feeder."
Speedy: "…was inside his tank all week."
cases.explain: This shows the rabbit got into the garden because it had a hole under the fence. Because of this, the rabbit is the one who ate the lettuce.

debate.story: Mrs. Gray's class planted lettuce in the school garden. On Friday the lettuce had big bites taken out of it. There were long thin tracks in the dirt and a rabbit hole under the fence. The bird feeder hangs right above the lettuce bed and was empty by Thursday. Hungry birds will come down for leaves when the seed runs out. Speedy the turtle was taken out to the garden on Wednesday to see the sun.
debate.question: Who ate the lettuce? Choose one answer and show the words.

suspects.why: thin tracks in the dirt and a hole under the fence
a feeder emptied by Thursday, right above the bed
taken out to the garden on Wednesday to see the sun

evidence: “There were long thin tracks in the dirt and a rabbit hole under the fence.”
arguments.against: “The bird feeder hangs right above the lettuce bed and was empty by Thursday.”

evidence: “The bird feeder hangs right above the lettuce bed and was empty by Thursday.”
“Hungry birds will come down for leaves when the seed runs out.”
arguments.against: “There were long thin tracks in the dirt and a rabbit hole under the fence.”

evidence: “Speedy the turtle was taken out to the garden on Wednesday to see the sun.”
arguments.against: “On Friday the lettuce had big bites taken out of it.”

debate.note: Big bites is the phrase that separates these. A bird takes a peck, a rabbit takes a mouthful, and a turtle takes its time. Ask the class to show with their hands how big a bite each suspect would leave, and then look at the lettuce again.

cases.title: The Empty Nest
cases.story: A robin built a nest in the bush outside Room 9. The class watched three blue eggs every day. One morning, the eggs were gone! Pieces of blue shell were at the bottom of the nest. The class heard tiny cheep-cheep sounds. Three fuzzy baby birds poked their heads up with their mouths open. No cats or snakes were seen near the bush. "The eggs didn’t disappear," said Mr. Gold. "They hatched!"
cases.question: What happened to the robin eggs?

suspects.why: pieces of shell, baby birds cheeping
no cats were seen near the bush
no snakes were seen

cases.answer: The robin eggs hatched.
proof: "Pieces of blue shell were at the bottom of the nest."
"Three fuzzy baby birds poked their heads up with their mouths open."
clears: Cat or snake: "No cats or snakes were seen near the bush."
cases.explain: This shows the eggs hatched because there are broken shells and baby birds in the nest. Because of this, the eggs turned into baby robins. (Science link: life cycles.)

debate.story: A robin built a nest in the bush outside Room 9. The class watched three blue eggs every day. One morning the eggs were gone. Pieces of blue shell lay at the bottom of the nest. Three fuzzy baby birds poked their heads up with their mouths open. A cat sits on the wall by that bush most afternoons. Shell broken by a hatching chick is cracked from the inside out.
debate.question: What happened to the eggs? Pick one and prove it from the story.

suspects.why: shell in the nest and three chicks with their mouths open
on the wall by that bush most afternoons
shell cracked from the inside out when a chick hatches

evidence: “Three fuzzy baby birds poked their heads up with their mouths open.”
“Pieces of blue shell lay at the bottom of the nest.”
arguments.against: “A cat sits on the wall by that bush most afternoons.”

evidence: “A cat sits on the wall by that bush most afternoons.”
arguments.against: “Three fuzzy baby birds poked their heads up with their mouths open.”

evidence: “Shell broken by a hatching chick is cracked from the inside out.”
arguments.against: “One morning the eggs were gone.”

debate.note: Three eggs gone and three chicks arrived is the arithmetic that answers this, and most children will see it at once. The useful part is the last sentence, which tells them how to prove it rather than assume it. Looking at which way a shell is bent is real science.

cases.title: The Earth Day Litter Mystery
cases.story: For Earth Day, the class went to clean up Maple Park. They found trash all around the picnic table! The trash can lid was off, and the bag inside was ripped open. Wrappers had little bite marks on them. Muddy paw prints with five fingers led to the creek. The park ranger said she emptied the can last week and closed the lid tight. That evening, a raccoon family came out to dig in the can again.
cases.question: Who made the mess at the park?

suspects.why: ripped bag, bite marks, five-finger prints
closed the lid tight
they came to clean it up

cases.answer: Raccoons made the mess at the park.
proof: "Wrappers had little bite marks on them."
"Muddy paw prints with five fingers led to the creek."
clears: Ranger: "The park ranger said she emptied the can last week and closed the lid tight."
cases.explain: This shows raccoons got into the trash because the wrappers were bitten and their prints led away. Because of this, raccoons made the mess.

debate.story: For Earth Day the class cleaned up Maple Park. Trash lay all around the picnic table. The can lid was off and the bag inside was ripped open. Wrappers had little bite marks on them. Muddy paw prints with five fingers led to the creek. The ranger emptied the can last week and left the lid leaning against it. A strong wind blew through the park on Tuesday night.
debate.question: Who made the mess? Make the case for one answer.

suspects.why: a ripped bag, bite marks and five-fingered prints
emptied the can and left the lid leaning against it
a strong wind through the park on Tuesday night

evidence: “Wrappers had little bite marks on them.”
“Muddy paw prints with five fingers led to the creek.”
arguments.against: “The ranger emptied the can last week and left the lid leaning against it.”

evidence: “The ranger emptied the can last week and left the lid leaning against it.”
arguments.against: “Wrappers had little bite marks on them.”

evidence: “A strong wind blew through the park on Tuesday night.”
“The can lid was off and the bag inside was ripped open.”
arguments.against: “Muddy paw prints with five fingers led to the creek.”

debate.note: Bite marks are the one thing wind cannot do, and the class should find them fast. A lid left leaning is not the same as a lid left tight, so the ranger is in the case now in a way she was not before. Three answers can all be partly true here.

cases.title: The Lost Field Trip Camera
cases.story: At the zoo, Ms. Ray took pictures with the class camera. When the class got back on the bus, the camera was gone! Ms. Ray checked her bag and her coat pockets. Then Ty remembered that she set it on the bench by the penguins to tie her shoe. The zoo worker at the penguin house found a camera on that bench. The bus driver had stayed on the bus the whole time. The monkeys were in a closed cage far away.
cases.question: Where did the camera go?

suspects.why: Ty saw her set it there, worker found it there
in a closed cage far away
stayed on the bus the whole time

cases.answer: Ms. Ray left the camera on the bench by the penguins.
proof: "Then Ty remembered that she set it on the bench by the penguins to tie her shoe."
"The zoo worker at the penguin house found a camera on that bench."
clears: Monkeys: "The monkeys were in a closed cage far away."
Driver: "The bus driver had stayed on the bus the whole time."
cases.explain: This shows the camera was on the bench because Ty saw her set it there and a worker found it there. Because of this, the camera was left behind, not stolen.

debate.story: At the zoo, Ms. Ray took pictures with the class camera. Back on the bus, the camera was gone. Ty remembered her setting it on the bench by the penguins. The zoo worker at the penguin house found a camera on that bench. Ms. Ray carried an open tote bag all afternoon. The bus driver loaded twelve bags into the hold while the class queued.
debate.question: Where is the camera? Choose one answer and quote the story.

suspects.why: set on the bench by the penguins, where a worker found one
an open tote carried all afternoon
loaded twelve bags into the hold while the class queued

evidence: “Ty remembered her setting it on the bench by the penguins.”
“The zoo worker at the penguin house found a camera on that bench.”
arguments.against: “Ms. Ray carried an open tote bag all afternoon.”

evidence: “Ms. Ray carried an open tote bag all afternoon.”
arguments.against: “The zoo worker at the penguin house found a camera on that bench.”

evidence: “The bus driver loaded twelve bags into the hold while the class queued.”
arguments.against: “Ty remembered her setting it on the bench by the penguins.”

debate.note: A camera on that bench is strong and it is still a camera, not the camera. Zoos have more than one visitor. Ask what would make it certain, and listen for children who say the pictures inside it would show the class.

cases.title: The Droopy Bean Plant
cases.story: The class planted bean seeds in cups. Every plant grew tall and green, except one. Jin’s plant was pale yellow and droopy. His cup had been moved into the dark supply closet to make room for a project. The other cups sat on the sunny windowsill. Jin watered his plant every day, and the soil was still wet. After one week back by the window, his plant turned green again.
cases.question: Why was Jin’s plant pale and droopy?

suspects.why: moved into the dark closet, green again by the window
he watered every day, soil was wet
it grew again by the window

cases.answer: Jin’s plant did not get sunlight.
proof: "His cup had been moved into the dark supply closet to make room for a project."
"After one week back by the window, his plant turned green again."
clears: Water: "Jin watered his plant every day, and the soil was still wet."
cases.explain: This shows the plant needed light because it turned green again in the sun. Because of this, being in the dark closet made it pale. (Science link: what plants need.)

debate.story: The class planted bean seeds in cups. Every plant grew tall and green except one. Jin's plant was pale yellow and droopy. His cup had been moved into the dark supply closet to make room. The other cups sat on the sunny windowsill. Jin watered his plant every day and the soil was still wet. Roots sitting in wet soil rot and cannot drink. Jin's seed came from the bottom of the packet.
debate.question: Why is Jin's plant droopy? Pick one answer and back it up.

suspects.why: moved into the dark closet, away from the sunny sill
watered every day, with soil that is still wet

suspects.who: 📦 A seed from the bottom of the packet
suspects.why: a seed taken from the bottom of the packet

evidence: “His cup had been moved into the dark supply closet to make room.”
“The other cups sat on the sunny windowsill.”
arguments.against: “Jin watered his plant every day and the soil was still wet.”

evidence: “Jin watered his plant every day and the soil was still wet.”
“Roots sitting in wet soil rot and cannot drink.”
arguments.against: “His cup had been moved into the dark supply closet to make room.”

evidence: “Jin's seed came from the bottom of the packet.”
arguments.against: “Every plant grew tall and green except one.”

debate.note: Watering every day used to clear the water and now it accuses it, which is a good surprise for a class that has met this case before. Pale and yellow fits the dark closet; droopy and wet fits the drowning. Both sentences are on the page and they point different ways.

cases.title: The Melted Ice Cream
cases.story: For the end-of-unit party, Mr. Fox bought ice cream and put it in the teacher lounge freezer. At 2:00, the ice cream was soup! The freezer door was open a crack, and a box of paper plates was stuck in it. Cold air was coming out into the room. Ms. Hall had put the paper plates on the top shelf that morning. The power was on, because the microwave and lights worked. "The door could not close!" said Mr. Fox.
cases.question: Why did the ice cream melt?

suspects.why: door open a crack, plates stuck in it
the microwave and lights worked
it would have stayed frozen with the door closed

cases.answer: The freezer door was left open, so the ice cream melted.
proof: "The freezer door was open a crack, and a box of paper plates was stuck in it."
"Cold air was coming out into the room."
clears: Power: "The power was on, because the microwave and lights worked."
cases.explain: This shows the freezer could not stay cold because the door was blocked open. Because of this, the ice cream melted. (Science link: solid to liquid.)

debate.story: Mr. Fox put ice cream in the teacher lounge freezer. At two o'clock it was soup. The freezer door was open a crack with a box of paper plates stuck in it. Cold air was coming out into the room. Ms. Hall put the plates on the top shelf that morning. The lounge window faces south and the sun falls on the freezer all afternoon. The freezer was unplugged for ten minutes while the kettle was moved.
debate.question: Why did the ice cream melt? Choose one and show the words.

suspects.why: a door held open a crack by a box of plates
ten minutes unplugged while the kettle was moved
a south window with sun on the freezer all afternoon

evidence: “The freezer door was open a crack with a box of paper plates stuck in it.”
“Cold air was coming out into the room.”
arguments.against: “The freezer was unplugged for ten minutes while the kettle was moved.”

evidence: “The freezer was unplugged for ten minutes while the kettle was moved.”
arguments.against: “Cold air was coming out into the room.”

evidence: “The lounge window faces south and the sun falls on the freezer all afternoon.”
arguments.against: “The freezer door was open a crack with a box of paper plates stuck in it.”

debate.note: Ten minutes is a short time and a whole morning is a long one, so this case can be argued with a clock. Cold air coming out into the room is the sentence that shows the door fault was still working at two. Ask which answer stops and which keeps going.

cases.title: The Field Day Ribbon
cases.story: On Field Day, Maya won a blue first-place ribbon. She clipped it to her water bottle and went to the sack race. When she came back, the ribbon was gone! A gust of wind blew everyone’s hats around. Maya saw something blue flapping against the fence at the edge of the field. It was her ribbon, caught on the wire.
