Her friend Ally had been in the sack race with her the whole time. The coach had all the extra ribbons locked in a box.
cases.question: What happened to Maya’s ribbon?

suspects.why: gust of wind, ribbon caught on the fence
in the sack race with her the whole time
extra ribbons were locked in a box

cases.answer: The wind blew Maya’s ribbon to the fence.
proof: "A gust of wind blew everyone’s hats around."
"It was her ribbon, caught on the wire."
clears: Ally: "Her friend Ally had been in the sack race with her the whole time."
Coach: "The coach had all the extra ribbons locked in a box."
cases.explain: This shows the wind carried the ribbon because it ended up on the fence after a big gust. Because of this, nobody took it.

debate.story: On Field Day, Maya won a blue first-place ribbon and clipped it to her water bottle. When she came back from the sack race it was gone. A gust of wind blew everyone's hats around. Something blue was flapping against the fence at the edge of the field. Ally finished the sack race early and went back for her bottle. The clip on Maya's ribbon was bent open before the race.
debate.question: Where did the ribbon go? Pick one answer and prove it.

suspects.why: a gust of wind and something blue on the fence
finished the sack race early and went back for her bottle
a clip already bent open before the race

evidence: “A gust of wind blew everyone's hats around.”
“Something blue was flapping against the fence at the edge of the field.”
arguments.against: “Ally finished the sack race early and went back for her bottle.”

evidence: “Ally finished the sack race early and went back for her bottle.”
arguments.against: “Something blue was flapping against the fence at the edge of the field.”

evidence: “The clip on Maya's ribbon was bent open before the race.”
arguments.against: “A gust of wind blew everyone's hats around.”

debate.note: Something blue is not the same as the ribbon, and a careful reader will say so before anybody runs to the fence. The bent clip explains how the ribbon came off and says nothing about where it went. Two answers can both be needed, and that is worth naming.

cases.title: The Popping Balloons
cases.story: On the last day of school, the class tied balloons to the playground fence. One by one, they started to pop! The balloons were in the bright, hot sun, and the thermometer said 90 degrees. The balloons in the shade by the door were still fine. No one was near the fence, because everyone was eating popsicles under the tree. "The heat made the air inside get bigger!" said Ms. Jade.
cases.question: Why did the balloons pop?

suspects.why: 90 degrees, sunny ones popped, shady ones were fine
everyone was under the tree
no clues point to birds

cases.answer: The hot sun made the balloons pop.
proof: "The balloons were in the bright, hot sun, and the thermometer said 90 degrees."
"The balloons in the shade by the door were still fine."
clears: Students: "No one was near the fence, because everyone was eating popsicles under the tree."
cases.explain: This shows the heat popped them because only the balloons in the sun popped. Because of this, the hot sun was the cause. (Science link: heat makes gas expand.)

debate.story: On the last day of school the class tied balloons to the playground fence. One by one they started to pop. The balloons were in bright sun and the thermometer said ninety degrees. The balloons in the shade by the door were still fine. The fence has a line of sharp wire ends along the top rail. The sunny balloons were blown up biggest because they went up first.
debate.question: Why did the balloons pop? Make the case for one answer.

suspects.why: ninety degrees, with the shady ones still fine
a line of sharp wire ends along the top rail
blown up biggest because they went up first

evidence: “The balloons were in bright sun and the thermometer said ninety degrees.”
“The balloons in the shade by the door were still fine.”
arguments.against: “The fence has a line of sharp wire ends along the top rail.”

evidence: “The fence has a line of sharp wire ends along the top rail.”
arguments.against: “The balloons in the shade by the door were still fine.”

evidence: “The sunny balloons were blown up biggest because they went up first.”
arguments.against: “On the last day of school the class tied balloons to the playground fence.”

debate.note: The shady balloons are the control and they are the best thing in the story, because they share the fence and not the sun. That beats the wire. The last sentence is the sly one: the sunny balloons were also the fullest, so sun and size travel together and the case cannot separate them.

cases.title: The Case of the Overdue Shelf
cases.story: Mr. Ruiz keeps the library's new books on a cart by the window. On Friday the whole top row was gone. The sign-out tablet showed no checkouts after lunch. A folded permission slip for the book fair lay under the cart. The custodian, Mrs. Ames, had waxed the floor and moved nothing. Ms. Patel's class had been in the gym since one o'clock. Then Mr. Ruiz found the books shelved neatly in the fiction aisle, in alphabetical order. Dev, the new helper, had been told to shelve returns and had shelved everything he saw.
cases.question: What happened to the new books?

suspects.why: told to shelve returns, shelved everything he saw
waxed the floor and moved nothing
in the gym since one o'clock

cases.answer: Dev shelved the new books in with the returns.
proof: “Then Mr. Ruiz found the books shelved neatly in the fiction aisle, in alphabetical order.”
“Dev, the new helper, had been told to shelve returns and had shelved everything he saw.”
clears: Mrs. Ames: “had waxed the floor and moved nothing.”
Ms. Patel's class: “had been in the gym since one o'clock.”
cases.explain: The books were never missing. Because Dev was told to shelve returns and shelved everything he saw, the new books ended up in the fiction aisle in alphabetical order.

debate.story: Mr. Ruiz keeps the library's new books on a cart by the window. On Friday the whole top row was gone. The books turned up shelved neatly in the fiction aisle, in alphabetical order. Dev, the new helper, had been told to shelve returns. Mrs. Ames waxed that aisle Friday and lifted the books down to do it. She put them back where she thought they went. Ms. Patel's class came back from the gym at ten past one. Three of them were sent to the library to pick a book. Nobody signed anything out.
debate.question: What happened to the new books? Say who you think moved them and prove it.

suspects.why: told to shelve returns, and the books turned up shelved
lifted every book down to wax, then put them back
back from the gym at ten past one, with three sent to the library

evidence: “Dev, the new helper, had been told to shelve returns.”
“The books turned up shelved neatly in the fiction aisle, in alphabetical order.”
arguments.against: “Mrs. Ames waxed that aisle Friday and lifted the books down to do it.”

evidence: “Mrs. Ames waxed that aisle Friday and lifted the books down to do it.”
“She put them back where she thought they went.”
arguments.against: “The books turned up shelved neatly in the fiction aisle, in alphabetical order.”

evidence: “Ms. Patel's class came back from the gym at ten past one.”
“Three of them were sent to the library to pick a book.”
arguments.against: “Nobody signed anything out.”

debate.note: Alphabetical order is the detail to hold the class to. It takes somebody who knows the system and is trying to be helpful, which fits Dev best and Mrs. Ames second. A student who picks the class has to explain why three children browsing would reshelve a whole row in order.

cases.title: The Case of the Cold Soup
cases.story: Nina packed hot tomato soup in a thermos on Tuesday. At lunch the soup was cold. Her thermos was sitting upright in her bag, and the lid was screwed on tight. Her brother Theo had packed the same soup and his was still steaming. Nina had filled hers from the pot before her mother turned the burner on. Theo had filled his afterward, once the pot was steaming. The thermos had kept the soup exactly as cold as it went in.
cases.question: Why was Nina's soup cold?

suspects.why: filled from the pot before the burner was on
lid screwed on tight, sitting upright in her bag
his soup was still steaming

cases.answer: The soup was already cold when Nina poured it in.
proof: “Nina had filled hers from the pot before her mother turned the burner on.”
“The thermos had kept the soup exactly as cold as it went in.”
clears: A broken thermos: “the lid was screwed on tight.”
Theo: “Theo had filled his afterward, once the pot was steaming.”
cases.explain: A thermos keeps food at the temperature it went in. Because Nina filled hers before her mother turned the burner on, the soup was cold from the start.

debate.story: Nina packed hot tomato soup in a thermos on Tuesday. At lunch the soup was cold. She filled hers from the pot before her mother turned the burner on. Her brother Theo had the same soup and his was still steaming. The two thermoses are the same model and the same colour. Nina's lid has a crack along the rim that she noticed last month. A cracked lid lets the heat straight out. Theo got to the counter first and both bags were open. Nobody wrote a name on either thermos.
debate.question: Why was Nina's soup cold? Pick one reason and back it from the story.

suspects.why: filled from the pot before the burner went on
a cracked lid that lets the heat straight out
first to the counter, with both bags open and no names

evidence: “She filled hers from the pot before her mother turned the burner on.”
“At lunch the soup was cold.”
arguments.against: “Nina's lid has a crack along the rim that she noticed last month.”

evidence: “Nina's lid has a crack along the rim that she noticed last month.”
“A cracked lid lets the heat straight out.”
arguments.against: “Her brother Theo had the same soup and his was still steaming.”

evidence: “Theo got to the counter first and both bags were open.”
“The two thermoses are the same model and the same colour.”
arguments.against: “She filled hers from the pot before her mother turned the burner on.”

debate.note: Two of these say the soup was never hot and one says it got cold on the way. Ask which one a thermometer at breakfast would have settled. The swap is the weakest and the most fun, and a student who argues it has to explain why Theo's soup was still steaming at lunch if he took the cracked one.

cases.title: The Case of the Shrinking Pencils
cases.story: Every Monday Mr. Dunn counted thirty sharpened pencils into the cup. By Friday there were thirty stubs. Nobody had taken a pencil home. The sharpener's drawer was packed tight with shavings, and the floor beneath it was clean. Mr. Dunn watched the cup and the sharpener for a whole week. Jonah sharpened his pencil eleven times on Wednesday alone, because he liked the sound. The pencils were all still there. They had simply been ground away a little at a time.
cases.question: Where did the pencils go?

suspects.why: drawer packed tight with shavings
nobody had taken a pencil home
the floor beneath it was clean

cases.answer: The sharpener ground the pencils down into stubs.
proof: “The sharpener's drawer was packed tight with shavings, and the floor beneath it was clean.”
“Jonah sharpened his pencil eleven times on Wednesday alone, because he liked the sound.”
clears: Taken home: “Nobody had taken a pencil home.”
The floor: “the floor beneath it was clean.”
cases.explain: The pencils never left the room. Because Jonah sharpened his pencil eleven times in one day, the shavings filled the drawer and the pencils became stubs.

debate.story: Every Monday Mr. Dunn counted thirty sharpened pencils into the cup. By Friday there were thirty stubs. The sharpener's drawer was packed tight with shavings. Jonah sharpened his pencil eleven times on Wednesday, because he liked the sound. Four pencils were found in coat pockets at the end of the week. The cup sits at the edge of a shelf above the heating vent. Two stubs were swept up from under the vent on Thursday. Mr. Dunn never counts what comes back in.
debate.question: Where did the pencils go? Choose one answer and quote the story.

suspects.why: a drawer packed tight, and eleven sharpenings in a day
four found in coat pockets at the end of the week
a cup on a shelf edge, and two stubs under the vent

evidence: “The sharpener's drawer was packed tight with shavings.”
“Jonah sharpened his pencil eleven times on Wednesday, because he liked the sound.”
arguments.against: “Four pencils were found in coat pockets at the end of the week.”

evidence: “Four pencils were found in coat pockets at the end of the week.”
“Mr. Dunn never counts what comes back in.”
arguments.against: “By Friday there were thirty stubs.”

evidence: “The cup sits at the edge of a shelf above the heating vent.”
“Two stubs were swept up from under the vent on Thursday.”
arguments.against: “The sharpener's drawer was packed tight with shavings.”

debate.note: There were thirty on Monday and thirty stubs on Friday, so nothing left the room and everything got shorter. That sentence is worth reading twice with the class. It makes the sharpener the strongest answer and it does not kill the others, because four in pockets and two under a vent are real pencils the count never missed.

cases.title: The Case of the Light Apple Crate
cases.story: The fourth grade picked apples all morning and filled six crates. Back at school, one crate weighed much less than the others. The orchard guide had taped a count to every lid. Crate four said forty apples and held twenty-two. A line of apples lay in the grass along the path from the bus. Nobody had eaten any, because the class had packed sandwiches. The bottom slat of crate four hung loose on one nail. It had been dropping apples the whole way back.
cases.question: Why was crate four so light?

suspects.who: 🪵 A loose slat in the crate
suspects.why: bottom slat hung loose on one nail
the class had packed sandwiches
had taped a count to every lid

cases.answer: The loose slat dropped apples along the path.
proof: “A line of apples lay in the grass along the path from the bus.”
“The bottom slat of crate four hung loose on one nail.”
clears: Eating: “Nobody had eaten any”
The guide: “had taped a count to every lid.”
cases.explain: The apples were lost on the way back, not at the orchard. Because the bottom slat hung loose on one nail, crate four left a line of apples along the path.

debate.story: The fourth grade picked apples all morning and filled six crates. Back at school, crate four weighed much less than the others. Its lid said forty apples and it held twenty-two. A line of apples lay in the grass along the path from the bus. The bottom slat of crate four hangs loose on one nail. The guide wrote the counts from memory at the end of the morning. Two students were seen eating apples on the bus. Nobody checked a crate before it was loaded.
debate.question: Why was crate four so light? Make the case for one answer.

suspects.who: 🪵 A loose slat in the crate
suspects.why: a bottom slat hanging on one nail, and apples along the path
two seen eating on the bus, and no crate checked before loading
counts written from memory at the end of the morning

evidence: “The bottom slat of crate four hangs loose on one nail.”
“A line of apples lay in the grass along the path from the bus.”
arguments.against: “The guide wrote the counts from memory at the end of the morning.”

evidence: “Two students were seen eating apples on the bus.”
“Nobody checked a crate before it was loaded.”
arguments.against: “A line of apples lay in the grass along the path from the bus.”

evidence: “The guide wrote the counts from memory at the end of the morning.”
“Its lid said forty apples and it held twenty-two.”
arguments.against: “The bottom slat of crate four hangs loose on one nail.”

debate.note: Eighteen apples are missing and two students eating on a bus do not account for eighteen. Get the class to do that subtraction out loud. The guide's count is the quiet answer: if the lid was wrong from the start, nothing went missing at all, and the apples in the grass came from somewhere else.

cases.title: The Case of the Bent Wheel
cases.story: Omar's bike wobbled badly on the ride to school. The front wheel had a flat spot, and two spokes were loose. His tires were full and the brakes held fine. On Saturday he had ridden down the park stairs with his cousin, who filmed it. The video shows the front wheel landing first on every step. His father spun the wheel and watched it rise and fall. Nothing else on the bike had changed. A wheel bends a little with each hard landing.
cases.question: What bent Omar's front wheel?

suspects.why: front wheel landed first on every step
his tires were full
the brakes held fine

cases.answer: Riding down the stairs bent the wheel.
proof: “The video shows the front wheel landing first on every step.”
“A wheel bends a little with each hard landing.”
clears: A flat tire: “His tires were full”
The brakes: “the brakes held fine.”
cases.explain: The damage came from the landings, not from the tire or the brakes. Because the front wheel landed first on every step, it bent a little each time.

debate.story: Omar's bike wobbled badly on the ride to school. The front wheel has a flat spot and two loose spokes. On Saturday he rode down the park stairs with his cousin, who filmed it. The video shows the front wheel landing first on every step. The front tire reads twelve pounds, where the side wall asks for forty. A soft tire lets the rim take the hit instead of the rubber. The front brake pad rubs the rim on one side only. Nothing else on the bike has changed.
debate.question: What bent Omar's front wheel? Argue for one cause.

suspects.why: the park stairs, with the front wheel landing first every time
twelve pounds in a tire that asks for forty
a front pad rubbing the rim on one side

evidence: “On Saturday he rode down the park stairs with his cousin, who filmed it.”
“The video shows the front wheel landing first on every step.”
arguments.against: “The front tire reads twelve pounds, where the side wall asks for forty.”

evidence: “The front tire reads twelve pounds, where the side wall asks for forty.”
“A soft tire lets the rim take the hit instead of the rubber.”
arguments.against: “The front wheel has a flat spot and two loose spokes.”

evidence: “The front brake pad rubs the rim on one side only.”
“Nothing else on the bike has changed.”
arguments.against: “The video shows the front wheel landing first on every step.”

debate.note: The tire and the stairs are not really rivals, and the better answers say so: a soft tire is why the stairs bent the wheel instead of bouncing off it. The brake is the odd one out, because a rubbing pad slows a wheel rather than bending one, and a student who spots that has used a rule the story never states.

cases.title: The Case of the Missing Guppy
cases.story: The class counted eight guppies on Friday and seven on Monday. The tank lid was on and the filter ran all weekend. No guppy floated at the top and none lay on the carpet. The big angelfish had been added two weeks earlier. Ms. Ortiz read the care card taped inside the cabinet. Angelfish eat anything that fits in their mouths, it said. The angelfish had not been fed since Thursday. It was the only fish in the tank big enough.
cases.question: What happened to the eighth guppy?

suspects.why: eats anything that fits, not fed since Thursday
the tank lid was on
the filter ran all weekend

cases.answer: The angelfish ate the guppy.
proof: “Angelfish eat anything that fits in their mouths, it said.”
“The angelfish had not been fed since Thursday.”
clears: Jumping out: “The tank lid was on”
The filter: “the filter ran all weekend.”
cases.explain: The guppy never left the tank. Because the angelfish eats anything that fits and had not been fed since Thursday, it was the only fish big enough to do it.

debate.story: The class counted eight guppies on Friday and seven on Monday. No guppy floated at the top. The big angelfish was added two weeks earlier and has not been fed since Thursday. The care card says angelfish eat anything that fits in their mouths. The tank lid was pushed back two inches to fit the new heater cord. The floor behind the tank was swept by the cleaners on Saturday night. The filter was making a dry rattle on Friday afternoon. A guppy can be pulled into an intake that has lost its sponge.
debate.question: What happened to the eighth guppy? Pick one answer and prove it.

suspects.why: unfed since Thursday, and it eats whatever fits
a lid pushed back two inches, and a floor swept on Saturday
a dry rattle on Friday, and an intake that can pull a guppy in

evidence: “The big angelfish was added two weeks earlier and has not been fed since Thursday.”
“The care card says angelfish eat anything that fits in their mouths.”

“A guppy can be pulled into an intake that has lost its sponge.”
arguments.against: “The care card says angelfish eat anything that fits in their mouths.”

debate.note: Nobody looked behind the tank before the cleaners came, which is the detail that keeps the jumping answer alive. Ask what each suspect would have left behind and whether anyone checked: the angelfish leaves nothing, the floor leaves a dried guppy, the filter leaves one in the intake. Only the last two can still be tested.

cases.title: The Case of the Thumping Wall
cases.story: Every afternoon at two the wall behind the reading corner thumped four times. Mr. Blake checked the pipes and found no air in them. The classroom above had music at ten, not at two. Outside, the basketball hoop stood against that same wall. At two o'clock the fifth grade had recess. Mr. Blake stepped outside and watched four students take turns shooting. Each miss hit the backboard and the wall shook. The thumping stopped the day the hoop was moved.
cases.question: What made the wall thump?

suspects.why: stands against that wall, each miss hit the backboard
no air in them
music at ten, not at two

cases.answer: Missed shots hitting the backboard shook the wall.
proof: “Outside, the basketball hoop stood against that same wall.”
“Each miss hit the backboard and the wall shook.”
clears: The pipes: “found no air in them.”
The class upstairs: “had music at ten, not at two.”
cases.explain: The noise came from outside the room. Because the hoop stood against that same wall, each miss hit the backboard and the wall shook.

debate.story: Every afternoon at two the wall behind the reading corner thumped four times. Outside, the basketball hoop stands against that same wall. At two o'clock the fifth grade has recess. Mr. Blake watched four students take turns shooting, and each miss hit the backboard. The hot water pipes run inside that wall and the boiler fires at two. A pipe knocks when hot water hits cold metal. The class upstairs moved its music lesson to two o'clock in October. Their drum kit sits above the reading corner.
debate.question: What made the wall thump? Choose one and back it up.

suspects.why: a hoop on that wall, and every miss hitting the backboard
pipes in the wall, and a boiler that fires at two
a music lesson moved to two, with a drum kit overhead

evidence: “Outside, the basketball hoop stands against that same wall.”
“Mr. Blake watched four students take turns shooting, and each miss hit the backboard.”
arguments.against: “The hot water pipes run inside that wall and the boiler fires at two.”

evidence: “The hot water pipes run inside that wall and the boiler fires at two.”
“A pipe knocks when hot water hits cold metal.”
arguments.against: “At two o'clock the fifth grade has recess.”

evidence: “The class upstairs moved its music lesson to two o'clock in October.”
“Their drum kit sits above the reading corner.”
arguments.against: “Outside, the basketball hoop stands against that same wall.”

debate.note: Three things now happen at two o'clock, so the time has stopped being evidence. That is the lesson here and it is worth naming: a clue that fits everybody fits nobody. What still separates them is four thumps, and the class should ask which suspect makes exactly four and then stops.

cases.title: The Case of the Bare Maple
cases.story: Two maples stand at the front of the school, planted the same spring. In October the one by the road had lost every leaf. The one by the field still held most of its own. Both had been watered by the same hose all summer. The road tree stands beside the bus lane, where the plows pile salt each winter. A soil test from the road tree came back high in salt. The field tree's test came back normal. Salt in the soil makes a tree drop its leaves early.
cases.question: Why did the road maple lose its leaves first?

suspects.why: soil test came back high in salt
watered by the same hose all summer
planted the same spring

cases.answer: Salt in the soil made the road tree drop its leaves early.
proof: “A soil test from the road tree came back high in salt.”
“Salt in the soil makes a tree drop its leaves early.”
clears: Water: “Both had been watered by the same hose all summer.”
Age: “planted the same spring.”
cases.explain: The two trees are the same age and got the same water. Because the road tree's soil came back high in salt, it dropped its leaves first.

debate.story: Two maples stand at the front of the school. In October the one by the road had lost every leaf. The one by the field still held most of its own. The road tree stands beside the bus lane, where the plows pile salt each winter. A soil test from the road tree came back high in salt. The hose reaches the field tree and stops four feet short of the road one. The road tree went in two springs after the field tree. A young tree drops its leaves sooner in a hard year.
debate.question: Why did the road maple lose its leaves first? Pick one and prove it.

suspects.why: beside the bus lane, with a soil test high in salt
a hose that stops four feet short of it
planted two springs later than the other

evidence: “The road tree stands beside the bus lane, where the plows pile salt each winter.”
“A soil test from the road tree came back high in salt.”
arguments.against: “The hose reaches the field tree and stops four feet short of the road one.”

“In October the one by the road had lost every leaf.”
arguments.against: “A soil test from the road tree came back high in salt.”

“A young tree drops its leaves sooner in a hard year.”
arguments.against: “The one by the field still held most of its own.”

debate.note: The soil test is the only measurement in the story and that counts for a lot. Say so, and then ask the harder question: a tree four feet past the end of a hose is also a thirsty tree, and thirst and salt do the same thing to a leaf. Nobody tested the field tree's soil either.

cases.title: The Case of the Sunken Pumpkin
cases.story: The class pumpkin sat on the sill from October first. By Halloween it had caved in on one side. The custodian had not moved it. No animal prints marked the sill or the floor. The radiator under the window had come on for the first time that week. The caved side was the side facing the glass, where the sun struck all afternoon. A second pumpkin in the cool hallway stayed firm. Heat dries a pumpkin from one side and the shell collapses.
cases.question: Why did the pumpkin cave in on one side?

suspects.why: radiator on, sun struck the glass side all afternoon
no prints on the sill or the floor
had not moved it

cases.answer: Heat at the window dried that side of the pumpkin.
proof: “The caved side was the side facing the glass, where the sun struck all afternoon.”
“Heat dries a pumpkin from one side and the shell collapses.”
clears: An animal: “No animal prints marked the sill or the floor.”
The custodian: “had not moved it.”
cases.explain: The pumpkin in the cool hallway stayed firm. Because the caved side faced the glass where the sun struck all afternoon, the heat dried that side and the shell collapsed.

debate.story: The class pumpkin sat on the sill from October first. By Halloween it had caved in on one side. The caved side faced the glass, where the sun struck all afternoon. The radiator under the window came on for the first time that week. A second pumpkin in the cool hallway stayed firm. Three small tooth marks show near the stem on the caved side. The custodian moved the pumpkin twice to clean the sill. He set it down hard the second time, and the class heard it.
debate.question: Why did the pumpkin cave in on one side? Make the case for one cause.

suspects.why: the sunny side, with the radiator on for the first time
three small tooth marks near the stem
moved twice, and set down hard the second time

evidence: “The caved side faced the glass, where the sun struck all afternoon.”
“The radiator under the window came on for the first time that week.”
arguments.against: “Three small tooth marks show near the stem on the caved side.”

“A second pumpkin in the cool hallway stayed firm.”

“He set it down hard the second time, and the class heard it.”
arguments.against: “The caved side faced the glass, where the sun struck all afternoon.”

debate.note: The tooth marks and the sunny side are on the same side of the pumpkin, which means the case has handed the class a coincidence and will not say which came first. The hallway pumpkin is the control and it works for two answers at once: it was never warm and it was never moved.

cases.title: The Case of the Painted Trail
cases.story: On Thursday a line of blue footprints crossed the gym floor. The art room had opened a gallon of blue paint that morning. The prints were the size of a grown-up's shoe. Coach Rivas had worn sneakers with a wavy sole, and the prints showed a flat heel. Mr. Shaw, the art teacher, had carried the open can to the kiln room through the gym. His boots have flat heels. A blue smear ran along the gym wall at hand height.
cases.question: Who left the blue footprints?

suspects.why: carried the open can through the gym, flat heels
wavy sole, but the prints show a flat heel
the prints are a grown-up's size

cases.answer: Mr. Shaw left the footprints while carrying the paint can.
proof: “Mr. Shaw, the art teacher, had carried the open can to the kiln room through the gym.”
“His boots have flat heels.”
clears: Coach Rivas: “had worn sneakers with a wavy sole”
A student: “The prints were the size of a grown-up's shoe.”
cases.explain: The prints have a flat heel and a grown-up's size. Because Mr. Shaw carried the open can through the gym and his boots have flat heels, the trail is his.

debate.story: On Thursday a line of blue footprints crossed the gym floor. The art room opened a gallon of blue paint that morning. Mr. Shaw carried the open can to the kiln room through the gym. His boots have flat heels, and the prints show a flat heel. Coach Rivas keeps a second pair of flat-heeled shoes in his office. He crossed the gym twice that morning to fetch cones. The prints measure nine inches, which is a big fourth grader or a small adult. A blue handprint sits on the wall at a child's height.
debate.question: Who left the blue footprints? Charge one of them and prove it.

suspects.why: carried the open can through the gym, in flat-heeled boots
a second pair of flat-heeled shoes, and two crossings that morning
prints of nine inches, and a handprint at a child's height

evidence: “Mr. Shaw carried the open can to the kiln room through the gym.”
“His boots have flat heels, and the prints show a flat heel.”
arguments.against: “A blue handprint sits on the wall at a child's height.”

evidence: “Coach Rivas keeps a second pair of flat-heeled shoes in his office.”
“He crossed the gym twice that morning to fetch cones.”
arguments.against: “The art room opened a gallon of blue paint that morning.”

evidence: “The prints measure nine inches, which is a big fourth grader or a small adult.”
“A blue handprint sits on the wall at a child's height.”
arguments.against: “His boots have flat heels, and the prints show a flat heel.”

debate.note: The heel used to tell the two adults apart and now it does not, because Coach Rivas turns out to own flat-heeled shoes as well. That is worth pointing at. Nine inches is the measurement that keeps the student in the case, and the handprint is the only evidence nobody can explain away.

cases.title: The Case of the Late Bus
cases.story: Bus 12 reached school at 8:40 every day this week instead of 8:20. The driver, Mr. Hahn, left the depot on time each morning. The route had not changed and no student was added. On Monday the city closed the bridge on Oak Street for repair. The detour sends Bus 12 around three extra blocks and through two lights. Mr. Hahn timed it himself at nineteen minutes added. The bridge reopens in April. Until then the bus will be late.
cases.question: Why is Bus 12 arriving late?

suspects.why: three extra blocks and two lights, nineteen minutes
left the depot on time each morning
no student was added

cases.answer: The bridge detour adds nineteen minutes to the route.
proof: “The detour sends Bus 12 around three extra blocks and through two lights.”
“Mr. Hahn timed it himself at nineteen minutes added.”
clears: A late start: “left the depot on time each morning.”
Extra stops: “The route had not changed and no student was added.”
cases.explain: The bus leaves on time and carries the same students. Because the closed bridge sends it around three extra blocks and through two lights, it arrives nineteen minutes late.

debate.story: Bus 12 reached school at 8:40 every day this week instead of 8:20. On Monday the city closed the bridge on Oak Street for repair. The detour sends Bus 12 around three extra blocks and through two lights. Mr. Hahn timed the detour himself at nineteen minutes added. The depot's sheet shows Bus 12 pulling out at 7:12 on three mornings, not 7:05. Two new families joined the route in January, at two new stops. Each stop takes about a minute with the lift. Nobody has written down what time the bus reaches the first stop.
debate.question: Why is Bus 12 arriving late? Pick one reason and quote the story.

suspects.why: three extra blocks and two lights, timed at nineteen minutes
pulling out at 7:12 on three mornings instead of 7:05
two new stops in January, about a minute each with the lift

evidence: “The detour sends Bus 12 around three extra blocks and through two lights.”
“Mr. Hahn timed the detour himself at nineteen minutes added.”
arguments.against: “The depot's sheet shows Bus 12 pulling out at 7:12 on three mornings, not 7:05.”

evidence: “The depot's sheet shows Bus 12 pulling out at 7:12 on three mornings, not 7:05.”
“Nobody has written down what time the bus reaches the first stop.”
arguments.against: “Bus 12 reached school at 8:40 every day this week instead of 8:20.”

evidence: “Two new families joined the route in January, at two new stops.”
“Each stop takes about a minute with the lift.”
arguments.against: “On Monday the city closed the bridge on Oak Street for repair.”

debate.note: This one is arithmetic and the class can do it. Twenty minutes are missing. The detour is nineteen, the late starts are seven on three days only, the new stops are two. Ask what each suspect adds up to against twenty, and which of them explains why the bus was late every single day.

cases.title: The Case of the Tarnished Trophy
cases.story: The chess trophy shone in September and looked brown by December. Nobody had touched it, because the case stays locked. The case sits beside the pool door, which is propped open each morning. Air from the pool room carries chlorine. The science teacher tested the trophy's surface and found silver, not gold. A silver spoon left by the same door had turned brown in a month. The soccer trophy in the front hall is still bright. Chlorine in the air darkens silver.
cases.question: Why did the chess trophy turn brown?

suspects.why: the air carries chlorine, a silver spoon turned brown
nobody had touched it, the case stays locked
the surface tested as silver, not gold

cases.answer: Chlorine in the air darkened the silver trophy.
proof: “Air from the pool room carries chlorine.”
“A silver spoon left by the same door had turned brown in a month.”
clears: Handling: “Nobody had touched it”
Paint: “found silver, not gold.”
cases.explain: The soccer trophy in the front hall is still bright. Because the chess case sits beside the propped pool door and chlorine darkens silver, that trophy turned brown.

debate.story: The chess trophy shone in September and looked brown by December. The case sits beside the pool door, which is propped open each morning. Air from the pool room carries chlorine. A silver spoon left by the same door turned brown in a month. The soccer trophy in the front hall is still bright. The case lock has been broken since October and the door swings open. The trophy was lifted out for photographs twice in November. Its base is bare metal under a thin coat that has worn through at the handles.
debate.question: Why did the chess trophy turn brown? Argue for one cause.

suspects.why: pool air carrying chlorine, and a spoon that browned in a month
a broken lock since October, and two trips out for photographs
a thin coat worn through at the handles, over bare metal

evidence: “Air from the pool room carries chlorine.”
“A silver spoon left by the same door turned brown in a month.”
arguments.against: “The case lock has been broken since October and the door swings open.”

evidence: “The case lock has been broken since October and the door swings open.”
“The trophy was lifted out for photographs twice in November.”
arguments.against: “The soccer trophy in the front hall is still bright.”

evidence: “Its base is bare metal under a thin coat that has worn through at the handles.”
“The chess trophy shone in September and looked brown by December.”
arguments.against: “A silver spoon left by the same door turned brown in a month.”

debate.note: The spoon is a clean little experiment nobody set up on purpose: same door, same air, same result. The broken lock is the interesting objection, because a case that will not shut lets more pool air in as well as more hands. Ask whether the lock helps the chlorine answer rather than beating it.

cases.title: The Case of the Early Dinner
cases.story: The fourth grade planned a Thanksgiving lunch for noon. The turkey came out of the oven at ten and was dry by twelve. The recipe said to roast it four hours at 325 degrees. Mrs. Kerr had set the dial to 425 by mistake. The oven light had been out for a month, so nobody checked the number. A thermometer in the bird read done two hours early. The rolls baked in the same oven had burned on the bottoms.
cases.question: Why was the turkey dry?

suspects.why: dial set to 425, rolls burned on the bottoms
a thermometer read done two hours early
said four hours at 325 degrees

cases.answer: The oven ran a hundred degrees too hot.
proof: “Mrs. Kerr had set the dial to 425 by mistake.”
“The rolls baked in the same oven had burned on the bottoms.”
clears: Cooking too long: “A thermometer in the bird read done two hours early.”
The recipe: “said to roast it four hours at 325 degrees.”
cases.explain: The turkey came out two hours early, so time was not the problem. Because the dial was set to 425 instead of 325, the oven ran a hundred degrees hot and the rolls burned too.

debate.story: The fourth grade planned a Thanksgiving lunch for noon. The turkey came out of the oven at ten and was dry by twelve. Mrs. Kerr had set the dial to 425 by mistake. The oven light had been out for a month, so nobody checked the number. The rolls baked in the same oven burned on the bottoms. The bird went in at six, which is four hours before it came out. The recipe card in the folder says three hours, not four. It also says to cover the breast with foil, and nobody did.
debate.question: Why was the turkey dry? Pick one cause and prove it from the story.

suspects.why: a dial set to 425, and rolls burned on the bottoms
in at six and out at ten, against a card that says three hours
a card that says three hours and asks for foil nobody used

evidence: “Mrs. Kerr had set the dial to 425 by mistake.”
“The rolls baked in the same oven burned on the bottoms.”
arguments.against: “The recipe card in the folder says three hours, not four.”

evidence: “The bird went in at six, which is four hours before it came out.”
“The oven light had been out for a month, so nobody checked the number.”
arguments.against: “Mrs. Kerr had set the dial to 425 by mistake.”

evidence: “The recipe card in the folder says three hours, not four.”
“It also says to cover the breast with foil, and nobody did.”
arguments.against: “The turkey came out of the oven at ten and was dry by twelve.”

debate.note: The burned rolls are the strongest evidence in the story because they were in the same oven and nothing about the recipe touched them. Hold the class to that. The other two answers have to explain why the rolls burned, and the honest ones admit that an hour too long at a hundred degrees too hot is the same mistake counted twice.

cases.title: The Case of the Flat Cupcakes
cases.story: Room 12 baked two dozen cupcakes for the class party. Every one came out flat and dense. Mrs. Lin tasted one and frowned. The class used the same recipe as last year. The flour, sugar and eggs were all fresh. The baking powder tin at the back of the cupboard expired in 2021. Ava had measured everything exactly and the oven ran at the right temperature. A test spoonful of the baking powder in water did not fizz.
cases.question: Why were the cupcakes flat?

suspects.why: expired in 2021, did not fizz in water
the same recipe as last year
ran at the right temperature

cases.answer: The baking powder was too old to make the cupcakes rise.
proof: “The baking powder tin at the back of the cupboard expired in 2021.”
“A test spoonful of the baking powder in water did not fizz.”
clears: The recipe: “The class used the same recipe as last year.”
The oven: “the oven ran at the right temperature.”
cases.explain: Everything else was the same as last year. Because the baking powder was from 2021 and did not fizz in water, it had no lift left and the cupcakes stayed flat.

debate.story: Room 12 baked two dozen cupcakes for the class party. Every one came out flat and dense. The baking powder tin at the back of the cupboard expired in 2021. A test spoonful of it in water did not fizz. Ava measured the flour by scooping the cup straight into the bag. Scooping packs in about half as much flour again as the recipe wants. The oven door was opened three times in the first ten minutes. A cake that is jolted early can fall before it sets.
debate.question: Why were the cupcakes flat? Choose one cause and back it up.

suspects.why: a tin that expired in 2021 and would not fizz
flour scooped from the bag, packing in half as much again
a door opened three times in the first ten minutes

evidence: “The baking powder tin at the back of the cupboard expired in 2021.”
“A test spoonful of it in water did not fizz.”
arguments.against: “Ava measured the flour by scooping the cup straight into the bag.”

evidence: “Ava measured the flour by scooping the cup straight into the bag.”
“Scooping packs in about half as much flour again as the recipe wants.”
arguments.against: “A test spoonful of it in water did not fizz.”

evidence: “The oven door was opened three times in the first ten minutes.”
“A cake that is jolted early can fall before it sets.”
arguments.against: “Every one came out flat and dense.”

debate.note: The water test is as close to proof as this story gets, and a student who leads with it is doing the right thing. Push them on dense, though. Dead powder makes a cake flat; too much flour makes it heavy. The word dense is doing work that the powder alone cannot explain.

cases.title: The Case of the Shrunken Mitten
cases.story: Priya's wool mittens fit in November and would not go on in January. Her hands had not grown. Her gloves from the same drawer still fit. The mittens had been soaked at recess and dried on the radiator. The care tag says to lay them flat and keep them away from heat. Her brother's wool hat, washed in hot water, had shrunk the same way. Wool fibers lock together and tighten when they are heated wet. The mittens are now a third smaller than they were.
cases.question: Why do the mittens no longer fit?

suspects.why: soaked at recess, dried on heat, the tag warns against it
her gloves from the same drawer still fit
they fit in November

cases.answer: Drying the wet mittens on the radiator shrank the wool.
proof: “The mittens had been soaked at recess and dried on the radiator.”
“Wool fibers lock together and tighten when they are heated wet.”
clears: Priya's hands: “Her gloves from the same drawer still fit.”
Always small: “Priya's wool mittens fit in November”
cases.explain: Her hands are the same size, because her gloves still fit. Because the soaked mittens dried on the radiator, the wool fibers locked together and tightened.

debate.story: Priya's wool mittens went on easily in November and will not go on in January. The mittens were soaked at recess and dried on the radiator. The care tag says to lay them flat and keep them away from heat. Wool fibers lock together and tighten when they are heated wet. The mittens are now a third smaller than they were. Priya has moved up two shoe sizes since September. Her gloves from the same drawer are a stretchy knit that gives with any hand. The mittens were a hand-me-down and had already been washed many times.
debate.question: Why will the mittens not go on? Argue for one cause.

suspects.why: soaked at recess and dried on a radiator the tag warns against
two shoe sizes up since September, with stretchy gloves that still give
a hand-me-down already washed many times

evidence: “The mittens were soaked at recess and dried on the radiator.”
“Wool fibers lock together and tighten when they are heated wet.”
arguments.against: “Priya has moved up two shoe sizes since September.”

evidence: “Priya has moved up two shoe sizes since September.”
“Her gloves from the same drawer are a stretchy knit that gives with any hand.”
arguments.against: “The mittens are now a third smaller than they were.”

evidence: “The mittens were a hand-me-down and had already been washed many times.”
“The care tag says to lay them flat and keep them away from heat.”
arguments.against: “Priya's wool mittens went on easily in November and will not go on in January.”

debate.note: The gloves used to prove Priya's hands had not grown and now they prove nothing, because a stretchy knit fits a hand of any size. That is the move worth naming. A third smaller is the fact that still decides it: hands do not grow by a third in two months, but wool does shrink by that much.

cases.title: The Case of the Collapsing Roof
cases.story: The gingerbread house stood up on Monday and fell in on Wednesday. The class had used royal icing on the walls and canned frosting on the roof. The walls still hold. Nobody had touched either house. Royal icing dries hard like cement, and canned frosting stays soft. The room had been warm all week with the heat on. A second house, iced entirely with royal icing, is still standing. The roof pieces slid apart along the frosting seam.
cases.question: Why did the roof fall in?

suspects.why: stays soft, and the seam slid apart
nobody had touched either house
the walls still hold

cases.answer: The canned frosting stayed soft and let the roof slide.
proof: “Royal icing dries hard like cement, and canned frosting stays soft.”
“The roof pieces slid apart along the frosting seam.”
clears: Knocking: “Nobody had touched either house.”
The walls: “The walls still hold.”
cases.explain: The house iced entirely with royal icing is still standing. Because the roof was stuck on with canned frosting, which stays soft, the pieces slid apart at the seam.

debate.story: The gingerbread house stood up on Monday and fell in on Wednesday. The class used royal icing on the walls and canned frosting on the roof. Royal icing dries hard like cement, and canned frosting stays soft. The roof pieces slid apart along the frosting seam. The room had been warm all week with the heat on. A second house, iced entirely with royal icing, has lost two candies from its roof. The roof slabs on the fallen house are the two biggest pieces in the kit. Nobody weighed anything before they built it.
debate.question: Why did the roof fall in? Pick one cause and prove it.

suspects.why: canned frosting that stays soft, and a seam that slid apart
a warm room all week, and a second house losing candies

suspects.who: 🧱 The weight of the roof slabs
suspects.why: the two biggest slabs in the kit, never weighed

evidence: “Royal icing dries hard like cement, and canned frosting stays soft.”
“The roof pieces slid apart along the frosting seam.”
arguments.against: “The room had been warm all week with the heat on.”

evidence: “The room had been warm all week with the heat on.”
“A second house, iced entirely with royal icing, has lost two candies from its roof.”
arguments.against: “The roof pieces slid apart along the frosting seam.”

evidence: “The roof slabs on the fallen house are the two biggest pieces in the kit.”
“Nobody weighed anything before they built it.”
arguments.against: “Royal icing dries hard like cement, and canned frosting stays soft.”

debate.note: The second house used to be a clean control and now it is slipping too, which means the warm room is doing something to everybody. The seam is still the best single piece of evidence, because it says exactly where the house let go. Ask whether warm frosting and soft frosting are really two different answers.

cases.title: The Case of the Half-Dark Strand
cases.story: Half of the hallway light strand went dark on Monday morning. The other half still glows. The plug is in and the fuse in the plug is whole. Mr. Cole pulled each bulb from the dark half and tested it. One bulb in the middle had a broken filament. The lights on this strand are wired in series, so one gap stops everything after it. The dark half starts exactly at that bulb. He replaced it and the whole strand lit.
cases.question: Why is half the strand dark?

suspects.why: a broken filament, and the dark half starts at that bulb
the plug is in and the fuse is whole
the other half still glows

cases.answer: One bulb with a broken filament stopped the rest of the strand.
proof: “One bulb in the middle had a broken filament.”
“The lights on this strand are wired in series, so one gap stops everything after it.”
clears: The plug: “The plug is in and the fuse in the plug is whole.”
A power cut: “The other half still glows.”
cases.explain: The strand is wired in series, so one gap stops everything after it. Because the bulb in the middle had a broken filament, every bulb past it went dark.

debate.story: Half of the hallway light strand went dark on Monday morning. The other half is still lit. Mr. Cole pulled each bulb from the dark half and tested it. One bulb in the middle had a broken filament. The lights on this strand are wired in series, so one gap stops everything after it. The dark half starts exactly at that bulb. The strand joins a second strand at a plug halfway along, right by that bulb. The plug is loose enough to turn in its socket. The dark half is the half plugged into the second strand.
debate.question: Why did half the strand go dark? Make the case for one cause.

suspects.why: a broken filament where the dark half begins
a loose plug joining the two strands, right at that point
a series wiring that stops everything after one gap

evidence: “One bulb in the middle had a broken filament.”
“The dark half starts exactly at that bulb.”
arguments.against: “The plug is loose enough to turn in its socket.”

evidence: “The strand joins a second strand at a plug halfway along, right by that bulb.”
“The plug is loose enough to turn in its socket.”
arguments.against: “One bulb in the middle had a broken filament.”

evidence: “The lights on this strand are wired in series, so one gap stops everything after it.”
“The dark half is the half plugged into the second strand.”
arguments.against: “The other half is still lit.”

debate.note: The broken bulb and the loose plug are in the same place, which is why this case will not resolve itself. Both would darken everything after them and the story cannot say which came first. The useful question is what one test would separate them, and the class should get to swapping the bulb and leaving the plug alone.

cases.title: The Case of the Slow Clock
cases.story: The classroom clock lost eleven minutes between Monday and Friday. The battery tested full in the meter. The hands move freely and nothing rubs the face. The clock hangs directly above the radiator, which ran all week. Mr. Ellis moved a second clock to the same spot on Tuesday. By Friday that one had lost nine minutes too. The paper tag inside says the clock is rated for cool rooms only. Nothing else in the room had changed. Heat makes the small motor run slow.
cases.question: Why is the clock losing time?

suspects.why: a second clock in the same spot lost nine minutes
tested full in the meter
the hands move freely and nothing rubs

cases.answer: Heat from the radiator makes the clock run slow.
proof: “Mr. Ellis moved a second clock to the same spot on Tuesday.”
“Heat makes the small motor run slow.”
clears: The battery: “The battery tested full in the meter.”
The hands: “The hands move freely and nothing rubs the face.”
cases.explain: A second clock in the same place lost nine minutes in the same week. Because the clock hangs directly above the radiator and heat makes the motor run slow, it loses time.

debate.story: The classroom clock lost eleven minutes between Monday and Friday. The clock hangs directly above the radiator, which ran all week. Mr. Ellis moved a second clock to the same spot on Tuesday. By Friday that one had lost nine minutes too. The paper tag inside says the clock is rated for cool rooms only. Both clocks take the same batteries from the same drawer, bought last spring. A cold battery and a hot battery both push less current than a fresh one. The second hand on each clock jerks twice before it moves on.
debate.question: Why did the clock lose time? Choose one cause and quote the story.

suspects.why: hung over a radiator that ran all week, and rated for cool rooms
the same drawer batteries, bought last spring, in both clocks
a second hand that jerks twice before it moves on

evidence: “The clock hangs directly above the radiator, which ran all week.”
“The paper tag inside says the clock is rated for cool rooms only.”
arguments.against: “Both clocks take the same batteries from the same drawer, bought last spring.”

evidence: “Both clocks take the same batteries from the same drawer, bought last spring.”
“A cold battery and a hot battery both push less current than a fresh one.”
arguments.against: “Mr. Ellis moved a second clock to the same spot on Tuesday.”

evidence: “The second hand on each clock jerks twice before it moves on.”
“By Friday that one had lost nine minutes too.”
arguments.against: “The paper tag inside says the clock is rated for cool rooms only.”

debate.note: The second clock is the experiment and it is a good one, but it shares a battery drawer with the first, so it tests the place and the batteries at the same time. That is the flaw to find. Ask what the test would have to look like to separate them, and the class will design a better one than the story did.

cases.title: The Case of the Lopsided Snowman
cases.story: The class built a snowman on Monday with three even balls. By Thursday the bottom ball had slumped to one side. Nobody had pushed it, because the yard was roped off. The snowman stands on the south side of the building. The sun hits that wall from noon until three. The shaded side of the bottom ball is still round. A puddle had frozen on the sunny side each night and melted again each day. The shaded side never dripped at all.
cases.question: Why did the snowman slump to one side?

suspects.why: the sun hits that wall from noon until three
the yard was roped off
it was built with three even balls

cases.answer: The sun melted the sunny side of the bottom ball.
proof: “The sun hits that wall from noon until three.”
“The shaded side of the bottom ball is still round.”
clears: Pushing: “the yard was roped off.”
Bad packing: “with three even balls.”
cases.explain: The shaded side is still round. Because the sun hits that wall from noon until three, only the sunny side melted and the snowman leaned.

debate.story: The class rolled three balls for a snowman on Monday and stacked them even. By Thursday the bottom ball had slumped to one side. The snowman stands on the south side of the building. The sun hits that wall from noon until three. A puddle froze on the sunny side each night and melted again each day. The shaded side never dripped at all. The rope around the yard was down on Tuesday for the gritting truck. Fresh boot prints circle the snowman on the slumped side. The bottom ball was rolled last, when the snow had gone sticky and wet.
debate.question: Why did the snowman slump? Pick one cause and prove it.

suspects.why: a south wall in sun from noon, with a side that melts and refreezes
a rope down on Tuesday, and fresh boot prints on the slumped side
a bottom ball rolled last, when the snow had gone sticky and wet

evidence: “The sun hits that wall from noon until three.”
“A puddle froze on the sunny side each night and melted again each day.”
arguments.against: “Fresh boot prints circle the snowman on the slumped side.”

evidence: “The rope around the yard was down on Tuesday for the gritting truck.”
“Fresh boot prints circle the snowman on the slumped side.”
arguments.against: “The shaded side never dripped at all.”

evidence: “The bottom ball was rolled last, when the snow had gone sticky and wet.”
“By Thursday the bottom ball had slumped to one side.”
arguments.against: “The sun hits that wall from noon until three.”

debate.note: The boot prints are on the slumped side, and so is the sun, so the case has put two suspects in the same place on purpose. The shaded side is the fact that does the most work: it never dripped and it never slumped, and nobody walked there either. Make the class say which of those two facts they are leaning on.

cases.title: The Case of the Empty Feeder
cases.story: The bird feeder emptied in two days instead of two weeks. The seed was the same mix the class always buys. No seed lay on the ground beneath it. The feeder hangs from a branch two feet from the trunk. Scratches run down the pole and along the branch above the feeder. A squirrel can jump four feet from a standing start. The class moved the feeder six feet out, away from every branch, and it lasted twelve days.
cases.question: What emptied the feeder?

suspects.why: scratches on the branch, and it can jump four feet
no seed lay on the ground beneath it
the same mix the class always buys

cases.answer: A squirrel reached the feeder from the branch.
proof: “Scratches run down the pole and along the branch above the feeder.”
“A squirrel can jump four feet from a standing start.”
clears: A leak: “No seed lay on the ground beneath it.”
Bad seed: “The seed was the same mix the class always buys.”
cases.explain: Moving the feeder six feet out made it last twelve days. Because a squirrel can jump four feet and left scratches on the branch above, it was reaching the feeder from the tree.

debate.story: The bird feeder emptied in two days instead of two weeks. The feeder hangs from a branch two feet from the trunk. Scratches run down the pole and along the branch above the feeder. A squirrel can jump four feet from a standing start. The base of the feeder has a crack where the two halves meet. A thin trail of seed runs from under the feeder into the long grass. The class switched to a finer mix in October that pours faster. Nobody has looked at the feeder between four o'clock and morning.
debate.question: Why did the feeder empty so fast? Argue for one cause.

suspects.why: scratches on the branch, and a jump of four feet
a crack where the two halves meet, and a seed trail into the grass
a finer mix since October that pours faster

evidence: “Scratches run down the pole and along the branch above the feeder.”
“A squirrel can jump four feet from a standing start.”
arguments.against: “The base of the feeder has a crack where the two halves meet.”

evidence: “The base of the feeder has a crack where the two halves meet.”
“A thin trail of seed runs from under the feeder into the long grass.”
arguments.against: “Scratches run down the pole and along the branch above the feeder.”

evidence: “The class switched to a finer mix in October that pours faster.”
“Nobody has looked at the feeder between four o'clock and morning.”
arguments.against: “The bird feeder emptied in two days instead of two weeks.”

debate.note: The seed trail is the piece that changes everything, because the old story said no seed lay on the ground. Now some does. Ask how much a crack can spill in two days against what a squirrel can carry, and whether a finer mix would run through a crack faster than a coarse one. Two of these answers may be one answer.

cases.title: The Case of the Gritty Cocoa
cases.story: The cocoa at the winter party was gritty at the bottom of every cup. The mix was fresh. The milk was cold from the fridge. The recipe says to stir the powder into a little hot milk first. Room 8 poured all the cold milk in at once and stirred twice. Room 9 followed the recipe and had no grit. Cocoa powder does not dissolve in cold liquid. A spoonful of the leftover grit dissolved at once in hot water.
cases.question: Why was the cocoa gritty?

suspects.why: powder does not dissolve in cold liquid
the mix was fresh
a spoonful dissolved at once in hot water

cases.answer: The cold milk left the cocoa powder undissolved.
proof: “Room 8 poured all the cold milk in at once and stirred twice.”
“Cocoa powder does not dissolve in cold liquid.”
clears: Old mix: “The mix was fresh.”
The grit: “A spoonful of the leftover grit dissolved at once in hot water.”
cases.explain: Room 9 followed the recipe and had no grit. Because Room 8 poured cold milk in all at once, and cocoa powder does not dissolve in cold liquid, the powder sank to the bottom.

debate.story: The cocoa at the winter party was gritty at the bottom of every cup. The recipe says to stir the powder into a little hot milk first. Room 8 poured all the cold milk in at once and stirred twice. Cocoa powder does not dissolve in cold liquid. Room 9 followed the recipe and had grit in four of its twenty cups. The tin Room 8 used had been open on the shelf since last winter. Damp powder goes lumpy and the lumps do not break up. Nobody sieved the powder in either room.
debate.question: Why was the cocoa gritty? Choose one cause and back it from the text.

suspects.why: cold milk poured in at once, and powder that will not dissolve cold
a tin open since last winter, going lumpy with damp
nobody sieving in either room, and grit in Room 9 too

evidence: “Room 8 poured all the cold milk in at once and stirred twice.”
“Cocoa powder does not dissolve in cold liquid.”
arguments.against: “Room 9 followed the recipe and had grit in four of its twenty cups.”

evidence: “The tin Room 8 used had been open on the shelf since last winter.”
“Damp powder goes lumpy and the lumps do not break up.”
arguments.against: “The recipe says to stir the powder into a little hot milk first.”

evidence: “Nobody sieved the powder in either room.”
“Room 9 followed the recipe and had grit in four of its twenty cups.”
arguments.against: “Cocoa powder does not dissolve in cold liquid.”

debate.note: Room 9 is the control and it has stopped being clean: four of its twenty cups were gritty too. That means the method cannot be the whole answer. Get the class to compare every cup in Room 8 against four in twenty, and to notice that two things can both be true and one can still be bigger.

cases.title: The Case of the Torn Valentines
cases.story: Twenty valentines went into the class mailbox and came out with torn corners. The mailbox is a cardboard box with a slot cut in the lid. The slot is three inches wide. Most of the envelopes are four inches across. Jamal pushed his through and the corner caught on the cardboard. Ms. Reyes had taped the slot edges, but the tape had peeled back. Every tear is on a corner, and all the tears face the same way.
cases.question: What tore the valentines?

suspects.why: the slot is three inches, the envelopes are four
all the tears face the same way
every tear is on a corner

cases.answer: The narrow slot tore the corners off the envelopes.
proof: “The slot is three inches wide.”
“Jamal pushed his through and the corner caught on the cardboard.”
clears: A student: “all the tears face the same way.”
A mouse: “Every tear is on a corner”
cases.explain: All the tears are on corners and face the same way, which a hand or a mouse would not do. Because the slot is three inches wide and the envelopes are four inches across, every corner caught.

debate.story: Twenty valentines went into the class mailbox and came out with torn corners. The mailbox is a cardboard box with a slot cut in the lid. The slot is three inches wide and most of the envelopes are four inches across. Jamal pushed his through and the corner caught on the cardboard. Ms. Reyes had taped the slot edges, but the tape had peeled back. The box was carried down two flights of stairs and dropped once. Each tear is at a corner, and every one of them points the same way. A gnawed hole the size of a thumb sits low on the back of the box.
debate.question: What tore the valentines? Pick one cause and prove it.

suspects.why: a three-inch slot for four-inch envelopes, with the tape peeled back
carried down two flights and dropped once
a gnawed hole the size of a thumb, low on the back

evidence: “The slot is three inches wide and most of the envelopes are four inches across.”
“Jamal pushed his through and the corner caught on the cardboard.”
arguments.against: “A gnawed hole the size of a thumb sits low on the back of the box.”

evidence: “The box was carried down two flights of stairs and dropped once.”
“Ms. Reyes had taped the slot edges, but the tape had peeled back.”
arguments.against: “Each tear is at a corner, and every one of them points the same way.”

evidence: “A gnawed hole the size of a thumb sits low on the back of the box.”
“Twenty valentines went into the class mailbox and came out with torn corners.”
arguments.against: “The slot is three inches wide and most of the envelopes are four inches across.”

debate.note: All the tears facing the same way is the fact that should decide this, and it is the one students walk past. Something that happens the same way twenty times in a row is a shape, not an accident. Ask what a mouse would leave and what a drop would leave, and whether either of them repeats exactly.

cases.title: The Case of the Quiet Volcano
cases.story: The science fair volcano fizzed at home and did nothing on stage. Mia used the same baking soda from the same box. The vinegar bottle on stage had been open since the last fair. Vinegar loses its strength once the bottle stays open. A fresh bottle made the model erupt over the table. The model itself had no cracks and the crater was clear. Mia poured the same amount both times. She measured it with the same cup.
cases.question: Why did the volcano not erupt on stage?

suspects.why: the bottle had been open since the last fair
the same box she used at home
no cracks and the crater was clear

cases.answer: The old vinegar had lost its strength.
proof: “The vinegar bottle on stage had been open since the last fair.”
“Vinegar loses its strength once the bottle stays open.”
clears: The baking soda: “Mia used the same baking soda from the same box.”
The model: “The model itself had no cracks and the crater was clear.”
cases.explain: A fresh bottle made the model erupt over the table. Because the stage bottle had been open since the last fair, the vinegar had lost its strength.

debate.story: The science fair volcano fizzed at home and did nothing on stage. The vinegar bottle on stage had been open since the last fair. Vinegar loses its strength once the bottle stays open. A fresh bottle made the model erupt over the table. The stage hall was eleven degrees colder than Mia's kitchen. A cold mixture reacts more slowly than a warm one. The baking soda box on stage had been left open beside a kettle. Damp baking soda gives off its gas early and has less left to give.
debate.question: Why did the volcano do nothing on stage? Make the case for one cause.

suspects.why: a bottle open since the last fair, and a fresh one that erupted
a hall eleven degrees colder than the kitchen
a box left open beside a kettle, giving its gas off early

evidence: “The vinegar bottle on stage had been open since the last fair.”
“A fresh bottle made the model erupt over the table.”
arguments.against: “The baking soda box on stage had been left open beside a kettle.”

evidence: “The stage hall was eleven degrees colder than Mia's kitchen.”
“A cold mixture reacts more slowly than a warm one.”
arguments.against: “A fresh bottle made the model erupt over the table.”

evidence: “The baking soda box on stage had been left open beside a kettle.”
“Damp baking soda gives off its gas early and has less left to give.”
arguments.against: “The science fair volcano fizzed at home and did nothing on stage.”

debate.note: The fresh bottle is nearly an experiment: same stage, same cold, same box, new vinegar, and it worked. That single sentence beats the cold hall and most of the baking soda argument. A student who finds it and says why it beats the others has done the whole job, whichever suspect they name.

cases.title: The Case of the Crooked Crown
cases.story: The paper crown for the play sat straight at dress rehearsal and tipped on opening night. Nobody had bent it, because it was kept flat in a box. The crown is held on with two bobby pins. On opening night Eli wore it over his costume wig. The wig is an inch thicker than his own hair. The pins no longer reached his hair at all. The crown sat on top of the wig instead of down in his hair.
cases.question: Why did the crown tip on opening night?

suspects.why: an inch thicker, so the pins no longer reached his hair
it was kept flat in a box
it is held on with two bobby pins

cases.answer: The wig held the crown too high for the pins to reach hair.
proof: “The wig is an inch thicker than his own hair.”
“The pins no longer reached his hair at all.”
clears: Bending: “it was kept flat in a box.”
Missing pins: “The crown is held on with two bobby pins.”
cases.explain: The crown sat straight at dress rehearsal, when Eli wore no wig. Because the wig is an inch thicker than his hair, the two pins could not reach hair and the crown tipped.

debate.story: The paper crown for the play sat straight at dress rehearsal and tipped on opening night. Two bobby pins are all that hold the crown on. On opening night Eli wore it over his costume wig. The wig is an inch thicker than his own hair. The pins no longer reached his hair at all. One pin was found bent flat in the costume box after the show. The crown was stored under three other hats and came out with a soft dent in the band. A dented band sits unevenly however it is pinned.
debate.question: Why did the crown tip? Choose one cause and quote the story.

suspects.why: a wig an inch thicker, so the pins reached no hair
one pin found bent flat in the costume box
a soft dent in the band from being stored under three hats

evidence: “The wig is an inch thicker than his own hair.”
“The pins no longer reached his hair at all.”
arguments.against: “One pin was found bent flat in the costume box after the show.”

evidence: “One pin was found bent flat in the costume box after the show.”
“Two bobby pins are all that hold the crown on.”
arguments.against: “On opening night Eli wore it over his costume wig.”

evidence: “The crown was stored under three other hats and came out with a soft dent in the band.”
“A dented band sits unevenly however it is pinned.”
arguments.against: “The paper crown for the play sat straight at dress rehearsal and tipped on opening night.”

debate.note: Two bobby pins used to clear the pins and now one of them is bent flat, which could be a cause or could be what a tipping crown does to a pin. The class should notice they cannot tell which. The wig is the only thing that changed between the two nights, and that is the argument to beat.

cases.title: The Case of the Silent Pedal
cases.story: The music room piano held its notes all year and stopped on Monday. The keys all sound. The damper pedal goes down and springs back up. Mr. Okafor looked underneath and found the pedal rod resting beside its slot instead of inside it. The piano had been rolled across the room on Friday for the concert. Nothing was dropped and nobody forced the pedal. A rod can shake loose when a piano is moved. He set the rod back in its slot and the notes held again.
cases.question: Why did the piano stop holding its notes?

suspects.why: found resting beside its slot, and the piano was moved
nothing was dropped and nobody forced the pedal
the keys all sound

cases.answer: The pedal rod had shaken loose out of its slot.
proof: “Mr. Okafor looked underneath and found the pedal rod resting beside its slot instead of inside it.”
“A rod can shake loose when a piano is moved.”
clears: Dropping: “Nothing was dropped and nobody forced the pedal.”
A broken key: “The keys all sound.”
cases.explain: He set the rod back in its slot and the notes held again. Because the piano was rolled across the room on Friday, the rod had shaken out of its slot.

debate.story: The music room piano held its notes all year and stopped on Monday. Mr. Okafor looked underneath and found the pedal rod resting beside its slot. The piano was rolled across the room on Friday for the concert. A rod can shake loose when a piano is moved. A music stand fell against the pedal during the concert and nobody picked it up until after. Three keys in the middle sound thin and will not ring on. The felt on the dampers is worn down to the cloth on those three. Nothing was written in the room log all week.
debate.question: Why did the piano stop holding its notes? Pick one cause and prove it.

suspects.why: found resting beside its slot after the piano was rolled
a music stand that fell against the pedal during the concert
three middle keys sounding thin, with felt worn to the cloth

evidence: “Mr. Okafor looked underneath and found the pedal rod resting beside its slot.”
“A rod can shake loose when a piano is moved.”
arguments.against: “A music stand fell against the pedal during the concert and nobody picked it up until after.”

evidence: “A music stand fell against the pedal during the concert and nobody picked it up until after.”
“The piano was rolled across the room on Friday for the concert.”
arguments.against: “A rod can shake loose when a piano is moved.”

evidence: “Three keys in the middle sound thin and will not ring on.”
“The felt on the dampers is worn down to the cloth on those three.”
arguments.against: “The music room piano held its notes all year and stopped on Monday.”

debate.note: The rod is out of its slot and that is a fact, but nothing in the story says what knocked it out, and two candidates happened on the same Friday. Worn felt is the odd one, because it takes years and the problem arrived on Monday. A student who argues the felt has to explain the date, and a student who ignores the date has not argued at all.

cases.title: The Case of the Diving Kite
cases.story: Maya's kite flew well in March and dove straight down in April. The sail has no tears and the strings are even. She flew it from the same field both times. In April she had tied on a shorter tail to make it look neater. A kite's tail keeps the nose pointed up into the wind. Her friend's kite, with its full tail, flew fine beside hers. Maya tied the long tail back on and the kite climbed.
cases.question: Why did the kite dive?

suspects.why: a tail holds the nose up, and a full tail flew fine beside it
the sail has no tears
she flew it from the same field both times

cases.answer: The shorter tail let the kite's nose drop.
proof: “In April she had tied on a shorter tail to make it look neater.”
“A kite's tail keeps the nose pointed up into the wind.”
clears: A torn sail: “The sail has no tears and the strings are even.”
The field: “She flew it from the same field both times.”
cases.explain: Maya tied the long tail back on and the kite climbed. Because the shorter tail could not hold the nose up into the wind, the kite dove.

debate.story: Maya's kite flew well in March and dove straight down in April. In April she tied on a shorter tail to make it look neater. A kite's tail keeps the nose pointed up into the wind. Her friend's kite, with its full tail, flew fine beside hers. The March flight was on the open field and the April one was behind the sports hall. Wind coming over a building breaks up into gusts that drop a kite. One of Maya's bridle strings has a knot that slipped an inch. An uneven bridle tips the kite before the wind even takes it.
debate.question: Why did the kite dive? Make the case for one cause.

suspects.why: a shorter tail, where a tail keeps the nose up
flown behind the sports hall, where wind breaks into gusts
a bridle knot slipped an inch, tipping the kite

evidence: “In April she tied on a shorter tail to make it look neater.”
“A kite's tail keeps the nose pointed up into the wind.”
arguments.against: “The March flight was on the open field and the April one was behind the sports hall.”

evidence: “The March flight was on the open field and the April one was behind the sports hall.”
“Wind coming over a building breaks up into gusts that drop a kite.”
arguments.against: “Her friend's kite, with its full tail, flew fine beside hers.”

evidence: “One of Maya's bridle strings has a knot that slipped an inch.”
“An uneven bridle tips the kite before the wind even takes it.”
arguments.against: “Maya's kite flew well in March and dove straight down in April.”

debate.note: The friend's kite is the best evidence in the story because it flew in the same April wind in the same place. That beats the building and leaves the tail and the bridle, both of which are on Maya's kite and not on her friend's. Ask which of the two changed in April, because only one of them did.

cases.title: The Case of the Wilted Shamrocks
cases.story: Room 9 grew shamrocks on two windowsills from the same packet of seed. The south window plants are pale and drooping. The north window plants are green. Both pots were watered on the same days with the same cup. The south sill sits above the heater vent, which has run since February. A thermometer on the south sill reads eighty-four degrees. The packet says shamrocks want a cool room. The soil in the south pot was dry an hour after watering.
cases.question: Why are the south window shamrocks wilting?

suspects.why: the sill reads eighty-four, and the packet wants a cool room
both pots were watered on the same days with the same cup
both came from the same packet

cases.answer: Heat from the vent dried the south pot out.
proof: “A thermometer on the south sill reads eighty-four degrees.”
“The packet says shamrocks want a cool room.”
clears: Water: “Both pots were watered on the same days with the same cup.”
Bad seed: “from the same packet of seed.”
