cases.explain: The north window plants are green on the same water and the same seed. Because the south sill sits above the heater vent and reads eighty-four degrees, that soil was dry an hour after watering.

debate.story: Room 9 grew shamrocks on two windowsills, sowing one packet across both. The south window plants are pale and drooping. The north window plants are green. The south sill sits above the heater vent, which has run since February. A thermometer on the south sill reads eighty-four degrees. The packet says shamrocks want a cool room. The soil in the south pot was dry an hour after watering. The south pot is a thin plastic one and the north pot is clay. The south window gets six hours of direct sun and the north window gets none.
debate.question: Why are the south plants drooping? Choose one cause and quote the story.

suspects.why: a sill at eighty-four degrees, over a vent, for a plant wanting cool
six hours of direct sun against none at the north window
a thin plastic pot that was dry an hour after watering

evidence: “The south sill sits above the heater vent, which has run since February.”
“A thermometer on the south sill reads eighty-four degrees.”
arguments.against: “The south window gets six hours of direct sun and the north window gets none.”

evidence: “The south window gets six hours of direct sun and the north window gets none.”
“The packet says shamrocks want a cool room.”
arguments.against: “The south sill sits above the heater vent, which has run since February.”

evidence: “The south pot is a thin plastic one and the north pot is clay.”
“The soil in the south pot was dry an hour after watering.”
arguments.against: “The north window plants are green.”

debate.note: Every difference in this story is on the south side, so pointing at the south side is not an answer by itself. The thermometer is the only number and it covers the vent and the sun together. The dry soil is the fact worth chasing: it tells you the plants were thirsty, and it does not tell you why.

cases.title: The Case of the Hallway Puddle
cases.story: A puddle appears outside the art room every Tuesday and never on other days. The roof above it was replaced in August and does not leak. The drinking fountain is forty feet away and dry. On Tuesdays the kiln runs all morning in the room next door. A kiln pushes damp air out through a vent above the art room door. The puddle sits directly under that vent. Mr. Shaw taped a paper towel to the vent and it was soaked by noon.
cases.question: Where is the puddle coming from?

suspects.why: the kiln runs Tuesdays and the puddle sits under the vent
the roof was replaced and does not leak
forty feet away and dry

cases.answer: Damp air from the kiln vent drips onto the floor.
proof: “A kiln pushes damp air out through a vent above the art room door.”
“The puddle sits directly under that vent.”
clears: A roof leak: “The roof above it was replaced in August and does not leak.”
The fountain: “The drinking fountain is forty feet away and dry.”
cases.explain: A paper towel taped to the vent was soaked by noon. Because the kiln runs on Tuesdays and pushes damp air through that vent, the puddle shows up under it on Tuesdays only.

debate.story: A puddle appears outside the art room every Tuesday and never on other days. On Tuesdays the kiln runs all morning in the room next door. A kiln pushes damp air out through a vent above the art room door. The puddle sits directly under that vent. Mr. Shaw taped a paper towel to the vent and it was soaked by noon. The floor is mopped every Tuesday morning by the early cleaner. A mop leaves water in a low spot, and that corner is the lowest in the hall. The drinking fountain was fixed in September and now runs on Tuesdays and Thursdays only.
debate.question: Where does the Tuesday puddle come from? Argue for one cause.

suspects.why: a kiln that runs Tuesdays, venting over the door above the puddle
a mop every Tuesday morning, and the lowest corner in the hall
a fountain running Tuesdays and Thursdays since September

evidence: “A kiln pushes damp air out through a vent above the art room door.”
“Mr. Shaw taped a paper towel to the vent and it was soaked by noon.”
arguments.against: “The floor is mopped every Tuesday morning by the early cleaner.”

evidence: “The floor is mopped every Tuesday morning by the early cleaner.”
“A mop leaves water in a low spot, and that corner is the lowest in the hall.”
arguments.against: “The puddle sits directly under that vent.”

evidence: “The drinking fountain was fixed in September and now runs on Tuesdays and Thursdays only.”
“A puddle appears outside the art room every Tuesday and never on other days.”
arguments.against: “Mr. Shaw taped a paper towel to the vent and it was soaked by noon.”

debate.note: The fountain argument fails on a day of the week and the class should find it: the fountain runs Thursdays too, and there is never a Thursday puddle. That is a clean piece of reasoning from a single word. The mop and the kiln both happen on Tuesday mornings and the story will not separate them.

cases.title: The Case of the Headless Sunflowers
cases.story: The school garden grew twelve sunflowers and nine lost their heads overnight. The stalks are cut clean at an angle, not torn. The fence is four feet high and has no gaps. Deer tracks run along the outside of the fence and stop there. A deer can reach over a four-foot fence without jumping it. The three sunflowers that kept their heads grew in the middle of the bed. The nine that lost them all stood within arm's reach of the fence.
cases.question: What took the sunflower heads?

suspects.who: 🦌 A deer reaching over the fence
suspects.why: tracks outside the fence, and only the near flowers lost heads
the stalks are cut clean at an angle, not torn
the fence has no gaps

cases.answer: A deer reached over the fence and took them.
proof: “Deer tracks run along the outside of the fence and stop there.”
“A deer can reach over a four-foot fence without jumping it.”
clears: Insects: “The stalks are cut clean at an angle, not torn.”
Something getting through: “The fence is four feet high and has no gaps.”
cases.explain: The nine that lost their heads all stood within arm's reach of the fence, and the three in the middle kept theirs. Because the deer tracks stop at the outside of the fence and a deer can reach over four feet, it never had to come in.

debate.story: The school garden grew twelve sunflowers and nine lost their heads overnight. Each stalk ends in a clean angled cut rather than a tear. Deer tracks run along the outside of the fence and stop there. A deer can reach over a four-foot fence without jumping it. The nine that lost their heads all stood within arm's reach of the fence. The gate was found unlatched on the morning the heads went. A pair of garden shears was left out on the bed all week. Shears cut a stalk clean at an angle, which is also how a deer's teeth leave one.
debate.question: What took the sunflower heads? Pick one and prove it from the story.

suspects.who: 🦌 A deer reaching over the fence
suspects.why: tracks outside the fence, and only the flowers within reach lost heads
a gate found unlatched on the morning the heads went
shears left out all week, which cut clean at an angle

evidence: “Deer tracks run along the outside of the fence and stop there.”
“The nine that lost their heads all stood within arm's reach of the fence.”
arguments.against: “The gate was found unlatched on the morning the heads went.”

evidence: “The gate was found unlatched on the morning the heads went.”
“A deer can reach over a four-foot fence without jumping it.”
arguments.against: “The nine that lost their heads all stood within arm's reach of the fence.”

evidence: “A pair of garden shears was left out on the bed all week.”
“Shears cut a stalk clean at an angle, which is also how a deer's teeth leave one.”
arguments.against: “Deer tracks run along the outside of the fence and stop there.”

debate.note: The clean angled cut used to rule out everything but a deer, and the story now says shears leave the same cut. Once a clue fits two suspects it stops choosing between them. What still chooses is which flowers were taken: nine within reach of the fence and three in the middle untouched. Anything that got through the gate could have reached all twelve.

cases.title: The Case of the Cold Nest
cases.story: A robin built a nest on the school ledge and sat on four eggs for nine days. On the tenth morning the robin was gone and the four eggs were cold. No shells lay on the ground and the nest was undamaged. The ledge is beside the gym door, which was propped open all week for painting. Workers walked past the nest about thirty times a day. Robins will abandon a nest that is disturbed too often. The week had been mild, with no night below fifty degrees.
cases.question: Why did the robin leave the nest?

suspects.why: workers passed thirty times a day, and robins abandon disturbed nests
no shells on the ground and the nest was undamaged
no night below fifty degrees

cases.answer: The robin abandoned the nest because people kept passing it.
proof: “Workers walked past the nest about thirty times a day.”
“Robins will abandon a nest that is disturbed too often.”
clears: A predator: “No shells lay on the ground and the nest was undamaged.”
Cold weather: “The week had been mild, with no night below fifty degrees.”
cases.explain: The eggs were still in the nest and nothing was broken, so nothing ate them. Because the gym door was propped open and workers passed about thirty times a day, the robin abandoned the nest.

debate.story: A robin built a nest on the school ledge and sat on four eggs for nine days. On the tenth morning the robin was gone and the four eggs were cold. The ledge is beside the gym door, which was propped open all week for painting. Workers walked past the nest about thirty times a day. Robins will abandon a nest that is disturbed too often. A magpie has been seen on the gym roof every morning since Monday. One egg is cracked along the side and still in the nest. The week had two nights at thirty-eight degrees, colder than the forecast said.
debate.question: Why did the robin leave the nest? Choose one cause and back it up.

suspects.why: a propped door and thirty passes a day, which robins abandon a nest for
a magpie on the gym roof every morning, and one egg cracked
two nights at thirty-eight degrees, colder than forecast

evidence: “The ledge is beside the gym door, which was propped open all week for painting.”
“Workers walked past the nest about thirty times a day.”
arguments.against: “A magpie has been seen on the gym roof every morning since Monday.”

evidence: “A magpie has been seen on the gym roof every morning since Monday.”
“One egg is cracked along the side and still in the nest.”
arguments.against: “Robins will abandon a nest that is disturbed too often.”

evidence: “The week had two nights at thirty-eight degrees, colder than the forecast said.”
“On the tenth morning the robin was gone and the four eggs were cold.”
arguments.against: “A robin built a nest on the school ledge and sat on four eggs for nine days.”

debate.note: A sitting robin keeps her own eggs warm, so cold nights explain cold eggs only after she has gone. That is a cause and effect to untangle out loud. The cracked egg is the hardest fact: it points at the magpie, and a bird that left in a hurry could have done it herself.

cases.title: The Case of the Litter by the Gate
cases.story: The playground is clean except for one corner by the back gate. Wrappers pile up there every week. The nearest trash can sits by the basketball court, ninety feet away. The wind on this field blows steadily from the west. The back gate corner is the east fence line. Ms. Diaz emptied the corner on Monday and it had refilled by Friday without anyone eating there. Wind carries loose wrappers until a fence stops them. Nothing else on the playground catches them first.
cases.question: Why does litter collect in that one corner?

suspects.why: the wind blows from the west and the corner is the east fence line
it refilled without anyone eating there
the nearest can sits ninety feet away

cases.answer: The wind blows loose wrappers against the east fence.
proof: “The wind on this field blows steadily from the west.”
“Wind carries loose wrappers until a fence stops them.”
clears: Eating there: “it had refilled by Friday without anyone eating there.”
The trash can: “The nearest trash can sits by the basketball court, ninety feet away.”
cases.explain: The corner refilled in a week with nobody eating there. Because the wind blows steadily from the west and the back gate corner is the east fence line, wrappers travel across the field and stop at that fence.

debate.story: The playground is clean except for one corner by the back gate. Wrappers pile up there every week. The wind on this field blows steadily from the west. The back gate corner is the east fence line. Wind carries loose wrappers until a fence stops them. The back gate is where the bus queue forms at half past three. The only bin on this side is ninety feet away by the basketball court. Ms. Diaz emptied the corner on Monday and it had refilled by Friday. The corner is the only part of the playground a duty teacher cannot see.
debate.question: Why does litter pile in that corner? Make the case for one cause.

suspects.why: a west wind and an east fence line that stops what it carries
where the bus queue forms, and the one corner no duty teacher sees
a nearest bin ninety feet away

evidence: “The wind on this field blows steadily from the west.”
“Wind carries loose wrappers until a fence stops them.”
arguments.against: “The back gate is where the bus queue forms at half past three.”

evidence: “The back gate is where the bus queue forms at half past three.”
“The corner is the only part of the playground a duty teacher cannot see.”
arguments.against: “The back gate corner is the east fence line.”

evidence: “The only bin on this side is ninety feet away by the basketball court.”
“Ms. Diaz emptied the corner on Monday and it had refilled by Friday.”
arguments.against: “Wind carries loose wrappers until a fence stops them.”

debate.note: The corner is now the windward fence line, the bus queue and the blind spot all at once, which is how real litter corners work. Ask the class for a test rather than a winner. Emptying it on a still weekend, or standing a duty teacher there for a week, would each rule out one suspect and cost nothing.

cases.title: The Case of the Dark Photographs
cases.story: The fourth grade took ninety photographs at the aquarium and eighty came out black. The ten that worked were all taken in the lobby. The camera battery was full. The lens was clean. A sign at the tank room door asks visitors to turn the flash off. Dev had turned the flash off as the sign asked. The tank rooms are lit only by the tanks themselves. A camera needs either light in the room or a flash.
cases.question: Why did eighty photographs come out black?

suspects.who: 🌑 No room light and no flash
suspects.why: the tank rooms are lit only by the tanks, and the flash was off
the camera battery was full
the lens was clean

cases.answer: The tank rooms were too dark once the flash was turned off.
proof: “The tank rooms are lit only by the tanks themselves.”
“A camera needs either light in the room or a flash.”
clears: The battery: “The camera battery was full.”
A dirty lens: “The lens was clean.”
cases.explain: The ten photographs that worked were all taken in the lobby, where there is room light. Because the tank rooms are lit only by the tanks and Dev had turned the flash off as the sign asked, the camera had no light to use.

debate.story: The fourth grade took ninety photographs at the aquarium and eighty came out black. The ten that worked were all taken in the lobby. A sign at the tank room door asks visitors to turn the flash off. Dev had turned the flash off as the sign asked. The tank rooms are lit only by the tanks themselves. A camera needs either light in the room or a flash. The battery warning blinked twice on the way in and nobody read it. A camera that is low on power stops firing the sensor before it stops showing a picture. The lens had a thumbprint across one half from the bus.
debate.question: Why did eighty photographs come out black? Pick one cause and prove it.

suspects.who: 🌑 No room light and no flash
suspects.why: no flash and rooms lit only by the tanks
a battery warning that blinked twice on the way in
a thumbprint across half the lens from the bus

evidence: “The tank rooms are lit only by the tanks themselves.”
“A camera needs either light in the room or a flash.”
arguments.against: “The battery warning blinked twice on the way in and nobody read it.”

evidence: “The battery warning blinked twice on the way in and nobody read it.”
“A camera that is low on power stops firing the sensor before it stops showing a picture.”
arguments.against: “The ten that worked were all taken in the lobby.”

evidence: “The lens had a thumbprint across one half from the bus.”
“Dev had turned the flash off as the sign asked.”
arguments.against: “The fourth grade took ninety photographs at the aquarium and eighty came out black.”

debate.note: The ten that worked are the control and they were all in the lobby, which is the bright room. That fits the light answer and works against the battery, because a flat battery does not care which room you stand in. The thumbprint would blur half a picture rather than blacken a whole one, and a student who says so is reasoning from what each cause would look like.

cases.title: The Case of the Leaning Bean
cases.story: Two bean plants grew in identical cups on the same shelf. One stands straight and one leans hard to the left. Both got the same water and the same soil. The straight plant sits under the ceiling light. The leaning plant sits two feet to the right of the window. Plants grow toward the strongest light they can reach. The leaning plant points directly at the window. Ms. Reed turned its cup around and in four days it had leaned the other way.
cases.question: Why does one bean plant lean?

suspects.why: it points at the window, and plants grow toward light
both got the same water and the same soil
turning the cup made it lean the other way instead

cases.answer: The plant leans toward the light from the window.
proof: “Plants grow toward the strongest light they can reach.”
“The leaning plant points directly at the window.”
clears: Water and soil: “Both got the same water and the same soil.”
A weak stem: “Ms. Reed turned its cup around and in four days it had leaned the other way.”
cases.explain: Turning the cup made the plant lean the other way within four days. Because plants grow toward the strongest light and this one points directly at the window, the window is what it is reaching for.

debate.story: Two bean plants grew in identical cups on the same shelf. One stands straight and one leans hard to the left. The leaning plant sits two feet to the right of the window. Plants grow toward the strongest light they can reach. The leaning plant points directly at the window. The straight plant sits under the ceiling light, which is on all day. The leaning plant's stem is thinner than the other's and bends at a touch. The shelf tilts about a finger's width down toward the window end.
debate.question: Why does one bean plant lean? Argue for one cause.

suspects.why: two feet from the window, and pointing directly at it
a thinner stem that bends at a touch
a shelf tilting a finger's width toward the window end

evidence: “The leaning plant points directly at the window.”
“Plants grow toward the strongest light they can reach.”
arguments.against: “The shelf tilts about a finger's width down toward the window end.”

evidence: “The leaning plant's stem is thinner than the other's and bends at a touch.”
“The straight plant sits under the ceiling light, which is on all day.”
arguments.against: “The leaning plant points directly at the window.”

evidence: “The shelf tilts about a finger's width down toward the window end.”
“Two bean plants grew in identical cups on the same shelf.”
arguments.against: “Plants grow toward the strongest light they can reach.”

debate.note: The tilt and the window are in the same direction, which the story does on purpose. The experiment that settled the old case is gone, so ask the class to invent it: turn the cup, or shim the shelf level, and see which way the plant goes next. One of those tests separates the three in four days.

cases.title: The Case of the Soupy Ice Cream
cases.story: The fifth grade sold ice cream at the spring fair and the last twenty cups were soup. The freezer was plugged in. Its light came on. A thermometer inside read twenty-two degrees, which is above freezing for ice cream. The lid had been propped open with a scoop since noon so servers could work faster. Warm air pours into a freezer whenever the lid is open. The first hundred cups, served before noon, were solid. Nothing about the recipe had changed that day.
cases.question: Why did the last cups melt?

suspects.why: propped open with a scoop since noon, and warm air pours in
it was plugged in and its light came on
the first hundred cups were solid

cases.answer: The propped lid let warm air into the freezer.
proof: “The lid had been propped open with a scoop since noon so servers could work faster.”
“Warm air pours into a freezer whenever the lid is open.”
clears: The freezer being off: “The freezer was plugged in.”
Bad ice cream: “The first hundred cups, served before noon, were solid.”
cases.explain: The first hundred cups, served before noon, were solid. Because the lid was propped open with a scoop from noon onward, warm air poured in and the thermometer read twenty-two degrees.

debate.story: The fifth grade sold ice cream at the spring fair. The last twenty cups were soup. A thermometer inside the freezer read twenty-two degrees, which is above freezing for ice cream. The lid had been propped open with a scoop since noon so servers could work faster. Warm air pours into a freezer whenever the lid is open. Every cup served before noon came out solid, a hundred of them. The freezer stands in full sun from eleven o'clock, and nobody moved it. The last twenty cups came from the tub nearest the lid opening. That tub had been dug into all morning and was half air by noon.
debate.question: Why were the last cups soup? Choose one cause and quote the story.

suspects.why: a lid propped open with a scoop since noon
standing in full sun from eleven, and never moved
the tub nearest the opening, half air by noon

evidence: “The lid had been propped open with a scoop since noon so servers could work faster.”
“Warm air pours into a freezer whenever the lid is open.”
arguments.against: “The freezer stands in full sun from eleven o'clock, and nobody moved it.”

evidence: “The freezer stands in full sun from eleven o'clock, and nobody moved it.”
“Every cup served before noon came out solid, a hundred of them.”
arguments.against: “The lid had been propped open with a scoop since noon so servers could work faster.”

evidence: “The last twenty cups came from the tub nearest the lid opening.”
“That tub had been dug into all morning and was half air by noon.”
arguments.against: “A thermometer inside the freezer read twenty-two degrees, which is above freezing for ice cream.”

debate.note: Noon is the hinge and three things happen near it: the lid goes up, the sun has been on the box for an hour, and one tub is nearly empty. The thermometer reading is the only measurement and it blames the whole freezer rather than any one of the three. A good answer uses the first hundred cups to date the problem.

cases.title: The Case of the Wrong Ribbon
cases.story: Field day ended with the fifty-meter ribbons handed out and one runner got the wrong color. Priya crossed the line second and received a third-place ribbon. The timer's sheet lists her at second. The ribbon table was sorted into three piles by color. The second and third place ribbons are both shades of blue. Under the tent canopy the two piles looked identical. Two other runners also received a ribbon that did not match the sheet. Nobody checked a ribbon against the sheet before handing it over.
cases.question: Why did Priya get the wrong ribbon?

suspects.why: both are shades of blue and looked identical under the canopy
the timer's sheet lists her at second
she crossed the line second

cases.answer: The second and third ribbons were both blue and got mixed up.
proof: “The second and third place ribbons are both shades of blue.”
“Under the tent canopy the two piles looked identical.”
clears: A timing mistake: “The timer's sheet lists her at second.”
Priya's finish: “Priya crossed the line second”
cases.explain: Two other runners also got a ribbon that did not match the sheet. Because the second and third place ribbons are both shades of blue and looked identical under the canopy, the piles were handed out wrong.

debate.story: Field day ended with the fifty-meter ribbons handed out and one runner got the wrong color. Priya came in second across the line and was handed a third-place ribbon. The ribbon table was sorted into three piles by color. The second and third place ribbons are both shades of blue. Under the tent canopy the two piles looked identical. Two other runners also received a ribbon that did not match the sheet. Nobody checked a ribbon against the sheet before handing it over. The timer wrote the places on a wet sheet and two lines are smudged. The finish judge and the timer disagreed about third place at the time.
debate.question: How did Priya get the wrong ribbon? Pick one cause and prove it.

suspects.why: two shades of blue that looked identical under the canopy
a wet sheet with two smudged lines, and a judge who disagreed

suspects.who: ✅ No ribbon checked against the sheet
suspects.why: no ribbon checked against the sheet before it was handed over

evidence: “The second and third place ribbons are both shades of blue.”
“Under the tent canopy the two piles looked identical.”
arguments.against: “The timer wrote the places on a wet sheet and two lines are smudged.”

evidence: “The timer wrote the places on a wet sheet and two lines are smudged.”
“The finish judge and the timer disagreed about third place at the time.”
arguments.against: “Priya came in second across the line and was handed a third-place ribbon.”

evidence: “Nobody checked a ribbon against the sheet before handing it over.”
“Two other runners also received a ribbon that did not match the sheet.”
arguments.against: “Under the tent canopy the two piles looked identical.”

debate.note: Three runners got the wrong ribbon, and that number is the evidence. One mistake can be a smudge; three in a row is a system. Ask what each suspect would produce: a smudged line makes one error, look-alike piles make many, and no checking makes every error survive. The last one is not a cause so much as the reason nothing was caught.

cases.title: The Case of the Popping Balloons
cases.story: The class blew up forty balloons for the last-day party and eleven popped by lunch. All eleven had been taped to the window side of the room. The balloons on the inside wall are still full. Nobody touched them and no pins were in the room. The window side was in direct sun from ten o'clock on. Air inside a balloon expands as it warms. The rubber stretches until it splits. The eleven popped between ten and twelve.
cases.question: Why did eleven balloons pop?

suspects.why: direct sun from ten, and they popped between ten and twelve
no pins were in the room
nobody touched them

cases.answer: The sun warmed the air inside and the rubber split.
proof: “The window side was in direct sun from ten o'clock on.”
“Air inside a balloon expands as it warms.”
clears: A pin: “no pins were in the room.”
Somebody popping them: “Nobody touched them”
cases.explain: The balloons on the inside wall are still full, and the eleven popped between ten and twelve. Because the window side was in direct sun from ten o'clock, the air inside expanded and the rubber stretched until it split.

debate.story: The class blew up forty balloons for the last-day party and eleven popped by lunch. All eleven had been taped to the window side of the room. The balloons on the inside wall are still full. The window side was in direct sun from ten o'clock on. Air inside a balloon expands as it warms, and the rubber stretches until it splits. The eleven popped between ten and twelve. The window-side balloons were blown up first and hardest, to get them done. The tape on that side was the rough kind and was pressed onto the rubber.
debate.question: Why did eleven balloons pop? Make the case for one cause.

suspects.why: direct sun from ten, and eleven popping between ten and twelve
blown up first and hardest, to get them done
rough tape pressed straight onto the rubber

evidence: “The window side was in direct sun from ten o'clock on.”
“Air inside a balloon expands as it warms, and the rubber stretches until it splits.”
arguments.against: “The window-side balloons were blown up first and hardest, to get them done.”

evidence: “The window-side balloons were blown up first and hardest, to get them done.”
“The eleven popped between ten and twelve.”
arguments.against: “The balloons on the inside wall are still full.”

evidence: “The tape on that side was the rough kind and was pressed onto the rubber.”
“All eleven had been taped to the window side of the room.”
arguments.against: “The window side was in direct sun from ten o'clock on.”

debate.note: Everything that happened to those eleven happened because they were on the window side, so the side is not an answer on its own. The timing is the strongest evidence left: they popped in the two hours after the sun arrived, and tape and overfilling do not wait for ten o'clock. A student who uses the clock is using the best thing in the story.

cases.title: The Case of the Rearranged Shelf
cases.story: Every book in the 500s was out of order on Monday morning. The call numbers ran backward from 599 to 500. Mrs. Kim checked the sign-out log and found no checkouts after Thursday. The custodian had waxed that aisle Friday night and said he moved nothing. A sixth-grade class had used the library Friday afternoon for a research lesson. Taped inside the back of the cart was a worksheet titled Practice Shelving: Reverse Order. One student had written her name at the top and answered all twelve questions correctly. The books were not lost. They had been shelved exactly as the worksheet told her to.
cases.question: Why were the books in backward order?

suspects.why: titled Reverse Order, with all twelve questions answered
waxed the aisle and said he moved nothing
no checkouts after Thursday
the books were not lost

cases.answer: A student shelved the books in reverse as the worksheet said.
proof: “Taped inside the back of the cart was a worksheet titled Practice Shelving: Reverse Order.”
“They had been shelved exactly as the worksheet told her to.”
clears: The custodian: “said he moved nothing.”
Checkouts: “found no checkouts after Thursday.”
cases.explain: Nothing was missing and nothing was damaged. Because the worksheet asked for reverse order and the student answered all twelve questions correctly, she shelved the whole range backward on purpose.

debate.story: Every book in the 500s was out of order on Monday morning. The call numbers ran backward from 599 to 500. The sign-out log shows three books taken Friday and all three back on the shelf. The custodian waxed that aisle Friday night. To wax it he lifted every book off and put it back. The aisle light had been out since Thursday. A sixth-grade class used the library Friday afternoon for a lesson on call numbers. Taped inside the cart was a worksheet titled Practice Shelving: Reverse Order. One student wrote her name on it and answered eleven of the twelve questions. Mrs. Kim saw a fifth grader slide a book behind the row on Friday. The whole row sits pushed back two inches from the shelf edge.
debate.question: Who put the books in backward order, and what in the case says so?

suspects.why: titled Reverse Order, taped in the cart after a lesson on call numbers
lifted every book off to wax, in an aisle with no light
three taken Friday, and all three back on the shelf
seen sliding a book behind a row that now sits pushed back

evidence: “Taped inside the cart was a worksheet titled Practice Shelving: Reverse Order.”
“A sixth-grade class used the library Friday afternoon for a lesson on call numbers.”
arguments.against: “One student wrote her name on it and answered eleven of the twelve questions.”

evidence: “To wax it he lifted every book off and put it back.”
“The aisle light had been out since Thursday.”
arguments.against: “The call numbers ran backward from 599 to 500.”

evidence: “Mrs. Kim saw a fifth grader slide a book behind the row on Friday.”
“The whole row sits pushed back two inches from the shelf edge.”
arguments.against: “Every book in the 500s was out of order on Monday morning.”

clears: Checkouts: “three books taken Friday and all three back on the shelf.”
debate.note: Three books cannot reorder a hundred, so the checkouts are out and everybody should say so. After that the case does not choose. The worksheet explains the exact backward order but not the one wrong answer. The custodian explains a whole shelf handled in the dark but not why it came back in perfect reverse. The hidden book explains a row pushed back but not a hundred call numbers. A strong answer names which fact its suspect cannot explain and says why it still picks that suspect.

cases.title: The Case of the Warm Milk
cases.story: Four students in Room 12 had warm milk at lunch and the rest were cold. All twenty cartons came out of the same cooler at 11:40. The four warm ones belonged to students who sit at the window table. Those four had put their cartons on the table at 11:45. The other sixteen also came out at 11:45 but stayed inside closed lunchboxes. The window table gets direct sun from 11:30 until one o'clock. A thermometer left on that table for ten minutes read eighty-one degrees. The cooler was working. The milk had been cold when it came out.
cases.question: Why was only some of the milk warm?

suspects.why: a thermometer there read eighty-one degrees
the cooler was working
the milk had been cold when it came out
all of it came out at 11:45

cases.answer: The sun on the window table warmed those four cartons.
proof: “The window table gets direct sun from 11:30 until one o'clock.”
“A thermometer left on that table for ten minutes read eighty-one degrees.”
clears: The cooler: “The cooler was working.”
Time out of the cooler: “The other sixteen also came out at 11:45 but stayed inside closed lunchboxes.”
cases.explain: All twenty cartons left the cooler together. Because only four sat on a table in direct sun while the rest stayed in closed lunchboxes, the sun warmed those four and nothing else.

debate.story: Four students in Room 12 had warm milk at lunch and the rest were cold. All twenty cartons came out of the same cooler at 11:40. The four warm ones belonged to students who sit at the window table. Those four set their cartons out at 11:45 and ate last, at 12:20. The window table gets direct sun from 11:30 until one o'clock. A thermometer left on that table for ten minutes read eighty-one degrees. The cooler door was propped open all morning for a delivery. Its dial reads forty, but nobody has checked the dial against a thermometer. The four warm cartons were the last four pulled from the back of the cooler. All twenty cartons carry the same date and came from one crate.
debate.question: Why was only some of the milk warm? Say who you would blame and prove it.

suspects.why: a thermometer on that table read eighty-one degrees
propped open all morning, and the dial has never been checked
all twenty cartons share one date and one crate
set out at 11:45 by the four who ate last

evidence: “The window table gets direct sun from 11:30 until one o'clock.”
“A thermometer left on that table for ten minutes read eighty-one degrees.”
arguments.against: “All twenty cartons came out of the same cooler at 11:40.”

evidence: “The cooler door was propped open all morning for a delivery.”
“Its dial reads forty, but nobody has checked the dial against a thermometer.”
“The four warm cartons were the last four pulled from the back of the cooler.”
arguments.against: “The four warm ones belonged to students who sit at the window table.”

evidence: “Those four set their cartons out at 11:45 and ate last, at 12:20.”
“Four students in Room 12 had warm milk at lunch and the rest were cold.”
arguments.against: “A thermometer left on that table for ten minutes read eighty-one degrees.”

clears: Bad milk: “All twenty cartons carry the same date and came from one crate.”
debate.note: One crate and one date rules the milk itself out. The other three all fit the same four children, which is what makes this hard: they sit in the sun, they waited longest, and theirs came from the back of a cooler propped open all morning. The best answers notice that the four warm cartons are warm for three reasons at once, and argue for the one they think did most of the work.

cases.title: The Case of the Vanishing Erasers
cases.story: Mr. Dunn bought a box of thirty pink erasers in September. By November eleven were gone. No student had taken one home, and the class had searched desks twice. Mr. Dunn found eight of them in the heating vent under the window. The vent sits directly below the pencil cup on the sill. An eraser is light and rolls, and the sill tilts half an inch toward the window. He put a strip of tape along the sill edge. Over the next six weeks nothing else fell. The missing three are probably further down the duct.
cases.question: Where did the erasers go?

suspects.who: 🕳️ The heating vent below the sill
suspects.why: eight were found in the vent
no student had taken one home
the class had searched desks twice

cases.answer: The erasers rolled off the tilted sill into the vent.
proof: “Mr. Dunn found eight of them in the heating vent under the window.”
“An eraser is light and rolls, and the sill tilts half an inch toward the window.”
clears: Taking them home: “No student had taken one home”
Desks: “the class had searched desks twice.”
cases.explain: Nothing else fell after tape went along the sill edge. Because the sill tilts toward the window and an eraser rolls, the erasers rolled off into the vent below.

debate.story: Mr. Dunn bought a box of thirty pink erasers in September. By November eleven were gone. He found three of them in the heating vent under the window. The vent sits directly below the pencil cup on the sill. An eraser is light and rolls, and the sill tilts half an inch toward the window. Two students were seen putting erasers in their pockets at the end of October. Erasers cost a nickel, and nobody counts them going out the door. The class searched desks once, in the first week of November, and found two. Nine desks were not opened, because those students were at band.
debate.question: Where did the other erasers go? Pick one answer and back it from the text.

suspects.who: 🕳️ The heating vent below the sill
suspects.why: three found in it, under a sill that tilts toward the window
two seen pocketing erasers, and nobody counts them going out
searched once, with nine desks never opened

evidence: “He found three of them in the heating vent under the window.”
“An eraser is light and rolls, and the sill tilts half an inch toward the window.”
arguments.against: “By November eleven were gone.”

evidence: “Two students were seen putting erasers in their pockets at the end of October.”
“Erasers cost a nickel, and nobody counts them going out the door.”
arguments.against: “He found three of them in the heating vent under the window.”

evidence: “The class searched desks once, in the first week of November, and found two.”
“Nine desks were not opened, because those students were at band.”
arguments.against: “The vent sits directly below the pencil cup on the sill.”

debate.note: Three of the eleven are accounted for by the vent and two by the desks, which leaves six that nothing in the case places. That gap is the exercise. Every answer here is partly right, so the argument is about which explanation covers the most erasers, and a strong one says out loud how many it has explained and how many it has not.

cases.title: The Case of the Bruised Apples
cases.story: The fifth grade picked four bushels and found a third of them bruised two days later. The bruises are all on one side and about the size of a thumb. Nobody dropped a crate. The truck ride was eight minutes on a paved road. The students had been told to pick with a twist, not a pull. Fourteen of them pulled instead, and a pulled apple comes away with the stem still attached. A loose stem in a crate presses into whatever it touches. The bruised apples were all in the two crates those fourteen filled. The unbruised crates have no stems loose inside them.
cases.question: What bruised the apples?

suspects.why: the bruised apples were in the crates those fourteen filled
eight minutes on a paved road
nobody dropped a crate

cases.answer: Loose stems in the crates pressed bruises into the apples.
proof: “A loose stem in a crate presses into whatever it touches.”
“The bruised apples were all in the two crates those fourteen filled.”
clears: The truck: “The truck ride was eight minutes on a paved road.”
A dropped crate: “Nobody dropped a crate.”
cases.explain: The unbruised crates have no stems loose inside them. Because fourteen students pulled instead of twisting, the stems came away with the fruit and pressed into the apples around them.

debate.story: The fifth grade picked four bushels and found a third of them bruised two days later. The bruises are all on one side and about the size of a thumb. The students had been told to pick with a twist, not a pull. Fourteen of them pulled instead. A pulled apple comes away with the stem still attached. A loose stem in a crate presses into whatever it touches. The truck ride was twenty minutes. The road behind the orchard is gravel and washboarded. One crate was set down hard at the loading dock and its corner split. The bruised apples came from two crates, and nobody wrote down which two.
debate.question: What bruised the apples? Name one cause and quote the case.

suspects.why: fourteen pulled instead of twisting, leaving the stems attached
twenty minutes over a washboarded gravel road
one set down hard enough to split its corner

evidence: “A pulled apple comes away with the stem still attached.”
“A loose stem in a crate presses into whatever it touches.”
arguments.against: “The bruised apples came from two crates, and nobody wrote down which two.”

evidence: “The truck ride was twenty minutes.”
“The road behind the orchard is gravel and washboarded.”
arguments.against: “The bruises are all on one side and about the size of a thumb.”

evidence: “One crate was set down hard at the loading dock and its corner split.”
“The fifth grade picked four bushels and found a third of them bruised two days later.”
arguments.against: “Fourteen of them pulled instead.”

debate.note: The sentence that used to settle this case is the one saying which crates the bruised apples came from, and it has been taken out. Now the stem explanation fits the size and shape of the bruise, the truck fits a third of the load, and the dropped crate fits one crate exactly. Ask which suspect explains the bruise being on one side only, and the room will divide usefully.

cases.title: The Case of the Pulling Brake
cases.story: Dev's bike pulled left every time he squeezed the brake. Both tires held the same pressure, and the frame sat straight against a wall. His father watched the wheels while Dev braked slowly in the driveway. The front brake pad on the left touched the rim a half second before the right one. One brake cable runs through a housing that had split near the handlebar. A split housing lets the cable stretch, which delays one side. His father replaced the housing and both pads met the rim together. The pull stopped on the first ride.
cases.question: Why did the bike pull to one side?

suspects.why: the left pad touched a half second early
both tires held the same pressure
the frame sat straight against a wall

cases.answer: A split housing delayed the right brake pad.
proof: “One brake cable runs through a housing that had split near the handlebar.”
“A split housing lets the cable stretch, which delays one side.”
clears: Tire pressure: “Both tires held the same pressure”
A bent frame: “the frame sat straight against a wall.”
cases.explain: The pull stopped once the housing was replaced and both pads met the rim together. Because the split housing let the cable stretch, the left pad gripped half a second before the right.

debate.story: Dev's bike pulled left every time he squeezed the brake. His father watched the wheels while Dev braked slowly in the driveway. The front brake pad on the left touched the rim a half second before the right one. One brake cable runs through a housing that had split near the handlebar. A split housing lets the cable stretch, which delays one side. The left tire reads thirty-four pounds and the right reads forty-one. A softer tire grips more and slows that wheel first. Dev's bike was hit in the rack in September and the front forks were straightened by hand. A frame held against a wall looks straight to the eye within a quarter inch.
debate.question: Why does the bike pull to one side? Make the case for one cause.

suspects.why: split near the handlebar, and the left pad lands first
thirty-four pounds on the left against forty-one on the right
hit in the rack in September and straightened by hand

evidence: “One brake cable runs through a housing that had split near the handlebar.”
“A split housing lets the cable stretch, which delays one side.”
arguments.against: “The left tire reads thirty-four pounds and the right reads forty-one.”

evidence: “The left tire reads thirty-four pounds and the right reads forty-one.”
“A softer tire grips more and slows that wheel first.”
arguments.against: “The front brake pad on the left touched the rim a half second before the right one.”

evidence: “Dev's bike was hit in the rack in September and the front forks were straightened by hand.”
“A frame held against a wall looks straight to the eye within a quarter inch.”
arguments.against: “Dev's bike pulled left every time he squeezed the brake.”

debate.note: All three now have a measurement behind them, and the pull is to the left in every one. The useful question is which of them explains why the bike only pulls when he brakes. Two of the three predict a pull all the time, and a student who notices that has done the real work whichever name they end up writing.

cases.title: The Case of the Gasping Fish
cases.story: The class goldfish hung near the surface and gulped at the air for two days. The water was clear and the filter ran all night. A test strip showed no ammonia and the right pH. The tank sits beside a radiator that came on when the weather turned. A thermometer in the water read eighty-two degrees, eight above the usual reading. Warm water holds less dissolved oxygen than cool water does. A fish at the surface is trying to reach the layer with the most oxygen. The class moved the tank four feet from the radiator. Within a day the fish swam low again.
cases.question: Why was the fish gulping at the surface?

suspects.why: the water read eighty-two degrees
the filter ran all night
no ammonia and the right pH

cases.answer: The warm water held too little oxygen.
proof: “A thermometer in the water read eighty-two degrees, eight above the usual reading.”
“Warm water holds less dissolved oxygen than cool water does.”
clears: The filter: “the filter ran all night.”
Water chemistry: “A test strip showed no ammonia and the right pH.”
cases.explain: The fish swam low again within a day of moving the tank. Because the radiator warmed the water to eighty-two degrees, the water held less oxygen and the fish went to the surface for it.

debate.story: The class goldfish hung near the surface and gulped at the air for two days. A fish at the surface is trying to reach the layer with the most oxygen. The tank sits beside a radiator that came on when the weather turned. A thermometer in the water read eighty-two degrees, eight above the usual reading. Warm water holds less dissolved oxygen than cool water does. The filter ran all night, but its outflow no longer breaks the surface since the water level dropped. Moving water is how most of the oxygen gets in. The test strip is from a tube that expired in March. Ammonia burns the gills, and a burned fish breathes fast wherever it is.
debate.question: Why is the fish gulping at the surface? Argue for one cause.

suspects.why: eighty-two degrees, eight above the usual reading
running, but its outflow no longer breaks the surface
tested with a strip from a tube that expired in March

evidence: “A thermometer in the water read eighty-two degrees, eight above the usual reading.”
“Warm water holds less dissolved oxygen than cool water does.”
arguments.against: “The filter ran all night, but its outflow no longer breaks the surface since the water level dropped.”

evidence: “Moving water is how most of the oxygen gets in.”
“The tank sits beside a radiator that came on when the weather turned.”
arguments.against: “A fish at the surface is trying to reach the layer with the most oxygen.”

evidence: “The test strip is from a tube that expired in March.”
“Ammonia burns the gills, and a burned fish breathes fast wherever it is.”
arguments.against: “A thermometer in the water read eighty-two degrees, eight above the usual reading.”

debate.note: Two of these take oxygen out of the water and one stops it going in, so the first two arguments agree about the mechanism and disagree about the cause. The chemistry argument is the interesting one, because the only reason it was ruled out before was a test strip, and the case now says the strip is nine months out of date. Evidence that cannot be trusted is not evidence that says no.

cases.title: The Case of the Rattling Vent
cases.story: A rattle came from the ceiling vent in Room 8 three or four times an hour. It stopped completely on Saturday and started again Monday. Mr. Blake found no loose screws. The duct is strapped tight. The rattle happens about ten seconds after the heat kicks on. A thin metal damper inside the duct swings when air first moves through it. The damper's pin had worn a groove and no longer held it steady. On Saturday the building heat was off, so the damper never moved. He shimmed the pin with a washer and the rattle stopped.
cases.question: What was rattling in the vent?

suspects.why: the damper swings when air first moves through
no loose screws were found
the duct is strapped tight

cases.answer: A worn pin let the damper swing and rattle.
proof: “A thin metal damper inside the duct swings when air first moves through it.”
“The damper's pin had worn a groove and no longer held it steady.”
clears: Loose screws: “Mr. Blake found no loose screws.”
The straps: “The duct is strapped tight.”
cases.explain: On Saturday the heat was off and the rattle stopped. Because the worn pin no longer held the damper steady, the damper swung every time the heat came on.

debate.story: A rattle came from the ceiling vent in Room 8 three or four times an hour. It stopped completely on Saturday and started again Monday. The rattle happens about ten seconds after the heat kicks on. A thin metal damper inside the duct swings when air first moves through it. The damper's pin has worn a groove and no longer holds it steady. Two screws on the ceiling grille turn freely without tightening. A loose grille buzzes when air pushes past it. The duct straps were fitted in August and one of them hangs an inch below the duct. On Saturday the building heat was off, so nothing moved in the duct at all.
debate.question: What is rattling in the vent? Pick a cause and prove it from the text.

suspects.why: worn into a groove, and the damper swings on the first air
two on the grille turn freely without tightening
one of them hangs an inch below the duct

evidence: “A thin metal damper inside the duct swings when air first moves through it.”
“The damper's pin has worn a groove and no longer holds it steady.”
arguments.against: “Two screws on the ceiling grille turn freely without tightening.”

evidence: “Two screws on the ceiling grille turn freely without tightening.”
“A loose grille buzzes when air pushes past it.”
arguments.against: “The rattle happens about ten seconds after the heat kicks on.”

evidence: “The duct straps were fitted in August and one of them hangs an inch below the duct.”
“It stopped completely on Saturday and started again Monday.”
arguments.against: “A thin metal damper inside the duct swings when air first moves through it.”

debate.note: Saturday no longer clears anybody, because the heat was off and all three suspects need moving air. That is worth saying aloud: a test that every suspect passes has told you nothing. The ten-second delay is the detail that still does work, and the strongest answers use it, whichever side they are arguing.

cases.title: The Case of the One Bare Branch
cases.story: One maple at the school entrance dropped the leaves from a single branch in September. The rest of the tree stayed green. The branch is on the north side, away from the parking lot and the road salt. No insect holes appear in the fallen leaves. A groundskeeper found a deep cut in the bark where that branch meets the trunk. The cut came from a string trimmer used around the base in August. Water travels to a branch through a thin layer just under the bark. A cut that circles part of that layer starves whatever is above it. The rest of the tree is fed by uncut bark.
cases.question: Why did one branch lose its leaves?

suspects.why: a deep cut where that branch meets the trunk
the branch is away from the road salt
no insect holes appear in the fallen leaves

cases.answer: A cut in the bark starved that one branch.
proof: “A groundskeeper found a deep cut in the bark where that branch meets the trunk.”
“A cut that circles part of that layer starves whatever is above it.”
clears: Road salt: “The branch is on the north side, away from the parking lot and the road salt.”
Insects: “No insect holes appear in the fallen leaves.”
cases.explain: The rest of the tree is fed by uncut bark and stayed green. Because the trimmer cut through the thin layer that carries water to that branch, only that branch lost its leaves.

debate.story: One maple at the school entrance dropped the leaves from a single branch in September. The rest of the tree stayed green. A groundskeeper found a deep cut in the bark where that branch meets the trunk. The cut came from a string trimmer used around the base in August. Water travels to a branch through a thin layer just under the bark. A cut that circles part of that layer starves whatever is above it. The branch is the lowest on the tree and the only one that reaches over the parking lot. Salt spray from the lot killed two shrubs on that side last winter. Three leaves in the fallen pile have small round holes near the stem.
debate.question: Why did one branch lose its leaves? Choose a cause and back it up.

suspects.why: deep, where that branch meets the trunk
the only branch over the lot, and salt killed shrubs on that side
small round holes in three of the fallen leaves

evidence: “A groundskeeper found a deep cut in the bark where that branch meets the trunk.”
“A cut that circles part of that layer starves whatever is above it.”
arguments.against: “The branch is the lowest on the tree and the only one that reaches over the parking lot.”

evidence: “The branch is the lowest on the tree and the only one that reaches over the parking lot.”
“Salt spray from the lot killed two shrubs on that side last winter.”
arguments.against: “One maple at the school entrance dropped the leaves from a single branch in September.”

evidence: “Three leaves in the fallen pile have small round holes near the stem.”
“The rest of the tree stayed green.”
arguments.against: “The cut came from a string trimmer used around the base in August.”

debate.note: The branch now has three things wrong with it at once, which is what makes it arguable. Push on timing: the cut was made in August and the leaves fell in September, the salt came last winter, and three holes is a small number out of a whole branch. A student who argues from how long each cause takes to show is reasoning well even if they pick the salt.

cases.title: The Case of the Pumpkin That Fell In
cases.story: The entrance pumpkin held its shape for three weeks and caved in overnight on the twenty-second day. No animal tracks or tooth marks appear anywhere on it. The custodian did not move it. The lid was never cut. The temperature dropped to twenty-six degrees that night, the first freeze of the fall. A pumpkin is about ninety percent water, and water expands when it freezes. Expanding ice pushes the cell walls apart, and they do not go back when the ice melts. The pumpkin in the lobby, in the same light, is still firm. The collapse happened the morning after the freeze.
cases.question: Why did the pumpkin cave in?

suspects.why: the temperature dropped to twenty-six degrees
no tracks or tooth marks appear on it
the custodian did not move it

cases.answer: Freezing water pushed the pumpkin's cell walls apart.
proof: “The temperature dropped to twenty-six degrees that night, the first freeze of the fall.”
“Expanding ice pushes the cell walls apart, and they do not go back when the ice melts.”
clears: An animal: “No animal tracks or tooth marks appear anywhere on it.”
The custodian: “The custodian did not move it.”
cases.explain: The lobby pumpkin in the same light is still firm. Because the night dropped to twenty-six degrees and a pumpkin is mostly water, the ice pushed the cell walls apart and the shell gave way as it thawed.

debate.story: The entrance pumpkin held its shape for three weeks and caved in overnight on the twenty-second day. Nobody saw it happen. The temperature dropped to twenty-six degrees that night, the first freeze of the fall. A pumpkin is about ninety percent water, and water expands when it freezes. Expanding ice pushes the cell walls apart, and they do not go back when the ice melts. Two shallow scratches run across the base where it meets the step. The custodian moved the pumpkin twice that week to sweep under it. A soft patch the size of a hand sits on the underside, and it smells sour. The lobby pumpkin, kept at room temperature, is still firm after twenty-four days.
debate.question: Why did the pumpkin cave in? Make the case for one cause.

suspects.why: twenty-six degrees that night, the first freeze of the fall
scratches across the base and a sour soft patch underneath
moved it twice that week to sweep under it

evidence: “The temperature dropped to twenty-six degrees that night, the first freeze of the fall.”
“Expanding ice pushes the cell walls apart, and they do not go back when the ice melts.”
arguments.against: “A soft patch the size of a hand sits on the underside, and it smells sour.”

evidence: “Two shallow scratches run across the base where it meets the step.”
“A soft patch the size of a hand sits on the underside, and it smells sour.”
arguments.against: “The entrance pumpkin held its shape for three weeks and caved in overnight on the twenty-second day.”

evidence: “The custodian moved the pumpkin twice that week to sweep under it.”
“The lobby pumpkin, kept at room temperature, is still firm after twenty-four days.”
arguments.against: “A pumpkin is about ninety percent water, and water expands when it freezes.”

debate.note: The lobby pumpkin is the strongest single fact in the case and it can be used on two sides. It was never frozen and never moved, so it supports the freeze and the custodian equally well. Ask the class what one extra fact would settle it, and the answer they should reach is whether the lobby pumpkin was ever outdoors.

cases.title: The Case of the Single Set of Prints
cases.story: Wet prints crossed the cafeteria floor on Wednesday in one direction only. Nothing led back. The prints start at the loading door and stop at the dish room. It had rained all morning and the delivery truck arrived at ten. The driver wore boots with a block tread, and the prints show a block tread. The dish room has a floor drain and a hose used at ten fifteen. Prints made on the way back would have been washed away by that hose. The kitchen staff wear non-slip shoes with a circular pattern. No circular prints appear anywhere on the floor.
cases.question: Who left the wet prints?

suspects.why: the prints show a block tread like his boots
no circular prints appear anywhere
the return prints would have been hosed away

cases.answer: The delivery driver left the prints in his block-tread boots.
proof: “The driver wore boots with a block tread, and the prints show a block tread.”
“The prints start at the loading door and stop at the dish room.”
clears: The kitchen staff: “No circular prints appear anywhere on the floor.”
Somebody still inside: “Prints made on the way back would have been washed away by that hose.”
cases.explain: The prints show a block tread and run one way only. Because the driver came in at ten in block-tread boots and the dish room floor was hosed at ten fifteen, his return prints were washed away.

debate.story: Wet prints crossed the cafeteria floor on Wednesday in one direction only. Nothing led back. The prints start at the loading door and stop at the dish room. It had rained all morning and the delivery truck arrived at ten. The driver wore boots with a block tread, and the prints show a block tread. The dish room has a floor drain and a hose that was used at ten fifteen. Two of the kitchen staff had been outside at the dumpster that morning. Their non-slip shoes have a block tread under the heel and circles under the toe. The dish room door was propped and nobody checked who was behind it. The prints stop at the drain, where the floor is always wet.
debate.question: Who left the wet prints? Charge one of them and prove it from the case.

suspects.why: block tread boots, and a truck that arrived at ten
outside at the dumpster, with block tread under the heel
a dish room door propped, and nobody checking behind it

evidence: “It had rained all morning and the delivery truck arrived at ten.”
“The driver wore boots with a block tread, and the prints show a block tread.”
arguments.against: “Two of the kitchen staff had been outside at the dumpster that morning.”

evidence: “Two of the kitchen staff had been outside at the dumpster that morning.”
“Their non-slip shoes have a block tread under the heel and circles under the toe.”
arguments.against: “The prints start at the loading door and stop at the dish room.”

evidence: “The dish room door was propped and nobody checked who was behind it.”
“The prints stop at the drain, where the floor is always wet.”
arguments.against: “Nothing led back.”

debate.note: The tread no longer tells the suspects apart, because the kitchen shoes turn out to have a block tread too. That is the move worth drawing out: evidence that fits two suspects is not evidence against either. What still does work is where the prints start and where they stop, and a strong answer argues from the route rather than the sole.

cases.title: The Case of the Half-Empty Bus
cases.story: Bus 7 arrived at school with eleven students on Tuesday instead of the usual twenty-six. Nobody was absent, and the attendance office counted all twenty-six in class by nine. The driver ran the normal route and made every stop. A city crew had closed Pine Street at six that morning for a water main. Fifteen of the students live on Pine Street or on the two streets behind it. The detour sign at the Pine Street corner pointed walkers toward the school's east gate. Walking from Pine Street to the east gate takes nine minutes. All twenty-six were at school. Only eleven were on the bus.
cases.question: Where were the other fifteen students?

suspects.why: fifteen live there and the sign sent walkers to the east gate
nobody was absent
the driver made every stop

cases.answer: Fifteen students walked because Pine Street was closed.
proof: “A city crew had closed Pine Street at six that morning for a water main.”
“The detour sign at the Pine Street corner pointed walkers toward the school's east gate.”
clears: Absences: “Nobody was absent”
A missed stop: “The driver ran the normal route and made every stop.”
cases.explain: All twenty-six were in class by nine. Because Pine Street was closed and the detour sign pointed walkers to the east gate, the fifteen who live there walked instead of riding.

debate.story: Bus 7 arrived at school with eleven students on Tuesday instead of the usual twenty-six. A city crew closed Pine Street at six that morning for a water main. Fifteen of the students live on Pine Street or the two streets behind it. The detour sign at the corner pointed walkers toward the school's east gate. Walking from Pine Street to the east gate takes nine minutes. The attendance office counted twenty-two in class by nine, not twenty-six. Four families reported a stomach bug going round that week. The driver's sheet shows he skipped the Elm Street stop to make up time. Six students wait at Elm Street. Nobody wrote down who boarded and who did not.
debate.question: Where were the other fifteen? Pick one explanation and back it from the text.

suspects.why: fifteen live there, and the sign sent walkers to the east gate
twenty-two counted in class, and a bug going round that week

“Four families reported a stomach bug going round that week.”
arguments.against: “Walking from Pine Street to the east gate takes nine minutes.”

evidence: “The driver's sheet shows he skipped the Elm Street stop to make up time.”
“Six students wait at Elm Street.”
arguments.against: “Fifteen of the students live on Pine Street or the two streets behind it.”

debate.note: Fifteen are missing from the bus and only four are missing from class, so no single suspect covers the whole number. That is the point. Ask the room to add up what their suspect explains: the closure covers fifteen but not the empty desks, the bug covers four, the skipped stop covers six. The best answers combine two and say so.

cases.title: The Case of the Cracked Trophy
cases.story: The science fair trophy developed a crack across its base between June and September. The case stayed locked and nobody signed it out. The crack runs in a straight line, not the star shape a blow would leave. The case sits against the south wall of the gym, which has no air conditioning in summer. A logger left in the case recorded swings from sixty-one degrees to ninety-four. The base is a marble slab glued to a plastic plate underneath. Marble and plastic expand by different amounts when they are heated. Two materials glued together that expand differently will pull apart at the joint. The crack follows the glue line exactly.
cases.question: What cracked the trophy base?

suspects.why: the crack follows the glue line exactly
the crack is straight, not the star shape a blow leaves
the case stayed locked and nobody signed it out

cases.answer: Heat made the marble and plastic pull apart at the glue line.
proof: “A logger left in the case recorded swings from sixty-one degrees to ninety-four.”
“Two materials glued together that expand differently will pull apart at the joint.”
clears: A blow: “The crack runs in a straight line, not the star shape a blow would leave.”
Handling: “The case stayed locked and nobody signed it out.”
cases.explain: The crack follows the glue line exactly. Because the gym swung between sixty-one and ninety-four degrees, the marble and the plastic expanded by different amounts and separated at the joint.

debate.story: The science fair trophy developed a crack across its base between June and September. The case sits against the south wall of the gym, which has no air conditioning. A logger left in the case recorded swings from sixty-one degrees to ninety-four. The base is a marble slab glued to a plastic plate underneath. Marble and plastic expand by different amounts when they are heated. Two materials glued together that expand differently pull apart at the joint. A chip the size of a pea is missing from one corner of the base. The crack begins at that corner. The case was unlocked for the summer open house and the trophy was handled. Nobody recorded who opened the case or when.
debate.question: What cracked the trophy base? Make the case for one cause.

suspects.why: sixty-one degrees to ninety-four, on a glued marble joint
a pea-sized chip at the corner the crack starts from
the case unlocked for the open house, with no record kept

arguments.against: “A chip the size of a pea is missing from one corner of the base.”

“The crack begins at that corner.”
arguments.against: “The case sits against the south wall of the gym, which has no air conditioning.”

evidence: “The case was unlocked for the summer open house and the trophy was handled.”
“Nobody recorded who opened the case or when.”
arguments.against: “Marble and plastic expand by different amounts when they are heated.”

debate.note: Heat explains why the joint was weak and the chip explains where the crack started, which means the two best answers are not really rivals. Let the argument run until somebody says so. A student who writes that the heat loosened the joint and a knock at the corner finished it has read the case better than one who picks a single name.

cases.title: The Case of the Underdone Turkey
cases.story: The fifth grade's holiday turkey came out browned on the outside and raw near the bone. The oven thermometer read 350 all afternoon. The bird roasted for the full four and a half hours the chart called for. It had come out of the freezer at nine that morning. A frozen turkey needs about twenty-four hours in a refrigerator for every five pounds. This one weighed sixteen pounds and had thawed for five hours on the counter. Heat moves through a roasting bird from the outside in. Ice at the center absorbs heat without the temperature rising. The outside finished while the middle was still thawing.
cases.question: Why was the turkey raw near the bone?

suspects.why: sixteen pounds thawed for only five hours
the thermometer read 350 all afternoon
it roasted the full time the chart called for

cases.answer: The turkey was still frozen in the middle.
proof: “A frozen turkey needs about twenty-four hours in a refrigerator for every five pounds.”
“This one weighed sixteen pounds and had thawed for five hours on the counter.”
clears: The oven: “The oven thermometer read 350 all afternoon.”
Time: “The bird roasted for the full four and a half hours the chart called for.”
cases.explain: The outside browned properly, so the oven and the time were fine. Because a sixteen-pound bird needs far more than five hours to thaw, ice at the center absorbed the heat and the middle stayed raw.

debate.story: The fifth grade's holiday turkey came out browned outside and raw near the bone. It had come out of the freezer at nine that morning. A frozen turkey needs about twenty-four hours in a refrigerator for every five pounds. This one weighed sixteen pounds and had thawed five hours on the counter. Heat moves through a roasting bird from the outside in. Ice at the center absorbs heat without the temperature rising. The oven dial was set to 350. The oven itself has not been checked in four years. The bird went in at noon and came out at four, and the chart asks for four and a half hours. Nobody opened the oven door to look.
debate.question: Why was the turkey raw near the bone? Choose a cause and prove it.

suspects.why: sixteen pounds thawed for five hours on a counter
a dial set to 350 on an oven unchecked for four years
noon to four against a chart that asks for four and a half

evidence: “This one weighed sixteen pounds and had thawed five hours on the counter.”
“Ice at the center absorbs heat without the temperature rising.”
arguments.against: “The oven itself has not been checked in four years.”

evidence: “The oven dial was set to 350.”
“The oven itself has not been checked in four years.”
arguments.against: “The fifth grade's holiday turkey came out browned outside and raw near the bone.”

evidence: “The bird went in at noon and came out at four, and the chart asks for four and a half hours.”
“Nobody opened the oven door to look.”
arguments.against: “A frozen turkey needs about twenty-four hours in a refrigerator for every five pounds.”

debate.note: A browned outside is the fact that does the most work and it is easy to walk past. An oven running cold would not brown anything, so the strongest answers use the browning to argue against the oven even while admitting it has not been checked in four years. Half an hour short is real and small; nineteen hours of thawing short is real and large.

cases.title: The Case of the Tough Cupcakes
cases.story: Room 11 baked two trays of cupcakes from one bowl of batter. The first tray is light and the second is dense and chewy. Both trays went into the same oven at the same temperature. Both came out after eighteen minutes. The class kept stirring the bowl while the first tray baked. Stirring wheat batter builds gluten, and gluten makes a cake chewy. The second tray sat in the bowl being stirred for eighteen extra minutes. The recipe says to stop mixing as soon as the flour disappears. Nobody added anything to the second half.
cases.question: Why was the second tray chewy?

suspects.why: the second half was stirred for eighteen extra minutes
both trays went in at the same temperature
both came out after eighteen minutes
nobody added anything to the second half

cases.answer: Extra stirring built gluten and made them chewy.
proof: “Stirring wheat batter builds gluten, and gluten makes a cake chewy.”
“The second tray sat in the bowl being stirred for eighteen extra minutes.”
clears: The oven: “Both trays went into the same oven at the same temperature.”
Baking time: “Both came out after eighteen minutes.”
cases.explain: One bowl of batter made both trays, so the ingredients were identical. Because the second half was stirred for eighteen extra minutes, the stirring built gluten and the cupcakes came out chewy.

debate.story: Room 11 baked two trays of cupcakes from one bowl of batter. The first tray is light and the second is dense and chewy. The class kept stirring the bowl while the first tray baked. Stirring wheat batter builds gluten, and gluten makes a cake chewy. The second tray sat in the bowl being stirred for eighteen extra minutes. The second tray went in straight after the first, into an oven already hot. An oven runs hotter on its second load than on its first. The timer was set for eighteen minutes. Nobody heard it over the mixer. Both trays were scooped from the same bowl and nothing was added to either.
debate.question: Why was the second tray chewy? Name a cause and quote the case.

suspects.why: eighteen extra minutes of stirring, which builds gluten
second into an oven already hot from the first tray
a timer nobody heard over the mixer
one bowl, and nothing added to either tray

evidence: “Stirring wheat batter builds gluten, and gluten makes a cake chewy.”
“The second tray sat in the bowl being stirred for eighteen extra minutes.”
arguments.against: “An oven runs hotter on its second load than on its first.”

evidence: “The second tray went in straight after the first, into an oven already hot.”
“An oven runs hotter on its second load than on its first.”
arguments.against: “The second tray sat in the bowl being stirred for eighteen extra minutes.”

evidence: “The timer was set for eighteen minutes.”
“Nobody heard it over the mixer.”
arguments.against: “The first tray is light and the second is dense and chewy.”

clears: A wrong ingredient: “Both trays were scooped from the same bowl and nothing was added to either.”
debate.note: One bowl rules the ingredients out and everybody should say so first. After that, three things happened to the second tray and only the second tray: it was stirred longer, it met a hotter oven, and nobody was listening for the timer. Dense and chewy is the detail to argue from, because overbaking dries a cake rather than making it chewy.

cases.title: The Case of the Stiff Gloves
cases.story: Noor's wool gloves came back from the wash stiff enough to stand up by themselves. The label says cold water and lay flat to dry. Her brother washed them in hot water and put them through the dryer. Wool fibers are covered in tiny scales that open in heat and lock together. Once locked, the scales do not release, and the wool stays matted and stiff. The gloves also came out two sizes smaller than before. A pair of her cotton gloves washed in the same load came out fine. Cotton has no scales. The wool gloves cannot be restored.
cases.question: Why did the gloves come out stiff?

suspects.why: heat opens the scales so they lock together
cotton gloves in the same load came out fine
the label says cold water and lay flat

cases.answer: Heat locked the wool scales together.
proof: “Her brother washed them in hot water and put them through the dryer.”
“Wool fibers are covered in tiny scales that open in heat and lock together.”
clears: The soap: “A pair of her cotton gloves washed in the same load came out fine.”
Cheap wool: “The label says cold water and lay flat to dry.”
cases.explain: The cotton gloves in the same load came out fine because cotton has no scales. Because the wool went through hot water and a dryer, the scales opened, locked together, and the gloves matted and shrank.

debate.story: Noor's wool gloves came back from the wash stiff enough to stand up by themselves. Her brother washed them in hot water and put them through the dryer. Wool fibers are covered in tiny scales that open in heat and lock together. Once locked, the scales do not release, and the wool stays matted and stiff. The gloves also came out two sizes smaller than before. He used a new detergent with an enzyme that the bottle says breaks down protein. Wool is a protein fiber. The gloves were bought at a market stall with no label of any kind. Two loose threads had already pulled free before the wash.
debate.question: Why did the gloves come out stiff? Argue for one cause.

suspects.why: hot water and a dryer, which open the scales
a new enzyme detergent that breaks down protein
a market stall with no label, and threads already pulling free

evidence: “Her brother washed them in hot water and put them through the dryer.”
“Wool fibers are covered in tiny scales that open in heat and lock together.”
arguments.against: “He used a new detergent with an enzyme that the bottle says breaks down protein.”

evidence: “He used a new detergent with an enzyme that the bottle says breaks down protein.”
“Wool is a protein fiber.”
arguments.against: “The gloves also came out two sizes smaller than before.”

evidence: “The gloves were bought at a market stall with no label of any kind.”
“Two loose threads had already pulled free before the wash.”
arguments.against: “Once locked, the scales do not release, and the wool stays matted and stiff.”
