proof: “The new one has a deeper cone and a wider blade.”
“A single turn in the new sharpener removes nearly three times the wood.”
clears: Sharpening more often: “Nobody was sharpening more often than they had in October.”
A different brand: “The pencils were the same brand from the same box.”
Pencils going missing: “nobody reported a pencil missing.”
cases.explain: Same pencils, same number of turns. Because the new sharpener's cone is deeper, each of those four turns eats about three times the wood, which is the jump from nine millimeters to twenty-six.

debate.story: Room 14 measured its pencils every Friday as a data lesson. In October the class lost an average of nine millimeters a week. In November that number jumped to twenty-six. The old sharpener broke on the first of November. The new one has a deeper cone and a wider blade. A single turn in the new sharpener removes nearly three times the wood. The new sharpener is electric and the class queued at it all November. Four pencils were never returned to the cup in the last week of November. Every pencil in the box is the same brand, bought in one order in September. Ms. Reyes measures what is in the cup on Friday, not what each child holds.
debate.question: Why did the pencils get shorter faster? Make the case for one answer.

suspects.why: a deeper cone taking nearly three times the wood a turn
an electric sharpener with a queue at it all November
one brand, bought in one order in September
four never returned to the cup in the last week

evidence: “The new one has a deeper cone and a wider blade.”
“A single turn in the new sharpener removes nearly three times the wood.”
arguments.against: “The new sharpener is electric and the class queued at it all November.”

evidence: “The new sharpener is electric and the class queued at it all November.”
“The old sharpener broke on the first of November.”
arguments.against: “A single turn in the new sharpener removes nearly three times the wood.”

evidence: “Four pencils were never returned to the cup in the last week of November.”
“Ms. Reyes measures what is in the cup on Friday, not what each child holds.”
arguments.against: “In November that number jumped to twenty-six.”

clears: A different brand: “Every pencil in the box is the same brand, bought in one order in September.”
debate.note: Nine to twenty-six is nearly three times, and so is the wood each turn takes, which makes the sharpener the neat answer. The queue argument is better than it looks, because a machine that is fun to use gets used more. The missing-pencil answer is about the measurement rather than the pencils: an average over a cup changes when pencils leave the cup.

cases.title: The Case of the Apple That Stayed White
cases.story: Six apple halves sat on a tray for the science fair. Five turned brown within an hour and one stayed white all afternoon. Every half came off the same apple and was cut with the same knife. All six sat side by side in the same light and air. A cut apple browns because an enzyme in the flesh reacts with oxygen. Acid slows that enzyme down and can stop it almost completely. Priya squeezed lemon over one half before she set the tray out. The lemon wedge was still on her desk at the end of the day. Nothing was covering the white half and no half was refrigerated.
cases.question: Why did one apple half stay white?

suspects.why: acid slows that enzyme down
no half was refrigerated
every half came off the same apple
nothing was covering the white half

cases.answer: Lemon juice kept the enzyme in that apple half from browning.
proof: “Acid slows that enzyme down and can stop it almost completely.”
“Priya squeezed lemon over one half before she set the tray out.”
clears: Being kept cold: “no half was refrigerated.”
A different apple: “Every half came off the same apple and was cut with the same knife.”
Something covering it: “Nothing was covering the white half and no half was refrigerated.”
cases.explain: Five of six browned under identical conditions. Because the only difference was acid on one half, and acid is what stops the browning enzyme, the lemon is the whole answer.

debate.story: Six apple halves sat on a tray for the science fair. Five turned brown within an hour and one stayed white all afternoon. A cut apple browns because an enzyme in the flesh reacts with oxygen. Acid slows that enzyme down and can stop it almost completely. Priya squeezed lemon over one half before she set the tray out. The white half sat at the end of the tray nearest the open window. A draught from that window kept that corner about eight degrees cooler. Cold slows the same enzyme that acid does. A paper label had been laid face down across the white half until noon. All six halves were cut from one apple with one knife.
debate.question: Why did one half stay white? Pick one cause and prove it.

suspects.why: lemon squeezed over it, and acid slows the enzyme
a draught keeping that corner eight degrees cooler
one apple, one knife, six halves
a paper label laid face down across it until noon

evidence: “Priya squeezed lemon over one half before she set the tray out.”
“Acid slows that enzyme down and can stop it almost completely.”
arguments.against: “A draught from that window kept that corner about eight degrees cooler.”

evidence: “A draught from that window kept that corner about eight degrees cooler.”
“Cold slows the same enzyme that acid does.”
arguments.against: “Priya squeezed lemon over one half before she set the tray out.”

evidence: “A paper label had been laid face down across the white half until noon.”
“A cut apple browns because an enzyme in the flesh reacts with oxygen.”
arguments.against: “Five turned brown within an hour and one stayed white all afternoon.”

clears: A different apple: “All six halves were cut from one apple with one knife.”
debate.note: The experiment has three things wrong with it and that is the lesson. One half got lemon, sat in the coldest spot, and spent the morning under a label, so whatever it proves, it does not prove the lemon. Ask the class how they would redo it, and insist that only one thing may change at a time.

cases.title: The Case of the Morning Flat Tire
cases.story: Marco's front tire read low every cold morning and fine every afternoon. He pumped it to forty pounds on Monday and it read thirty-two at dawn. By three o'clock the same tire read thirty-nine. He dunked the tube in a bucket twice and no bubbles came up. The valve held when he pressed soapy water around it. Gas takes up less room when it gets colder and presses out less hard. The shed was thirty-eight degrees at dawn and seventy-one in the afternoon. His rear tire, pumped the same morning, swung by the same amount. A tire losing air does not come back up on its own.
cases.question: Why was the tire low only in the mornings?

suspects.who: 🌡️ Cold air taking up less room
suspects.why: gas presses out less hard when colder

suspects.who: 🕳️ A slow leak in the tube
suspects.why: no bubbles came up in the bucket
the valve held when he pressed soapy water around it

suspects.who: ⚖️ Too much weight on the front
suspects.why: his rear tire swung by the same amount

cases.answer: Cold air in the tire pressed out less hard at dawn.
proof: “Gas takes up less room when it gets colder and presses out less hard.”
“The shed was thirty-eight degrees at dawn and seventy-one in the afternoon.”
clears: A slow leak: “He dunked the tube in a bucket twice and no bubbles came up.”
A bad valve: “The valve held when he pressed soapy water around it.”
Too much weight: “His rear tire, pumped the same morning, swung by the same amount.”
cases.explain: The number goes down and then comes back, which no leak does. Because the shed swings more than thirty degrees between dawn and afternoon, the air inside is simply pressing out less hard when it is cold.

debate.story: Marco's front tire read low every cold morning and fine every afternoon. He pumped it to forty pounds on Monday and it read thirty-two at dawn. By three o'clock the same tire read thirty-nine. Gas takes up less room when it gets colder and presses out less hard. The shed was thirty-eight degrees at dawn and seventy-one in the afternoon. The tube was patched twice last summer and one patch has lifted at its edge. A patch that lifts in the cold can seal again as the rubber warms. The valve core turns with a finger and has never been tightened. His rear tire, pumped the same morning, held forty all week.
debate.question: Why does the front tire read low in the morning? Argue for one cause.

suspects.who: 🌡️ Cold air taking up less room
suspects.why: thirty-eight degrees at dawn against seventy-one by afternoon

suspects.who: 🕳️ A slow leak in the tube
suspects.why: a patch lifted at its edge since last summer
a core that turns with a finger and was never tightened

suspects.who: ⚖️ Too much weight on the front
suspects.why: a rear tire that held forty all week

evidence: “Gas takes up less room when it gets colder and presses out less hard.”
“The shed was thirty-eight degrees at dawn and seventy-one in the afternoon.”
arguments.against: “The tube was patched twice last summer and one patch has lifted at its edge.”

evidence: “The tube was patched twice last summer and one patch has lifted at its edge.”
“A patch that lifts in the cold can seal again as the rubber warms.”
arguments.against: “By three o'clock the same tire read thirty-nine.”

evidence: “The valve core turns with a finger and has never been tightened.”
“He pumped it to forty pounds on Monday and it read thirty-two at dawn.”
arguments.against: “Gas takes up less room when it gets colder and presses out less hard.”

clears: Weight on the front: “His rear tire, pumped the same morning, held forty all week.”
debate.note: The rear tire is the control and it does two jobs: it clears the weight and it makes trouble for the cold answer, because a rear tire sits in the same cold shed. A student who notices that has found the best objection in the case. A leak that reseals when it warms is the one explanation that survives it.

cases.title: The Case of the Cloudy Fishtank
cases.story: The classroom tank ran clear for two years and went cloudy in four days. Nobody added a fish and nobody changed the food. The water tested high for ammonia for the first time ever. A healthy tank carries bacteria in the filter that eat ammonia as fast as it appears. Those bacteria live in the filter sponge, not in the water. Ms. Oyelaran replaced the whole filter cartridge on Sunday, sponge and all. The new cartridge came sealed and sterile out of the box. The cloudiness began on Wednesday and the ammonia climbed all week. The heater, the light and the pump were all working normally.
cases.question: Why did the tank go cloudy?

suspects.why: the bacteria live in the filter sponge
nobody added a fish
nobody changed the food
the heater, light and pump were all working normally

cases.answer: Replacing the filter sponge threw out the bacteria that eat ammonia.
proof: “Those bacteria live in the filter sponge, not in the water.”
“Ms. Oyelaran replaced the whole filter cartridge on Sunday, sponge and all.”
clears: A new fish: “Nobody added a fish and nobody changed the food.”
Overfeeding: “nobody changed the food.”
Broken equipment: “The heater, the light and the pump were all working normally.”
cases.explain: Cleaning the filter is what broke the tank. Because the ammonia-eating bacteria lived in the sponge that went in the bin, nothing was left to eat the ammonia, and it climbed for the first time in two years.

debate.story: The classroom tank ran clear for two years and went cloudy in four days. The water tested high for ammonia for the first time ever. A healthy tank carries bacteria in the filter that eat ammonia as fast as it appears. Those bacteria live in the filter sponge, not in the water. Ms. Oyelaran replaced the whole filter cartridge on Sunday, sponge and all. The new cartridge came sealed and sterile out of the box. A student fed the fish on Friday and again on Monday, not knowing about the other. The heater has read two degrees high since the thermostat was knocked in October. Warm water speeds up everything that rots in a tank. The fish count has been six since last spring.
debate.question: Why did the tank go cloudy? Choose one cause and quote the story.

suspects.why: a sealed sterile cartridge, sponge and all
six fish since last spring
fed Friday and Monday by two people who did not know
a heater reading two degrees high since October

evidence: “Ms. Oyelaran replaced the whole filter cartridge on Sunday, sponge and all.”
“The new cartridge came sealed and sterile out of the box.”
arguments.against: “A student fed the fish on Friday and again on Monday, not knowing about the other.”

evidence: “A student fed the fish on Friday and again on Monday, not knowing about the other.”
“The water tested high for ammonia for the first time ever.”
arguments.against: “Those bacteria live in the filter sponge, not in the water.”

evidence: “The heater has read two degrees high since the thermostat was knocked in October.”
“Warm water speeds up everything that rots in a tank.”
arguments.against: “The classroom tank ran clear for two years and went cloudy in four days.”

clears: A new fish: “The fish count has been six since last spring.”
debate.note: The heater has been wrong since October and the tank went cloudy in four days, so the dates do most of the work here. Make the class use them. Sunday's cartridge and the double feeding both land in the same week, and the better answers notice that a tank with no bacteria left cannot handle a double feed either.

cases.title: The Case of the Hum in Room 9
cases.story: A low hum filled Room 9 every afternoon and nobody could find it. The hum never came before one o'clock and always stopped by three. Custodians checked the pipes, the vents and the lights and found nothing. The sound meter read the same with the lights off as with them on. Room 9 shares a wall with the gym, where a ceiling fan runs on a timer. That fan starts at one and shuts off at three every school day. A room will ring back at a sound when the sound matches the room's own pitch. The gym fan turns at a rate that matches Room 9 almost exactly. Nothing in Room 9 itself was switched on at one.
cases.question: What was making the hum?

suspects.who: 🌀 The gym fan on its timer
suspects.why: that fan starts at one and shuts off at three
the meter read the same with the lights off
custodians checked the pipes and found nothing
nothing in Room 9 itself was switched on at one

cases.answer: The gym fan rang the room back at its own pitch.
proof: “A room will ring back at a sound when the sound matches the room's own pitch.”
“The gym fan turns at a rate that matches Room 9 almost exactly.”
clears: The lights: “The sound meter read the same with the lights off as with them on.”
The pipes: “Custodians checked the pipes, the vents and the lights and found nothing.”
Something in Room 9: “Nothing in Room 9 itself was switched on at one.”
cases.explain: The hum keeps the fan's hours exactly. Because the fan's rate matches the pitch Room 9 rings at, a sound made next door gets amplified by the room itself, which is why nothing inside it had to be running.

debate.story: A low hum filled Room 9 every afternoon and nobody could find it. The hum never came before one o'clock and always stopped by three. Room 9 shares a wall with the gym, where a ceiling fan runs on a timer. That fan starts at one and shuts off at three every school day. A room will ring back at a sound when the sound matches the room's own pitch. The gym fan turns at a rate that matches Room 9 almost exactly. The overhead lights in Room 9 switch to a second ballast at one each day. An old ballast hums at a steady low pitch of its own. The projector in Room 9 is left on standby and its fan runs warm by one. The pipes were capped off in August when the old boiler went, and carry nothing.
debate.question: What is humming in Room 9? Pick one and prove it from the text.

suspects.who: 🌀 The gym fan on its timer
suspects.why: a gym fan on a timer from one to three, turning at a matching rate
a second ballast switching in at one, humming low
pipes capped off in August, carrying nothing
a projector left on standby, its fan warm by one

evidence: “That fan starts at one and shuts off at three every school day.”
“The gym fan turns at a rate that matches Room 9 almost exactly.”
arguments.against: “The overhead lights in Room 9 switch to a second ballast at one each day.”

evidence: “The overhead lights in Room 9 switch to a second ballast at one each day.”
“An old ballast hums at a steady low pitch of its own.”
arguments.against: “The hum never came before one o'clock and always stopped by three.”

evidence: “The projector in Room 9 is left on standby and its fan runs warm by one.”
“A room will ring back at a sound when the sound matches the room's own pitch.”
arguments.against: “That fan starts at one and shuts off at three every school day.”

clears: The pipes: “The pipes were capped off in August when the old boiler went, and carry nothing.”
debate.note: Three things now start at one o'clock, so one o'clock has stopped being evidence. Three is where the case still has teeth: the gym fan stops at three and the hum stops at three, while a ballast and a projector run until the last bell. A student who argues from the stop rather than the start is reading more carefully.

cases.title: The Case of the Early Bare Tree
cases.story: Four maples line the school drive and one stood bare three weeks early. All four were planted the same spring and are the same height. A tree drops its leaves when it stops sending water and food to them. Drought and heat both start that shutdown sooner than cold does. The bare tree stands at the end of the row beside the asphalt lot. A thermometer in its bed read nine degrees warmer than the beds of the other three. The lot drains away from that bed instead of into it. The groundskeeper watered all four on the same schedule all summer. No insect damage or disease was found on any of the four.
cases.question: Why did one maple go bare early?

suspects.who: 🅿️ Heat and dryness beside the lot
suspects.why: nine degrees warmer and the lot drains away from that bed
no insect damage or disease was found
the groundskeeper watered all four on the same schedule
all four were planted the same spring

cases.answer: Heat and dry soil beside the asphalt shut that tree down early.
proof: “Drought and heat both start that shutdown sooner than cold does.”
“A thermometer in its bed read nine degrees warmer than the beds of the other three.”
clears: Insects or disease: “No insect damage or disease was found on any of the four.”
Less watering: “The groundskeeper watered all four on the same schedule all summer.”
An older tree: “All four were planted the same spring and are the same height.”
cases.explain: Four identical trees, one different spot. Because the bed by the asphalt runs nine degrees hotter and sheds its water instead of holding it, that tree hit the heat-and-drought trigger weeks before the others.

debate.story: Four maples line the school drive and one stood bare three weeks early. A tree drops its leaves when it stops sending water and food to them. Drought and heat both start that shutdown sooner than cold does. The bare tree stands at the end of the row beside the asphalt lot. A thermometer in its bed read nine degrees warmer than the beds of the other three. The lot drains away from that bed instead of into it. The hose reaches the first three beds and the fourth is watered by bucket. Whoever carries the bucket has skipped it on four of the last ten rounds. The bare tree was replaced in its second year and is two years younger. A pest survey in July found nothing on any of the four.
debate.question: Why did one maple go bare early? Make the case for one cause.

suspects.who: 🅿️ Heat and dryness beside the lot
suspects.why: nine degrees warmer, beside a lot that drains away from it
a pest survey in July that found nothing
watered by bucket, and skipped four rounds in ten
replaced in its second year, two years younger than the rest

evidence: “A thermometer in its bed read nine degrees warmer than the beds of the other three.”
“The lot drains away from that bed instead of into it.”
arguments.against: “Whoever carries the bucket has skipped it on four of the last ten rounds.”

evidence: “The hose reaches the first three beds and the fourth is watered by bucket.”
“Whoever carries the bucket has skipped it on four of the last ten rounds.”
arguments.against: “A thermometer in its bed read nine degrees warmer than the beds of the other three.”

evidence: “The bare tree was replaced in its second year and is two years younger.”
“Four maples line the school drive and one stood bare three weeks early.”
arguments.against: “The lot drains away from that bed instead of into it.”

clears: Insects or disease: “A pest survey in July found nothing on any of the four.”
debate.note: Heat and dryness are the same shutdown by two routes, which the second sentence says outright. That makes the first two answers allies rather than rivals, and the strongest work in the room will be the student who says so and then argues which route matters more. The younger tree is the weakest case and it is not nothing.

cases.title: The Case of the Collapsed Pumpkin
cases.story: The front-step pumpkin stood firm on Friday and sat flat on Monday. No animal tracks, teeth marks or holes were found anywhere on it. The skin was unbroken and the stem was still attached. Saturday night dropped to twenty-six degrees and Sunday climbed back to fifty. Water swells as it freezes and pushes outward on whatever holds it. A pumpkin is mostly water held inside stiff cell walls. When those walls burst, the flesh goes soft and the shape gives way. The pumpkin felt heavy and wet rather than dried out and light. It had sat on that step through three warmer weeks without changing at all.
cases.question: What flattened the pumpkin?

suspects.why: water swells as it freezes and pushes outward
no animal tracks, teeth marks or holes were found
the skin was unbroken and the stem was still attached
it felt heavy and wet rather than dried out

cases.answer: Water froze inside the pumpkin and burst its cell walls.
proof: “Saturday night dropped to twenty-six degrees and Sunday climbed back to fifty.”
“When those walls burst, the flesh goes soft and the shape gives way.”
clears: An animal: “No animal tracks, teeth marks or holes were found anywhere on it.”
A hole letting it rot: “The skin was unbroken and the stem was still attached.”
Drying out: “The pumpkin felt heavy and wet rather than dried out and light.”
cases.explain: Three warm weeks changed nothing and one freezing night changed everything. Because the water inside swelled as it froze, it broke the cell walls from within, which is why the skin is whole and the pumpkin still flat.

debate.story: The front-step pumpkin stood firm on Friday and sat flat on Monday. Saturday night dropped to twenty-six degrees and Sunday climbed back to fifty. Water swells as it freezes and pushes outward on whatever holds it. A pumpkin is mostly water held inside stiff cell walls. When those walls burst, the flesh goes soft and the shape gives way. A split runs two inches along the base where it met the wet step. Soft rot starts at a split and spreads through the flesh in days. The step faces south and the pumpkin had sat in full sun for three weeks. A pumpkin that dries from one side caves toward the dry side. No tracks, teeth marks or droppings were found on the step or around it.
debate.question: Why did the pumpkin collapse? Choose one cause and back it up.

suspects.why: twenty-six degrees on Saturday night and fifty on Sunday
no tracks, teeth marks or droppings anywhere near it
a two-inch split at the base, on a wet step
three weeks of full sun on a south-facing step

evidence: “Saturday night dropped to twenty-six degrees and Sunday climbed back to fifty.”
“When those walls burst, the flesh goes soft and the shape gives way.”
arguments.against: “A split runs two inches along the base where it met the wet step.”

evidence: “A split runs two inches along the base where it met the wet step.”
“Soft rot starts at a split and spreads through the flesh in days.”
arguments.against: “The front-step pumpkin stood firm on Friday and sat flat on Monday.”

evidence: “The step faces south and the pumpkin had sat in full sun for three weeks.”
“A pumpkin that dries from one side caves toward the dry side.”
arguments.against: “Water swells as it freezes and pushes outward on whatever holds it.”

clears: An animal: “No tracks, teeth marks or droppings were found on the step or around it.”
debate.note: Friday firm, Monday flat, is the strongest fact and it fits the freeze best, because rot takes days and drying takes weeks. Hold the class to that timescale. The split is the real complication: it could be where the rot got in, or it could be where the frozen flesh gave way, and the story will not say which.

cases.title: The Case of the One-Sided Footprints
cases.story: Frost covered the field on Tuesday and footprints showed on only half of it. The prints ran in a clear line along the fence and stopped at the open grass. Whoever walked it did not turn around at that line. The fence throws shade over the north half until nearly noon. The open half takes direct sun from eight o'clock onward. Frost melts wherever the sun reaches it and holds wherever it does not. Both halves were frosted when the custodian opened up at seven. The groundskeeper walked the whole field at seven-fifteen on his usual round. By the time the class came out at ten, half the frost was gone.
cases.question: Why did the footprints stop halfway?

suspects.who: ☀️ Sun melting the frost on the open half
suspects.why: frost melts wherever the sun reaches it
whoever walked it did not turn around at that line
both halves were frosted at seven
the groundskeeper walked the whole field

cases.answer: The sun melted the frost that held the prints on the open half.
proof: “Frost melts wherever the sun reaches it and holds wherever it does not.”
“By the time the class came out at ten, half the frost was gone.”
clears: Somebody turning around: “Whoever walked it did not turn around at that line.”
Only half frosting: “Both halves were frosted when the custodian opened up at seven.”
A second person: “The groundskeeper walked the whole field at seven-fifteen on his usual round.”
cases.explain: The prints did not stop; the frost did. Because the fence shades the north half until noon and the open half takes sun from eight, only the shaded prints were still there at ten.

debate.story: Frost covered the field on Tuesday and footprints showed on only half of it. The prints ran in a clear line along the fence and stopped at the open grass. The fence throws shade over the north half until nearly noon. The open half takes direct sun from eight o'clock onward. Frost melts wherever the sun reaches it and holds wherever it does not. By the time the class came out at ten, half the frost was gone. The line of prints ends at a gate that opens onto the lane. A second, smaller set of prints crosses the shaded half at an angle. The custodian's round takes him along the fence and back the same way. The whole field was white in the seven o'clock photograph on the office wall.
debate.question: Why did the prints show on only half the field? Pick one and prove it.

suspects.who: ☀️ Sun melting the frost on the open half
suspects.why: shade until noon on one half, sun from eight on the other
a round that goes along the fence and back the same way
a seven o'clock photograph showing the whole field white
a second, smaller set crossing the shaded half

evidence: “Frost melts wherever the sun reaches it and holds wherever it does not.”
“By the time the class came out at ten, half the frost was gone.”
arguments.against: “The line of prints ends at a gate that opens onto the lane.”

evidence: “The custodian's round takes him along the fence and back the same way.”
“The prints ran in a clear line along the fence and stopped at the open grass.”
arguments.against: “The open half takes direct sun from eight o'clock onward.”

evidence: “A second, smaller set of prints crosses the shaded half at an angle.”
“The line of prints ends at a gate that opens onto the lane.”
arguments.against: “Frost melts wherever the sun reaches it and holds wherever it does not.”

clears: Only half frosting: “The whole field was white in the seven o'clock photograph on the office wall.”
debate.note: The photograph settles one suspect cleanly and everybody should use it. After that the question splits in two, and it is worth naming them separately: why the prints stop, and who made them. The sun answers the first and says nothing about the second, which is why the gate and the smaller prints are still in play.

cases.title: The Case of the Bus That Was Late Twice
cases.story: Bus 12 ran on time all month except on Tuesdays and Thursdays. On those two days it reached school between nine and twelve minutes late. The same driver drove the same route at the same hour every day. The bus left the depot on time on all five mornings. Traffic counts on the route showed no difference between the days. A freight line crosses the route at the halfway point. The rail yard schedules a loaded outbound train for Tuesday and Thursday mornings. A loaded freight at that crossing holds traffic for about ten minutes. The driver logged a stopped train at the crossing on both late days.
cases.question: Why was Bus 12 late only on Tuesdays and Thursdays?

suspects.who: 🚂 The Tuesday and Thursday freight train
suspects.why: a loaded freight holds traffic for about ten minutes
the bus left the depot on time on all five mornings
traffic counts showed no difference between the days
the same driver drove the same route at the same hour

cases.answer: A loaded freight train blocked the crossing on both days.
proof: “The rail yard schedules a loaded outbound train for Tuesday and Thursday mornings.”
“The driver logged a stopped train at the crossing on both late days.”
clears: Leaving late: “The bus left the depot on time on all five mornings.”
Heavier traffic: “Traffic counts on the route showed no difference between the days.”
A different driver: “The same driver drove the same route at the same hour every day.”
cases.explain: Nine to twelve minutes late, and a crossing that holds traffic about ten. Because the yard runs that loaded train on exactly those two mornings, the delay matches both the days and the length.

debate.story: Bus 12 ran on time all month except on Tuesdays and Thursdays. On those two days it reached school between nine and twelve minutes late. A freight line crosses the route at the halfway point. The rail yard schedules a loaded outbound train for Tuesday and Thursday mornings. A loaded freight at that crossing holds traffic for about ten minutes. The driver logged a stopped train at the crossing on both late days. The depot sheet shows Bus 12 leaving at 7:09 on Tuesdays and Thursdays and 7:01 on the other three. A relief driver covers those two mornings and has driven the route since September. The regular driver clocks in at the depot on all five days. A traffic count found the same number of cars on all five mornings.
debate.question: Why is Bus 12 late on two days? Pick one cause and prove it from the text.

suspects.who: 🚂 The Tuesday and Thursday freight train
suspects.why: a loaded freight scheduled for those two mornings, logged both times
leaving at 7:09 on those two days and 7:01 on the others
traffic counts that show no difference between the days
a relief driver who covers those two mornings

evidence: “The rail yard schedules a loaded outbound train for Tuesday and Thursday mornings.”
“The driver logged a stopped train at the crossing on both late days.”
arguments.against: “The depot sheet shows Bus 12 leaving at 7:09 on Tuesdays and Thursdays and 7:01 on the other three.”

evidence: “The depot sheet shows Bus 12 leaving at 7:09 on Tuesdays and Thursdays and 7:01 on the other three.”
“On those two days it reached school between nine and twelve minutes late.”
arguments.against: “A loaded freight at that crossing holds traffic for about ten minutes.”

evidence: “A relief driver covers those two mornings and has driven the route since September.”
“The regular driver clocks in at the depot on all five days. A traffic count found the same number of cars on all five mornings.”
arguments.against: “The driver logged a stopped train at the crossing on both late days.”

clears: Heavier traffic: “A traffic count found the same number of cars on all five mornings.”
debate.note: This one is arithmetic. The lateness is nine to twelve minutes, the train is about ten, and the late start is eight. Ask what the two together would come to and whether the bus is late enough for both. The relief driver is the weakest and the most human, and a student who argues it has to say what a different driver actually does differently.

cases.title: The Case of the Dull Trophy
cases.story: The 1998 trophy went dull and grey in the case over one winter break. The four trophies beside it stayed bright the whole time. Nobody opened the case and the lock was never broken. Silver turns dark when sulfur in the air reacts with its surface. Rubber bands and some foam release small amounts of sulfur as they age. The dull trophy sits on a foam pad that the others do not have. The custodian added that pad in December to stop a wobble. All five trophies were polished on the same day in November. The case holds the same air and light for every shelf.
cases.question: Why did one trophy go dull?

suspects.who: 🧽 Sulfur from the new foam pad
suspects.why: some foam releases small amounts of sulfur as it ages
all five trophies were polished on the same day in November
nobody opened the case and the lock was never broken
the case holds the same air and light for every shelf

cases.answer: Sulfur from the foam pad darkened the silver on that trophy.
proof: “Silver turns dark when sulfur in the air reacts with its surface.”
“The dull trophy sits on a foam pad that the others do not have.”
clears: Missing a polish: “All five trophies were polished on the same day in November.”
Somebody handling it: “Nobody opened the case and the lock was never broken.”
Light in the case: “The case holds the same air and light for every shelf.”
cases.explain: Five trophies, one new object. Because the pad went in during December and aging foam gives off the sulfur that darkens silver, the only trophy touching foam is the only one that went grey.

debate.story: The 1998 trophy went dull and grey in the case over one winter break. The four trophies beside it stayed bright the whole time. Silver turns dark when sulfur in the air reacts with its surface. Rubber bands and some foam release small amounts of sulfur as they age. The dull trophy sits on a foam pad that the others do not have. The custodian added that pad in December to stop a wobble. The 1998 trophy is the only one on the bottom shelf, beside the floor vent. The case lock was found open twice in January and the door ajar once. Every one of the five was polished on the same November afternoon.

debate.note: Two things are true of this trophy and no other: it has a foam pad and it sits alone by the vent. Both put more air past it than the rest get, which is why the vent argument is better than it first looks. The open lock is the one that explains dullness without explaining why only one went dull.

cases.title: The Case of the Cold Half Turkey
cases.story: The cafeteria turkey came out done on the left and underdone on the right. One thermometer read one hundred seventy-five degrees and the other one hundred forty-two. The bird was one piece and went in at one temperature. It roasted the full four hours the recipe called for. The oven was set to three hundred twenty-five and held it all morning. Ovens move heat with air, and anything blocking that air leaves a cold pocket. A full sheet of foil-covered rolls sat on the rack beside the right side. Those rolls went in at the same time as the turkey. A thermometer placed in the empty left half of the oven read correctly.
cases.question: Why was half the turkey underdone?

suspects.who: 🥖 The tray of rolls blocking the air
suspects.why: anything blocking that air leaves a cold pocket
it roasted the full four hours the recipe called for
the oven held three hundred twenty-five all morning
the bird was one piece and went in at one temperature

cases.answer: The tray of rolls blocked the hot air on the turkey's right side.
proof: “Ovens move heat with air, and anything blocking that air leaves a cold pocket.”
“A full sheet of foil-covered rolls sat on the rack beside the right side.”
clears: Not enough time: “It roasted the full four hours the recipe called for.”
A cold oven: “The oven was set to three hundred twenty-five and held it all morning.”
Two different birds: “The bird was one piece and went in at one temperature.”
cases.explain: One bird, one oven, two readings thirty degrees apart. Because an oven cooks by moving air and the rolls sat in the way on one side only, the blocked half never got the heat the other half did.

debate.story: The cafeteria turkey came out done on the left and underdone on the right. One thermometer read one hundred seventy-five degrees and the other one hundred forty-two. Ovens move heat with air, and anything blocking that air leaves a cold pocket. A full sheet of foil-covered rolls sat on the rack beside the right side. Those rolls went in at the same time as the turkey. The oven's fan motor has been replaced twice and the right vent is taped over. A fan pushing from one side only heats that side. The bird sat on a steel tray that overhangs the rack by four inches on the right. Steel under a bird shields it from the heat coming up underneath. It roasted for the whole four hours the recipe asks for.
debate.question: Why was one side of the turkey underdone? Make the case for one cause.

suspects.who: 🥖 The tray of rolls blocking the air
suspects.why: a full sheet of foil-covered rolls beside the right side
the full four hours the recipe called for
a right vent taped over, so that side never reaches temperature
a steel tray overhanging the rack by four inches on the right

“Those rolls went in at the same time as the turkey.”
arguments.against: “The oven's fan motor has been replaced twice and the right vent is taped over.”

evidence: “The oven's fan motor has been replaced twice and the right vent is taped over.”
“A fan pushing from one side only heats that side.”
arguments.against: “Ovens move heat with air, and anything blocking that air leaves a cold pocket.”

evidence: “The bird sat on a steel tray that overhangs the rack by four inches on the right.”
“Steel under a bird shields it from the heat coming up underneath. It roasted for the whole four hours the recipe asks for.”
arguments.against: “A full sheet of foil-covered rolls sat on the rack beside the right side.”

clears: Not enough time: “It roasted for the whole four hours the recipe asks for.”
debate.note: All three open answers block heat on the right, so the class is arguing about which blockage matters most rather than about where the problem is. That is a fair argument and the way to settle it is a test: move the rolls, untape the vent, change the tray, one at a time. A student who proposes that has done better than one who simply picks.

cases.title: The Case of the Cupcakes That Waited
cases.story: Two dozen cupcakes came out of the same oven and one dozen stayed flat. Both trays used the same bowl of batter mixed at the same time. Both went in at three hundred fifty and came out after nineteen minutes. Cupcakes rise on gas bubbles that baking soda makes when it meets acid. Those bubbles start forming the moment the wet and dry are stirred together. The first tray went in at once and the second waited forty minutes on the counter. Nobody opened the oven door while either tray was baking. The flat tray was the one that waited. Both trays were filled from the top of the same bowl.
cases.question: Why was one dozen flat?

suspects.who: ⏳ The forty-minute wait on the counter
suspects.why: the bubbles start the moment wet and dry are stirred
nobody opened the oven door while either tray was baking
both trays used the same bowl of batter
both went in at three hundred fifty

cases.answer: The batter that waited forty minutes had lost its bubbles.
proof: “Those bubbles start forming the moment the wet and dry are stirred together.”
“The first tray went in at once and the second waited forty minutes on the counter.”
clears: The oven door: “Nobody opened the oven door while either tray was baking.”
A different batter: “Both trays used the same bowl of batter mixed at the same time.”
A cooler oven: “Both went in at three hundred fifty and came out after nineteen minutes.”
cases.explain: Same batter, same oven, same time in it. Because the gas starts the instant the batter is stirred, the tray that sat for forty minutes had already let most of its bubbles go before it ever got hot.

debate.story: Two dozen cupcakes came out of the same oven and one dozen stayed flat. Cupcakes rise on gas bubbles that baking soda makes when it meets acid. Those bubbles start forming the moment the wet and dry are stirred together. The first tray went in at once and the second waited forty minutes on the counter. The flat tray was the one that waited. The second tray was filled from the bottom of the bowl, where the batter had settled. Batter that settles is heavier at the bottom than at the top. The second tray went into an oven that had already run for twenty minutes. One bowl of batter was mixed at one time and split between the two trays.
debate.question: Why did one tray stay flat? Pick one cause and back it up.

suspects.who: ⏳ The forty-minute wait on the counter
suspects.why: forty minutes on the counter, with bubbles forming from the first stir
a door nobody opened while either tray was baking
one bowl of batter, mixed at one time

suspects.who: 🥣 Batter from the bottom of the bowl
suspects.why: filled from the bottom of the bowl, where the batter had settled

evidence: “Those bubbles start forming the moment the wet and dry are stirred together.”
“The first tray went in at once and the second waited forty minutes on the counter.”
arguments.against: “The second tray was filled from the bottom of the bowl, where the batter had settled.”

evidence: “The second tray went into an oven that had already run for twenty minutes.”
“Two dozen cupcakes came out of the same oven and one dozen stayed flat.”
arguments.against: “The flat tray was the one that waited.”

evidence: “The second tray was filled from the bottom of the bowl, where the batter had settled.”
“Batter that settles is heavier at the bottom than at the top.”
arguments.against: “Those bubbles start forming the moment the wet and dry are stirred together.”

clears: A different batter: “One bowl of batter was mixed at one time and split between the two trays.”
debate.note: Same bowl rules the recipe out, and everything left is about the forty minutes: the gas escaped, the batter settled, and the oven changed. Those are three consequences of one delay, and the honest answer says so. Ask which of the three would still have happened if the bowl had been stirred again before the second tray was filled.

cases.title: The Case of the Wet Mittens Inside
cases.story: Ivy's mittens came in soaked on the inside and dry on the outside. The outer shell is coated and water beaded on it all recess. No snow got past the cuffs, which she had tucked under her sleeves. The puddles on the blacktop were shallow and she never put her hands in. Working hands give off water as vapor, and a coated shell will not let vapor out. Vapor turns back into water when it reaches the cold inside of the shell. Ivy dug in the snowbank for the whole twenty minutes. Her classmates in uncoated knit mittens came in damp all the way through. The mittens weighed more coming in than they did going out.
cases.question: Why were the mittens wet inside?

suspects.who: 💦 Her own hands giving off vapor
suspects.why: a coated shell will not let vapor out
no snow got past the cuffs
she never put her hands in
water beaded on the outside all recess

cases.answer: Vapor from her hands condensed inside the coated mitten shell.
proof: “Working hands give off water as vapor, and a coated shell will not let vapor out.”
“Vapor turns back into water when it reaches the cold inside of the shell.”
clears: Snow in the cuffs: “No snow got past the cuffs, which she had tucked under her sleeves.”
Puddles: “The puddles on the blacktop were shallow and she never put her hands in.”
A hole in the shell: “The outer shell is coated and water beaded on it all recess.”
cases.explain: The water came from the inside out. Because a coated shell keeps vapor in as well as rain out, twenty minutes of digging put enough water in the air inside the mitten to soak it from within.

debate.story: Ivy's mittens came in soaked on the inside and dry on the outside. Working hands give off water as vapor, and a coated shell will not let vapor out. Vapor turns back into water when it reaches the cold inside of the shell. Ivy dug in the snowbank for the whole twenty minutes. The mittens weighed more coming in than they did going out. The left cuff had worked out from under her sleeve by the end of recess. She packed snowballs with bare hands for five minutes and put the mittens back on wet. The seam across the right palm has come unstitched for about an inch. Her classmates in uncoated knit mittens came in damp all the way through.
debate.question: Why were the mittens wet inside? Argue for one cause.

suspects.who: 💦 Her own hands giving off vapor
suspects.why: a coated shell that will not let her own vapor out
a left cuff worked out from under her sleeve by the end

“Vapor turns back into water when it reaches the cold inside of the shell.”
arguments.against: “The left cuff had worked out from under her sleeve by the end of recess.”

evidence: “The left cuff had worked out from under her sleeve by the end of recess.”
“Ivy dug in the snowbank for the whole twenty minutes.”
arguments.against: “The mittens weighed more coming in than they did going out.”

evidence: “The seam across the right palm has come unstitched for about an inch.”
“Her classmates in uncoated knit mittens came in damp all the way through.”
arguments.against: “Working hands give off water as vapor, and a coated shell will not let vapor out.”

clears: Wet hands from snowballs: “She packed snowballs with bare hands for five minutes and put the mittens back on wet.”
debate.note: Both mittens came in soaked, and the cuff fault is on the left while the seam fault is on the right. That is the detail that beats both of them, and it is one sentence apart from each. The vapor answer is the only one that acts on both hands at once, which is a good reason to prefer it and worth making the class say out loud.

cases.title: The Case of the Cracked Gingerbread
cases.story: Six gingerbread walls came off one baking sheet and two cracked in half. The dough was rolled from one batch and cut with the same cutter. All six baked eleven minutes and came out looking identical. A sheet of baked dough shrinks a little as it cools and gives up water. Dough cooling unevenly shrinks unevenly, and the stress splits it at the thinnest line. Four walls cooled on a rack in the open kitchen for an hour. The two that cracked were moved straight to the cold windowsill. A thermometer on that sill read thirty-one degrees that afternoon. Nobody touched, stacked or dropped any of the six walls.
cases.question: Why did two walls crack?

suspects.who: 🪟 Cooling fast on the cold sill
suspects.why: dough cooling unevenly shrinks unevenly
nobody touched, stacked or dropped any of the six
the dough was rolled from one batch
all six baked eleven minutes

cases.answer: The two walls moved to the cold sill cooled unevenly and split.
proof: “Dough cooling unevenly shrinks unevenly, and the stress splits it at the thinnest line.”
“The two that cracked were moved straight to the cold windowsill.”
clears: Somebody handling them: “Nobody touched, stacked or dropped any of the six walls.”
A different batch: “The dough was rolled from one batch and cut with the same cutter.”
Baking too long: “All six baked eleven minutes and came out looking identical.”
cases.explain: Six identical walls, two different cooling spots. Because a thirty-one degree sill pulls heat out of one face far faster than the other, the shrinking went uneven and the dough split where it was thinnest.

debate.story: Six gingerbread walls came off one baking sheet and two cracked in half. A sheet of baked dough shrinks a little as it cools and gives up water. Dough cooling unevenly shrinks unevenly, and the stress splits it at the thinnest line. Four walls cooled on a rack in the open kitchen for an hour. The two that cracked were moved straight to the cold windowsill. A thermometer on that sill read thirty-one degrees that afternoon. The two cracked walls were cut from the last of the dough, rolled thin to make them fit. A thin wall carries the same shrinking stress across less gingerbread. The sill walls were laid flat on the stone and the rack walls had air underneath. No wall was lifted, stacked or knocked by anybody.

suspects.why: moved straight to a sill reading thirty-one degrees
nobody touching, stacking or dropping any of the six

“A thermometer on that sill read thirty-one degrees that afternoon.”
arguments.against: “The two cracked walls were cut from the last of the dough, rolled thin to make them fit.”

“A thin wall carries the same shrinking stress across less gingerbread.”
arguments.against: “A thermometer on that sill read thirty-one degrees that afternoon.”

evidence: “The sill walls were laid flat on the stone and the rack walls had air underneath. No wall was lifted, stacked or knocked by anybody.”
“Dough cooling unevenly shrinks unevenly, and the stress splits it at the thinnest line.”
arguments.against: “Six gingerbread walls came off one baking sheet and two cracked in half.”

clears: Somebody handling them: “No wall was lifted, stacked or knocked by anybody.”
debate.note: The same two walls are the thin ones, the cold ones and the ones on stone, so every difference lands on the same pair. That is the hardest shape a case can take and it is worth naming. The sentence about uneven cooling is the rule in the story, and the stone answer is the only one that uses it directly.

cases.title: The Case of the Half-Dark String
cases.story: Half the hallway light string went dark and the other half stayed lit. The dark half runs from the twenty-sixth bulb to the fiftieth. Each half of this string is wired so the current passes through every bulb in turn. When one bulb in such a line fails, the whole line it belongs to goes out. The lit half is wired as its own separate line. Mr. Cole tested the outlet and it carried full power. He checked the plug and the cord and found no break or fray. The twenty-sixth bulb rattled when he shook it and its filament was broken. Every other bulb in the dark half tested fine in a working socket.
cases.question: Why did half the string go dark?

suspects.why: when one bulb in such a line fails, the whole line goes out
he tested the outlet and it carried full power
he found no break or fray
every other bulb in the dark half tested fine

cases.answer: One broken bulb opened the line that half the string runs on.
proof: “When one bulb in such a line fails, the whole line it belongs to goes out.”
“The twenty-sixth bulb rattled when he shook it and its filament was broken.”
clears: The outlet: “Mr. Cole tested the outlet and it carried full power.”
A break in the cord: “He checked the plug and the cord and found no break or fray.”
All the bulbs: “Every other bulb in the dark half tested fine in a working socket.”
cases.explain: Twenty-five bulbs went out and twenty-four of them still work. Because that half is one line with the current running through every bulb in turn, the single broken filament at number twenty-six is enough to darken all of them.

debate.story: Half the hallway light string went dark and the other half stayed lit. The dark half runs from the twenty-sixth bulb to the fiftieth. Each half of this string is wired so the current passes through every bulb in turn. When one bulb in such a line fails, the whole line it belongs to goes out. The twenty-sixth bulb rattled when he shook it and its filament was broken. The socket for the twenty-sixth bulb is cracked and the bulb sits loose in it. A bulb that is not seated breaks the line as surely as a broken filament does. Water from a leaking window ran down the wall behind bulbs twenty-six to thirty. The outlet reads full power on the tester and runs the lit half fine.
debate.question: Why did half the string go dark? Pick one cause and prove it from the text.

suspects.why: a twenty-sixth bulb that rattles, with a broken filament
an outlet that tested at full power
a cracked socket where the bulb sits loose
water running down the wall behind bulbs twenty-six to thirty

evidence: “The twenty-sixth bulb rattled when he shook it and its filament was broken.”
“When one bulb in such a line fails, the whole line it belongs to goes out.”
arguments.against: “The socket for the twenty-sixth bulb is cracked and the bulb sits loose in it.”

evidence: “The socket for the twenty-sixth bulb is cracked and the bulb sits loose in it.”
“A bulb that is not seated breaks the line as surely as a broken filament does.”
arguments.against: “The twenty-sixth bulb rattled when he shook it and its filament was broken.”

evidence: “Water from a leaking window ran down the wall behind bulbs twenty-six to thirty.”
“The dark half runs from the twenty-sixth bulb to the fiftieth.”
arguments.against: “Each half of this string is wired so the current passes through every bulb in turn.”

clears: The outlet: “The outlet reads full power on the tester and runs the lit half fine.”
debate.note: Everything in this case points at bulb twenty-six and the class should say so before arguing. The question underneath is what caused what: a cracked socket lets a bulb rattle, rattling breaks a filament, and water gets into a cracked socket. Ordering those three is the real work, and the story deliberately leaves the order out.

cases.title: The Case of the Clock That Lost Four Minutes
cases.story: The hallway clock lost about four minutes a day all through January. It had kept time to the second for the six years before that. The battery tested at full voltage and the hands moved freely. Nothing was rubbing the hands and the glass had not been struck. This clock keeps time with a thin metal wheel that turns at a fixed rate. Metal expands when it warms and that makes the wheel turn more slowly. The clock hangs directly above a radiator that was replaced in December. A thermometer taped beside the clock read ninety-four degrees in January. The identical clock at the far end of the hall kept perfect time.
cases.question: Why was the clock losing time?

suspects.why: metal expands when it warms and turns more slowly
the battery tested at full voltage
nothing was rubbing the hands
it had kept time to the second for six years

cases.answer: Heat from the radiator expanded the wheel and slowed the clock.
proof: “Metal expands when it warms and that makes the wheel turn more slowly.”
“A thermometer taped beside the clock read ninety-four degrees in January.”
clears: A weak battery: “The battery tested at full voltage and the hands moved freely.”
Something rubbing: “Nothing was rubbing the hands and the glass had not been struck.”
A faulty clock: “It had kept time to the second for the six years before that.”
cases.explain: Six perfect years, then four minutes a day the month a radiator went in underneath it. Because the wheel that sets the rate runs slower as it warms, ninety-four degrees is enough to cost four minutes every day.

debate.story: The hallway clock lost about four minutes a day all through January. For six years before that it had not drifted by a second. This clock keeps time with a thin metal wheel that turns at a fixed rate. Metal expands when it warms and that makes the wheel turn more slowly. The clock hangs directly above a radiator that was replaced in December. A thermometer taped beside the clock read ninety-four degrees in January. The battery was changed in December from the drawer of mixed spares. A battery that reads full voltage can still fail under load. The identical clock at the far end of the hall was also rehung in December. That one hangs over the stairwell, where the air is cold and still. The hands swing freely and the glass is unmarked.
debate.question: Why did the clock lose four minutes a day? Make the case for one cause.

suspects.why: a new radiator below it, and ninety-four degrees beside it
a December battery from the drawer of mixed spares
nothing rubbing the hands and no struck glass
rehung in December, over a radiator rather than a cold stairwell

evidence: “The clock hangs directly above a radiator that was replaced in December.”
“A thermometer taped beside the clock read ninety-four degrees in January.”
arguments.against: “The battery was changed in December from the drawer of mixed spares.”

evidence: “The battery was changed in December from the drawer of mixed spares.”
“A battery that reads full voltage can still fail under load.”
arguments.against: “Metal expands when it warms and that makes the wheel turn more slowly.”

evidence: “The identical clock at the far end of the hall was also rehung in December.”
“That one hangs over the stairwell, where the air is cold and still. The hands swing freely and the glass is unmarked.”
arguments.against: “For six years before that it had not drifted by a second.”

clears: Something rubbing the hands: “The hands swing freely and the glass is unmarked.”
debate.note: The second clock used to be a clean control and it has stopped being one, because it was also rehung in December and it is also somewhere with a temperature. It is still useful, just not as proof. Three things changed in December and only one of them is measured, which is why the thermometer reading carries the most weight.

cases.title: The Case of the Snow That Melted in Stripes
cases.story: Snow on the playground melted in stripes and left white bands between them. The bare stripes sit directly over the black rubber safety mat. The white bands sit over the light grey concrete beside it. Air temperature was thirty-four degrees across the whole playground. Dark surfaces take in more sunlight and give that heat back as warmth. Light surfaces throw much of the same sunlight away again. A surface thermometer read fifty-one on the rubber and thirty-six on the concrete. The snow fell evenly, and a ruler showed the same depth everywhere at dawn. No salt, sand or shovel had been anywhere near the playground all winter.
cases.question: Why did the snow melt in stripes?

suspects.who: ⬛ The dark rubber mat taking in sunlight
suspects.why: the rubber read fifty-one and the concrete thirty-six
no salt, sand or shovel had been near the playground
a ruler showed the same depth everywhere at dawn
air temperature was thirty-four degrees across the whole playground

cases.answer: The dark rubber mat took in sunlight and melted the snow above it.
proof: “Dark surfaces take in more sunlight and give that heat back as warmth.”
“A surface thermometer read fifty-one on the rubber and thirty-six on the concrete.”
clears: Salt: “No salt, sand or shovel had been anywhere near the playground all winter.”
Uneven snowfall: “The snow fell evenly, and a ruler showed the same depth everywhere at dawn.”
Warmer air: “Air temperature was thirty-four degrees across the whole playground.”
cases.explain: The air was the same everywhere and the ground was not. Because the black mat sat at fifty-one degrees while the concrete sat at thirty-six, the snow melted exactly where the dark surface was and nowhere else.

debate.story: Snow on the playground melted in stripes and left white bands between them. The bare stripes sit directly over the black rubber safety mat. The white bands sit over the light grey concrete beside it. Dark surfaces take in more sunlight and give that heat back as warmth. Light surfaces throw much of the same sunlight away again. A surface thermometer read fifty-one on the rubber and thirty-six on the concrete. The heating pipe to the gym runs under the rubber strip and not under the concrete. A buried pipe warms the ground above it whatever the sun is doing. The rubber strip is a hand's width lower than the concrete and water collects along it. suspects.why: fifty-one degrees on the dark rubber against thirty-six on the concrete
