“Water carries dye out of fabric a little at a time.”
arguments.against: “Sunlight breaks down the dyes in fabric and lightens the color over time.”

clears: Two different ribbons: “The ribbon runs unbroken from end to end and was never cut.”
debate.note: One ribbon, two colors, is the fact that makes this case work at all, and every answer has to respect it. All three open suspects act on the south stretch and nowhere else, so position cannot choose between them. Dates can: all season for the sun, May onward for the sprinkler, one afternoon in June for the thinner.

cases.title: The Case of the Balloons That Sank Overnight
cases.story: Thirty foil balloons touched the gym ceiling on Friday and rested on the floor on Monday. None of them had popped and every knot still held. Foil holds helium far better than latex and these were all foil. A gas shrinks when it cools and takes up less room than it did warm. A balloon floats only while it pushes aside more air than it weighs. A balloon that shrinks pushes aside less air and stops floating. The gym heat is switched off from Friday evening until Monday morning. A logger in the gym recorded sixty-eight degrees Friday and forty-one on Sunday. Every balloon measured smaller around on Monday than it had on Friday.
cases.question: Why did the balloons sink?

suspects.who: 🌡️ The cold gym shrinking the gas
suspects.why: a balloon that shrinks pushes aside less air and stops floating
foil holds helium far better than latex and these were all foil
none of them had popped and every knot still held
every balloon measured smaller around on Monday

cases.answer: The cold weekend gym shrank the helium until the balloons sank.
proof: “A logger in the gym recorded sixty-eight degrees Friday and forty-one on Sunday.”
“Every balloon measured smaller around on Monday than it had on Friday.”
clears: Helium leaking: “Foil holds helium far better than latex and these were all foil.”
A leak or a pop: “None of them had popped and every knot still held.”
Heavier ribbons: “Every balloon measured smaller around on Monday than it had on Friday.”
cases.explain: The measurement is the proof: they are smaller, not emptier. Because the heat went off and the gym fell to forty-one degrees, the helium shrank, each balloon pushed aside less air, and thirty of them stopped floating at once.

debate.story: Thirty foil balloons touched the gym ceiling on Friday and rested on the floor on Monday. A gas shrinks when it cools and takes up less room than it did warm. A balloon floats only while it pushes aside more air than it weighs. A balloon that shrinks pushes aside less air and stops floating. The gym heat is switched off from Friday evening until Monday morning. A logger in the gym recorded sixty-eight degrees Friday and forty-one on Sunday. The gym was at sixty-six degrees by nine on Monday and the balloons stayed down. A foil balloon loses a little helium through its valve over several days. Each balloon was retied on Friday with a longer ribbon and a small paper weight. Every knot still held and not one balloon had popped.
debate.question: Why did the balloons sink? Pick one cause and prove it from the text.

suspects.who: 🌡️ The cold gym shrinking the gas
suspects.why: sixty-eight degrees on Friday and forty-one on Sunday
a valve that loses a little helium over several days
every knot holding and not one popped
retied Friday with a longer ribbon and a paper weight

evidence: “A logger in the gym recorded sixty-eight degrees Friday and forty-one on Sunday.”
“The gym heat is switched off from Friday evening until Monday morning.”
arguments.against: “The gym was at sixty-six degrees by nine on Monday and the balloons stayed down.”

evidence: “A foil balloon loses a little helium through its valve over several days.”
“The gym was at sixty-six degrees by nine on Monday and the balloons stayed down.”
arguments.against: “A gas shrinks when it cools and takes up less room than it did warm.”

evidence: “Each balloon was retied on Friday with a longer ribbon and a small paper weight.”
“A balloon floats only while it pushes aside more air than it weighs.”
arguments.against: “Thirty foil balloons touched the gym ceiling on Friday and rested on the floor on Monday.”

clears: A leak or a pop: “Every knot still held and not one balloon had popped.”
debate.note: One sentence breaks the old answer wide open: the gym was warm again on Monday morning and the balloons were still down. Cold shrinks a balloon and warmth gives it back, so a cold weekend alone should have undone itself. A student who finds that line has found the strongest argument in the case, whichever side they take it to.

cases.title: The Case of the Overdue Twenty
cases.story: Twenty books from Ms. Ortiz's class showed overdue on March 17. The library had changed its loan period from fourteen days to twenty-one on March 1. Her class checked the books out on March 2, and every printed slip reads March 23. The catalog listed all twenty as due March 16. A power cut on March 10 shut the system down for most of a day. Staff rebuilt the catalog from a backup copy made on February 26. The new twenty-one-day rule was entered into the system on March 1. Nothing borrowed after March 11 has shown overdue at all. No librarian edited a due date, and the log confirms it. The slips and the catalog disagree by exactly seven days.
cases.question: Why does the catalog call the twenty books overdue?

suspects.why: staff rebuilt the catalog from a backup copy made on February 26
nothing borrowed after March 11 has shown overdue at all
no librarian edited a due date, and the log confirms it
every printed slip reads March 23

cases.answer: The rebuilt catalog is running the old fourteen-day rule.
proof: “Staff rebuilt the catalog from a backup copy made on February 26.”
“The new twenty-one-day rule was entered into the system on March 1.”
clears: The power cut: “Nothing borrowed after March 11 has shown overdue at all.”
A librarian: “No librarian edited a due date, and the log confirms it.”
The class: “every printed slip reads March 23.”
cases.explain: Everything in the story happened. The order is what settles it: the backup was made on February 26 and the new rule went in on March 1, so the copy staff restored had never heard of the twenty-one-day loan. The books are due March 23, exactly as the slips say.

cases.title: The Case of the Warm Milk at Third Lunch
cases.story: Milk cartons were cold at first lunch and warm at third. The cooler door was propped open from 10:40 to 11:05 for a delivery. A thermometer inside the cooler read 38 degrees at 10:30. It read 51 at 11:10 and was back to 39 by noon. Cartons for third lunch were stacked on the open counter at 11:00. Third lunch begins at 12:35, and those cartons had sat out since. The delivery truck's cartons were checked on arrival and read 36 degrees. The cooler motor ran all day without stopping once. First lunch cartons came straight from the cooler at 11:15. That counter sits beside the ovens on the warm side of the kitchen. Nobody touched the thermostat, and the setting is logged each morning.
cases.question: Why was the milk warm at third lunch?

suspects.who: 🥛 The cartons stacked on the counter
suspects.why: cartons for third lunch were stacked on the open counter at 11:00
it read 51 at 11:10 and was back to 39 by noon
the delivery truck's cartons were checked on arrival and read 36 degrees
the cooler motor ran all day without stopping once

cases.answer: The third lunch cartons had been out on the counter since 11:00.
proof: “Cartons for third lunch were stacked on the open counter at 11:00.”
“Third lunch begins at 12:35, and those cartons had sat out since.”
clears: The propped door: “It read 51 at 11:10 and was back to 39 by noon.”
The truck: “The delivery truck's cartons were checked on arrival and read 36 degrees.”
The motor: “The cooler motor ran all day without stopping once.”
cases.explain: The door really was propped open, and that really did warm the cooler. It also recovered by noon, half an hour before third lunch began. The cartons that spent ninety minutes on a counter are the ones that were warm.

cases.title: The Case of the Full Shavings Bin
cases.story: Mr. Reyes empties the sharpener bin at three o'clock every afternoon. On Tuesday morning at nine the bin was full to the rim. His first period class had not arrived yet when he found it. The custodian empties the wastebaskets nightly but never opens the sharpener. Chess club met in the room from 3:15 to 4:30 on Monday afternoon. They had worked through a packet of score sheets in pencil. The sharpener itself turned smoothly and showed no jam at all. Monday's last class left at 2:50, before the bin was emptied. Nobody has a key to the room except Mr. Reyes and the custodian. Tuesday's bin held shavings from at least two dozen sharpened pencils. The bin was empty when he locked up Monday at three.
cases.question: Who filled the shavings bin?

suspects.why: chess club met in the room from 3:15 to 4:30 on Monday afternoon
the custodian empties the wastebaskets nightly but never opens the sharpener
Monday's last class left at 2:50, before the bin was emptied
the sharpener itself turned smoothly and showed no jam at all

cases.answer: Chess club filled the bin after Mr. Reyes emptied it.
proof: “The bin was empty when he locked up Monday at three.”
“Chess club met in the room from 3:15 to 4:30 on Monday afternoon.”
clears: The custodian: “the custodian empties the wastebaskets nightly but never opens the sharpener.”
Monday's last class: “Monday's last class left at 2:50, before the bin was emptied.”
A jam: “The sharpener itself turned smoothly and showed no jam at all.”
cases.explain: Monday's last class really did sharpen pencils, and the bin really did hold their shavings. Then it was emptied at three. Only the group that used the room after three could have refilled it.

cases.title: The Case of the Tray That Browned
cases.story: Two trays of apple slices went out for the tasting at nine o'clock. Tray A came out brown at the edges and tray B stayed pale and clean. Both trays were cut from the same bag of the same variety. Both got two spoons of lemon juice brushed over every slice. Both sat on the same counter in the same room all morning. Tray A was cut at 8:00 and the juice went on at 8:20. Tray B was cut at 8:30 and brushed within a minute. Cut apple begins browning the moment the flesh meets air. Lemon juice slows the browning that follows but cannot lift what is done. Nobody opened a window or ran a fan over either tray. The refrigerator was not used for either tray.
cases.question: Why did only tray A brown?

suspects.who: ⏱️ The twenty-minute gap on tray A
suspects.why: tray A was cut at 8:00 and the juice went on at 8:20
both trays were cut from the same bag of the same variety

suspects.who: 🍋 Less lemon juice on tray A
suspects.why: both got two spoons of lemon juice brushed over every slice
the refrigerator was not used for either tray

cases.answer: Tray A sat cut and bare for twenty minutes before the juice went on.
proof: “Tray A was cut at 8:00 and the juice went on at 8:20.”
“Lemon juice slows the browning that follows but cannot lift what is done.”
clears: Variety: “Both trays were cut from the same bag of the same variety.”
The juice: “Both got two spoons of lemon juice brushed over every slice.”
The refrigerator: “The refrigerator was not used for either tray.”
cases.explain: Both trays got the same treatment, so the only difference is when they got it. Twenty minutes of bare cut flesh is browning the lemon juice arrived too late to prevent.

cases.title: The Case of the Brake That Faded
cases.story: Nadia's rear brake went soft at the bottom of the long hill on Pine Road. At the top of that same hill it had gripped perfectly well. Next morning it gripped perfectly well again from the first squeeze. The short hill on Vine is steeper and her brake has never faded there. Pine Road falls gently for almost a mile without a level stretch. Vine drops hard for one block and then flattens out completely. Her pads were measured on Saturday and sit well within the wear limit. The day was dry and her rims were clean and dry throughout. Rubbing a brake builds heat, and heat builds the longer the rubbing lasts. On Pine she held the brake lightly the whole way down.
cases.question: Why did the brake fade on Pine and not on Vine?

suspects.who: 🔥 Heat from a mile of steady braking
suspects.why: on Pine she held the brake lightly the whole way down
her pads were measured on Saturday and sit well within the wear limit
the day was dry and her rims were clean and dry throughout
the short hill on Vine is steeper and her brake has never faded there

cases.answer: A mile of steady braking on Pine built up heat in the rim.
proof: “Pine Road falls gently for almost a mile without a level stretch.”
“Rubbing a brake builds heat, and heat builds the longer the rubbing lasts.”
clears: The pads: “Her pads were measured on Saturday and sit well within the wear limit.”
Wet rims: “The day was dry and her rims were clean and dry throughout.”
Steepness: “The short hill on Vine is steeper and her brake has never faded there.”
cases.explain: Steepness is the obvious answer and the story rules it out: Vine is steeper and never fades. What Pine has is length. The brake works the whole way down, and the heat has a mile to build.

cases.title: The Case of the Cloud That Came Late
cases.story: The class tank turned milky on a Thursday and stayed that way for a week. Two new fish had been added a full two weeks before the cloud appeared. The gravel had been scrubbed clean in hot water on the Monday before. Invisible bacteria live in tank gravel and break down fish waste there. Hot water kills those bacteria, and a new colony takes about a week to build. Waste builds up with nothing to break it down, and the water clouds. Feeding has been one pinch a day since September and has not changed. The filter was opened on Thursday and its motor and pads were clean. The cloud began three days after the gravel was scrubbed. The two new fish had swum in clear water for a fortnight.
cases.question: What clouded the tank?

suspects.who: 🧼 Scrubbing the gravel in hot water
suspects.why: the gravel had been scrubbed clean in hot water on the Monday before
the two new fish had swum in clear water for a fortnight
feeding has been one pinch a day since September and has not changed
the filter was opened on Thursday and its motor and pads were clean

cases.answer: Scrubbing the gravel killed the bacteria that break down waste.
proof: “Hot water kills those bacteria, and a new colony takes about a week to build.”
“The cloud began three days after the gravel was scrubbed.”
clears: The new fish: “The two new fish had swum in clear water for a fortnight.”
Feeding: “Feeding has been one pinch a day since September and has not changed.”
The filter: “The filter was opened on Thursday and its motor and pads were clean.”
cases.explain: New fish are the first thing anyone suspects, and these fish are real. They had also been in the tank for two weeks of clear water. The cloud starts three days after the scrub, which is exactly how long it takes for waste to build with no bacteria left to eat it.

cases.title: The Case of the Hum That Quit at Noon
cases.story: A low hum filled Room 12 every morning and was gone by afternoon. Four things in the room run on electricity and might be making it. The projector is switched on at 8:05 and left on until the last bell. The fluorescent lights are on from 7:30 until the building closes at six. The drinking fountain's chiller cycles on and off all day and all night. The heating blower runs on a timer from 6:00 in the morning until noon. Mr. Dale stood under each one in turn with the room otherwise silent. The hum was loudest at the ceiling vent and faint everywhere else. On Tuesday the blower was shut off at nine and the hum stopped then. On Wednesday the timer ran as usual and the hum lasted until twelve.
cases.question: What is making the hum?

suspects.why: the heating blower runs on a timer from 6:00 in the morning until noon
the projector is switched on at 8:05 and left on until the last bell
the fluorescent lights are on from 7:30 until the building closes at six
the drinking fountain's chiller cycles on and off all day and all night

cases.answer: The heating blower hums, and its timer stops it at noon.
proof: “The heating blower runs on a timer from 6:00 in the morning until noon.”
“On Tuesday the blower was shut off at nine and the hum stopped then.”
clears: The projector: “The projector is switched on at 8:05 and left on until the last bell.”
The lights: “The fluorescent lights are on from 7:30 until the building closes at six.”
The chiller: “The drinking fountain's chiller cycles on and off all day and all night.”
cases.explain: All four really do hum, and three of them are still running at one o'clock when the room is quiet. Only one stops when the noise stops. The Tuesday test moves the ending, which is as close to proof as this case gets.

cases.title: The Case of the Side That Bared First
cases.story: The maple by the lot dropped every leaf on its east side in September. Its west side held green leaves into the middle of October. Salt is spread on that lot each winter and runs off toward the tree. A crew trenched a cable line along the east side of the tree in July. Roots cut in July cannot carry water to the branches above them. A tree sheds leaves it cannot supply, and the shedding shows up weeks later. The street lamp on the east side has burned every night for nine years. The whole tree was watered on the same schedule all summer long. Last winter's salt was spread in January, eight months before the drop. The trench ran within three feet of the trunk on the east side only.
cases.question: Why did only the east side go bare early?

suspects.why: a crew trenched a cable line along the east side of the tree in July
last winter's salt was spread in January, eight months before the drop
the street lamp on the east side has burned every night for nine years
the whole tree was watered on the same schedule all summer long

cases.answer: The July trench cut the roots feeding the east branches.
proof: “A crew trenched a cable line along the east side of the tree in July.”
“A tree sheds leaves it cannot supply, and the shedding shows up weeks later.”
clears: Salt: “Last winter's salt was spread in January, eight months before the drop.”
The lamp: “The street lamp on the east side has burned every night for nine years.”
Drought: “The whole tree was watered on the same schedule all summer long.”
cases.explain: Salt and the lamp are both on the east side, which is what makes them tempting. The lamp has been there nine years without doing this, and the salt went down in January. Only the trench happened on the side that bared, at a distance of weeks rather than months.

cases.title: The Case of the Pumpkin That Caved on Friday
cases.story: The front-step pumpkin was carved on Monday and caved in on Friday. It stood firm through Tuesday, Wednesday and most of Thursday. A flat slice had been cut off its base on Monday so it would sit level. That cut face rested all week on concrete still damp from Sunday's rain. Cut squash takes on water and softens from the cut inward over days. Wednesday's rain fell for an hour and the step is under a deep overhang. The candle inside is an electric one that gives off no heat at all. The uncarved gourd beside it sat on the same damp concrete and is firm. Thursday reached sixty-one degrees, which is mild for the end of October. The collapse began at the base and spread upward from there.
cases.question: Why did the pumpkin cave in?

suspects.who: 🪚 The cut base on damp concrete
suspects.why: that cut face rested all week on concrete still damp from Sunday's rain
the step is under a deep overhang
the candle inside is an electric one that gives off no heat at all
thursday reached sixty-one degrees, which is mild for the end of October

cases.answer: The cut base drew up water from the damp concrete all week.
proof: “Cut squash takes on water and softens from the cut inward over days.”
“The collapse began at the base and spread upward from there.”
clears: The rain: “the step is under a deep overhang.”
The candle: “The candle inside is an electric one that gives off no heat at all.”
The gourd test: “The uncarved gourd beside it sat on the same damp concrete and is firm.”
cases.explain: The gourd is the control. It sat on the same wet concrete all week and is still firm, so damp concrete alone does nothing. What the pumpkin had and the gourd did not is a cut face against it, soaking since Monday.

cases.title: The Case of the Prints That Went One Way
cases.story: Muddy prints led from the side door to the gym and stopped there. No prints at all led back out of the gym toward any door. The side door is the only unlocked way in before eight o'clock. Coach Benn found the prints at 7:35 and photographed them at once. The custodian mopped that hall at 8:10, well after the photographs. The other three doors were still bolted at 7:35 and the log confirms it. Wet mud prints; mud that has dried on a sole prints nothing. The lot outside was soft from rain that had stopped at 6:40. The gym floor is sealed wood and shows a wet print clearly. Whoever walked in at seven was in the gym for half an hour.
cases.question: Why are there no prints leading out?

suspects.why: wet mud prints; mud that has dried on a sole prints nothing
the other three doors were still bolted at 7:35 and the log confirms it
the custodian mopped that hall at 8:10, well after the photographs

suspects.who: 🪵 A floor that will not take a print
suspects.why: the gym floor is sealed wood and shows a wet print clearly

cases.answer: The mud dried on the soles before anyone walked back out.
proof: “Wet mud prints; mud that has dried on a sole prints nothing.”
“Whoever walked in at seven was in the gym for half an hour.”
clears: A second door: “The other three doors were still bolted at 7:35 and the log confirms it.”
The mopping: “The custodian mopped that hall at 8:10, well after the photographs.”
The floor: “The gym floor is sealed wood and shows a wet print clearly.”
cases.explain: The mopping really did happen and really does erase prints. It happened at 8:10, and the prints were photographed at 7:35. Half an hour inside a warm gym is all the drying a sole needs.

cases.title: The Case of the Bus That Lost Its Lead
cases.story: Bus 14 reaches school on time Monday, Wednesday and Friday and late on Tuesday and Thursday. It leaves the depot at 7:10 every single morning of the week. The same driver has held the route since September without one day off. The freight crossing on Mill Street closes its gates from 7:38 to 7:44 each weekday. On Monday, Wednesday and Friday the bus runs the stops in numbered order. On Tuesday and Thursday it runs them in reverse to balance the ride times. Running forward, it clears Mill Street at 7:31, before the gates come down. Running in reverse, it reaches Mill Street at 7:40 with the gates already down. Traffic counts on Mill Street are logged daily and vary by less than two percent. The late arrivals run between five and seven minutes behind.
cases.question: Why is bus 14 late on Tuesdays and Thursdays?

suspects.why: running in reverse, it reaches Mill Street at 7:40 with the gates already down
the same driver has held the route since September without one day off
traffic counts on Mill Street are logged daily and vary by less than two percent
it leaves the depot at 7:10 every single morning of the week

cases.answer: In reverse order the bus reaches the Mill Street crossing while the gates are down.
proof: “On Tuesday and Thursday it runs them in reverse to balance the ride times.”
“Running forward, it clears Mill Street at 7:31, before the gates come down.”
clears: The driver: “The same driver has held the route since September without one day off.”
Traffic: “Traffic counts on Mill Street are logged daily and vary by less than two percent.”
A late start: “It leaves the depot at 7:10 every single morning of the week.”
cases.explain: The crossing closes every weekday, so it cannot be blamed on its own. What changes is when the bus gets there. Forward it arrives seven minutes early; reversed it arrives two minutes into a six-minute closure.

cases.title: The Case of the Trophy That Dulled in the Case
cases.story: The silver relay trophy was polished bright in May and locked in the display case. By late September its surface had gone grey and faintly yellow all over. The case has not been opened since June, and only Ms. Pike holds a key. The trophy was handled with cotton gloves both times it was moved. The same tin of polish has been used on it every spring for ten years. In August the case floor was relined with a dark wool felt. Wool gives off a trace of sulfur, and sulfur turns silver grey over weeks. The hall's humidity is logged hourly and has held steady since spring. The brass plaque beside the trophy looks exactly as it did in May. The dulling was first noticed about five weeks after the relining.
cases.question: What dulled the trophy?

suspects.why: in August the case floor was relined with a dark wool felt
the trophy was handled with cotton gloves both times it was moved
the same tin of polish has been used on it every spring for ten years
the hall's humidity is logged hourly and has held steady since spring

cases.answer: The wool felt added in August gives off sulfur that tarnishes silver.
proof: “Wool gives off a trace of sulfur, and sulfur turns silver grey over weeks.”
“The dulling was first noticed about five weeks after the relining.”
clears: Fingerprints: “The trophy was handled with cotton gloves both times it was moved.”
The polish: “The same tin of polish has been used on it every spring for ten years.”
Humidity: “The hall's humidity is logged hourly and has held steady since spring.”
cases.explain: A polish used for ten years without this happening is not the new thing in the case. The felt is, and it went in five weeks before the grey appeared. The brass plaque is untouched because sulfur goes after silver.

cases.title: The Case of the Turkey That Was Not Done
cases.story: The turkey went into the oven at eleven for a four-hour roast. At three o'clock the thermometer read 150 instead of the 165 it needed. The thermometer was checked in boiling water that morning and read correctly. An oven thermometer sat on the rack beside the bird the whole time. It showed the oven climbing from cold and reaching 325 only at 11:35. The door was opened twice, for under a minute each time, to baste. The bird was fully thawed in the refrigerator over the three previous days. Its weight matched the four-hour chart exactly, with nothing added or removed. A roast times from the moment the oven holds its temperature, not from loading. The bird had thirty-five fewer minutes of real roasting than anyone counted.
cases.question: Why was the turkey still underdone at three?

suspects.why: it showed the oven climbing from cold and reaching 325 only at 11:35
the thermometer was checked in boiling water that morning and read correctly
the door was opened twice, for under a minute each time, to baste
the bird was fully thawed in the refrigerator over the three previous days

cases.answer: The oven did not reach 325 until 11:35, so the roast lost thirty-five minutes.
proof: “It showed the oven climbing from cold and reaching 325 only at 11:35.”
“A roast times from the moment the oven holds its temperature, not from loading.”
clears: The thermometer: “The thermometer was checked in boiling water that morning and read correctly.”
The door: “The door was opened twice, for under a minute each time, to baste.”
A frozen bird: “The bird was fully thawed in the refrigerator over the three previous days.”
cases.explain: Nothing was wrong with the bird, the oven or the thermometer. The clock started at eleven and the oven started at 11:35, and the thirty-five minutes between them were counted as roasting when they were not.

cases.title: The Case of the Cupcakes That Sank
cases.story: Every cupcake on the left tray sank into a crater in the middle. The right tray, baked after it, came out domed and even. Both trays came from one bowl of batter mixed at the same time. Both were filled two-thirds full, the way the class has always filled them. The baking powder was fresh and fizzed hard when dropped into vinegar. A cake sets its structure about two-thirds of the way through its bake. Cool air reaching a cake before it sets will drop the risen middle. The bake is eighteen minutes, and the oven door was opened at minute eight. It was opened to slide the right tray in beside the left one. The right tray was still liquid batter when the door was opened.
cases.question: Why did only the left tray sink?

suspects.who: 🚪 The door opened at minute eight
suspects.why: the bake is eighteen minutes, and the oven door was opened at minute eight
both trays came from one bowl of batter mixed at the same time
the baking powder was fresh and fizzed hard when dropped into vinegar
both were filled two-thirds full, the way the class has always filled them

cases.answer: The door opened at minute eight, before the left tray had set.
proof: “A cake sets its structure about two-thirds of the way through its bake.”
“The right tray was still liquid batter when the door was opened.”
clears: Too much powder: “Both trays came from one bowl of batter mixed at the same time.”
Old powder: “The baking powder was fresh and fizzed hard when dropped into vinegar.”
Overfilling: “Both were filled two-thirds full, the way the class has always filled them.”
cases.explain: One bowl of batter went onto both trays, so nothing about the recipe can explain a difference. The door opened once, at minute eight. The left tray was risen and not yet set; the right tray had not started.

cases.title: The Case of the Mittens Wet Inside
cases.story: Eleven pairs of mittens came back from recess soaked on the inside. The outsides of all eleven pairs were dry to the touch. These mittens have a sealed shell that was tested under a tap in November. Their cuffs are elastic and were worn under coat sleeves the whole time. Recess ran from 11:45 to 12:00 and the snow had stopped on Sunday. The hand dryer in the washroom has been broken since the Friday before. The class washed hands at 11:40 and went straight outside without drying them. Damp skin inside a sealed mitten has nowhere to send its water. The three students who skipped the sink came back with dry mittens. Nobody knelt, dug or threw snow during the fifteen minutes outside.
cases.question: Why were the mittens wet inside?

suspects.why: the class washed hands at 11:40 and went straight outside without drying them
their cuffs are elastic and were worn under coat sleeves the whole time
these mittens have a sealed shell that was tested under a tap in November
nobody knelt, dug or threw snow during the fifteen minutes outside

cases.answer: Damp hands went straight into the mittens at 11:40.
proof: “The class washed hands at 11:40 and went straight outside without drying them.”
“The three students who skipped the sink came back with dry mittens.”
clears: Snow: “Their cuffs are elastic and were worn under coat sleeves the whole time.”
A leak: “These mittens have a sealed shell that was tested under a tap in November.”
Sweat: “Nobody knelt, dug or threw snow during the fifteen minutes outside.”
cases.explain: The three who skipped the sink are the test. Same recess, same mittens, same weather, dry hands going in and dry mittens coming back. The water was already on the inside before anyone stepped outdoors.

cases.title: The Case of the Gingerbread That Split
cases.story: Four of the six gingerbread walls cracked across the middle by evening. The two that held were the ones iced last, at half past eleven. The dough was rolled to a quarter inch everywhere and measured in four places. All six walls came out of the oven together at ten o'clock. The first four were iced and joined at ten past ten, straight from the rack. Warm baked dough keeps shrinking a little as it cools to room temperature. Set icing cannot shrink with it, so the dough splits where the icing holds. The last two sat untouched for ninety minutes and were cool to the touch. Nobody dropped a wall or leaned on the finished house at any point. The same bowl of icing was used on all six walls.
cases.question: Why did four walls crack and two hold?

suspects.who: ⏲️ Icing the walls while still warm
suspects.why: the first four were iced and joined at ten past ten, straight from the rack
the dough was rolled to a quarter inch everywhere and measured in four places
the same bowl of icing was used on all six walls
nobody dropped a wall or leaned on the finished house at any point

cases.answer: The four cracked walls were iced warm and shrank under set icing.
proof: “Warm baked dough keeps shrinking a little as it cools to room temperature.”
“The last two sat untouched for ninety minutes and were cool to the touch.”
clears: Thin dough: “The dough was rolled to a quarter inch everywhere and measured in four places.”
The icing: “The same bowl of icing was used on all six walls.”
A knock: “Nobody dropped a wall or leaned on the finished house at any point.”
cases.explain: Six walls, one dough, one bowl of icing, one oven. The only difference is the ninety minutes the last two spent cooling before anything was stuck to them.

cases.title: The Case of the String That Went Half Dark
cases.story: Half the light string went dark on Tuesday and the other half stayed lit. The dark half runs from the sixteenth bulb to the end of the string. An extension cord was added on Monday and the whole string lit all Monday evening. On Tuesday morning a bulb was borrowed from the string for a craft project. It came out of the sixteenth socket and was never put back. In this older string the bulbs sit in series, in one unbroken circuit. Removing any bulb breaks that circuit and darkens every bulb after it. The lit half proves the outlet and the fuse in the plug are fine. Every remaining bulb was pressed and checked and sits firmly in its socket. The darkness began the same morning the bulb was taken.
cases.question: Why did half the string go dark?

suspects.who: 🔌 The bulb taken from socket sixteen
suspects.why: it came out of the sixteenth socket and was never put back
the lit half proves the outlet and the fuse in the plug are fine
an extension cord was added on Monday and the whole string lit all Monday evening
every remaining bulb was pressed and checked and sits firmly in its socket

cases.answer: A bulb was taken from the sixteenth socket and the circuit broke there.
proof: “Removing any bulb breaks that circuit and darkens every bulb after it.”
“The dark half runs from the sixteenth bulb to the end of the string.”
clears: The fuse: “The lit half proves the outlet and the fuse in the plug are fine.”
The cord: “An extension cord was added on Monday and the whole string lit all Monday evening.”
A loose bulb: “Every remaining bulb was pressed and checked and sits firmly in its socket.”
cases.explain: The extension cord is new and the cord is not the problem, because the string worked all Monday evening with it. The break is at socket sixteen, which is exactly where the lit half ends and the dark half starts.

cases.title: The Case of the Clocks That Agreed With Each Other
cases.story: All sixteen hall clocks read 2:14 when the office clock read 3:00. They have read exactly forty-six minutes slow every day since Tuesday. The hall clocks run on the building supply and carry no batteries at all. The office clock runs on a battery and has kept perfect time throughout. Tuesday's power cut began at 9:12 and the supply came back at 9:58. A clock that runs slow falls further behind every day that passes. These clocks have lost forty-six minutes and have not lost a second since. Nobody has opened a clock case or touched a hand all week. Sixteen clocks could not all be reset by hand to the same wrong minute. The gap has stayed at forty-six minutes through four school days.
cases.question: Why are all sixteen clocks forty-six minutes slow?

suspects.why: tuesday's power cut began at 9:12 and the supply came back at 9:58
a clock that runs slow falls further behind every day that passes
the hall clocks run on the building supply and carry no batteries at all
sixteen clocks could not all be reset by hand to the same wrong minute

cases.answer: The clocks stood still for the forty-six minutes of the power cut.
proof: “Tuesday's power cut began at 9:12 and the supply came back at 9:58.”
“These clocks have lost forty-six minutes and have not lost a second since.”
clears: A slow mechanism: “A clock that runs slow falls further behind every day that passes.”
Batteries: “The hall clocks run on the building supply and carry no batteries at all.”
Resetting: “Nobody has opened a clock case or touched a hand all week.”
cases.explain: A slow clock keeps getting slower, and these have been forty-six minutes behind for four days running. That is not a clock losing time. That is sixteen clocks that stopped together for forty-six minutes and started again.

cases.title: The Case of the Pile That Outlasted the Other
cases.story: Two snow piles were plowed from the same storm on the same Friday. The lot pile was gone by Sunday and the field pile lasted until Thursday. Both were measured at plowing and stood within a foot of the same height. Neither pile was salted, and the salt barrel has not been opened since January. Both sit in full sun from nine in the morning until four. The lot pile was pushed onto asphalt that had baked in sun since Wednesday. The field pile was pushed onto grass that had been under old snow all week. Dark asphalt holds the day's heat and keeps giving it back for hours. Ground that has been covered by snow all week is already at freezing. The snow that landed on warm asphalt started melting from underneath at once.
cases.question: Why did the lot pile melt four days sooner?

suspects.who: 🌡️ The warm asphalt under the lot pile
suspects.why: the lot pile was pushed onto asphalt that had baked in sun since Wednesday
both were measured at plowing and stood within a foot of the same height
neither pile was salted, and the salt barrel has not been opened since January
both sit in full sun from nine in the morning until four

cases.answer: The lot pile sat on asphalt that was already warm when the snow landed.
proof: “Dark asphalt holds the day's heat and keeps giving it back for hours.”
“The snow that landed on warm asphalt started melting from underneath at once.”
clears: Size: “Both were measured at plowing and stood within a foot of the same height.”
Salt: “Neither pile was salted, and the salt barrel has not been opened since January.”
Shade: “Both sit in full sun from nine in the morning until four.”
cases.explain: Same storm, same hour, same sun, same size. What differs is what the ground had been doing in the days before the plow came: one surface spent three days collecting heat and the other spent a week under snow.

cases.title: The Case of the Feeder on the Open Post
cases.story: The feeder went quiet on a Saturday after a winter of steady visitors. The seed was opened that same week and is dry, clean and sweet-smelling. A window film went up in March, and the birds fed through all of April. A hawk was seen in the yard once, in February, and not since. On Friday the class moved the feeder from the hedge to an open post. The post stands eleven feet from the nearest branch or shrub. Small birds feed where cover is within a short hop of the perch. A bird on an open post can be seen from every direction at once. Nothing else about the feeder, the seed or the yard was changed. The visits stopped the morning after the move.
cases.question: Why did the birds stop coming?

suspects.who: 🪵 The move to the open post
suspects.why: on Friday the class moved the feeder from the hedge to an open post
the seed was opened that same week and is dry, clean and sweet-smelling
a window film went up in March, and the birds fed through all of April
a hawk was seen in the yard once, in February, and not since

cases.answer: The feeder now stands eleven feet from any cover.
proof: “Small birds feed where cover is within a short hop of the perch.”

The film: “A window film went up in March, and the birds fed through all of April.”
The hawk: “A hawk was seen in the yard once, in February, and not since.”
cases.explain: The film and the hawk are both real and both scare birds. They are also months old, and the birds kept feeding after each one. The feeder moved on Friday and the visits stopped on Saturday.

cases.title: The Case of the Cocoa Full of Lumps
cases.story: The first pot of cocoa came out lumpy and the second came out smooth. Both pots used powder from the same tin, opened in November and still dry. Both were stirred for a full minute by the clock, without stopping. Both pots of milk were heated to the same 160 degrees on the same burner. For the first pot the powder was poured straight into the hot milk. For the second the powder was stirred into a splash of cold milk first. Cocoa powder meeting hot liquid seals on the outside of each clump instantly. That seal traps dry powder inside, and stirring cannot reach what is sealed. Cold milk wets the powder through before any sealing can happen. The lumps in the first pot were dry powder when they were cut open.
cases.question: Why was only the first pot lumpy?

suspects.who: 🥛 Powder going straight into hot milk
suspects.why: for the first pot the powder was poured straight into the hot milk
both pots used powder from the same tin, opened in November and still dry
both were stirred for a full minute by the clock, without stopping
both pots of milk were heated to the same 160 degrees on the same burner

cases.answer: The powder met hot milk before it had been wetted by cold milk.
proof: “Cocoa powder meeting hot liquid seals on the outside of each clump instantly.”
“The lumps in the first pot were dry powder when they were cut open.”
clears: Old powder: “Both pots used powder from the same tin, opened in November and still dry.”
Stirring: “Both were stirred for a full minute by the clock, without stopping.”
Heat: “Both pots of milk were heated to the same 160 degrees on the same burner.”
cases.explain: Same tin, same minute of stirring, same temperature. The order is the whole difference. Once a clump seals, a minute of stirring is a minute spent on the outside of it.

cases.title: The Case of the Valentines One Bag Over
cases.story: Almost every student got the card meant for whoever sits beside them. Nobody got a card at random, and nobody got two cards from one person. The room was locked from Wednesday afternoon until Thursday morning. Two students share the first name Jordan, which would explain exactly two mix-ups. On Wednesday the cards were sorted into bags arranged in seating order. On Thursday morning a helper lined the bags up in alphabetical order. The labels stayed on the bags, but the cards had already been dropped in. Cards sorted by position go wrong the moment the positions change. The mix-up runs the same direction for the whole class, not here and there. The first bag in both orders is the only one that is correct.

suspects.why: on Thursday morning a helper lined the bags up in alphabetical order
the room was locked from Wednesday afternoon until Thursday morning
two students share the first name Jordan, which would explain exactly two mix-ups
the labels stayed on the bags, but the cards had already been dropped in

cases.answer: The cards were sorted by seating order and the bags were then reordered.
proof: “On Wednesday the cards were sorted into bags arranged in seating order.”
“Cards sorted by position go wrong the moment the positions change.”
clears: A student: “The room was locked from Wednesday afternoon until Thursday morning.”
The Jordans: “Two students share the first name Jordan, which would explain exactly two mix-ups.”
The labels: “The labels stayed on the bags, but the cards had already been dropped in.”
cases.explain: Two students with one name explains two errors, and this is a whole class of them going the same way. The cards were dropped in on Wednesday against one order and read out on Thursday against another.

cases.title: The Case of the Volcano That Would Not Fizz
cases.story: Monday's volcano gave a weak gurgle where Friday's model had erupted properly. Both cones were built on the same mold from the same batch of paste. Friday's soda went into the cone and the vinegar followed within a minute. Monday's soda had been loaded into its cone on Friday afternoon. That cone's papier-mache was still damp when the soda went in. Baking soda reacts slowly with damp acidic paste and gives up its gas quietly. Over a weekend a damp cone can use up most of the soda inside it. The soda scraped out on Monday no longer fizzed in a test cup.
cases.question: Why did Monday's volcano barely erupt?

suspects.who: 📅 Soda left in a damp cone since Friday
suspects.why: monday's soda had been loaded into its cone on Friday afternoon
the vinegar was tested on fresh soda in a cup and fizzed hard
both received two level spoons of baking soda, measured with the same spoon
both cones were built on the same mold from the same batch of paste

cases.answer: The soda spent the weekend reacting quietly with the damp cone.
proof: “Over a weekend a damp cone can use up most of the soda inside it.”
“The soda scraped out on Monday no longer fizzed in a test cup.”
clears: The vinegar: “The vinegar was tested on fresh soda in a cup and fizzed hard.”
The amount: “Both received two level spoons of baking soda, measured with the same spoon.”
The cone: “Both cones were built on the same mold from the same batch of paste.”
cases.explain: Two level spoons went into each cone, so the amount is not the problem. One of them had three days to be spent before anyone poured anything. The test cup settles it: that soda was already finished.

cases.title: The Case of the Crown That Shrank
cases.story: Dev's paper crown closed easily at ten o'clock and would not meet at half past eleven. The strip was cut to twenty-two inches, measured twice with a checked tape. His head measures twenty-one inches and has not changed since September. The strip was brushed all over with wet paste before the gems went on. Paper takes up water, swells a little, and gives that length back as it dries. At ten the paste was wet and the strip was still damp through. By half past eleven the crown was dry, stiff and about an inch short. No one trimmed the strip, and the cut ends still show the original marks. The other crowns, glued at the ends only, all still close.
cases.question: Why would the crown not close by half past eleven?

suspects.why: the strip was brushed all over with wet paste before the gems went on
the strip was cut to twenty-two inches, measured twice with a checked tape
no one trimmed the strip, and the cut ends still show the original marks
his head measures twenty-one inches and has not changed since September

cases.answer: The pasted strip was swollen at ten and gave the length back as it dried.
proof: “Paper takes up water, swells a little, and gives that length back as it dries.”
“The other crowns, glued at the ends only, all still close.”
clears: The measurement: “The strip was cut to twenty-two inches, measured twice with a checked tape.”
Trimming: “No one trimmed the strip, and the cut ends still show the original marks.”
A growing head: “His head measures twenty-one inches and has not changed since September.”
cases.explain: The crowns pasted only at the ends are the control, and they all still fit. Dev's was wet from end to end when he measured it against his head, and twenty-two inches of damp paper is not twenty-two inches of dry paper.

cases.title: The Case of the Piano That Soured in Four Days
cases.story: The hall piano was tuned on Monday and sounded wrong by Friday morning. The same tuner tuned the chapel piano the same afternoon, and it still holds. The hall piano was not moved, opened or played by anyone over the weekend. The hall is heated and the radiators were switched on for the season on Tuesday. The chapel has no radiator and sat at the same temperature all week. Dry heat pulls moisture out of wood over several days, not all at once. A soundboard that loses moisture shrinks, and shrinking wood slackens every string. The hall's humidity gauge fell from forty-two percent Tuesday to twenty-four by Friday. The chapel's gauge has not moved from forty-one percent all week. Both pianos are the same make and were last serviced in the same month.
cases.question: Why did only the hall piano go out of tune?

suspects.why: the hall is heated and the radiators were switched on for the season on Tuesday
the same tuner tuned the chapel piano the same afternoon, and it still holds
the hall piano was not moved, opened or played by anyone over the weekend
both pianos are the same make and were last serviced in the same month

cases.answer: The radiators dried the hall air and the soundboard shrank.
proof: “The hall's humidity gauge fell from forty-two percent Tuesday to twenty-four by Friday.”
“A soundboard that loses moisture shrinks, and shrinking wood slackens every string.”
clears: The tuner: “The same tuner tuned the chapel piano the same afternoon, and it still holds.”
Playing: “The hall piano was not moved, opened or played by anyone over the weekend.”
Age: “Both pianos are the same make and were last serviced in the same month.”
cases.explain: The chapel piano is the control: same tuner, same afternoon, same make, still in tune. The one thing the hall got that the chapel did not was a radiator switched on the day after the tuning.

cases.title: The Case of the Kite That Waited for Four
cases.story: The kite would not climb at noon and flew well at four, three days running. The same kite, tail and string were used at both hours each day. The spars were checked for cracks on the first afternoon and are sound. The rooftop weather station logged the wind at nine miles an hour all day. A line of tall pines runs along the whole west edge of the field. The morning wind comes from the west and the pines break it before the field. By mid-afternoon the wind swings around to the south every day. The south side of the field is open ground with nothing standing on it. A rooftop reading is taken above the trees and misses what they do below. The windsock on the field hangs limp at noon and stands out at four.
cases.question: Why would the kite only fly after four?

suspects.who: 🌲 The pines blocking the morning wind
suspects.why: the morning wind comes from the west and the pines break it before the field
the rooftop weather station logged the wind at nine miles an hour all day
the same kite, tail and string were used at both hours each day
the spars were checked for cracks on the first afternoon and are sound

cases.answer: The pines break the west wind at noon, and the wind swings south by four.
proof: “A line of tall pines runs along the whole west edge of the field.”
“The windsock on the field hangs limp at noon and stands out at four.”
clears: Wind speed: “The rooftop weather station logged the wind at nine miles an hour all day.”
The tail: “The same kite, tail and string were used at both hours each day.”
A spar: “The spars were checked for cracks on the first afternoon and are sound.”
cases.explain: The rooftop number says the wind never changed, and it is measured above the trees. The windsock on the ground says otherwise. What changes at four is not how hard the wind blows but which side of the field it arrives from.

cases.title: The Case of the Shamrock on Its Own Clock
cases.story: The shamrock folded its leaves at ten past four every day for a week. It folded at ten past four on the cloudy Tuesday as well as the bright Monday. On Wednesday it sat in a dark supply closet from noon onward. It folded at ten past four in the closet, with no light reaching it at all. On Thursday the lamp above it was left burning all afternoon and evening. It folded at ten past four under the lamp, exactly as on every other day. Some plants fold on a daily rhythm their own cells keep without any cue. The room was held at seventy degrees by thermostat the whole week. It was watered every morning at eight on the same schedule as always. Nothing in the week shifted that folding by more than two minutes.
cases.question: What makes the shamrock fold at ten past four?

suspects.why: some plants fold on a daily rhythm their own cells keep without any cue
it folded at ten past four in the closet, with no light reaching it at all
it was watered every morning at eight on the same schedule as always
the room was held at seventy degrees by thermostat the whole week

cases.answer: The plant keeps its own daily rhythm, with or without light.
proof: “It folded at ten past four in the closet, with no light reaching it at all.”
“It folded at ten past four under the lamp, exactly as on every other day.”
clears: Light: “It folded at ten past four in the closet, with no light reaching it at all.”
Water: “It was watered every morning at eight on the same schedule as always.”
Cooling: “The room was held at seventy degrees by thermostat the whole week.”
cases.explain: Light is the answer everybody reaches for, and the week was built to test it. Darkness at noon did not move the folding and a lamp burning past midnight did not move it either. The clock is inside the plant.

cases.title: The Case of the Puddle That Outlived the Rain
cases.story: One puddle in the lot is still there three days after every rain. The rest of the lot dries within a few hours of the last drop. Rain falls on the whole lot at once and in the same amount. The storm drain twenty feet away was flushed in May and runs freely. The spot sits in open sun from morning until late afternoon. A crew dug up that spot in June to reach a water line underneath. Soil that has been dug and refilled settles over the months that follow. A level laid across the spot shows it sitting an inch below the lot. Water runs downhill and collects wherever the surface drops below its surroundings. The puddle's outline matches the edges of the June patch almost exactly.
cases.question: Why does one puddle stay for days?

suspects.why: a crew dug up that spot in June to reach a water line underneath
the storm drain twenty feet away was flushed in May and runs freely
the spot sits in open sun from morning until late afternoon
rain falls on the whole lot at once and in the same amount

cases.answer: The June patch settled an inch below the rest of the lot.
proof: “A level laid across the spot shows it sitting an inch below the lot.”
“The puddle's outline matches the edges of the June patch almost exactly.”
clears: The drain: “The storm drain twenty feet away was flushed in May and runs freely.”
Shade: “The spot sits in open sun from morning until late afternoon.”
The rain: “Rain falls on the whole lot at once and in the same amount.”
cases.explain: The drain is clear and the sun reaches it, so nothing is stopping the water from leaving. Something is holding it. The outline of the puddle is the outline of a hole dug in June and refilled, which has been sinking ever since.

cases.title: The Case of the Bed That Grew Nothing
cases.story: Not one seed came up in the raised bed, six weeks after planting. Seed from the same packet was laid on a damp towel indoors as a test. Those sprouted in four days, which rules out a problem with the seed. The bed was netted from the day of planting and shows no bird marks. It was watered every evening and the soil is damp four inches down. On March 28 the bed was treated against weeds before the season began. That product coats the soil and stops any seed from sprouting for six weeks. The class planted its seeds on April 2, five days after the treatment. Weeds have not come up in that bed either, anywhere along its length. The bed beside it, left untreated, is thick with both seedlings and weeds.
cases.question: Why did nothing come up?

suspects.why: on March 28 the bed was treated against weeds before the season began
those sprouted in four days, which rules out a problem with the seed
the bed was netted from the day of planting and shows no bird marks
it was watered every evening and the soil is damp four inches down

cases.answer: The bed was treated five days before the seeds went in.
proof: “That product coats the soil and stops any seed from sprouting for six weeks.”
“Weeds have not come up in that bed either, anywhere along its length.”
clears: The seed: “Those sprouted in four days, which rules out a problem with the seed.”
Birds: “The bed was netted from the day of planting and shows no bird marks.”
Water: “It was watered every evening and the soil is damp four inches down.”
cases.explain: The bare weeds are the clue nobody looks at. A bed that grows no weeds either is not a bed with a seed problem. It was treated on March 28 to stop seeds, and seeds went into it on April 2.

cases.title: The Case of the Egg That Rose
cases.story: One egg floated upright in the bowl while the other five lay flat on the bottom. All six were raw and none had been boiled at any point. Every shell was checked under a lamp and not one carried a crack. The bowl held plain tap water with no salt or sugar added. A shell is slightly porous, and an egg loses water through it over weeks. As water leaves, the air pocket at the blunt end grows larger and lighter. Five of the eggs came from a carton dated the twelfth of this month. The floating egg came from a carton at the back dated five weeks earlier. The older egg's air pocket measured almost twice the width of the others. Nothing else about the six eggs differed in size, color or handling.
cases.question: Why did one egg float?

suspects.why: the floating egg came from a carton at the back dated five weeks earlier
every shell was checked under a lamp and not one carried a crack
the bowl held plain tap water with no salt or sugar added
all six were raw and none had been boiled at any point

cases.answer: The floating egg is five weeks older and has lost water through its shell.
proof: “As water leaves, the air pocket at the blunt end grows larger and lighter.”
“The older egg's air pocket measured almost twice the width of the others.”
clears: A crack: “Every shell was checked under a lamp and not one carried a crack.”
Salt: “The bowl held plain tap water with no salt or sugar added.”
Boiling: “All six were raw and none had been boiled at any point.”
cases.explain: All six eggs are in the same water, so the water cannot explain a difference. What one egg has that the others do not is five extra weeks of losing water through a shell that lets it go.

cases.title: The Case of the Shadow That Jumped
cases.story: The class marks the pole's shadow at ten o'clock on the first of each month. The October mark and the November mark sit nearly a hand apart. Two weeks of autumn moves the midday sun by only a small amount. A jump that size would take months of the season changing, not weeks. The pole stands in concrete and was checked for lean before each marking. Both marks were photographed, and the chalk lines are clear in both pictures. The clocks were set back one hour on the last Sunday in October. The October mark was made before that change and the November mark after. Ten o'clock in November falls an hour earlier in the sun's own day. The same student made both marks, standing in the same place each time.
cases.question: Why did the shadow jump so far in a month?

suspects.why: the clocks were set back one hour on the last Sunday in October
a jump that size would take months of the season changing, not weeks
the pole stands in concrete and was checked for lean before each marking
the same student made both marks, standing in the same place each time

cases.answer: Ten o'clock in November is an hour earlier in the sun's day than ten in October.
proof: “The clocks were set back one hour on the last Sunday in October.”
“The October mark was made before that change and the November mark after.”
clears: The season: “A jump that size would take months of the season changing, not weeks.”
The pole: “The pole stands in concrete and was checked for lean before each marking.”
The observer: “The same student made both marks, standing in the same place each time.”
cases.explain: The season really does move the shadow, which is why the class marks it. It moves slowly. An hour of the sun's travel in a single Sunday night moves it far more, and that is what sits between these two marks.

cases.title: The Case of the One Blurred Runner
cases.story: Three runners came out sharp in the finish photograph and the fourth came out smeared. The camera was braced on a fence post and the background is perfectly sharp. All four runners were the same distance from the lens when the shutter opened. The shutter stayed open for one sixtieth of a second on every frame. A subject moving across the frame crosses many pixels in that time. A subject moving straight toward the lens barely shifts across the frame at all. Three of the runners were driving directly at the camera down the straight. The fourth had already crossed the line and was turning left off the track. The timing sheet shows she ran the slowest of the four. Her smear runs sideways across the picture, not toward or away from it.
cases.question: Why was only one runner blurred?

suspects.who: ↔️ Her sideways motion across the frame
suspects.why: her smear runs sideways across the picture, not toward or away from it
the camera was braced on a fence post and the background is perfectly sharp
all four runners were the same distance from the lens when the shutter opened
the timing sheet shows she ran the slowest of the four

cases.answer: She was moving across the frame while the others came straight at the lens.
proof: “A subject moving across the frame crosses many pixels in that time.”
“The fourth had already crossed the line and was turning left off the track.”
clears: A shaken camera: “The camera was braced on a fence post and the background is perfectly sharp.”

Her speed: “The timing sheet shows she ran the slowest of the four.”
cases.explain: Speed is the first guess and the timing sheet kills it: she was the slowest on the track. One sixtieth of a second is the same for all four. What differs is the direction they spent it travelling.

cases.title: The Case of the Bean That Leaned at Night
cases.story: The bean plant leans away from the window and toward the back of the room. A plant bends toward whatever light reaches it for the most hours. The window faces east and gives direct sun from seven until about one. The grow lamp at the back of the room is on a timer each day. That timer runs the lamp from two in the afternoon until midnight. Ten hours of lamp against six hours of morning sun is not a close contest. The pot was turned a quarter turn weekly and the lean came back each time. Its roots have room, and the soil was changed three weeks ago. The stem is thick, straight and shows no damage at any point. The lean points directly at the lamp and not at any corner of the room.
cases.question: Why does the plant lean away from the window?

suspects.who: 💡 The grow lamp on its timer
suspects.why: that timer runs the lamp from two in the afternoon until midnight
the window faces east and gives direct sun from seven until about one
its roots have room, and the soil was changed three weeks ago
the stem is thick, straight and shows no damage at any point

cases.answer: The lamp gives ten hours of light a day and the window gives six.
proof: “Ten hours of lamp against six hours of morning sun is not a close contest.”
“The lean points directly at the lamp and not at any corner of the room.”
clears: The window: “The window faces east and gives direct sun from seven until about one.”
The pot: “Its roots have room, and the soil was changed three weeks ago.”
The stem: “The stem is thick, straight and shows no damage at any point.”
cases.explain: Sunlight is brighter than a lamp, which is why this looks wrong. A plant answers to hours as well as brightness, and the lamp is on for ten of them while the sun is on that window for six.

cases.title: The Case of the Two Bowls on One Table
cases.story: Ice cream in the metal bowl was soup in ten minutes and the ceramic bowl held firm. Both scoops came from the same carton at one o'clock exactly. Both bowls sat side by side on the same table in the same room. Metal carries heat quickly, which is the answer everybody offered first. A second metal bowl was taken straight from the cupboard and tested next. Its scoop lasted as long as the ceramic one did, to within a minute. The first metal bowl had been in the dish rack by the sunny window since noon. It measured ninety-one degrees when the ice cream went into it. The cupboard bowl and the ceramic bowl both measured sixty-eight degrees. A warm bowl has heat of its own to give before the room's heat matters.

suspects.who: ☀️ An hour in the sunny dish rack
suspects.why: the first metal bowl had been in the dish rack by the sunny window since noon
its scoop lasted as long as the ceramic one did, to within a minute
both scoops came from the same carton at one o'clock exactly
both bowls sat side by side on the same table in the same room

cases.answer: That bowl was already ninety-one degrees when the scoop went in.
proof: “It measured ninety-one degrees when the ice cream went into it.”
“A warm bowl has heat of its own to give before the room's heat matters.”

The scoop: “Both scoops came from the same carton at one o'clock exactly.”
The room: “Both bowls sat side by side on the same table in the same room.”
cases.explain: The second metal bowl is the whole case. Same metal, same table, same carton, and it behaved like the ceramic one. The difference was never the material. It was the hour the first bowl spent in the sun before anyone used it.

cases.title: The Case of the Ribbon Faded on One Side

the covered spot proves the dye was the same color on every ribbon
none of them has ever been washed or cleaned in any way
the heating vent below the board blows on all of them equally

cases.title: The Case of the Balloons on the Floor
cases.story: Every latex balloon was on the floor by morning and every foil balloon was still up. All of them were filled from the same tank between two and three yesterday. Not one balloon showed a tear, a pinhole or a loose knot. Eighteen hours had passed between filling and the morning they were found down.

suspects.why: latex is full of tiny gaps, and helium atoms are small enough to slip through
cold air would have brought the foil balloons down as well as the latex
each was filled to the same marked ring on the side of the nozzle
all of them were filled from the same tank between two and three yesterday

cases.title: The Case of the Book in Two Places
cases.story: The circulation report shows one copy of Hatchet checked out to two students at once. Neither student has ever met the other, and both have the book in hand. Ms. Vega holds both copies on the desk, and the spines are plainly different ages. The older copy was bought in 2011 and the newer one replaced a lost book in 2019. Every item in the catalog is supposed to carry a barcode of its own. The 2019 replacement was entered by copying the record of the book it replaced. Copying a record copies its barcode, and two items then answer to one number. The scanner was tested forty times on known items and misread nothing. Neither student's card has been lent, and both scanned their own at the desk. The system clock agrees with the office clock to the second. A report can only be as good as the records it adds up.
cases.question: How is one book checked out twice?

suspects.why: the 2019 replacement was entered by copying the record of the book it replaced
neither student's card has been lent, and both scanned their own at the desk
the scanner was tested forty times on known items and misread nothing
the system clock agrees with the office clock to the second
a report can only be as good as the records it adds up

cases.answer: Two books share one barcode, so the catalog sees a single copy.
proof: “The 2019 replacement was entered by copying the record of the book it replaced.”
“Copying a record copies its barcode, and two items then answer to one number.”

The scanner: “The scanner was tested forty times on known items and misread nothing.”
The clock: “The system clock agrees with the office clock to the second.”
The report: “A report can only be as good as the records it adds up.”
cases.explain: Nothing in the library did anything strange. Two real books are in two real hands. The catalog has only one record between them, so every true fact about both gets written into one line and comes out looking impossible.

cases.title: The Case of the Log That Read 38 All Week
cases.story: Food in the staff refrigerator spoiled over a week in which the log read 38 degrees daily. The log has a line for each weekday and a space for initials. All five lines read exactly 38, with no variation of even a single degree. All five were written in the same blue pen in one continuous hand. A refrigerator opened and closed all day does not hold one reading for five days. The thermometer inside was tested in ice water on Friday and read 32 correctly. The compressor runs and the door seal grips a sheet of paper firmly. No power interruption was recorded in the building at any point that week. A dial thermometer left in overnight on Friday read 47 by morning. The log was filled in on Friday afternoon from memory for the whole week. A record written after the fact is a memory, not a measurement.
cases.question: Why did the food spoil when the log said 38?

suspects.who: 📝 A log filled in from memory
suspects.why: the log was filled in on Friday afternoon from memory for the whole week
the thermometer inside was tested in ice water on Friday and read 32 correctly
the compressor runs and the door seal grips a sheet of paper firmly
no power interruption was recorded in the building at any point that week
a dial thermometer left in overnight on Friday read 47 by morning

cases.answer: The log was written on Friday from memory and never measured anything.
proof: “All five were written in the same blue pen in one continuous hand.”
“A refrigerator opened and closed all day does not hold one reading for five days.”
clears: The thermometer: “The thermometer inside was tested in ice water on Friday and read 32 correctly.”
The seal: “The compressor runs and the door seal grips a sheet of paper firmly.”
A power cut: “No power interruption was recorded in the building at any point that week.”
cases.explain: The refrigerator really is running warm, and the Friday dial reading of 47 shows it. The log hid that for five days, and it hid it by never being a log. Five identical numbers in one pen is a page somebody filled out, not a week somebody measured.

cases.title: The Case of the Fifty Missing Pencils
cases.story: The order was for two hundred pencils and the supply closet holds one hundred and fifty. The invoice says two hundred and the delivery was signed for by the office. Eight boxes arrived, and every box label reads twenty-five count in bold print. Eight boxes at twenty-five each is the two hundred the invoice charged for. Mr. Hale opened every box and counted what was inside each one. Six boxes held twenty-five pencils and two held exactly eighteen apiece. The supplier changed its packaging in the autumn and kept printing the old label. The closet has been locked since the delivery and only Mr. Hale holds a key. No pencil has been handed out from that closet since the boxes arrived. Six twenty-fives and two eighteens come to one hundred and eighty-six, not two hundred. The count on the shelf was taken from the labels and not from the pencils.
cases.question: Where did the fifty pencils go?

suspects.why: the supplier changed its packaging in the autumn and kept printing the old label
the closet has been locked since the delivery and only Mr. Hale holds a key
the invoice says two hundred and the delivery was signed for by the office
no pencil has been handed out from that closet since the boxes arrived
the count on the shelf was taken from the labels and not from the pencils

cases.answer: Two boxes labelled twenty-five held eighteen pencils each.
proof: “Six boxes held twenty-five pencils and two held exactly eighteen apiece.”
“The supplier changed its packaging in the autumn and kept printing the old label.”
clears: Somebody taking them: “The closet has been locked since the delivery and only Mr. Hale holds a key.”
Handing them out: “No pencil has been handed out from that closet since the boxes arrived.”
The shelf count: “The count on the shelf was taken from the labels and not from the pencils.”
cases.explain: The delivery was short and nobody noticed, because everyone who counted was reading labels. The school was charged for two hundred and received one hundred and eighty-six. The remaining gap is the shelf count, which also trusted the print on the box.

cases.title: The Case of the Heavier Apples
cases.story: Group C's apples each weighed about forty grams more than every other group's. All four groups drew their apples from the same crate on the same morning. The apples were measured with a caliper and matched across groups to within a millimetre. Each group used an identical digital scale from the same classroom set. Group C weighed each apple sitting in a small plastic tray for steadiness. The other three groups set each apple directly on the scale plate. A scale zeroed empty counts whatever sits on it, tray included. The trays from that set weigh thirty-nine grams each on a checked balance. Group C zeroed its scale before the tray went on and not after. Every group recorded the number in the display without adjusting it. The apples themselves were never weighed, only the apples plus something else.
cases.question: Why were group C's apples heavier?

suspects.why: group C weighed each apple sitting in a small plastic tray for steadiness
the apples were measured with a caliper and matched across groups to within a millimetre
each group used an identical digital scale from the same classroom set
all four groups drew their apples from the same crate on the same morning
every group recorded the number in the display without adjusting it

cases.answer: Group C weighed the tray along with every apple.
proof: “Group C zeroed its scale before the tray went on and not after.”
“The trays from that set weigh thirty-nine grams each on a checked balance.”
clears: Bigger apples: “The apples were measured with a caliper and matched across groups to within a millimetre.”
The scale: “Each group used an identical digital scale from the same classroom set.”
The crate: “All four groups drew their apples from the same crate on the same morning.”
cases.explain: Nothing is wrong with the scale and nothing is wrong with the apples. The thirty-nine grams of tray is in every one of group C's numbers, which is why the gap is the same size every time instead of varying the way a real difference would.

cases.title: The Case of the Ride That Grew
cases.story: Priya's bike computer says she rode fourteen miles on a route the map measures at eleven. It has said the same thing on four different rides this month. The map distance was checked twice with a measuring wheel along the whole route. She did not take a detour, and her riding partner's computer read eleven. A bike computer counts wheel turns and multiplies by the wheel size it is set to. Her setting reads 2096 millimetres, the figure for a 700c road wheel. Her bike has 26-inch wheels, which roll about 2070 millimetres a turn. A wrong setting cannot change the distance ridden, only the distance displayed. The magnet is tight and a loose one would undercount, not overcount. Her partner's computer is set to the wheel size that partner's bike actually has. The ratio between fourteen and eleven is far larger than those two wheel figures explain.
cases.question: Why does the computer read three miles long?

suspects.why: a wrong setting cannot change the distance ridden, only the distance displayed
the map distance was checked twice with a measuring wheel along the whole route
she did not take a detour, and her riding partner's computer read eleven
the magnet is tight and a loose one would undercount, not overcount
the ratio between fourteen and eleven is far larger than those two wheel figures explain

cases.answer: The computer is set for a wheel her bike does not have.
proof: “Her setting reads 2096 millimetres, the figure for a 700c road wheel.”
“A wrong setting cannot change the distance ridden, only the distance displayed.”
clears: The map: “The map distance was checked twice with a measuring wheel along the whole route.”
A detour: “She did not take a detour, and her riding partner's computer read eleven.”
The magnet: “The magnet is tight and a loose one would undercount, not overcount.”
cases.explain: Priya rode eleven miles. She has ridden eleven miles every time. The only thing that grew is a number on a display, and the last line is the warning: the gap is bigger than the wheel figures alone account for, so the setting is further off than she thinks.

cases.title: The Case of the Test That Said Zero
cases.story: The nitrate test reads zero every week while the fish hang near the surface and eat poorly. Zero nitrate in a stocked tank that has run since September is not believable. Something is always breaking down waste, and the end of that process is nitrate. The kit's second bottle must be shaken hard for thirty seconds before use. Its contents settle into a layer that will not mix on its own. The class has been adding drops from a bottle nobody has shaken since October. The kit's printed expiry is next June, so it has not run out of date. The tank's filter runs, the heater holds 76, and the water is clear. A sample taken to the pet shop on Saturday tested at 80 parts per million. A reading of zero from an unshaken bottle is not a measurement of anything.
cases.question: Why does the test read zero?

suspects.why: the class has been adding drops from a bottle nobody has shaken since October
the kit's printed expiry is next June, so it has not run out of date
zero nitrate in a stocked tank that has run since September is not believable
the tank's filter runs, the heater holds 76, and the water is clear
a reading of zero from an unshaken bottle is not a measurement of anything

cases.answer: The second bottle has not been shaken, so the test cannot work.
proof: “The kit's second bottle must be shaken hard for thirty seconds before use.”
“A sample taken to the pet shop on Saturday tested at 80 parts per million.”
clears: An expired kit: “The kit's printed expiry is next June, so it has not run out of date.”
A clean tank: “Zero nitrate in a stocked tank that has run since September is not believable.”
The heater: “The tank's filter runs, the heater holds 76, and the water is clear.”
cases.explain: The fish were telling the truth the whole time and the kit was not. The pet shop sample settles it at 80. A result that is too good to be true is worth testing against something outside the instrument that produced it.

cases.title: The Case of the Quiet Reading
