cases.story: A phone app recorded Room 4 at 55 decibels, which the report called a quiet classroom. Every teacher who has taught in Room 4 describes it as among the loudest in the building. The app stamps each reading with the time it was taken, and the stamps survive. All six readings fall between 10:05 and 10:08 on three different mornings. Room 4 holds silent independent reading from ten o'clock until ten fifteen. A measurement describes the moment it was taken and nothing on either side of it. A sound meter borrowed from the district read 78 decibels at 1:30 that same week. The phone's microphone was clear and the app had been calibrated in August. The app's own readings during group work on Thursday reached 74 decibels. The report quoted only the six morning figures and left the Thursday ones out.
cases.question: Why does the report call Room 4 quiet?

suspects.why: all six readings fall between 10:05 and 10:08 on three different mornings
the phone's microphone was clear and the app had been calibrated in August
a sound meter borrowed from the district read 78 decibels at 1:30 that same week
the app's own readings during group work on Thursday reached 74 decibels
the report quoted only the six morning figures and left the Thursday ones out

cases.answer: All six readings were taken during the quietest fifteen minutes of the day.
proof: “Room 4 holds silent independent reading from ten o'clock until ten fifteen.”
“A measurement describes the moment it was taken and nothing on either side of it.”
clears: The microphone: “The phone's microphone was clear and the app had been calibrated in August.”
A quiet room: “A sound meter borrowed from the district read 78 decibels at 1:30 that same week.”
Calibration: “The app's own readings during group work on Thursday reached 74 decibels.”
cases.explain: The app worked. Every number it produced is accurate for the three minutes it covers. The report turned six accurate numbers about silent reading into a claim about a whole school day, and dropped the Thursday figures that would have shown the difference.

cases.title: The Case of the Quadrat by the Fence
cases.story: Group B counted 340 fallen leaves in its square where the other groups counted around 90. All five groups used a square frame measured at one metre on every side. All five counted whole leaves only, with torn pieces left out by agreement. All five counted on the same Friday morning within half an hour of each other. Group B set its frame directly against the base of the north fence. Wind pushes fallen leaves until something stops them, and a fence stops them. Leaves pile deep along a barrier and thin out across open ground. The other four frames were set at random points across the open lawn. A sample taken where a thing collects will not describe the ground around it. Group B counted carefully and counted correctly, and its number is still wrong for the lawn.
cases.question: Why is group B's count four times the others?

suspects.why: group B set its frame directly against the base of the north fence
all five groups used a square frame measured at one metre on every side
all five counted whole leaves only, with torn pieces left out by agreement
all five counted on the same Friday morning within half an hour of each other
group B counted carefully and counted correctly, and its number is still wrong for the lawn

cases.answer: Group B sampled the one place on the lawn where leaves pile up.
proof: “Wind pushes fallen leaves until something stops them, and a fence stops them.”
“A sample taken where a thing collects will not describe the ground around it.”
clears: A bigger frame: “All five groups used a square frame measured at one metre on every side.”
Torn pieces: “All five counted whole leaves only, with torn pieces left out by agreement.”
The hour: “All five counted on the same Friday morning within half an hour of each other.”
cases.explain: This is the hardest kind of wrong number to catch, because nobody made a mistake. Group B's 340 is a true count of a real square metre. Where the square was placed is what makes it useless for describing the lawn.

cases.title: The Case of the Pumpkin That Gained Weight
cases.story: The pumpkin lost weight for three weeks, gained nine ounces in week four, and lost again after. A cut pumpkin drying on a porch loses water steadily and does not take it back. The same scale was used every week and its serial number is on every sheet. The scale was checked against a two-pound weight before and after week four. Every reading was photographed, and week four's photograph matches the sheet exactly. Weeks one, two, three and five were weighed at noon in dry weather. Week four was weighed at seven in the morning after a night of heavy rain. The porch rail is open on the weather side and the pumpkin sat in the wet. Water sitting on a surface is weighed along with whatever is under it. Nine ounces is about half a cup, which a wet pumpkin skin can easily hold.
cases.question: Why does week four show a gain?

suspects.why: week four was weighed at seven in the morning after a night of heavy rain
the scale was checked against a two-pound weight before and after week four
every reading was photographed, and week four's photograph matches the sheet exactly
a cut pumpkin drying on a porch loses water steadily and does not take it back
the same scale was used every week and its serial number is on every sheet

cases.answer: Week four weighed the pumpkin plus a night of rain sitting on it.
proof: “Water sitting on a surface is weighed along with whatever is under it.”
“Nine ounces is about half a cup, which a wet pumpkin skin can easily hold.”
clears: The scale: “The scale was checked against a two-pound weight before and after week four.”
A miscopy: “Every reading was photographed, and week four's photograph matches the sheet exactly.”
A real gain: “A cut pumpkin drying on a porch loses water steadily and does not take it back.”
cases.explain: Every check anyone ran was a check on the scale or the record, and both were fine. The thing nobody checked was what was on the pumpkin when it went on the scale. Four of the five weighings had a rule nobody had written down: noon, and dry.

cases.title: The Case of the Print That Measured Twelve
cases.story: The print in the flowerbed measured eleven and a half inches, pointing to a very large shoe. Nobody at the school wears a shoe that size, and the search stalled there. The print was never measured in the bed itself before the rain came. It was measured from a photograph, using a brick in the frame as the scale. The measurer assumed the bricks were eight inches long, as most bricks are. The school's walls are built of a seven-inch brick used only in this county. Every length taken from that photograph is therefore about one part in eight too large. Corrected to a seven-inch brick, the print measures just over ten inches. A print pressed into soft soil also spreads wider than the sole that made it. A measurement is only as good as the thing it was compared against.
cases.question: Why did the print measure so large?

suspects.why: the measurer assumed the bricks were eight inches long, as most bricks are
corrected to a seven-inch brick, the print measures just over ten inches
it was measured from a photograph, using a brick in the frame as the scale
a print pressed into soft soil also spreads wider than the sole that made it
a measurement is only as good as the thing it was compared against

cases.answer: The scale brick was seven inches, not the eight that was assumed.
proof: “The school's walls are built of a seven-inch brick used only in this county.”
“Every length taken from that photograph is therefore about one part in eight too large.”
clears: A huge shoe: “Corrected to a seven-inch brick, the print measures just over ten inches.”
A ruler: “It was measured from a photograph, using a brick in the frame as the scale.”
The soil: “A print pressed into soft soil also spreads wider than the sole that made it.”
cases.explain: No ruler was wrong and no photograph was faked. One assumption was carried into every number without being checked, and it was off by an inch. The soil spreading the print pushes the real shoe smaller still.

cases.title: The Case of the Vanishing Riders
cases.story: The October report shows ridership on route 6 down thirty percent from September. Enrollment along that route rose by four students over the same month. The driver says the bus is as full as it has ever been in her years there. Riders are counted by a hand tally the driver keeps at the front door. In late September the school began letting students board through the rear door. The tally sheet has no line for the rear door and never has had one. Students boarding at the rear are not counted anywhere in the system. The fare box counts nothing, since this route has never charged a fare. The tally sheet's total and the number of bodies on the bus stopped matching in September. A count that only looks at one door measures that door, not the bus.
cases.question: Why does ridership appear to have fallen?

suspects.why: in late september the school began letting students board through the rear door
enrollment along that route rose by four students over the same month
riders are counted by a hand tally the driver keeps at the front door
the fare box counts nothing, since this route has never charged a fare
the tally sheet has no line for the rear door and never has had one

cases.answer: Students boarding at the rear door are not counted at all.
proof: “Students boarding at the rear are not counted anywhere in the system.”
“A count that only looks at one door measures that door, not the bus.”
clears: Fewer riders: “Enrollment along that route rose by four students over the same month.”
A broken counter: “Riders are counted by a hand tally the driver keeps at the front door.”
The fare box: “The fare box counts nothing, since this route has never charged a fare.”
cases.explain: Nothing happened to ridership. Something happened to the counting. The drop is exactly the size of the change in how students get on, and the report has no way of knowing that because its sheet was printed before the rear door opened.

cases.title: The Case of the Trophy With the Wrong Year
cases.story: The relay trophy is engraved 1998, and the record book says the team won in 1997. Somebody proposed that the engraver made a mistake and should be billed for it. The case holds eleven other trophies from eleven other seasons on the same shelf. Every one of them is engraved with a year one later than its season in the book. An error repeated eleven times in the same direction is not an error. Trophies in this league are presented at the spring banquet following the autumn season. The engraving records the year of presentation, which the league has always done. The record book records the year of the season, which is a different thing. The plate on the 1998 trophy is original and shows no sign of replacement. Two records can disagree completely and both be perfectly correct.
cases.question: Why does the trophy say 1998?

suspects.why: the engraving records the year of presentation, which the league has always done
an error repeated eleven times in the same direction is not an error
the record book records the year of the season, which is a different thing
the plate on the 1998 trophy is original and shows no sign of replacement
every one of them is engraved with a year one later than its season in the book

cases.answer: The engraving records the spring banquet, not the autumn season.
proof: “Trophies in this league are presented at the spring banquet following the autumn season.”
“Two records can disagree completely and both be perfectly correct.”
clears: The engraver: “An error repeated eleven times in the same direction is not an error.”
The record book: “The record book records the year of the season, which is a different thing.”
A replaced plate: “The plate on the 1998 trophy is original and shows no sign of replacement.”
cases.explain: The clue is the pattern. One trophy off by a year is a mistake; twelve off by a year in the same direction is a rule nobody wrote down. Both records are accurate about different events, and the only error was assuming they were about the same one.

cases.title: The Case of the Thermometer in the Wrong Place
cases.story: The probe read 181 degrees, well past done, and the thigh ran pink when it was carved. The thermometer was tested in boiling water that morning and read 212 exactly. The oven was checked with a second thermometer and held its setting all afternoon. The recipe asks for the probe in the thickest part of the thigh, clear of bone. The cook pushed the probe in until it met resistance and stopped there. Resistance in a thigh means bone, and bone sits right against the oven's heat. Bone carries heat faster than meat and runs hotter than the flesh around it. A reading taken against bone describes the bone, not the meat beside it. Moved an inch back into the muscle, the same probe read 154. Nothing was wrong with the thermometer, the oven, the bird or the recipe.
cases.question: Why did the probe read done when the thigh was not?

suspects.why: resistance in a thigh means bone, and bone sits right against the oven's heat
the thermometer was tested in boiling water that morning and read 212 exactly
the oven was checked with a second thermometer and held its setting all afternoon
the recipe asks for the probe in the thickest part of the thigh, clear of bone
a reading taken against bone describes the bone, not the meat beside it

cases.answer: The probe was touching bone, which runs hotter than the meat.
proof: “Bone carries heat faster than meat and runs hotter than the flesh around it.”
“Moved an inch back into the muscle, the same probe read 154.”
clears: The thermometer: “The thermometer was tested in boiling water that morning and read 212 exactly.”
The oven: “The oven was checked with a second thermometer and held its setting all afternoon.”
The recipe: “The recipe asks for the probe in the thickest part of the thigh, clear of bone.”
cases.explain: The same probe gives two readings thirty degrees apart an inch from each other, which settles that the instrument is fine. Pushing in until something stops you is exactly the instruction the recipe warns against, and it puts the tip on the hottest thing in the bird.

cases.title: The Case of the Cup That Was Not a Cup
cases.story: Period 2's cupcakes came out dry and tough and period 4's came out tender. Both classes worked from the same printed recipe, which asks for one cup of flour. Both drew that flour from the same sack in the same storeroom. Both baked on the middle rack of the same oven at the same setting. Both trays came out when the same timer reached eighteen minutes. Period 2 scooped the measuring cup straight down into the sack and levelled it. Period 4 spooned flour loosely into the cup and then levelled it off. Scooping packs flour into a cup and spooning leaves it loose. One cup of flour weighs anywhere from 120 to 150 grams depending on how it is filled. Weighed afterwards, period 2's cup came to 148 grams and period 4's to 123. That is a fifth more flour in a recipe where a fifth is the difference.
cases.question: Why were period 2's cupcakes dry?

suspects.who: 🥄 Scooping the cup into the sack
suspects.why: period 2 scooped the measuring cup straight down into the sack and levelled it
both baked on the middle rack of the same oven at the same setting
both drew that flour from the same sack in the same storeroom
both trays came out when the same timer reached eighteen minutes

suspects.who: 📝 The one cup in the recipe
suspects.why: one cup of flour weighs anywhere from 120 to 150 grams depending on how it is filled

cases.answer: Period 2 packed twenty-five grams more flour into the same cup.
proof: “Weighed afterwards, period 2's cup came to 148 grams and period 4's to 123.”
“That is a fifth more flour in a recipe where a fifth is the difference.”
clears: The oven: “Both baked on the middle rack of the same oven at the same setting.”
The flour: “Both drew that flour from the same sack in the same storeroom.”
Overbaking: “Both trays came out when the same timer reached eighteen minutes.”
cases.explain: Both classes followed the recipe exactly, which is the point. A cup measures space, and flour can be loose or packed in the same space. The recipe never said which, so following it precisely still produced two different cakes — and the fifth suspect, that one cup, is as much to blame as the scooping.

cases.title: The Case of the Log That Balanced
cases.story: The lost and found log shows fourteen pairs of mittens turned in and fourteen claimed. By that record nothing is missing, and yet three students are still without mittens. Mr. Oyelaran emptied the bin and laid out everything that had come through it. Seven of the fourteen entries turned out to be single mittens, not pairs. The log has one column headed pairs and no column for a single at all. Whoever logged a lone mitten wrote it in the only column there was. Seven singles counted as seven pairs inflates the record by seven mittens. Claimed items were logged the same way, which is why the two totals still match. Two wrong numbers that are wrong by the same amount will balance perfectly. The bin itself is empty and has been checked twice by two people.
cases.question: Why are mittens missing when the log balances?

suspects.why: seven of the fourteen entries turned out to be single mittens, not pairs
the bin itself is empty and has been checked twice by two people
claimed items were logged the same way, which is why the two totals still match
two wrong numbers that are wrong by the same amount will balance perfectly
the log has one column headed pairs and no column for a single at all

cases.answer: Seven single mittens were logged in the only column there was.
proof: “The log has one column headed pairs and no column for a single at all.”
“Seven singles counted as seven pairs inflates the record by seven mittens.”
clears: The bin: “The bin itself is empty and has been checked twice by two people.”
Wrong claims: “Claimed items were logged the same way, which is why the two totals still match.”
A counting error: “Two wrong numbers that are wrong by the same amount will balance perfectly.”
cases.explain: A balanced record feels like proof and is not. Both sides of this one were inflated the same way by the same form, so they agree with each other and disagree with the coat rack. The missing column is doing all the damage.

cases.title: The Case of the Dial That Said 350
cases.story: Every gingerbread batch comes out pale and soft though the dial is set to 350. The recipe has worked in three other kitchens without a single change to it. An oven thermometer hung from the middle rack reads 325 after a full hour. A second oven thermometer from a different shop reads 324 on the same rack. Two instruments that agree with each other and disagree with a dial are worth believing. The dial is a request for a temperature and not a report of one. An oven's dial can drift years out of true without anything looking wrong. Set to 375, the dial brings the rack thermometers to 350 and the batches brown properly. The bake time was held at twelve minutes throughout, exactly as written. Nothing about the dough, the recipe or the timing was ever the problem.
cases.question: Why do the batches come out pale?

suspects.why: an oven thermometer hung from the middle rack reads 325 after a full hour
the recipe has worked in three other kitchens without a single change to it
the bake time was held at twelve minutes throughout, exactly as written
a second oven thermometer from a different shop reads 324 on the same rack
nothing about the dough, the recipe or the timing was ever the problem

cases.answer: The dial says 350 while the oven holds 325.
proof: “The dial is a request for a temperature and not a report of one.”
“Set to 375, the dial brings the rack thermometers to 350 and the batches brown properly.”
clears: The recipe: “The recipe has worked in three other kitchens without a single change to it.”
The time: “The bake time was held at twelve minutes throughout, exactly as written.”
A bad thermometer: “A second oven thermometer from a different shop reads 324 on the same rack.”
cases.explain: Two thermometers from two shops agreeing within a degree is as close to independent confirmation as a kitchen gets. The dial is the one voice disagreeing, and the test at 375 proves the point by making the problem go away.

cases.title: The Case of the Twenty-Five Watt Label
cases.story: The display breaker trips within a minute every time the last string is plugged in. The circuit is rated for 1800 watts and the plan called for well under that. Each box is labelled twenty-five watts, and the plan multiplied twenty-five by twenty strings. Five hundred watts is nowhere near 1800, so the plan looked comfortable. The twenty-five watts on the box is the rating of a replacement bulb, not the string. Each string holds a hundred bulbs and the fine print gives its total as 240 watts. Twenty strings at 240 watts each comes to 4800 watts on one circuit. The breaker was swapped for a new one and trips in exactly the same way. The extension cords are rated for fifteen amps and are cool to the touch. A number on a box means nothing until you know what it is a number for.
cases.question: Why does the breaker keep tripping?

suspects.why: the twenty-five watts on the box is the rating of a replacement bulb, not the string
the breaker was swapped for a new one and trips in exactly the same way
the extension cords are rated for fifteen amps and are cool to the touch
the circuit is rated for 1800 watts and the plan called for well under that
each box is labelled twenty-five watts, and the plan multiplied twenty-five by twenty strings

cases.answer: The twenty-five watts is one bulb, and each string draws 240.
proof: “Each string holds a hundred bulbs and the fine print gives its total as 240 watts.”
“Twenty strings at 240 watts each comes to 4800 watts on one circuit.”
clears: The breaker: “The breaker was swapped for a new one and trips in exactly the same way.”
The cords: “The extension cords are rated for fifteen amps and are cool to the touch.”
The circuit: “The circuit is rated for 1800 watts and the plan called for well under that.”
cases.explain: The breaker is doing its job correctly. The plan asked a circuit built for 1800 watts to carry 4800, and it did so because of one number read as the wrong kind of number. The last line is the lesson: a figure without its unit attached is not information.

cases.title: The Case of the Time That Was Too Good
cases.story: The hand-timed hundred metres came out four tenths faster than the electronic system's time. The electronic system starts on the gun's electrical signal and stops at a beam. The hand timer stood at the finish line, a hundred metres from the starter. He started his watch when he heard the gun rather than when he saw the smoke. Sound travels a hundred metres in roughly three tenths of a second. A watch started three tenths late records a run three tenths shorter than it was. Human reaction at the finish adds a little more in the same direction. Both systems were tested against each other over a fifty metre run and differed by half as much. The stopwatch itself was checked against a time signal and keeps accurate time. A faster time is not always a faster runner.
cases.question: Why was the hand time faster?

suspects.why: he started his watch when he heard the gun rather than when he saw the smoke
a faster time is not always a faster runner
the stopwatch itself was checked against a time signal and keeps accurate time
the electronic system starts on the gun's electrical signal and stops at a beam
human reaction at the finish adds a little more in the same direction

cases.answer: The watch started three tenths late, when the sound of the gun arrived.
proof: “Sound travels a hundred metres in roughly three tenths of a second.”
“A watch started three tenths late records a run three tenths shorter than it was.”
clears: A faster run: “A faster time is not always a faster runner.”
The stopwatch: “The stopwatch itself was checked against a time signal and keeps accurate time.”
The electronic system: “The electronic system starts on the gun's electrical signal and stops at a beam.”
cases.explain: The fifty metre test is the confirmation: half the distance, half the error, which is exactly what a sound delay does and not what a broken watch does. The runner ran the slower time. The watch recorded a shorter race.

cases.title: The Case of the Storm Measured Twice
cases.story: The weather station reported four inches and the school's own board recorded nine. Both numbers were taken honestly, and neither observer made an arithmetic error. The school clears its measuring board and takes a fresh reading every six hours. It took four readings through the storm and added them to reach nine inches. The station takes one reading at the end, measuring the depth that is still lying. Snow settles under its own weight from the moment it lands. Four separate fresh falls summed will always exceed the depth left at the end. Both methods are standard, and each answers a question the other does not. The school ruler and the station gauge were compared afterwards and agree exactly. The storm ran for just under twenty-four hours from first flake to last. Drifting was ruled out because both sites are flat, open and sheltered from wind.
cases.question: Why do the two snow totals disagree?

suspects.why: it took four readings through the storm and added them to reach nine inches
drifting was ruled out because both sites are flat, open and sheltered from wind
the school ruler and the station gauge were compared afterwards and agree exactly
both numbers were taken honestly, and neither observer made an arithmetic error

suspects.who: ❄️ One of the two being wrong
suspects.why: both methods are standard, and each answers a question the other does not

cases.answer: The school summed four fresh falls and the station measured what was left lying.
proof: “Snow settles under its own weight from the moment it lands.”
“Four separate fresh falls summed will always exceed the depth left at the end.”
clears: Drifting: “Drifting was ruled out because both sites are flat, open and sheltered from wind.”
The ruler: “The school ruler and the station gauge were compared afterwards and agree exactly.”
Arithmetic: “Both numbers were taken honestly, and neither observer made an arithmetic error.”
cases.explain: Nobody is wrong here, which is the hard part. Nine inches of snow fell and four inches were lying at the end, and both sentences are true at once. The disagreement is between two definitions of how much snow, not between two measurements.

cases.title: The Case of the Forty Chickadees
cases.story: The tally sheet records forty chickadees at the feeder in one hour on Saturday. The yard is small, and forty chickadees at once would fill the hedge completely. The observer marked the sheet every time a chickadee landed on the perch. One bird in the yard carries a numbered band from a ringing project nearby. That banded bird was recorded six separate times within the same hour. A tally of landings counts visits and cannot count individuals at all. Three observers watched together and their sheets agree within one mark. A photograph taken at the busiest moment shows seven birds in the frame. Seven birds making six visits each in an hour comes to about forty landings. The feeder holds four perches and never showed more than four birds at once. Nothing is wrong with the counting; the sheet simply counts a different thing.
cases.question: Were there really forty chickadees?

suspects.who: 🔁 Repeat visits by the same birds
suspects.why: that banded bird was recorded six separate times within the same hour
a photograph taken at the busiest moment shows seven birds in the frame
three observers watched together and their sheets agree within one mark
the observer marked the sheet every time a chickadee landed on the perch
a tally of landings counts visits and cannot count individuals at all

cases.answer: About seven birds made forty landings between them.
proof: “That banded bird was recorded six separate times within the same hour.”
“Seven birds making six visits each in an hour comes to about forty landings.”
clears: A flock of forty: “A photograph taken at the busiest moment shows seven birds in the frame.”
A miscount: “Three observers watched together and their sheets agree within one mark.”
The view: “The observer marked the sheet every time a chickadee landed on the perch.”
cases.explain: The banded bird is the whole case. It is one bird, and it is on the sheet six times, which proves the sheet counts landings. Forty is a perfectly accurate number and the word after it is wrong.

cases.title: The Case of the Ninety-Two Percent
cases.story: The report says ninety-two percent of students prefer the school's cocoa to the shop's. Two hundred students answered, which is a reasonable number for a school this size. The question was worded plainly and offered both options in a neutral order. Every form was tallied twice by two different students and the totals matched. The survey was handed out at the cocoa stand to students buying cocoa. Everyone asked had already chosen to spend money on the thing being asked about. A sample drawn from the people who already prefer something will prefer it. Students who dislike the cocoa had no way of entering the survey at all. The same question asked in homerooms the following week came back at fifty-four percent. Nobody who dislikes the cocoa was ever likely to be standing in that line. Who you ask decides your answer before the question is read.
cases.question: Why is the ninety-two percent misleading?

suspects.why: the survey was handed out at the cocoa stand to students buying cocoa
two hundred students answered, which is a reasonable number for a school this size
the question was worded plainly and offered both options in a neutral order
every form was tallied twice by two different students and the totals matched
who you ask decides your answer before the question is read

cases.answer: Everyone surveyed had already bought cocoa at the stand.
proof: “A sample drawn from the people who already prefer something will prefer it.”
“The same question asked in homerooms the following week came back at fifty-four percent.”
clears: Sample size: “Two hundred students answered, which is a reasonable number for a school this size.”
The question: “The question was worded plainly and offered both options in a neutral order.”
The tally: “Every form was tallied twice by two different students and the totals matched.”
cases.explain: Everything about this survey was done carefully except the one thing nobody thought of as a choice. The homeroom result at fifty-four percent is the same question asked of everybody, and it is thirty-eight points away.

cases.title: The Case of the Average Fourteen Cards
cases.story: The report says students received fourteen valentines on average, and most students feel cheated. Twenty-eight students were counted and the total came to three hundred and ninety-two. Three hundred and ninety-two divided by twenty-eight is exactly fourteen, so the arithmetic holds. Every bag was counted twice and no card was counted in two bags. No student's bag was opened twice, and each count was initialled by two people. Three students run the school's social accounts and received eighty-one, seventy-four and sixty-eight. The remaining twenty-five students received between two and nine cards each. Lined up in order, the middle student in the class received five cards. A mean can sit far outside the range where almost everybody actually is. Half the class got five or fewer and the report still says fourteen. The mean and the middle are both true and they describe different classrooms.
cases.question: Why does the average feel wrong?

suspects.who: 📈 A mean pulled by three large counts
suspects.why: three students run the school's social accounts and received eighty-one, seventy-four and sixty-eight
three hundred and ninety-two divided by twenty-eight is exactly fourteen, so the arithmetic holds
every bag was counted twice and no card was counted in two bags
no student's bag was opened twice, and each count was initialled by two people
a mean can sit far outside the range where almost everybody actually is

cases.answer: Three students received over two hundred cards between them.
proof: “The remaining twenty-five students received between two and nine cards each.”
“Lined up in order, the middle student in the class received five cards.”
clears: Division: “Three hundred and ninety-two divided by twenty-eight is exactly fourteen, so the arithmetic holds.”
Missed bags: “Every bag was counted twice and no card was counted in two bags.”
The mean: “A mean can sit far outside the range where almost everybody actually is.”
cases.explain: Fourteen is correct and useless. Not one student in this class received fourteen valentines, and half received five or fewer. The middle student is the number that describes the room, and the report did not ask for it.

cases.title: The Case of the Eruption Nobody Saw
cases.story: Group D's data sheet records no reaction at all, and the class wrote their model off. Their vinegar came from the same jug that worked for the other five groups. Their baking soda was weighed on the same balance to the same two grams. Their cone was built on the same mold, and its vent is the same width. The instructions ask each group to observe for thirty seconds after pouring. Group D's vinegar had been stored on the cold windowsill and was near freezing. A cold reaction runs slower and takes longer to build enough gas to rise. The group recorded nothing, packed up and left the room at the thirty-second mark. The custodian found their cone overflowed and the table wet that evening. A sheet that says no reaction is a record of what somebody watched.
cases.question: Why does the sheet say no reaction?

suspects.why: their vinegar had been stored on the cold windowsill and was near freezing
their baking soda was weighed on the same balance to the same two grams
their vinegar came from the same jug that worked for the other five groups
their cone was built on the same mold, and its vent is the same width
the group recorded nothing, packed up and left the room at the thirty-second mark

cases.answer: The cold vinegar erupted after the group had stopped watching.
proof: “A cold reaction runs slower and takes longer to build enough gas to rise.”
“The custodian found their cone overflowed and the table wet that evening.”
clears: The soda: “Their baking soda was weighed on the same balance to the same two grams.”
The vinegar: “Their vinegar came from the same jug that worked for the other five groups.”
The vent: “Their cone was built on the same mold, and its vent is the same width.”
cases.explain: The custodian's wet table is evidence nobody collected on purpose. The model worked. The observation window was built for a warm reaction, and a sheet that says no reaction is only ever a report about the seconds somebody was looking.

cases.title: The Case of the Crown an Inch Short
cases.story: Nine of the twenty-eight crowns would not close, all by about the same small amount. Each student measured their own head with the same cloth tape and wrote the number down. The tape was checked against a metre rule and is accurate along its whole length. The strips were cut to exactly the number each student had written. The assembly step glues one end over the other with a one-inch overlap. An inch of overlap takes an inch out of the circle the strip can make. Nobody added that inch to the length before cutting, because nobody wrote it down. Nineteen crowns closed because those students measure a head smaller than their strip. The nine that failed are the nine largest measurements in the class. A missing allowance shows up first wherever the margin was already thinnest.
cases.question: Why would nine crowns not close?

suspects.why: the assembly step glues one end over the other with a one-inch overlap
the tape was checked against a metre rule and is accurate along its whole length
the strips were cut to exactly the number each student had written
each student measured their own head with the same cloth tape and wrote the number down
nobody added that inch to the length before cutting, because nobody wrote it down

cases.answer: Every strip was cut an inch short of what the overlap needs.
proof: “An inch of overlap takes an inch out of the circle the strip can make.”
“The nine that failed are the nine largest measurements in the class.”
clears: The tape: “The tape was checked against a metre rule and is accurate along its whole length.”
The cutting: “The strips were cut to exactly the number each student had written.”
The measurements: “Each student measured their own head with the same cloth tape and wrote the number down.”
cases.explain: All twenty-eight crowns are an inch short. Nineteen of them closed anyway because those heads had an inch to spare. Which nine failed tells you the error is the same size for everybody, which is what a missing allowance looks like.

cases.title: The Case of the App That Said 440
cases.story: The tuning app calls every note on the piano correct and the piano sounds flat beside the flute. A warm flute does go sharp, which would explain part of a gap like this. The flute was played cold from its case and the gap was just as wide. The piano was also checked against a steel tuning fork, which needs no battery. It sounded flat against the fork by the same amount it did against the flute. An app's reference pitch can be changed in its settings by a single tap. This app's reference is set to 435 hertz rather than the standard 440. Every note it calls correct is therefore a little flat of where it should be. The app's microphone was tested on the fork and read the fork as flat too. An instrument that calls a known standard wrong is telling you about itself.
cases.question: Why does the app say the piano is in tune?

suspects.why: this app's reference is set to 435 hertz rather than the standard 440
the flute was played cold from its case and the gap was just as wide
it sounded flat against the fork by the same amount it did against the flute
the app's microphone was tested on the fork and read the fork as flat too
the piano was also checked against a steel tuning fork, which needs no battery

cases.answer: The app is set to 435 hertz, so flat notes read as correct.
proof: “This app's reference is set to 435 hertz rather than the standard 440.”
“Every note it calls correct is therefore a little flat of where it should be.”
clears: The flute: “The flute was played cold from its case and the gap was just as wide.”
The microphone: “The app's microphone was tested on the fork and read the fork as flat too.”
The fork: “The piano was also checked against a steel tuning fork, which needs no battery.”
cases.explain: A warm flute really does go sharp, which is why that suspect is here and why it had to be tested rather than argued about. The fork settles everything. A fork cannot be out of tune, and the app called it flat.

cases.title: The Case of the Four Hundred Foot Kite
cases.story: The club recorded a kite altitude of four hundred feet by counting the string let out. Four hundred feet of string did leave the reel, and the count was careful. A kite's string is never a straight line from the hand to the kite. It hangs in a curve, and it leaves the hand at an angle well below vertical. The line angle was photographed that day and measured at about forty-five degrees. At forty-five degrees, four hundred feet of string reaches roughly two hundred and eighty feet up. The curve of the line takes a further bite out of that number. The reel's counter was checked against a tape and counts accurately. A second club measured the same kite by sighting angles from two points. Their figure came to two hundred and sixty feet, not four hundred.
cases.question: How high was the kite really?

suspects.why: it hangs in a curve, and it leaves the hand at an angle well below vertical
the reel's counter was checked against a tape and counts accurately
four hundred feet of string did leave the reel, and the count was careful
the line angle was photographed that day and measured at about forty-five degrees
their figure came to two hundred and sixty feet, not four hundred

cases.answer: Four hundred feet of string at forty-five degrees is far less than four hundred feet up.
proof: “At forty-five degrees, four hundred feet of string reaches roughly two hundred and eighty feet up.”
“The curve of the line takes a further bite out of that number.”
clears: The counter: “The reel's counter was checked against a tape and counts accurately.”
A miscount: “Four hundred feet of string did leave the reel, and the count was careful.”
The photograph: “The line angle was photographed that day and measured at about forty-five degrees.”
cases.explain: Every number the club wrote down is correct. Four hundred feet of string went out. What they recorded was the length of the string and what they reported was the height of the kite, and those are two sides of a triangle.

cases.title: The Case of the Plant That Grew Four Centimetres
cases.story: The chart shows the shamrock growing four centimetres in a week after months of slow growth. Nothing about the light, the water or the room changed during that week. Four centimetres in seven days would be remarkable for a plant of this kind. Measurements in weeks one through five were taken from the rim of the pot. Week six's measurement was taken from the surface of the soil instead. The soil sits about four centimetres below the rim of that pot. Measuring from a lower starting point adds the distance between the two points. Two students share the task and each had their own idea of where to start. Week seven, measured from the rim again, shows the plant back at its week five height. A growth chart records the distance between two points, and one of them moved.
cases.question: Did the plant really grow four centimetres?

suspects.why: week six's measurement was taken from the surface of the soil instead
week seven, measured from the rim again, shows the plant back at its week five height
nothing about the light, the water or the room changed during that week
measuring from a lower starting point adds the distance between the two points
a growth chart records the distance between two points, and one of them moved

cases.answer: Week six was measured from the soil and the others from the rim.
proof: “The soil sits about four centimetres below the rim of that pot.”
“Week seven, measured from the rim again, shows the plant back at its week five height.”
clears: Real growth: “Week seven, measured from the rim again, shows the plant back at its week five height.”
Conditions: “Nothing about the light, the water or the room changed during that week.”
The chart: “A growth chart records the distance between two points, and one of them moved.”
cases.explain: Week seven is the proof, and it looks at first like the plant shrank. It did not. The jump and the drop are the same four centimetres, which is the distance from the rim to the soil, appearing once and then disappearing again.

cases.title: The Case of the Gauge Under the Tree
cases.story: The school's rain gauge recorded two tenths of an inch from a storm that left standing water everywhere. Two tenths of an inch does not fill a parking lot or float a leaf. The gauge was emptied, checked for cracks and found sound and dry. It was read at eight the next morning, before any evaporation could matter. The gauge stands beneath the spreading branches of a large maple by the fence. A canopy catches most of the rain that falls on it and sheds it elsewhere. A gauge under a tree measures what gets through the tree, not what falls. The county station four miles away recorded one and three tenths of an inch. A second gauge placed in the open lawn that week recorded one and two tenths. Rain gauges are supposed to stand clear of anything overhead for exactly this reason.
cases.question: Why did the gauge read two tenths?

suspects.why: the gauge stands beneath the spreading branches of a large maple by the fence
the gauge was emptied, checked for cracks and found sound and dry
it was read at eight the next morning, before any evaporation could matter
a second gauge placed in the open lawn that week recorded one and two tenths
rain gauges are supposed to stand clear of anything overhead for exactly this reason

cases.answer: The maple caught most of the rain before it reached the gauge.
proof: “A canopy catches most of the rain that falls on it and sheds it elsewhere.”
“A gauge under a tree measures what gets through the tree, not what falls.”
clears: A crack: “The gauge was emptied, checked for cracks and found sound and dry.”
The reading time: “It was read at eight the next morning, before any evaporation could matter.”
A light storm: “A second gauge placed in the open lawn that week recorded one and two tenths.”
cases.explain: The gauge is accurate. It accurately reports the rain that reached it, which is the question nobody was asking. Where an instrument stands is part of what it measures, and this one has been measuring a maple tree for years.

cases.title: The Case of the Forty Percent Garden
cases.story: The germination report says forty percent where the seed packet promises eighty-five. The class counted every seedling in every row and the count itself was careful. Seed was sown at the depth the packet gives, in soil tested at sixty-eight degrees. The bed was watered every morning and never allowed to dry out. The count was taken on day seven, which is when the project sheet asked for it. This species takes fourteen to twenty-one days to come up, as the packet also states. A count taken at day seven catches only the earliest seeds in a slow species. Counted again on day twenty-one, the same bed came to eighty-three percent. The forty percent and the eighty-three percent are the same bed on two mornings. A germination rate without a date attached is not a rate at all.
cases.question: Why did germination look so poor?

suspects.why: the count was taken on day seven, which is when the project sheet asked for it
counted again on day twenty-one, the same bed came to eighty-three percent
seed was sown at the depth the packet gives, in soil tested at sixty-eight degrees
the bed was watered every morning and never allowed to dry out
a germination rate without a date attached is not a rate at all

cases.answer: The count was taken a week before most of the seed was due up.
proof: “This species takes fourteen to twenty-one days to come up, as the packet also states.”
“A count taken at day seven catches only the earliest seeds in a slow species.”
clears: The seed: “Counted again on day twenty-one, the same bed came to eighty-three percent.”
Cold soil: “Seed was sown at the depth the packet gives, in soil tested at sixty-eight degrees.”
Watering: “The bed was watered every morning and never allowed to dry out.”
cases.explain: The seed was fine and the bed was fine and the counting was fine. The project sheet asked for a number on a day the species had not finished answering, and forty percent is a true count of an unfinished process.

cases.title: The Case of the Large Eggs That Were Not
cases.story: The carton is marked large and the twelve eggs inside visibly differ in size. Two of them are noticeably smaller than the others and one is clearly bigger. A customer complained that the carton had been packed with the wrong grade. The farm's grader was checked and is sorting correctly to the published standard. That standard sets a minimum weight for a dozen, not for each individual egg. A dozen graded large must weigh at least twenty-four ounces in total. The twelve in this carton weigh twenty-five and a half ounces together. Individual eggs within a correctly graded dozen vary and are supposed to. The two small eggs and the large one are all inside the allowed spread. The carton was packed and sealed at the farm and has not been opened since. A grade printed on a carton describes the carton and not any egg in it.
cases.question: Is the carton wrongly graded?

suspects.why: that standard sets a minimum weight for a dozen, not for each individual egg
the twelve in this carton weigh twenty-five and a half ounces together
the farm's grader was checked and is sorting correctly to the published standard
a grade printed on a carton describes the carton and not any egg in it
individual eggs within a correctly graded dozen vary and are supposed to

cases.answer: Large is a weight for the whole dozen, not for each egg.
proof: “A dozen graded large must weigh at least twenty-four ounces in total.”
“The twelve in this carton weigh twenty-five and a half ounces together.”
clears: The grader: “The farm's grader was checked and is sorting correctly to the published standard.”
The label: “A grade printed on a carton describes the carton and not any egg in it.”
The weighing: “Individual eggs within a correctly graded dozen vary and are supposed to.”
cases.explain: Nothing is wrong and nobody is at fault. The complaint comes from reading a word about twelve eggs as though it were a word about one. Twenty-five and a half ounces clears the standard with room to spare.

cases.title: The Case of the Sunrise Nine Minutes Late
cases.story: The almanac gives sunrise at 6:42 and the class first saw the sun at 6:51. The observation was made from the playground on four clear mornings running. The classroom clock agrees with the national time signal to the second. The almanac's figure is calculated for the city centre at a flat sea horizon. The school sits in a valley with a wooded ridge standing to the east. The sun must climb above that ridge before anyone on the playground can see it. An almanac describes a horizon that most places on the ground do not have. From the hilltop above the school the sun appeared at 6:43 on the same morning. The ridge adds the same eight or nine minutes every clear day of the week. Both times are correct for the horizon each one was measured against.
cases.question: Why was sunrise nine minutes late?

suspects.why: the sun must climb above that ridge before anyone on the playground can see it
the classroom clock agrees with the national time signal to the second
both times are correct for the horizon each one was measured against
the almanac's figure is calculated for the city centre at a flat sea horizon
the observation was made from the playground on four clear mornings running

cases.answer: The ridge to the east hides the sun for nine more minutes.
proof: “An almanac describes a horizon that most places on the ground do not have.”
“From the hilltop above the school the sun appeared at 6:43 on the same morning.”
clears: The clock: “The classroom clock agrees with the national time signal to the second.”
The almanac: “Both times are correct for the horizon each one was measured against.”
The observing: “The observation was made from the playground on four clear mornings running.”
cases.explain: The hilltop test is what turns an argument into an answer. Same sun, same morning, same town, two horizons nine minutes apart. The almanac was never wrong; it was answering for a sea horizon the playground does not have.

cases.title: The Case of the Photographs Out of Order
cases.story: Sorted by timestamp, the trip photographs show the group arriving before they left. Pictures from two cameras were put into one folder and sorted automatically. The sorting program reads each file's recorded time and does nothing else to it. Every photograph from the second camera sits exactly sixty minutes behind the first. A gap of exactly one hour, repeated across ninety files, is not a coincidence. The clocks were last compared in March, before the spring change of hour. The second camera's clock was never moved forward when the clocks changed. One camera's photographs were checked against a phone and match it to the minute. Nobody edited a file, and the original recorded times are all intact. Both cameras sat in the same bag and travelled the same route all week. A timestamp records what a camera believed the time to be.
cases.question: Why are the photographs out of order?

suspects.why: the second camera's clock was never moved forward when the clocks changed
the sorting program reads each file's recorded time and does nothing else to it
one camera's photographs were checked against a phone and match it to the minute
nobody edited a file, and the original recorded times are all intact
a timestamp records what a camera believed the time to be

cases.answer: One camera's clock was never moved forward in the spring.
proof: “Every photograph from the second camera sits exactly sixty minutes behind the first.”
“A gap of exactly one hour, repeated across ninety files, is not a coincidence.”
clears: The program: “The sorting program reads each file's recorded time and does nothing else to it.”
The phone: “One camera's photographs were checked against a phone and match it to the minute.”
Edited files: “Nobody edited a file, and the original recorded times are all intact.”
cases.explain: Exactly sixty minutes, ninety times over, is the signature. Drift is ragged and an hour is a decision. One camera has been honestly recording a time that stopped being the time one Sunday in spring.

cases.title: The Case of the Fertiliser by the Window
cases.story: The fertilised beans grew half again as tall as the unfertilised ones in four weeks. The report concluded that the fertiliser works and recommended it for the whole school. All sixteen pots were watered on the same schedule with the same measured amount. All sixteen pots are the same size and were filled from the same bag of soil. The eight fertilised pots were lined up along the window and the other eight by the door. Light falling on a windowsill is several times what reaches a doorway. Two things changed between the groups, and only one of them was the fertiliser. In week five the two trays were swapped end for end without changing anything else. By week eight the plants at the window were taller whichever tray they came from. An experiment with two differences cannot tell you which one did the work.
cases.question: Did the fertiliser make the plants taller?

suspects.why: by week eight the plants at the window were taller whichever tray they came from
two things changed between the groups, and only one of them was the fertiliser
all sixteen pots were watered on the same schedule with the same measured amount
all sixteen pots are the same size and were filled from the same bag of soil
an experiment with two differences cannot tell you which one did the work

cases.answer: The fertilised pots were also the pots at the window.
proof: “The eight fertilised pots were lined up along the window and the other eight by the door.”
“By week eight the plants at the window were taller whichever tray they came from.”
clears: Watering: “All sixteen pots were watered on the same schedule with the same measured amount.”
Pot size: “All sixteen pots are the same size and were filled from the same bag of soil.”
The report: “An experiment with two differences cannot tell you which one did the work.”
cases.explain: The swap in week five is the move that rescues the experiment. The height followed the window and not the fertiliser, which is the one thing the first four weeks could never have shown. The fertiliser may still help; this study cannot say so.

cases.title: The Case of the Soft Ice Cream in a Cold Freezer
cases.story: The ice cream in the door rack is soft while the freezer's display reads zero degrees. The display takes its reading from a sensor mounted at the back wall. Cold air sinks and pools at the bottom and back of a freezer compartment. The door rack sits at the front, at the top, and swings into the room when opened. A thermometer left in the door rack overnight read nineteen degrees by morning. A thermometer left at the back on the same night read one degree. The compressor ran normally all night and the door seal passed a paper test. A tub moved from the door rack to the back shelf was firm within three hours. A sensor reports the temperature where the sensor is and nowhere else. The display has been accurate about the back wall this whole time.
cases.question: Why is the ice cream soft?

suspects.why: a thermometer left in the door rack overnight read nineteen degrees by morning
a thermometer left at the back on the same night read one degree
the compressor ran normally all night and the door seal passed a paper test
a tub moved from the door rack to the back shelf was firm within three hours
a sensor reports the temperature where the sensor is and nowhere else

cases.answer: The door rack runs nineteen degrees while the sensor reads the cold back wall.
proof: “Cold air sinks and pools at the bottom and back of a freezer compartment.”
“A tub moved from the door rack to the back shelf was firm within three hours.”
clears: The display: “A thermometer left at the back on the same night read one degree.”
The compressor: “The compressor ran normally all night and the door seal passed a paper test.”
The recipe: “A tub moved from the door rack to the back shelf was firm within three hours.”
cases.explain: The display is telling the truth and the truth is about one spot. Moving the tub is the experiment that settles it: the same ice cream firmed up in three hours without anybody changing a setting.

cases.title: The Case of the Ribbons That Matched Indoors
cases.story: The two rolls of ribbon matched perfectly in the storeroom and clashed badly on stage. Both were checked against each other under the storeroom's fluorescent tube. Nobody compared them under daylight or under the stage lights before the show. Two dyes can reflect light identically under one kind of lamp and differently under another. A fluorescent tube and a stage lamp do not give out the same mix of colours. Held side by side at the window in daylight, the two ribbons plainly differ. The rolls came from different dye lots, which the labels on the cores record. A dye lot difference invisible under one lamp is not invisible under all of them. Both rolls were handled carefully and neither has faded or been washed. A colour match is a statement about a pair of ribbons and a particular light.
cases.question: Why did the ribbons clash on stage?

suspects.why: both were checked against each other under the storeroom's fluorescent tube
a dye lot difference invisible under one lamp is not invisible under all of them
both rolls were handled carefully and neither has faded or been washed
held side by side at the window in daylight, the two ribbons plainly differ
the rolls came from different dye lots, which the labels on the cores record

cases.answer: The two ribbons were only ever matched under the storeroom tube.
proof: “Two dyes can reflect light identically under one kind of lamp and differently under another.”
“Nobody compared them under daylight or under the stage lights before the show.”
clears: Fading: “Both rolls were handled carefully and neither has faded or been washed.”
The eyes: “Held side by side at the window in daylight, the two ribbons plainly differ.”
The labels: “The rolls came from different dye lots, which the labels on the cores record.”
cases.explain: The dye lots really are different and the labels said so. The test that was run could not detect it, because a match under one lamp is not a match. The ribbons never changed; the light did.

cases.title: The Case of the Three Hundred Who Were Four Hundred
cases.story: The attendance figure is three hundred and four hundred and twenty balloons were given out. The balloon table counted its stock before the doors opened and again at the end. Four hundred and twenty left the table, and each visitor took exactly one. Volunteers refused second balloons, and the table was watched the whole evening. The attendance count was made by two staff walking the hall at a quarter to seven. They counted everybody standing in the hall at that one moment and wrote it down. People arrived from five thirty and others left before seven to catch buses. A count of who is present at one moment cannot total who came all evening. The balloon figure adds up every visitor across three hours of the event. Both numbers are right about different questions, and only one of them is attendance.
cases.question: How many people came?

suspects.who: ⏱️ A count taken at one moment
suspects.why: the attendance count was made by two staff walking the hall at a quarter to seven
volunteers refused second balloons, and the table was watched the whole evening
the balloon table counted its stock before the doors opened and again at the end
they counted everybody standing in the hall at that one moment and wrote it down
both numbers are right about different questions, and only one of them is attendance

cases.answer: Four hundred and twenty came, and three hundred were in the hall at once.
proof: “A count of who is present at one moment cannot total who came all evening.”
“The balloon figure adds up every visitor across three hours of the event.”
clears: Second balloons: “Volunteers refused second balloons, and the table was watched the whole evening.”
The stock count: “The balloon table counted its stock before the doors opened and again at the end.”
The walk-through: “They counted everybody standing in the hall at that one moment and wrote it down.”
cases.explain: Three hundred is a true count of a crowded room at a quarter to seven. It is the wrong kind of number for the question, because people kept arriving and leaving. The balloons counted each visitor once and never counted anyone twice.

cases.title: The Case of the Damp Bottom Shelf
cases.story: Forty books on the bottom shelf of the north wall have swollen covers and wavy pages. The damage is worst at the wall end of the shelf and fades along it. Books on the top shelf, directly under the roof, are dry and flat. A roof leak runs downward, so the top shelf would be the wet one. The room's humidity reads forty-four percent, which is normal for the building. Air that damp would affect every shelf in the room equally, and it has not. A spilled bottle soaks one patch and leaves the books beside it untouched. This damage runs along four metres of shelving in a single gradient. The plaster behind that shelf is blistered from the skirting board upward. A hot water pipe runs inside the north wall at floor level. Water escaping at floor level wets what sits lowest and nearest, which is exactly the pattern on the shelf. The cleaning crew have not mopped that aisle since the damage was reported.
cases.question: What is wetting the books?

suspects.who: 🚰 A pipe inside the north wall
suspects.why: a hot water pipe runs inside the north wall at floor level
a roof leak runs downward, so the top shelf would be the wet one
air that damp would affect every shelf in the room equally, and it has not
a spilled bottle soaks one patch and leaves the books beside it untouched
the cleaning crew have not mopped that aisle since the damage was reported

cases.answer: A pipe in the north wall is wetting the shelf from floor level.
proof: “The plaster behind that shelf is blistered from the skirting board upward.”
“Water escaping at floor level wets what sits lowest and nearest, which is exactly the pattern on the shelf.”
“The damage is worst at the wall end of the shelf and fades along it.”
clears: A roof leak: “Books on the top shelf, directly under the roof, are dry and flat.”
Humidity: “The room's humidity reads forty-four percent, which is normal for the building.”
A bottle: “This damage runs along four metres of shelving in a single gradient.”
The cleaners: “The cleaning crew have not mopped that aisle since the damage was reported.”
cases.explain: Each suspect predicts a shape. A roof leak predicts damage from the top down, humidity predicts it everywhere at once, a bottle predicts one patch. The shape on the shelf is lowest and nearest a wall, which is the only prediction left standing, and the blistered plaster confirms it.

cases.title: The Case of the Friday Sandwich
cases.story: Mira's sandwich is slimy on Fridays and fine the other four days of the week. The bread comes from one loaf bought on Sunday and used all week. If the bread were the problem, Thursday's sandwich would be worse than Monday's. The deli meat is sliced fresh on Thursday evening for Friday only. Meat sliced the night before would spoil in the refrigerator too, and it does not. The mayonnaise jar is opened on Monday and used every day from the same spoon. Mayonnaise would affect every sandwich in the week, not one of them. The lunchbox is washed in hot water on Thursday night after school. It is dried with a cloth and the lid is clipped shut while the seams are still wet. A sealed box with water trapped in its seams grows a film overnight. Thursday is the only night the box is both washed and closed. A box left open on the rack on other nights is dry by morning.
cases.question: Why is the Friday sandwich slimy?

suspects.who: 📦 The box clipped shut while wet
suspects.why: it is dried with a cloth and the lid is clipped shut while the seams are still wet
if the bread were the problem, Thursday's sandwich would be worse than Monday's
meat sliced the night before would spoil in the refrigerator too, and it does not
mayonnaise would affect every sandwich in the week, not one of them
a box left open on the rack on other nights is dry by morning

cases.answer: The lunchbox is clipped shut on Thursday night with water in its seams.
proof: “A sealed box with water trapped in its seams grows a film overnight.”
“Thursday is the only night the box is both washed and closed.”
“A box left open on the rack on other nights is dry by morning.”
clears: The bread: “If the bread were the problem, Thursday's sandwich would be worse than Monday's.”
The meat: “Meat sliced the night before would spoil in the refrigerator too, and it does not.”
The mayonnaise: “Mayonnaise would affect every sandwich in the week, not one of them.”
The wash: “A box left open on the rack on other nights is dry by morning.”
cases.explain: Three of the four food suspects are ruled out by a prediction about other days: each would spoil more than one sandwich a week. Washing is not the fault either, since the box is washed on other nights too. What happens only on Thursday is washing and closing in the same move.

cases.title: The Case of the Breaking Leads
cases.story: Pencils from the new box snap their points within a word or two of sharpening. Pencils from the old box sharpen in the same sharpener and write all period. If the sharpener's blade were dull, pencils from both boxes would break. The two boxes are the same brand and the same HB grade, printed on the barrel. A softer grade would smudge as well as snap, and these do not smudge at all. Pressing hard would break points for one student and not for a whole class. Every student using the new box reports the same thing within a day. A pencil's lead is one thin rod running the full length of the barrel. A sharp knock cracks that rod in several places without marking the wood. Each crack becomes a break as soon as the sharpener exposes it. The new box arrived in a carton the delivery driver dropped on the step. The old box has sat on the shelf since September and has not been moved.
cases.question: Why do the new pencils keep snapping?

suspects.why: the new box arrived in a carton the delivery driver dropped on the step
if the sharpener's blade were dull, pencils from both boxes would break
a softer grade would smudge as well as snap, and these do not smudge at all
pressing hard would break points for one student and not for a whole class
a sharp knock cracks that rod in several places without marking the wood

cases.answer: The dropped carton cracked the leads inside the new pencils.
proof: “A sharp knock cracks that rod in several places without marking the wood.”
“Each crack becomes a break as soon as the sharpener exposes it.”
“The new box arrived in a carton the delivery driver dropped on the step.”
clears: The sharpener: “If the sharpener's blade were dull, pencils from both boxes would break.”
The grade: “A softer grade would smudge as well as snap, and these do not smudge at all.”
Pressing: “Every student using the new box reports the same thing within a day.”
The wood: “A sharp knock cracks that rod in several places without marking the wood.”
cases.explain: The old box is the control for the sharpener, the printed grade is the control for the lead, and a whole class is the control for pressing. What is left is a box that was dropped, and a lead that can be broken in six places while the pencil still looks perfect.

cases.title: The Case of the Bowl That Ripened
cases.story: Five apples in the kitchen bowl went soft and brown within four days of being picked. Six apples from the same tree, left in a dish on the counter, are still firm. The two groups were picked on the same morning from the same branch. A bad batch would have gone soft in the dish as well as in the bowl. Bruising shows as a brown patch where the fruit was struck, not as softening throughout. None of the five carries a mark on its skin anywhere. The bowl is wood and the dish is china, and neither reacts with fruit. The bowl also held two bananas that were spotted brown when the apples went in. Ripening fruit gives off ethylene gas, which ripens other fruit near it. Gas pools in a deep bowl and disperses from a shallow dish. Two pears that shared the bowl have gone soft as well, and the pears in the dish are hard.
cases.question: What ripened the apples?

suspects.why: the bowl also held two bananas that were spotted brown when the apples went in
a bad batch would have gone soft in the dish as well as in the bowl
none of the five carries a mark on its skin anywhere
the bowl is wood and the dish is china, and neither reacts with fruit
the two groups were picked on the same morning from the same branch

cases.answer: Ethylene from the bananas ripened everything in the bowl.
proof: “Ripening fruit gives off ethylene gas, which ripens other fruit near it.”
“Gas pools in a deep bowl and disperses from a shallow dish.”
“Two pears that shared the bowl have gone soft as well, and the pears in the dish are hard.”
clears: A bad batch: “A bad batch would have gone soft in the dish as well as in the bowl.”
Bruising: “None of the five carries a mark on its skin anywhere.”
The bowl: “The bowl is wood and the dish is china, and neither reacts with fruit.”
The tree: “The two groups were picked on the same morning from the same branch.”
cases.explain: The pears are the test that separates the last two explanations. Something about the fruit itself would not touch a pear, and something about the bowl would not have spared the dish. A gas that fills a bowl ripens whatever is in it, pears included.

cases.title: The Case of the Wheel That Would Not Stay True
cases.story: The rear wheel pulls out of true within a week of every truing, and the front wheel never does. Both wheels run the same roads, the same potholes and the same rider. If potholes were the cause, the front wheel would go out first and harder. The rim was checked for cracks and dents and is straight when the spokes are even. A cracked rim would hold a bend in one place rather than drifting slowly. The hub bearings spin smoothly and have no play when the wheel is rocked. The same two spokes are loose at every truing, and both are on the chain side. A rear wheel is dished, so its chain-side spokes pull at a steeper angle. Spokes at a steeper angle carry more tension and lose it first if they were set low. Tension was measured after the last truing and those two read well under the others. Nothing on the front wheel is dished, which is why nothing on it moves.
cases.question: Why does only the rear wheel go out of true?

suspects.who: 🔧 Two chain-side spokes set at low tension
suspects.why: tension was measured after the last truing and those two read well under the others
if potholes were the cause, the front wheel would go out first and harder
a cracked rim would hold a bend in one place rather than drifting slowly
the hub bearings spin smoothly and have no play when the wheel is rocked
both wheels run the same roads, the same potholes and the same rider

cases.answer: Two chain-side spokes were left at low tension and keep letting go.
proof: “A rear wheel is dished, so its chain-side spokes pull at a steeper angle.”
“Spokes at a steeper angle carry more tension and lose it first if they were set low.”
“The same two spokes are loose at every truing, and both are on the chain side.”
clears: Potholes: “If potholes were the cause, the front wheel would go out first and harder.”
The rim: “A cracked rim would hold a bend in one place rather than drifting slowly.”
The bearings: “The hub bearings spin smoothly and have no play when the wheel is rocked.”
The rider: “Both wheels run the same roads, the same potholes and the same rider.”
cases.explain: The front wheel is the control for everything the bike meets: same roads, same rider, same potholes, and it stays true. The difference is inside the rear wheel, where dishing puts the chain-side spokes under more load, and the same two keep failing because they were never brought up to tension.

cases.title: The Case of the Algae on One Pane
cases.story: Green film coats the left pane of the tank and leaves the other three clear. Overfeeding raises nutrients in the water, and water circulates past every pane equally. Nutrients in the water would green all four sides rather than one. The tap water was tested for phosphate and came back at almost nothing. Phosphate would also feed algae everywhere the water touches, which is everywhere. The tank's own lamp sits centred above it and lights all four panes the same. The left pane faces a west window about a metre away. Algae need light, and more light on one surface grows more algae there. The green stops in a sharp horizontal line two thirds of the way up the pane. A shelf above the window casts a shadow across the tank at exactly that height. The film is thickest at the end of weeks with clear afternoons. Scraping the pane clean leaves it green again within nine or ten days.
cases.question: Why is only one pane green?

suspects.who: 🪟 Afternoon light from the west window
suspects.why: the left pane faces a west window about a metre away
nutrients in the water would green all four sides rather than one
the tap water was tested for phosphate and came back at almost nothing
the tank's own lamp sits centred above it and lights all four panes the same
overfeeding raises nutrients in the water, and water circulates past every pane equally

cases.answer: Window light on the left pane is growing the algae there.
proof: “Algae need light, and more light on one surface grows more algae there.”
“The green stops in a sharp horizontal line two thirds of the way up the pane.”
“A shelf above the window casts a shadow across the tank at exactly that height.”
clears: Overfeeding: “Nutrients in the water would green all four sides rather than one.”
Phosphate: “The tap water was tested for phosphate and came back at almost nothing.”
The lamp: “The tank's own lamp sits centred above it and lights all four panes the same.”
The filter: “Overfeeding raises nutrients in the water, and water circulates past every pane equally.”
cases.explain: Anything carried in the water reaches all four panes, so a one-sided problem cannot be a water problem. The shadow line is the proof: the algae stop exactly where the light stops, which no nutrient could arrange.

cases.title: The Case of the Cabinet That Buzzed
cases.story: A hard buzz comes from the display cabinet whenever the projector runs, and stops the moment it is switched off. The projector itself hums steadily and that hum is a different, softer sound. A loose cabinet screw would buzz when anything shook the room, including footsteps. Walking heavily past the cabinet produces no sound at all. The buzz only happens at the projector's high fan speed and never at the low one. Every object has a frequency at which it vibrates easily, and a push at that rate sets it going. The glass shelf inside the cabinet rests loose in its brackets at both ends. Laying a folded cloth under one end of that shelf silences the buzz completely. Removing the cloth brings the buzz back on the next high-speed run. The radiator was off all week and the buzz happened anyway. The cabinet door latch was tightened on Monday and made no difference.
cases.question: What is buzzing?

suspects.why: the glass shelf inside the cabinet rests loose in its brackets at both ends
walking heavily past the cabinet produces no sound at all
the projector itself hums steadily and that hum is a different, softer sound
the radiator was off all week and the buzz happened anyway
the cabinet door latch was tightened on Monday and made no difference

cases.answer: The loose glass shelf vibrates at the projector's high fan speed.
proof: “Every object has a frequency at which it vibrates easily, and a push at that rate sets it going.”
“Laying a folded cloth under one end of that shelf silences the buzz completely.”
“Removing the cloth brings the buzz back on the next high-speed run.”
clears: A loose screw: “Walking heavily past the cabinet produces no sound at all.”
The projector: “The projector itself hums steadily and that hum is a different, softer sound.”
The radiator: “The radiator was off all week and the buzz happened anyway.”
The latch: “The cabinet door latch was tightened on Monday and made no difference.”
cases.explain: The cloth is the experiment that settles it, and it is run twice: in and the buzz stops, out and the buzz returns. The high fan speed matters because only one speed pushes at the rate the shelf answers to.

cases.title: The Case of the Sticky Leaves
cases.story: The young leaves at the tips of the lime tree are curled, and the path beneath it is sticky. Drought curls leaves from the edges inward and leaves nothing sticky behind. The tree has been watered twice a week and the soil is damp a spade deep. Leaf diseases usually show as spots or patches with a clear edge. The curled leaves have no spots and are an even green underneath the curl. Salt damage browns leaf margins, and these margins are not browned. Aphids feed on new growth and excrete a sugary liquid called honeydew. Honeydew falls on whatever is below, which is why the path is tacky. Ants farm aphids for that honeydew and carry them to fresh shoots. A steady column of ants runs up the trunk and out along the tip branches. Curling is confined to this year's shoots and none of the older leaves are affected.
cases.question: What is wrong with the lime tree?

suspects.why: aphids feed on new growth and excrete a sugary liquid called honeydew
the tree has been watered twice a week and the soil is damp a spade deep
the curled leaves have no spots and are an even green underneath the curl
salt damage browns leaf margins, and these margins are not browned
curling is confined to this year's shoots and none of the older leaves are affected

cases.answer: Aphids are feeding on the new shoots and dripping honeydew.
