proof: “Honeydew falls on whatever is below, which is why the path is tacky.”
“Ants farm aphids for that honeydew and carry them to fresh shoots.”
“A steady column of ants runs up the trunk and out along the tip branches.”
clears: Drought: “The tree has been watered twice a week and the soil is damp a spade deep.”
Disease: “The curled leaves have no spots and are an even green underneath the curl.”
Salt: “Salt damage browns leaf margins, and these margins are not browned.”
Old leaves: “Curling is confined to this year's shoots and none of the older leaves are affected.”
cases.explain: Only one explanation predicts both symptoms at once. Drought, disease and salt each account for damaged leaves and none of them accounts for a sticky path. The ants are the confirmation: they are there because the honeydew is.

cases.title: The Case of the Pumpkin That Rotted Inward
cases.story: One of the two carved pumpkins collapsed in five days and the other is firm after two weeks. Both were carved on the same afternoon from the same patch and the same size. Both stood side by side on the same step in the same weather. A crack in the shell lets water and spores in, and shows as a line on the outside. Neither pumpkin carries a crack or a soft patch anywhere on its skin. A bruise from dropping shows as a dark sunken spot within a day or two. The candles in both are electric and give off no heat at all. The collapsed one was hollowed quickly and left with pulp and seeds clinging inside. The firm one was scraped down to clean wall with a metal spoon. Wet pulp holds moisture against the cut wall and feeds the moulds that soften it. The collapse began on the inner wall and worked outward to the skin.
cases.question: Why did one pumpkin collapse?

suspects.why: the collapsed one was hollowed quickly and left with pulp and seeds clinging inside
neither pumpkin carries a crack or a soft patch anywhere on its skin
a bruise from dropping shows as a dark sunken spot within a day or two
the candles in both are electric and give off no heat at all
both stood side by side on the same step in the same weather

cases.answer: Pulp left inside held moisture against the cut wall.
proof: “Wet pulp holds moisture against the cut wall and feeds the moulds that soften it.”
“The collapse began on the inner wall and worked outward to the skin.”
“The firm one was scraped down to clean wall with a metal spoon.”
clears: A crack: “Neither pumpkin carries a crack or a soft patch anywhere on its skin.”
A bruise: “A bruise from dropping shows as a dark sunken spot within a day or two.”
The candle: “The candles in both are electric and give off no heat at all.”
The weather: “Both stood side by side on the same step in the same weather.”
cases.explain: Three suspects predict damage you could see from outside, and the skin is unmarked on both. The rot ran the other way, inside to out, which points at the one thing that differed: what was left clinging to the inner wall.

cases.title: The Case of the Prints in the Frost
cases.story: A line of prints crosses the frosted lawn from the hedge to the bins and back. Each print shows four toes and a small triangular pad behind them. A human boot leaves a continuous sole mark with no separate toes at all. These prints are forty millimetres across, far smaller than any boot. Claw marks show clearly in front of every toe in the trail. A cat walks with its claws drawn in and leaves no claw marks in soft frost. A dog's trail runs in two loose lines, with the hind feet landing wide of the front. This trail runs almost in a single line, one print nearly in front of the last. A fox places each hind foot into the print its front foot just left. That habit is what produces a near single line of prints. The stride measures thirty centimetres, which is short for a dog of this foot size. Nothing has disturbed the bin lids and nothing has been dragged across the grass.
cases.question: What made the prints?

suspects.why: a fox places each hind foot into the print its front foot just left
a dog's trail runs in two loose lines, with the hind feet landing wide of the front
a cat walks with its claws drawn in and leaves no claw marks in soft frost
a human boot leaves a continuous sole mark with no separate toes at all
nothing has disturbed the bin lids and nothing has been dragged across the grass

cases.answer: A fox crossed the lawn, registering its hind feet in the front prints.
proof: “Claw marks show clearly in front of every toe in the trail.”
“This trail runs almost in a single line, one print nearly in front of the last.”
“That habit is what produces a near single line of prints.”
clears: A dog: “A dog's trail runs in two loose lines, with the hind feet landing wide of the front.”
A cat: “A cat walks with its claws drawn in and leaves no claw marks in soft frost.”
A person: “A human boot leaves a continuous sole mark with no separate toes at all.”
The bins: “Nothing has disturbed the bin lids and nothing has been dragged across the grass.”
cases.explain: Two features have to be explained together. Claws rule out the cat and a single line rules out the dog, and only one animal in the list does both at once. Either feature alone would leave two suspects standing.

cases.title: The Case of the Bus That Was Late in the Rain
cases.story: Route 9 runs five minutes late on wet mornings and on time on dry ones. Routes 4 and 11 cover the same main roads and keep to time in any weather. If rain slowed the traffic, all three routes would run late together. The wheelchair lift is used on Tuesdays only, and the late mornings fall on every weekday. Ridership is logged daily and rises by two or three students when it rains. Three extra students board in about twelve seconds, which is not five minutes. The driver's timing sheet shows the whole delay appearing between stops six and eight. Stop seven has no shelter, and the nearest cover is a shop porch across the road. On wet mornings the students wait in that porch and start crossing when the bus appears. Waiting for a group to cross a road takes far longer than letting them step aboard. On dry mornings those same students stand at the pole and board immediately.
cases.question: Why is route 9 late in the rain?

suspects.who: 🏪 Students sheltering across the road at stop seven
suspects.why: on wet mornings the students wait in that porch and start crossing when the bus appears
if rain slowed the traffic, all three routes would run late together
the wheelchair lift is used on Tuesdays only, and the late mornings fall on every weekday
three extra students board in about twelve seconds, which is not five minutes
the driver's timing sheet shows the whole delay appearing between stops six and eight

cases.answer: At stop seven the students shelter across the road and have to cross.
proof: “Stop seven has no shelter, and the nearest cover is a shop porch across the road.”
“Waiting for a group to cross a road takes far longer than letting them step aboard.”
“On dry mornings those same students stand at the pole and board immediately.”
clears: Traffic: “If rain slowed the traffic, all three routes would run late together.”
The lift: “The wheelchair lift is used on Tuesdays only, and the late mornings fall on every weekday.”
Extra riders: “Three extra students board in about twelve seconds, which is not five minutes.”
The driver: “The driver's timing sheet shows the whole delay appearing between stops six and eight.”
cases.explain: The other two routes are the control for weather and traffic. The timing sheet then narrows five minutes to a single stop, and the only thing that changes at that stop when it rains is which side of the road the students are standing on.

cases.title: The Case of the Cracked Trophy Base
cases.story: The marble base of the county trophy has split, and the eleven trophies beside it are sound. A fall chips a corner or scuffs an edge before it cracks a base through. There is no chip, scuff or dust mark anywhere on the base or the shelf. Cold and heat craze a stone surface into a web of fine lines across the whole face. These are three clean cracks and there is no crazing anywhere on it. The case is unheated and its temperature log has not moved four degrees all year. The cracks all begin at the bolt hole in the centre and run outward from it. A bolt tightened too far pushes outward on the stone around the hole. Stone takes enormous pressure from above and very little pushing out from inside. The column was refitted in August with a new bolt and a spanner rather than by hand. The eleven sound trophies have never had their columns off.
cases.question: What cracked the base?

suspects.why: the column was refitted in August with a new bolt and a spanner rather than by hand
there is no chip, scuff or dust mark anywhere on the base or the shelf
the case is unheated and its temperature log has not moved four degrees all year
the cracks all begin at the bolt hole in the centre and run outward from it
the eleven sound trophies have never had their columns off

cases.answer: A bolt driven in with a spanner split the stone from the hole outward.
proof: “A bolt tightened too far pushes outward on the stone around the hole.”
“Stone takes enormous pressure from above and very little pushing out from inside.”
“The cracks all begin at the bolt hole in the centre and run outward from it.”
clears: A fall: “There is no chip, scuff or dust mark anywhere on the base or the shelf.”
Heat and cold: “These are three clean cracks and there is no crazing anywhere on it.”
The marble: “The cracks all begin at the bolt hole in the centre and run outward from it.”
The shelf: “The eleven sound trophies have never had their columns off.”
cases.explain: Where cracks start is the evidence. A fall starts them at the point of impact and temperature starts them everywhere at once. These start at a hole that had a bolt driven into it, and the eleven trophies that were never taken apart are all intact.

cases.title: The Case of the Pale Turkey
cases.story: The turkey came out of the oven cooked through and the colour of raw pastry. The thigh read 176 degrees, so the oven cannot have been running too cool. An oven too cool would have left the meat underdone as well as the skin pale. The bird was rubbed with oil before it went in, so it is not a dry skin. The meat is juicy and the skin is soft rather than dried out. Browning needs a dry surface and heat reaching it directly, and neither was available. The bird was covered with foil at the start and the foil was never taken off. Foil holds steam against the skin for the whole of the roast. A surface held wet cannot brown however long it stays in the oven. The same oven browned a chicken to a deep gold last Sunday. That chicken was roasted uncovered from the first minute to the last.
cases.question: Why is the skin pale?

suspects.who: 🫙 Foil left on for the whole roast
suspects.why: the bird was covered with foil at the start and the foil was never taken off
an oven too cool would have left the meat underdone as well as the skin pale
the bird was rubbed with oil before it went in, so it is not a dry skin
the thigh read 176 degrees, so the oven cannot have been running too cool
the same oven browned a chicken to a deep gold last Sunday

cases.answer: Foil kept steam against the skin for the whole roast.
proof: “Browning needs a dry surface and heat reaching it directly, and neither was available.”
“Foil holds steam against the skin for the whole of the roast.”
“A surface held wet cannot brown however long it stays in the oven.”
clears: A cool oven: “An oven too cool would have left the meat underdone as well as the skin pale.”
No fat: “The bird was rubbed with oil before it went in, so it is not a dry skin.”
Time: “The thigh read 176 degrees, so the oven cannot have been running too cool.”
The bird: “That chicken was roasted uncovered from the first minute to the last.”
cases.explain: A cooked thigh and a pale skin cannot both be explained by heat or time, because either would have left the meat underdone too. What separates skin from meat is the surface, and the surface spent the whole roast under foil in its own steam.

cases.title: The Case of the Tray That Browned on One Side
cases.story: Cupcakes at the back left of every tray come out dark and the ones at the front right stay pale. It happens with the light tray and with the dark one, so the tray is not the cause. A dark tray would brown everything resting on it rather than one corner. The batter is poured from one jug and measured to the gram into every cup. Uneven batter would put the dark ones in a different place each time. The dark ones appear in the same corner of the oven on every single bake. Rotating the tray halfway through the bake produces an evenly coloured batch. If the tray carried the fault, turning it would simply move the dark side around. An oven with a hot corner browns whatever happens to be sitting in it. The element behind that corner was replaced last term and sits closer to the shelf. The oven thermometer reads nine degrees higher when moved to that corner.
cases.question: Why does one corner always brown?

suspects.who: ♨️ A hot corner in the oven
suspects.why: an oven with a hot corner browns whatever happens to be sitting in it
a dark tray would brown everything resting on it rather than one corner
uneven batter would put the dark ones in a different place each time
if the tray carried the fault, turning it would simply move the dark side around
the dark ones appear in the same corner of the oven on every single bake

cases.answer: One corner of the oven runs about nine degrees hotter.
proof: “The element behind that corner was replaced last term and sits closer to the shelf.”
“The oven thermometer reads nine degrees higher when moved to that corner.”
“Rotating the tray halfway through the bake produces an evenly coloured batch.”
clears: A dark tray: “It happens with the light tray and with the dark one, so the tray is not the cause.”
The batter: “The batter is poured from one jug and measured to the gram into every cup.”
The tray: “If the tray carried the fault, turning it would simply move the dark side around.”
Bake time: “The dark ones appear in the same corner of the oven on every single bake.”
cases.explain: The rotation test is the one that decides it. If the fault travelled with the tray, turning the tray would turn the dark side with it. The dark side stayed where it was in the oven, which means the oven owns it, and the thermometer says by how much.

cases.title: The Case of the Mittens That Shrank
cases.story: Two pairs of wool mittens went into the wash the same size and one pair came out child-sized. Both pairs are the same wool from the same maker and the same batch. A fault in the wool would have shrunk both pairs, and one is unchanged. Both were washed in the same machine on the same hot cycle in the same load. Hot water alone swells wool fibres and lets them relax again as they dry. Wool felts when heat and movement act together, because the scales on each fibre lock. Once those scales interlock they cannot be pulled apart and the shrinking is permanent. The shrunken pair went into the tumble dryer on a high heat setting. The unchanged pair was laid flat on a rack and left to dry overnight. A dryer supplies heat and constant tumbling at the same time. Neither pair was stretched, pinned or worn between the wash and the measuring.
cases.question: Why did only one pair shrink?

suspects.why: the shrunken pair went into the tumble dryer on a high heat setting
both were washed in the same machine on the same hot cycle in the same load
a fault in the wool would have shrunk both pairs, and one is unchanged
neither pair was stretched, pinned or worn between the wash and the measuring
the unchanged pair was laid flat on a rack and left to dry overnight

cases.answer: The dryer gave heat and tumbling together, which felts wool.
proof: “Wool felts when heat and movement act together, because the scales on each fibre lock.”
“Once those scales interlock they cannot be pulled apart and the shrinking is permanent.”
“A dryer supplies heat and constant tumbling at the same time.”
clears: The hot wash: “Both were washed in the same machine on the same hot cycle in the same load.”
The wool: “A fault in the wool would have shrunk both pairs, and one is unchanged.”
Stretching: “Neither pair was stretched, pinned or worn between the wash and the measuring.”
The rack: “The unchanged pair was laid flat on a rack and left to dry overnight.”
cases.explain: Both pairs got the heat, so heat alone cannot be the answer. Felting needs two things at once, and only one pair met the second. That is why the rule in the story names heat and movement together rather than either on its own.

cases.title: The Case of the Gingerbread That Spread
cases.story: Half the gingerbread figures baked into flat blobs and half held their shape perfectly. Every figure was cut from one bowl of dough mixed and weighed in one go. A shortage of flour would have spread every figure from that bowl, not half. Too much baking soda leaves a soapy taste, and these taste exactly as they should. All of them went into the same oven on the same shelf at the same setting. Butter in dough must be firm when it meets the oven or it melts before the flour sets. Dough that melts first spreads outward, and dough that sets first holds its edge. The first sheet was cut and baked straight away from dough at room temperature. The second sheet was cut and then chilled for thirty minutes before it went in. The spread figures are all from the first sheet without a single exception. Nobody opened the oven door during either bake.
cases.question: Why did half the figures spread?

suspects.who: 🧈 Room-temperature butter in the first sheet
suspects.why: the first sheet was cut and baked straight away from dough at room temperature
a shortage of flour would have spread every figure from that bowl, not half
too much baking soda leaves a soapy taste, and these taste exactly as they should
all of them went into the same oven on the same shelf at the same setting
nobody opened the oven door during either bake

cases.answer: The first sheet went in warm, so its butter melted before the flour set.
proof: “Butter in dough must be firm when it meets the oven or it melts before the flour sets.”
“Dough that melts first spreads outward, and dough that sets first holds its edge.”
“The spread figures are all from the first sheet without a single exception.”
clears: Flour: “A shortage of flour would have spread every figure from that bowl, not half.”
Soda: “Too much baking soda leaves a soapy taste, and these taste exactly as they should.”
The oven: “All of them went into the same oven on the same shelf at the same setting.”
The door: “Nobody opened the oven door during either bake.”
cases.explain: One bowl of dough and one oven means the recipe and the oven are controls for each other. The only thing that differed between the sheets was thirty minutes in the refrigerator, and the split in the results is exactly the split between the sheets.

cases.title: The Case of the String That Flickered
cases.story: The whole light string flickers together several times a second, all hundred bulbs at once. A loose bulb interrupts its own circuit and flickers that bulb or that half. Every bulb in the string dims and brightens in step, which one loose bulb cannot do. A failing outlet would also affect the lamp plugged into the socket beside it. That lamp has burned steadily in the same socket all evening. These are LED bulbs, which switch on and off far faster than old filament bulbs. The string is plugged into a wall switch fitted with a dimmer last spring. A dimmer chops the current on and off to lower the brightness of a filament lamp. A filament glows through those gaps and an LED follows them exactly. Moving the string to an undimmed socket in the hall stops the flicker completely. Plugging it back into the dimmed switch brings the flicker straight back.
cases.question: Why does the whole string flicker?

suspects.why: the string is plugged into a wall switch fitted with a dimmer last spring
every bulb in the string dims and brightens in step, which one loose bulb cannot do
that lamp has burned steadily in the same socket all evening
moving the string to an undimmed socket in the hall stops the flicker completely
plugging it back into the dimmed switch brings the flicker straight back

cases.answer: A dimmer is chopping the current and the LEDs follow every gap.
proof: “A dimmer chops the current on and off to lower the brightness of a filament lamp.”
“A filament glows through those gaps and an LED follows them exactly.”
“Moving the string to an undimmed socket in the hall stops the flicker completely.”
clears: A loose bulb: “Every bulb in the string dims and brightens in step, which one loose bulb cannot do.”
The outlet: “That lamp has burned steadily in the same socket all evening.”
Cold: “Moving the string to an undimmed socket in the hall stops the flicker completely.”
The lead: “Plugging it back into the dimmed switch brings the flicker straight back.”
cases.explain: A hundred bulbs moving in step says the supply is doing it, not any bulb. The dimmer has been there since spring and filament bulbs never showed it, because a filament stays hot through the gaps. The swap test confirms it in both directions.

cases.title: The Case of the Clock That Gained
cases.story: The hall pendulum clock gains four minutes a day, every day, by the same amount. A clock gaining the same amount daily has a pendulum swinging slightly too fast. A pendulum's speed is set by its length and by nothing else that matters here. Shortening a pendulum makes each swing quicker and makes the clock gain. Winding has nothing to do with rate, because the escapement meters the power out. The clock was wound fully on Sunday and gained four minutes that day as usual. Heat lengthens a steel rod and would make this clock lose rather than gain. The hall has been colder, not warmer, since the gaining started in October. The clock was carried to the hall from the office in late September. The bob rests on a nut that is turned to raise or lower it along the rod. A bob carried by the rod swings loose and seats higher when the clock is set down.
cases.question: Why does the clock gain four minutes a day?

suspects.who: 🔩 The bob seated higher after the move
suspects.why: a bob carried by the rod swings loose and seats higher when the clock is set down
heat lengthens a steel rod and would make this clock lose rather than gain
winding has nothing to do with rate, because the escapement meters the power out
a clock gaining the same amount daily has a pendulum swinging slightly too fast
the hall has been colder, not warmer, since the gaining started in October

cases.answer: The bob sits higher than it did, so the pendulum is effectively shorter.
proof: “A pendulum's speed is set by its length and by nothing else that matters here.”
“Shortening a pendulum makes each swing quicker and makes the clock gain.”
“The clock was carried to the hall from the office in late September.”
clears: Temperature: “Heat lengthens a steel rod and would make this clock lose rather than gain.”
Winding: “The clock was wound fully on Sunday and gained four minutes that day as usual.”
The hall: “The hall has been colder, not warmer, since the gaining started in October.”
The escapement: “A clock gaining the same amount daily has a pendulum swinging slightly too fast.”
cases.explain: Temperature is the trap, because it does change a pendulum and the season did change. It runs the wrong way: a colder hall shortens the rod less, not more. What else happened in late September is the move, and carrying a clock is how a bob ends up seated somewhere new.

cases.title: The Case of the Roof With No Snow
cases.story: Number 14 lost its snow in a day while every other roof in the terrace stayed white for a week. All eight houses face the same way and get the same hours of sun. If the sun were doing it, the south slopes of all eight would clear together. The north slope of number 14 is bare as well, and every other north slope is covered. A chimney warms the tiles around it and melts a ring a metre or so across. Number 14's chimney was capped years ago and the ring around it is no different from the rest. Snow on a roof melts from below when heat escapes through the ceiling beneath it. The loft of number 14 was cleared in August and the insulation taken up for rewiring. It has not been put back, and the other seven lofts are insulated as before. A thermal camera shows the whole roof of 14 running six degrees warmer than its neighbours. Rain ran off all eight roofs equally on the night before the snow.
cases.question: Why did one roof clear so fast?

suspects.why: the loft of number 14 was cleared in August and the insulation taken up for rewiring
if the sun were doing it, the south slopes of all eight would clear together
number 14's chimney was capped years ago and the ring around it is no different from the rest
all eight houses face the same way and get the same hours of sun
rain ran off all eight roofs equally on the night before the snow

cases.answer: Heat escaping through an uninsulated loft melted the snow from below.
proof: “Snow on a roof melts from below when heat escapes through the ceiling beneath it.”
“It has not been put back, and the other seven lofts are insulated as before.”
“A thermal camera shows the whole roof of 14 running six degrees warmer than its neighbours.”
clears: The sun: “The north slope of number 14 is bare as well, and every other north slope is covered.”
The chimney: “Number 14's chimney was capped years ago and the ring around it is no different from the rest.”
The angle: “All eight houses face the same way and get the same hours of sun.”
The rain: “Rain ran off all eight roofs equally on the night before the snow.”
cases.explain: The bare north slope is the observation that does the work. Anything arriving from outside, sun most of all, would clear a south slope before a north one. A roof bare on both sides is being warmed from underneath.

cases.title: The Case of the Feeder Emptied Overnight
cases.story: The feeder is full at dusk and empty at dawn, four nights running. Birds at this latitude do not feed in darkness and are gone from the garden by sunset. Squirrels work in daylight and tear at a feeder rather than emptying it tidily. A squirrel also wrenches the lid off, and this lid is still clipped down. Spilled seed would lie on the ground beneath, and the ground is bare and clean. Something has been taking the seed out through the ports and eating all of it. The metal pole carries a greasy smear running from the ground to the tray. Small dark droppings sit along the top edge of the tray each morning. The plastic around two ports has been gnawed into a wider opening. Rats climb smooth poles easily, feed after dark, and gnaw to make an opening bigger. A trail camera set on the third night recorded movement at ten past one.
cases.question: What is emptying the feeder?

suspects.why: rats climb smooth poles easily, feed after dark, and gnaw to make an opening bigger
birds at this latitude do not feed in darkness and are gone from the garden by sunset
a squirrel also wrenches the lid off, and this lid is still clipped down
spilled seed would lie on the ground beneath, and the ground is bare and clean
the plastic around two ports has been gnawed into a wider opening

cases.answer: A rat is climbing the pole and feeding through the gnawed ports.
proof: “The metal pole carries a greasy smear running from the ground to the tray.”
“The plastic around two ports has been gnawed into a wider opening.”
“Rats climb smooth poles easily, feed after dark, and gnaw to make an opening bigger.”
clears: Birds: “Birds at this latitude do not feed in darkness and are gone from the garden by sunset.”
A squirrel: “A squirrel also wrenches the lid off, and this lid is still clipped down.”
Spilling: “Spilled seed would lie on the ground beneath, and the ground is bare and clean.”
A person: “A trail camera set on the third night recorded movement at ten past one.”
cases.explain: Four facts have to be true together: after dark, up a smooth pole, through the ports rather than the lid, and nothing dropped. Each suspect fails at least one of them, and one animal in the list does all four as a matter of habit.

cases.title: The Case of the Cocoa That Went Cold
cases.story: The cocoa in the flask is barely warm by noon, three hours after it was poured in boiling. A failed vacuum lets heat out through the wall, which makes the outside of a flask warm to the touch. This flask is cold on the outside after three hours, as a working vacuum should be. The stopper seals and no steam escapes when the flask is tipped. The flask holds a litre and only a third of a litre of cocoa was poured in. The rest of the space is air, and the liquid loses heat into it until both are the same temperature. A small amount of liquid warming a large volume of air cools a long way doing it. The flask was not rinsed with hot water before the cocoa went in. A cold steel flask takes heat from the drink to warm itself as well. Filled to the brim the next day, the same flask was still hot at noon. Nothing about the cocoa recipe changed between the two days.
cases.question: Why did the cocoa go cold?

suspects.who: 💨 Air filling two thirds of the flask
suspects.why: the flask holds a litre and only a third of a litre of cocoa was poured in
this flask is cold on the outside after three hours, as a working vacuum should be
the stopper seals and no steam escapes when the flask is tipped
a cold steel flask takes heat from the drink to warm itself as well
nothing about the cocoa recipe changed between the two days

cases.answer: Two thirds of the flask was air, and the cocoa heated all of it.
proof: “The rest of the space is air, and the liquid loses heat into it until both are the same temperature.”
“A small amount of liquid warming a large volume of air cools a long way doing it.”
“Filled to the brim the next day, the same flask was still hot at noon.”
clears: A failed vacuum: “This flask is cold on the outside after three hours, as a working vacuum should be.”
The stopper: “The stopper seals and no steam escapes when the flask is tipped.”
The cocoa: “Nothing about the cocoa recipe changed between the two days.”
Preheating: “A cold steel flask takes heat from the drink to warm itself as well.”
cases.explain: Preheating is a real effect and it is in the story on purpose, because it would cost a few degrees rather than most of them. The full flask the next day is the test: same flask, same stopper, same recipe, and the only change is how much air was shut in with the drink.

cases.title: The Case of the Ink That Stayed Wet
cases.story: Eleven of the twenty-six valentines came out of the pile with the writing smeared sideways. Every card was written with the same gel pen from the same packet. If the pen were at fault, all twenty-six would have smeared rather than eleven. All twenty-six were written at the same table within the same twenty minutes. All twenty-six were stacked together in one pile as soon as they were finished. Gel ink soaks into an absorbent surface and sits on top of a sealed one. Ink that sits on the surface stays wet far longer and wipes with the lightest touch. The eleven smeared cards are all the glossy ones from the shop packet. The fifteen clean ones are matte card cut from the classroom stock. Rubbing a finger across a fresh line on each kind shows the difference in seconds. The room was dry and the heating had been on since morning.
cases.question: Why did eleven cards smear?

suspects.why: the eleven smeared cards are all the glossy ones from the shop packet
if the pen were at fault, all twenty-six would have smeared rather than eleven
all twenty-six were stacked together in one pile as soon as they were finished
the room was dry and the heating had been on since morning
all twenty-six were written at the same table within the same twenty minutes

cases.answer: Gel ink cannot soak into glossy card, so it was still wet when stacked.
proof: “Gel ink soaks into an absorbent surface and sits on top of a sealed one.”
“Ink that sits on the surface stays wet far longer and wipes with the lightest touch.”
“The fifteen clean ones are matte card cut from the classroom stock.”
clears: The pen: “If the pen were at fault, all twenty-six would have smeared rather than eleven.”
Stacking: “All twenty-six were stacked together in one pile as soon as they were finished.”
Damp air: “The room was dry and the heating had been on since morning.”
Drying time: “All twenty-six were written at the same table within the same twenty minutes.”
cases.explain: Stacking and drying time are both real causes of smearing, and both are ruled out the same way: every card got the same treatment. The split in the results matches the split in the paper exactly, and the rub test shows why in a few seconds.

cases.title: The Case of the Foam That Would Not Hold
cases.story: The outdoor volcano gushed and flattened in two seconds while the indoor one held a standing foam. Both used the same measured soda and the same bottle of vinegar. A weaker reaction would produce less gas, and the outdoor one fizzed hard and loud. Wind pushes a foam sideways rather than collapsing it where it stands. The air was still enough that a ribbon on the stake barely moved. Carbon dioxide on its own escapes as bubbles that burst the moment they form. A little dish soap gives each bubble a skin that holds it together in a foam. The indoor mixture had a squeeze of dish soap added to the vinegar. The outdoor batch was mixed in a hurry and the soap was left out. Both cones were the same mould and both vents the same width. The outdoor cone shows the same wet ring a strong eruption always leaves.
cases.question: Why did the outdoor foam collapse?

suspects.who: 🧼 No dish soap in the outdoor batch
suspects.why: the outdoor batch was mixed in a hurry and the soap was left out
the air was still enough that a ribbon on the stake barely moved
a weaker reaction would produce less gas, and the outdoor one fizzed hard and loud
both cones were the same mould and both vents the same width
the outdoor cone shows the same wet ring a strong eruption always leaves

cases.answer: Without soap the gas escaped as bubbles that burst at once.
proof: “Carbon dioxide on its own escapes as bubbles that burst the moment they form.”
“A little dish soap gives each bubble a skin that holds it together in a foam.”
“The indoor mixture had a squeeze of dish soap added to the vinegar.”
clears: Wind: “The air was still enough that a ribbon on the stake barely moved.”
A weak reaction: “A weaker reaction would produce less gas, and the outdoor one fizzed hard and loud.”
The cone: “Both cones were the same mould and both vents the same width.”
The cold: “The outdoor cone shows the same wet ring a strong eruption always leaves.”
cases.explain: The reaction was not the problem and the wet ring proves it: as much gas came out of the outdoor cone as the indoor one. What the outdoor batch had no way of doing was holding that gas, because nothing in it could make a bubble that lasted.

cases.title: The Case of the Crowns That Rubbed Off
cases.story: Gold came off nine crowns onto nine pairs of hands, and the other seventeen are clean. All twenty-six were painted on Monday morning and left on the same rack. All twenty-six had the same two days to dry before they were worn. If drying time were the problem, every crown would mark a hand. None of the twenty-six was sealed with varnish or any other finish. A lack of sealant would leave all of them vulnerable rather than nine. Poster paint binds with a starch that stays soluble and lifts with warm skin. Acrylic paint sets into a plastic film that holds together once it is dry. The nine that rubbed were painted from the gold poster paint pot. The seventeen that did not were painted with the gold acrylic. Both pots were opened the same morning and neither had dried out. Every crown was handled by the same twenty-six students for the same hour.
cases.question: Why did nine crowns rub off?

suspects.why: the nine that rubbed were painted from the gold poster paint pot
if drying time were the problem, every crown would mark a hand
a lack of sealant would leave all of them vulnerable rather than nine
both pots were opened the same morning and neither had dried out
all twenty-six were painted on Monday morning and left on the same rack

cases.answer: Poster paint stays soluble and lifts off onto warm hands.
proof: “Poster paint binds with a starch that stays soluble and lifts with warm skin.”
“Acrylic paint sets into a plastic film that holds together once it is dry.”
“The nine that rubbed were painted from the gold poster paint pot.”
clears: Drying time: “All twenty-six had the same two days to dry before they were worn.”
No sealant: “A lack of sealant would leave all of them vulnerable rather than nine.”
The pot: “Both pots were opened the same morning and neither had dried out.”
The paper: “All twenty-six were painted on Monday morning and left on the same rack.”
cases.explain: Three of the suspects would have damaged all twenty-six, which is the test that removes them. The nine and the seventeen split exactly along which pot was used, and the two paints differ in a way that decides whether dry means finished.

cases.title: The Case of the Note That Buzzed
cases.story: One note on the hall piano buzzes, and the eighty-seven others sound clean. A broken string makes a note thin and quiet rather than adding a buzz to it. The note is as loud as its neighbours and the buzz rides on top of the tone. A tuning pin slipping would drop that note in pitch over a few days. The note has held its pitch exactly against a fork for three weeks. A failed damper lets a note ring on after the key is released. This note stops dead the moment the key comes up, as it should. The buzz also appears faintly when the note an octave below is played. Something lying loose on the soundboard rattles when a note at its own pitch sets the board moving. A nearby note will shake it a little and the octave will shake it less. A two pence coin was found lying flat on the soundboard under the lid.
cases.question: What is buzzing?

suspects.why: a two pence coin was found lying flat on the soundboard under the lid
a broken string makes a note thin and quiet rather than adding a buzz to it
the note has held its pitch exactly against a fork for three weeks
this note stops dead the moment the key comes up, as it should
the buzz also appears faintly when the note an octave below is played

cases.answer: A coin on the soundboard rattles when that note sets the board moving.
proof: “Something lying loose on the soundboard rattles when a note at its own pitch sets the board moving.”
“A nearby note will shake it a little and the octave will shake it less.”
“The buzz also appears faintly when the note an octave below is played.”
clears: A broken string: “The note is as loud as its neighbours and the buzz rides on top of the tone.”
A tuning pin: “The note has held its pitch exactly against a fork for three weeks.”
A damper: “This note stops dead the moment the key comes up, as it should.”
The key: “The buzz also appears faintly when the note an octave below is played.”
cases.explain: The octave is the clue that moves this from one note to the whole instrument. A fault in a single string or key cannot be heard from a different key, so whatever buzzes is not part of that note at all. It is sitting on the board all of them share.

cases.title: The Case of the Kite That Stalled
cases.story: The kite climbs for twenty feet, stops, slides backward and dives into the grass. A kite with too little tail spins on its own axis rather than stalling and sliding back. This kite tracks straight with no spin at all before it stops. Adding two metres of tail changed nothing about the climb or the dive. Wind too strong for a kite pulls hard on the line and then overflies. The line is slack through the whole flight and the meter reads nine miles an hour. The bridle knot sets the angle the kite meets the wind at. A knot too far back tips the nose up until the wind stops flowing over the sail. A sail the wind has stopped flowing over stops lifting and falls backward. The line is new, unkinked and runs freely off the reel. The knot had been slid two centimetres back when the kite was packed away last autumn. Moved forward again to its mark, the kite climbs steadily and stays up.
cases.question: Why does the kite stall?

suspects.who: 🪢 The bridle knot set too far back
suspects.why: a knot too far back tips the nose up until the wind stops flowing over the sail
a kite with too little tail spins on its own axis rather than stalling and sliding back
the line is slack through the whole flight and the meter reads nine miles an hour
this kite tracks straight with no spin at all before it stops
the line is new, unkinked and runs freely off the reel

cases.answer: The bridle knot sat two centimetres back, tipping the nose too high.
proof: “The bridle knot sets the angle the kite meets the wind at.”
“A sail the wind has stopped flowing over stops lifting and falls backward.”
“Moved forward again to its mark, the kite climbs steadily and stays up.”
clears: Tail: “Adding two metres of tail changed nothing about the climb or the dive.”
Strong wind: “The line is slack through the whole flight and the meter reads nine miles an hour.”
A spar: “This kite tracks straight with no spin at all before it stops.”
The line: “The line is new, unkinked and runs freely off the reel.”
cases.explain: The way it falls is the evidence. A tail problem makes a kite spin and a wind problem makes it pull. Climbing, stopping and sliding backward is what a sail does when its angle is too steep, and moving the knot back to its mark proves it.

cases.title: The Case of the Yellowing Shamrock
cases.story: The shamrock's lower leaves have yellowed one by one while the top growth stays green. A plant short of water wilts first and its leaf edges go dry and crisp. These leaves are soft and yellow, with no crisp edge anywhere on them. The soil is still wet to the knuckle three days after the last watering. Too little light makes new growth pale, thin and stretched toward the window. The new growth is compact and a strong green. Roots take in air from the gaps between soil particles as well as water. Waterlogged soil fills those gaps, the roots cannot work, and the oldest leaves yellow first. The pot is a decorative one with no drainage hole in the bottom. Water poured in has nowhere to leave and sits around the roots until it evaporates. The plant was repotted into it in September and the yellowing began in October.
cases.question: Why are the lower leaves yellowing?

suspects.who: 🪣 A pot with no drainage hole
suspects.why: the pot is a decorative one with no drainage hole in the bottom
the soil is still wet to the knuckle three days after the last watering
the new growth is compact and a strong green
waterlogged soil fills those gaps, the roots cannot work, and the oldest leaves yellow first
the plant was repotted into it in September and the yellowing began in October

cases.answer: The pot cannot drain, so the roots are sitting in water.
proof: “Roots take in air from the gaps between soil particles as well as water.”
“The pot is a decorative one with no drainage hole in the bottom.”
“Water poured in has nowhere to leave and sits around the roots until it evaporates.”
clears: Too little water: “The soil is still wet to the knuckle three days after the last watering.”
Too little light: “The new growth is compact and a strong green.”
Feeding: “The plant was repotted into it in September and the yellowing began in October.”
Old leaves: “A plant short of water wilts first and its leaf edges go dry and crisp.”
cases.explain: Soft yellow and crisp brown are different symptoms, and the first one rules out thirst immediately. Healthy new growth rules out light and food. What is left is a root problem, and the pot explains it: there is no way for water to leave.

cases.title: The Case of the Puddle at the Low End
cases.story: Water stands against the back wall of the shed after every rain, and the front stays dry. A leaking roof drips onto whatever is directly below it and wets a patch. The floor beneath the roof joint is dry and the boards there show no stain. Groundwater rising through a floor darkens the boards evenly across the whole slab. These boards are dry a hand's width from the wet edge and stay dry as they dry out. A blocked gutter overflows in a sheet and would wet the ground outside the wall. The ground outside that wall is no wetter than the ground outside the others. Water runs downhill and stops where the fall stops. A spirit level laid across the floor shows the back wall sitting nineteen millimetres low. The door sill at the front sits highest, so water entering anywhere runs back. Rain blows under the door in a south-westerly, and the shed faces south-west.
cases.question: Why does water collect at the back wall?

suspects.who: 📐 A floor that falls to the back
suspects.why: a spirit level laid across the floor shows the back wall sitting nineteen millimetres low
the floor beneath the roof joint is dry and the boards there show no stain
these boards are dry a hand's width from the wet edge and stay dry as they dry out
the ground outside that wall is no wetter than the ground outside the others
rain blows under the door in a south-westerly, and the shed faces south-west

cases.answer: The floor falls nineteen millimetres to the back, so water runs there.
proof: “Water runs downhill and stops where the fall stops.”
“A spirit level laid across the floor shows the back wall sitting nineteen millimetres low.”
“The door sill at the front sits highest, so water entering anywhere runs back.”
clears: The roof: “The floor beneath the roof joint is dry and the boards there show no stain.”
Groundwater: “These boards are dry a hand's width from the wet edge and stay dry as they dry out.”
The gutter: “The ground outside that wall is no wetter than the ground outside the others.”
cases.explain: Rain really does blow under that door, and that is where the water gets in. Where it ends up is a different question, and the level answers it: whatever enters this shed anywhere runs to the back, because the back is the bottom.

cases.title: The Case of the Row That Did Not Come Up
cases.story: Row three of the seed bed is bare and rows one, two, four and five are thick with seedlings. All five rows were sown from one packet on one afternoon by one person. A dead packet would have left all five rows empty rather than one. All five were watered by the same hose for the same count of seconds. Row three is the one nearest the fence on the south side of the bed. A seed needs its own water, and roots already in the soil take water first. The fence carries a mature privet hedge whose roots run out under the bed. Digging a trench along row three turned up privet roots every few centimetres. A soil moisture meter reads row three at less than half the others two hours after watering. Birds take seed before it germinates and leave scratch marks in the surface. The surface of row three is smooth and shows no scratching at all.
cases.question: Why is row three bare?

suspects.why: the fence carries a mature privet hedge whose roots run out under the bed
a dead packet would have left all five rows empty rather than one
all five were watered by the same hose for the same count of seconds
the surface of row three is smooth and shows no scratching at all
row three is the one nearest the fence on the south side of the bed

cases.answer: Privet roots under row three are drinking the water first.
proof: “A seed needs its own water, and roots already in the soil take water first.”
“Digging a trench along row three turned up privet roots every few centimetres.”
“A soil moisture meter reads row three at less than half the others two hours after watering.”
clears: The packet: “A dead packet would have left all five rows empty rather than one.”
Watering: “All five were watered by the same hose for the same count of seconds.”
Birds: “The surface of row three is smooth and shows no scratching at all.”
cases.explain: Shade is the obvious guess for a row beside a fence, and a fence on the south side shades very little at midday. The meter is the measurement that matters: the same water went on and half of it was gone two hours later, which is what established roots do to a seedling.

cases.title: The Case of the Egg That Would Not Peel
cases.story: Six boiled eggs peeled cleanly and six tore their whites away in ragged lumps. All twelve were boiled together in one pan for the same eleven minutes. All twelve went into the same iced water for the same ten minutes afterward. If the boiling or the cooling were at fault, all twelve would behave alike. The shell of an egg is held to the white by a membrane that loosens as an egg ages. A fresh egg grips that membrane tightly and tears when it is pulled away. The six that peeled cleanly came from a carton dated three weeks ago. The six that tore came from a carton collected from the farm on Saturday. Vinegar in the water is said to help, and no vinegar was used on either batch. Cracking an egg before cooling is said to help, and none of the twelve was cracked. Both cartons were stored side by side in the same refrigerator.
cases.question: Why did six eggs refuse to peel?

suspects.why: the six that tore came from a carton collected from the farm on Saturday
all twelve were boiled together in one pan for the same eleven minutes
all twelve went into the same iced water for the same ten minutes afterward
vinegar in the water is said to help, and no vinegar was used on either batch
cracking an egg before cooling is said to help, and none of the twelve was cracked

cases.answer: The six that tore were laid two days before, and fresh eggs grip the membrane.
proof: “The shell of an egg is held to the white by a membrane that loosens as an egg ages.”
“A fresh egg grips that membrane tightly and tears when it is pulled away.”
“The six that peeled cleanly came from a carton dated three weeks ago.”
clears: Boiling: “All twelve were boiled together in one pan for the same eleven minutes.”
Cooling: “All twelve went into the same iced water for the same ten minutes afterward.”
Vinegar: “Vinegar in the water is said to help, and no vinegar was used on either batch.”
Cracking: “Cracking an egg before cooling is said to help, and none of the twelve was cracked.”
cases.explain: Everything done to these eggs was done to all twelve, which removes every step of the method at once. The last two suspects are the kitchen remedies people reach for, and neither was applied to either batch, so neither can explain a difference between them.

cases.title: The Case of the Shadow That Was Too Short
cases.story: The metre stick casts a shadow forty centimetres shorter at school than the same stick casts at home. Both readings were taken at noon on the same day with the same stick. A clock an hour out would move a shadow, but both readings used the same phone. The stick was held against a spirit level and read vertical in both places. A stick leaning away from the sun casts a longer shadow, not a shorter one. The two sites are eleven kilometres apart, which changes the sun's angle by almost nothing. The school stick stood on the sloping tarmac of the car park. A slope tilts the ground the shadow falls on and changes the length it measures. The home stick stood on a patio checked level with the same spirit level. Measured again on level ground at school, the shadow matched the home reading within a centimetre. Both shadows were measured with the same tape from the base of the stick.
cases.question: Why was the school shadow shorter?

suspects.why: the school stick stood on the sloping tarmac of the car park
a clock an hour out would move a shadow, but both readings used the same phone
a stick leaning away from the sun casts a longer shadow, not a shorter one
the two sites are eleven kilometres apart, which changes the sun's angle by almost nothing
both shadows were measured with the same tape from the base of the stick

cases.answer: The school shadow fell on sloping ground, which shortens it.
proof: “A slope tilts the ground the shadow falls on and changes the length it measures.”
“The home stick stood on a patio checked level with the same spirit level.”
“Measured again on level ground at school, the shadow matched the home reading within a centimetre.”
clears: The clock: “A clock an hour out would move a shadow, but both readings used the same phone.”
Leaning: “A stick leaning away from the sun casts a longer shadow, not a shorter one.”
Distance: “The two sites are eleven kilometres apart, which changes the sun's angle by almost nothing.”
The tape: “Both shadows were measured with the same tape from the base of the stick.”
cases.explain: A shadow measurement has three parts: the stick, the sun and the ground. The stick was checked, the sun is the same sun eleven kilometres away, and nobody thought about the ground. Repeating it on level tarmac is the test, and the difference disappears.

cases.title: The Case of the Photographs That Went Green
cases.story: Every photograph taken in the gym has a green cast and the same camera is fine outdoors. A faulty sensor would tint every photograph the camera takes, wherever it is. Three hundred shots taken on the field the same afternoon are perfectly neutral. A dirty lens softens a picture and dulls it rather than colouring it green. The lens was cleaned and the next gym shot came out as green as the last. White balance tells a camera which light it is working under so it can correct for it. The camera was left on its daylight setting for both the field and the gym. Older fluorescent tubes give out a spiky light with far more green in it than daylight. The gym is lit by twenty-eight fluorescent tubes and has no windows. A shot taken in the gym on the fluorescent white balance setting came out neutral. The same tubes were fitted when the gym was built in 1998.
cases.question: Why are the gym photographs green?

suspects.who: 💡 Fluorescent light on a daylight setting
suspects.why: the camera was left on its daylight setting for both the field and the gym
three hundred shots taken on the field the same afternoon are perfectly neutral
the lens was cleaned and the next gym shot came out as green as the last
a shot taken in the gym on the fluorescent white balance setting came out neutral
the same tubes were fitted when the gym was built in 1998

cases.answer: Fluorescent tubes are green-heavy and the camera was set for daylight.
proof: “White balance tells a camera which light it is working under so it can correct for it.”
“Older fluorescent tubes give out a spiky light with far more green in it than daylight.”
“A shot taken in the gym on the fluorescent white balance setting came out neutral.”
clears: The sensor: “Three hundred shots taken on the field the same afternoon are perfectly neutral.”
The lens: “The lens was cleaned and the next gym shot came out as green as the last.”
The walls: “A shot taken in the gym on the fluorescent white balance setting came out neutral.”
cases.explain: The field shots clear the camera and the cleaned lens clears the glass, which leaves the room. The green walls answer is tempting and the setting test kills it: the same walls photograph neutral once the camera is told what light it is standing in.

cases.title: The Case of the Seedling That Leaned Back
cases.story: The bean seedling leans toward the window, and turning the pot does not keep it straight. Within two days of every turn the stem has bent back toward the glass again. A plant leaning because its stem is weak would fall in whatever direction it was pushed. This stem is firm and holds whatever angle it has grown to. Roots crowded on one side of a pot would tip a plant once and not repeatedly. The pot was knocked out and the roots are even all the way round. A plant bends toward light because the cells on the shaded side grow longer than the lit ones. That growth happens at the tip, which is why a turned plant bends back within days. Covering the tip with a small foil cap stopped the bending entirely for a week. Uncovering the tip started it again within three days. The window is the only light source in the room during the day.
cases.question: Why does the seedling keep leaning back?

suspects.why: a plant bends toward light because the cells on the shaded side grow longer than the lit ones
this stem is firm and holds whatever angle it has grown to
the pot was knocked out and the roots are even all the way round
within two days of every turn the stem has bent back toward the glass again
covering the tip with a small foil cap stopped the bending entirely for a week

cases.answer: The tip senses the window light and regrows the bend after every turn.
proof: “That growth happens at the tip, which is why a turned plant bends back within days.”
“Covering the tip with a small foil cap stopped the bending entirely for a week.”
“Uncovering the tip started it again within three days.”
clears: A weak stem: “This stem is firm and holds whatever angle it has grown to.”
Crowded roots: “The pot was knocked out and the roots are even all the way round.”
The turning: “Within two days of every turn the stem has bent back toward the glass again.”
The cap: “Covering the tip with a small foil cap stopped the bending entirely for a week.”
cases.explain: The cap is the experiment, and it is the tip that is capped rather than the leaves. Light still fell on the whole plant and the bending stopped, which locates the sensing in the tip and nowhere else.

cases.title: The Case of the Ice Cream That Grew Crystals
cases.story: The tub in the door of the freezer is gritty with ice crystals and the tub at the back is smooth. Both were bought on the same day from the same shop and opened the same evening. A poor recipe would make both tubs gritty rather than one of them. Both tubs carry the same brand, flavour and batch code on the lid. Ice cream grows crystals when it part-thaws and refreezes, because small crystals melt and regrow as big ones. The freezer's own temperature log reads a steady minus eighteen all week. That sensor sits at the back of the compartment beside the smooth tub. Opening the freezer door swings the door shelf out into room-temperature air. The door is opened perhaps twenty times a day in this house. A thermometer taped to the door shelf recorded minus six at four in the afternoon. Moving the gritty tub to the back shelf stopped any further crystals forming.
cases.question: Why is one tub gritty?

suspects.why: opening the freezer door swings the door shelf out into room-temperature air
a poor recipe would make both tubs gritty rather than one of them
both tubs carry the same brand, flavour and batch code on the lid
the freezer's own temperature log reads a steady minus eighteen all week
that sensor sits at the back of the compartment beside the smooth tub

cases.answer: The door tub part-thaws every time the door opens and refreezes coarser.
proof: “Ice cream grows crystals when it part-thaws and refreezes, because small crystals melt and regrow as big ones.”
“A thermometer taped to the door shelf recorded minus six at four in the afternoon.”
“Moving the gritty tub to the back shelf stopped any further crystals forming.”
clears: The recipe: “A poor recipe would make both tubs gritty rather than one of them.”
The batch: “Both tubs carry the same brand, flavour and batch code on the lid.”
The freezer: “The freezer's own temperature log reads a steady minus eighteen all week.”
cases.explain: The log says the freezer is fine and the log is telling the truth about the one spot it measures. The door shelf is twelve degrees warmer and swings into the kitchen twenty times a day, and moving the tub is the test that closes it.

cases.title: The Case of the Ribbon That Frayed
cases.story: Half the medal ribbons have frayed into loose threads at both cut ends and half have not. Every ribbon came off the same roll on the same afternoon. A weak weave would fray every ribbon from that roll rather than half of them. All of them have hung on the same board in the same room since the spring. Scissors leave a clean cut that begins to unravel as soon as the ribbon is handled. A heated blade melts the cut edge of a synthetic ribbon and seals the threads together. The frayed half were cut with the craft scissors from the supply drawer. The sound half were cut with the hot knife borrowed from the technology room. Running a finger along a sealed end finds a hard glassy ridge that the cut ends do not have. Nobody has washed, pinned or ironed any of the ribbons since they were cut. The two halves were cut within an hour of each other.
cases.question: Why did half the ribbons fray?

suspects.why: the frayed half were cut with the craft scissors from the supply drawer
a weak weave would fray every ribbon from that roll rather than half of them
all of them have hung on the same board in the same room since the spring
nobody has washed, pinned or ironed any of the ribbons since they were cut
the two halves were cut within an hour of each other

cases.answer: The frayed half were cut with scissors instead of a hot knife.
proof: “A heated blade melts the cut edge of a synthetic ribbon and seals the threads together.”
“The sound half were cut with the hot knife borrowed from the technology room.”
“Running a finger along a sealed end finds a hard glassy ridge that the cut ends do not have.”
clears: The weave: “A weak weave would fray every ribbon from that roll rather than half of them.”
The board: “All of them have hung on the same board in the same room since the spring.”
Washing: “Nobody has washed, pinned or ironed any of the ribbons since they were cut.”
Age: “The two halves were cut within an hour of each other.”
cases.explain: One roll, one room, one hour, and still two outcomes, so nothing about the ribbon or its life explains it. The glassy ridge is the physical evidence that the two ends were made differently, and it is only on the half that held.

cases.title: The Case of the Balloon That Burst Alone
cases.story: Twelve balloons were tied along the railing and only the one at the south end burst. All twelve came from one bag and were inflated by the same pump to the same mark. A weak balloon from a bad bag would be as likely to be any of the twelve. The pump has a gauge and every balloon was taken to the same reading. Latex weakens where sunlight falls on it, and weakened latex gives way under pressure. The south end of the railing is the only part in direct sun after eleven o'clock. The other eleven sit in the shade of the building all day. The air inside a balloon in sunlight also warms and pushes outward harder. A thermometer held against the south end balloon read nine degrees above the others. Nothing sharp projects from the railing anywhere along its length. The burst happened at twenty past two, in the hottest part of the afternoon.
cases.question: Why did one balloon burst?

suspects.who: ☀️ Direct sun on the south end
suspects.why: the south end of the railing is the only part in direct sun after eleven o'clock
a weak balloon from a bad bag would be as likely to be any of the twelve
the pump has a gauge and every balloon was taken to the same reading
nothing sharp projects from the railing anywhere along its length
a thermometer held against the south end balloon read nine degrees above the others

cases.answer: The south end balloon sat in the sun, which weakened it and warmed its air.
proof: “Latex weakens where sunlight falls on it, and weakened latex gives way under pressure.”
“The air inside a balloon in sunlight also warms and pushes outward harder.”
“The burst happened at twenty past two, in the hottest part of the afternoon.”
clears: A weak balloon: “A weak balloon from a bad bag would be as likely to be any of the twelve.”
Over-inflation: “The pump has a gauge and every balloon was taken to the same reading.”
Something sharp: “Nothing sharp projects from the railing anywhere along its length.”
The others: “The other eleven sit in the shade of the building all day.”
cases.explain: The sun does two things here at once, and both push the same way: it weakens the latex from outside and it expands the air from inside. That is why the one balloon in the sun is also the one that goes, and why it goes at the hottest hour rather than the moment it was tied.

cases.title: The Case of the Chute That Stopped Squeaking
cases.story: Three odd things turned up in the library in the same week. Books returned through the outside drop chute arrive with curled, wavy pages. The carpet under the chute has a dark square the size of a doormat. And the brass chute flap, which squeaked for nine years, has gone completely silent. Rain blowing in through the chute would curl the pages, but rain cannot silence a flap. The wet bags readers carry in would mark the whole entrance, not one square under the chute. The reading room humidifier runs on the far side of the building behind two closed doors. A drinks spill soaks the carpet once and dries within a day, and this square has stayed dark since Monday. The flap's return spring snapped on Sunday night, and the flap now hangs open. A flap that rests open never swings, so it cannot squeak. An open chute lets night air and rain straight down onto the books below. It also lets that wet air settle on one square of carpet and keep it damp. The caretaker has not touched the carpet or the chute since the complaints began.
cases.question: What is behind all three problems?

suspects.why: the flap's return spring snapped on Sunday night, and the flap now hangs open
rain blowing in through the chute would curl the pages, but rain cannot silence a flap
the wet bags readers carry in would mark the whole entrance, not one square under the chute
the reading room humidifier runs on the far side of the building behind two closed doors
a drinks spill soaks the carpet once and dries within a day

cases.answer: A snapped spring has left the chute flap hanging open.
proof: “The flap's return spring snapped on Sunday night, and the flap now hangs open.”
“A flap that rests open never swings, so it cannot squeak.”
“An open chute lets night air and rain straight down onto the books below.”
clears: Rain: “rain cannot silence a flap.”
Wet bags: “would mark the whole entrance, not one square under the chute.”
The humidifier: “runs on the far side of the building behind two closed doors.”
A spill: “soaks the carpet once and dries within a day, and this square has stayed dark since Monday.”
cases.explain: Rain can curl pages. A spill can darken carpet. Neither can quiet a hinge. Only one thing in the case sits upstream of all three: a flap stuck open stops swinging, lets the weather in, and holds damp air over the square beneath it. When a single cause accounts for three symptoms that look unrelated, that is the cause.

cases.title: The Case of the Ice Pack That Never Melted
cases.story: Dev's yogurt is warm by lunchtime every day this term. Two other things go with it, and nobody has put them together. His ice pack is still frozen rock hard at noon. The outside of his bag is cold to the touch when he lifts it off the rack. A freezer that failed overnight would send out a soft ice pack, and his comes out solid. Worn insulation would let the cold leak out, so the pack would be melting faster, not slower. The radiator by the bag rack would warm the bag from the outside, and the outside is the cold part. A pack too small for the box would still sweat and soften by noon. Since Dev got the new bag in September, he has clipped the ice pack into the outside mesh pocket. There is a zipped insulated wall between that pocket and the food. The pack has been chilling the outer shell and the air around it all morning. Nothing cold has been inside the box with the yogurt since term began. An ice pack with no warm food beside it has almost nothing to melt it.
cases.question: Why is the yogurt warm?

suspects.who: 🧊 The pack in the outside pocket
suspects.why: he has clipped the ice pack into the outside mesh pocket, with an insulated wall between it and the food
a freezer that failed overnight would send out a soft ice pack, and his comes out solid
worn insulation would let the cold leak out, so the pack would be melting faster, not slower
the radiator would warm the bag from the outside, and the outside is the cold part
a pack too small for the box would still sweat and soften by noon

cases.answer: The ice pack is clipped outside the insulated wall, not inside with the food.
proof: “There is a zipped insulated wall between that pocket and the food.”
“Nothing cold has been inside the box with the yogurt since term began.”
“An ice pack with no warm food beside it has almost nothing to melt it.”
clears: A failed freezer: “a freezer that failed overnight would send out a soft ice pack, and his comes out solid.”
Worn insulation: “the pack would be melting faster, not slower.”
The radiator: “would warm the bag from the outside, and the outside is the cold part.”
A small pack: “a pack too small for the box would still sweat and soften by noon.”
cases.explain: Warm yogurt alone has four plausible causes. Add the pack that will not melt and the shell that is cold, and only one survives. The cold is on the wrong side of the insulation, which is why the food never gets it and the pack never spends it. Three facts, one place they all come from.

cases.title: The Case of the Pencils That Snapped Every Time
cases.story: Lia cannot keep a point on a pencil for a single paragraph. Three facts sit beside the snapping, and each has been shrugged off on its own. The wooden barrels of her pencils have hairline splits running along the grain. A pencil from the same box, kept in Omar's tray, has written all week without breaking. Cheap pencils would fail for Omar too, and his came out of Lia's box. A blunt sharpener blade tears the wood at the tip and leaves the lead below it whole. Pressing too hard snaps a point at the paper, not three centimetres inside the wood. Lia carries her pencil case clipped to the outside of her rucksack, and it hits the stair rail every morning. A dropped case cracks the lead along its whole length inside the unbroken wood. It also splits the barrel along the grain, which is where wood gives way first. A lead cracked end to end has a break waiting wherever the sharpener happens to stop. Omar's pencil has never been in that case.
cases.question: Why do Lia's pencils break and Omar's does not?

suspects.who: 🎒 The case banging the stair rail
suspects.why: she carries her pencil case clipped to the outside of her rucksack, and it hits the stair rail every morning
cheap pencils would fail for Omar too, and his came out of Lia's box
a blunt sharpener blade tears the wood at the tip and leaves the lead below it whole
pressing too hard snaps a point at the paper, not three centimetres inside the wood

cases.answer: The pencil case is knocked against the stair rail every morning.
proof: “A dropped case cracks the lead along its whole length inside the unbroken wood.”
“It also splits the barrel along the grain, which is where wood gives way first.”
“A lead cracked end to end has a break waiting wherever the sharpener happens to stop.”
clears: Cheap pencils: “cheap pencils would fail for Omar too, and his came out of Lia's box.”
The sharpener: “a blunt sharpener blade tears the wood at the tip and leaves the lead below it whole.”
Pressing hard: “pressing too hard snaps a point at the paper, not three centimetres inside the wood.”
cases.explain: The snapping has three companions: split barrels, a twin pencil that works, and breaks deep inside the wood. A bad batch cannot explain Omar's. A bad blade cannot explain the splits. Only the daily knock reaches all of it, because it damages the lead and the wood at once, everywhere along their length.

cases.title: The Case of the Tuesday Apples
cases.story: Apples from the Tuesday crate bruise within a day of reaching the classrooms. Two more things are true of that crate and of no other. Its cardboard base is damp enough to tear when lifted. And the fruit inside tastes mealy and dry even where it is not bruised. Rough handling bruises apples, but it does not make them mealy and it leaves the box dry. Old stock goes mealy, yet every crate on the delivery comes off the same pallet on the same morning. A roof leak would wet the crate below it as well, and the crate below is bone dry. The variety is identical in all five crates, and four of them are fine. The Tuesday crate is the one left on the loading dock overnight because the store room is locked on Mondays. Temperatures on the dock drop below freezing and climb again by morning. Freezing bursts the cells inside the fruit, which is what makes an apple both soft and mealy. Thawing releases that water, and the crate stands in it until the apples are handed out.
cases.question: What is wrong with the Tuesday crate?

suspects.who: 🧊 A night on the loading dock
suspects.why: the Tuesday crate is left on the dock overnight, where temperatures drop below freezing and climb again by morning
rough handling bruises apples, but it does not make them mealy and it leaves the box dry
every crate on the delivery comes off the same pallet on the same morning
a roof leak would wet the crate below it as well, and the crate below is bone dry
the variety is identical in all five crates, and four of them are fine

cases.answer: The crate freezes and thaws overnight on the loading dock.
proof: “Temperatures on the dock drop below freezing and climb again by morning.”
“Freezing bursts the cells inside the fruit, which is what makes an apple both soft and mealy.”
“Thawing releases that water, and the crate stands in it until the apples are handed out.”
clears: Handling: “it does not make them mealy and it leaves the box dry.”
Old stock: “every crate on the delivery comes off the same pallet on the same morning.”
A leak: “the crate below is bone dry.”
The variety: “the variety is identical in all five crates, and four of them are fine.”
cases.explain: Bruised, mealy and damp look like three faults. Freezing and thawing is one event that produces all three, because burst cells go soft, taste dry, and let their water out. Every other suspect accounts for exactly one column of the table and leaves the other two unexplained.

cases.title: The Case of the Punctures on the Inside
cases.story: Noor's back tyre goes soft every three or four days, and she has mended it six times. Two details have come up every time and nobody has used them. All six holes are on the inner face of the tube, the side against the wheel. And the cloth rim tape under the tube has slid about a centimetre off true. Thorns and glass pierce a tyre from the outside, and they leave a mark in the tread above the hole. The tread has no cuts anywhere on it. A leaking valve lets air out steadily but leaves no hole to patch, and she has patched six. A worn pump seal would fail to put air in, and the tyre is hard when she sets off. The rim tape exists to cover the spoke ends that poke through the rim bed. Where it has slipped, one spoke end stands proud of the rim with nothing over it. Every time the wheel turns, the tube presses against that end from the inside. That is the only thing touching the tube on the face where all six holes are.
cases.question: What keeps puncturing the tube?

suspects.who: 🔩 A spoke end through the slipped tape
suspects.why: where the tape has slipped, one spoke end stands proud of the rim with nothing over it
thorns and glass pierce a tyre from the outside, and the tread has no cuts anywhere on it
a leaking valve leaves no hole to patch, and she has patched six
a worn pump seal would fail to put air in, and the tyre is hard when she sets off

cases.answer: A bare spoke end is pressing through where the rim tape slipped.
proof: “Where it has slipped, one spoke end stands proud of the rim with nothing over it.”
“Every time the wheel turns, the tube presses against that end from the inside.”
“That is the only thing touching the tube on the face where all six holes are.”
clears: Thorns: “the tread has no cuts anywhere on it.”
The valve: “a leaking valve lets air out steadily but leaves no hole to patch, and she has patched six.”
The pump: “the tyre is hard when she sets off.”
cases.explain: A slow puncture on its own has four ordinary causes. Add which face the holes are on and where the rim tape sits, and three of the four are gone. The holes are on the inside, so the thing making them is on the inside, and only one thing in the case is.

cases.title: The Case of the Four O'Clock Fish
cases.story: Three complaints about the class tank have been written in the log, on different pages, by different people. The glass grows a green film within three days of being scraped clean. The fish crowd the surface and gulp every afternoon, though they swim low all morning. The thermometer reads nineteen degrees at nine o'clock and twenty-three at four. Overfeeding feeds algae, but it does not warm four degrees of water by teatime. A tired filter would let waste build up slowly and would not keep office hours. Too many fish would crowd the surface in the morning as well as the afternoon. The heater has been unplugged since October, and the plug sits on the shelf beside the tank. The tank was moved in September to the sill under the south window. From half past one the sun falls directly on that glass and stays there until the room is locked. Light is what algae grow on, and sunlight through glass is far stronger than the room lamps. Warm water also holds less dissolved oxygen than cold water does.
cases.question: What is behind all three log entries?

suspects.who: ☀️ The afternoon sun on the sill
suspects.why: from half past one the sun falls directly on that glass and stays there until the room is locked
overfeeding feeds algae, but it does not warm four degrees of water by teatime
a tired filter would let waste build up slowly and would not keep office hours
too many fish would crowd the surface in the morning as well as the afternoon
the heater has been unplugged since October, and the plug sits on the shelf beside the tank

cases.answer: Afternoon sun through the south window is heating and lighting the tank.
proof: “From half past one the sun falls directly on that glass and stays there until the room is locked.”
“Light is what algae grow on, and sunlight through glass is far stronger than the room lamps.”
“Warm water also holds less dissolved oxygen than cold water does.”
clears: Overfeeding: “it does not warm four degrees of water by teatime.”
The filter: “a tired filter would let waste build up slowly and would not keep office hours.”
Too many fish: “too many fish would crowd the surface in the morning as well as the afternoon.”
The heater: “the heater has been unplugged since October, and the plug sits on the shelf beside the tank.”
cases.explain: Algae, gasping and a rising thermometer were logged as three problems. Sunlight is one cause with three outputs: it feeds the algae, it warms the water, and warm water carries less oxygen, so the fish come up for air exactly when the sun has been on the glass longest.

cases.title: The Case of the Rattle on Windy Days
