cases.question: Why did pencil use triple?

suspects.why: a hand sharpener takes about a millimetre off a pencil and the electric one takes four before it stops
forty more pupils is seven percent of six hundred, or about sixty-three pencils at last year's rate
breakages were counted for a fortnight and ran at four a day, which is roughly a hundred and fifty over a year
a sample of thirty bags on one afternoon turned up eleven
issuing by the box changes how pencils leave the shelf but not how fast they are used up

cases.answer: The electric sharpener eats four times as much pencil per sharpening.
proof: “Those four together cannot reach three hundred.”
“A pencil that used to last nine weeks now lasts three.”
“Three times the consumption on nine hundred is twenty-seven hundred, and twenty-seven hundred is the gap.”
clears: More pupils: “about sixty-three pencils at last year's rate.”
Breakages: “roughly a hundred and fifty over a year.”
Taken home: “a sample of thirty bags on one afternoon turned up eleven.”
Issuing by the box: “changes how pencils leave the shelf but not how fast they are used up.”
cases.explain: Growth, breakage and pilfering are all real and all small, and the box system moves pencils without consuming them. The sharpener is the only suspect that multiplies rather than adds, and multiplying is what a threefold rise needs. Four millimetres a sharpening is nothing to watch and everything to the total.

cases.title: The Case of the Orchard That Lost Three Quarters
cases.story: The school orchard picked four hundred kilograms last autumn and ninety this one, and four causes have been proposed by four different people. Each of them is genuinely at work in that orchard. The neighbour's new hedge shades two of the eleven trees, so at the very worst it can cost two elevenths of the crop. Wasp damage was counted on a sample of two hundred apples and came to five percent. The trees have not been pruned for three years, which the county guide says costs about fifteen percent of a yield. Apples crop heavily one year and lightly the next, which can halve a harvest on its own. Put every one of those at its maximum and you still have well over a hundred and fifty kilograms. The weather station logged minus three degrees on the night of the twenty-second of April. The trees were in full flower that night, and a frost at full flower kills the flowers outright. No flower means no fruit at all from that tree, not a reduced crop. The two trees against the south wall flower a week later than the rest, and they carried most of the ninety kilograms.
cases.question: What took three quarters of the crop?

suspects.why: the weather station logged minus three degrees on the night of the twenty-second of April, when the trees were in full flower
the hedge shades two of the eleven trees, so at the very worst it can cost two elevenths of the crop
wasp damage was counted on a sample of two hundred apples and came to five percent
the county guide says three years without pruning costs about fifteen percent of a yield
apples crop heavily one year and lightly the next, which can halve a harvest on its own

cases.answer: A frost on the night of the twenty-second killed the blossom.
proof: “Put every one of those at its maximum and you still have well over a hundred and fifty kilograms.”
“No flower means no fruit at all from that tree, not a reduced crop.”
“The two trees against the south wall flower a week later than the rest, and they carried most of the ninety kilograms.”
clears: The hedge: “at the very worst it can cost two elevenths of the crop.”
Wasps: “came to five percent.”
No pruning: “costs about fifteen percent of a yield.”
Biennial cropping: “which can halve a harvest on its own.”
cases.explain: Four real reductions, stacked at their worst, still leave more than a hundred and fifty kilograms on the trees. Only the frost works by subtraction to zero rather than by percentage, and the two late-flowering trees prove it: they missed the cold night and they carried the harvest.

cases.title: The Case of the Ride That Took Thirteen Minutes Longer
cases.story: Noor's five-kilometre ride to school has gone from eighteen minutes to thirty-one, and she has four theories, all of them founded on something real. The new traffic lights at the bridge were timed over a week and cost her an average of forty seconds. Her rear tyre is soft, and the cycling club's own figures put a soft tyre at about a minute over five kilometres. The roadworks detour was measured on the map at six hundred extra metres, which is two minutes at her speed. There has been a headwind most mornings this month, worth perhaps a minute on an exposed road. Those four add up to four and a half minutes against a loss of thirteen. The rear brake was adjusted in March and the pad has sat against the rim ever since. A wheel lifted off the ground and spun by hand stops in two seconds, where a free wheel spins for forty. A brake that never lets go is working against her for every metre of the ride, uphill, downhill and flat. Nothing else in the list is still costing her anything once she is past it.
cases.question: What is taking the extra time?

suspects.why: the rear brake was adjusted in March and the pad has sat against the rim ever since
the new traffic lights at the bridge were timed over a week and cost her an average of forty seconds
the cycling club's own figures put a soft tyre at about a minute over five kilometres
the detour was measured on the map at six hundred extra metres, which is two minutes at her speed
there has been a headwind most mornings this month, worth perhaps a minute on an exposed road

cases.answer: A brake pad has been dragging on the rim since March.
proof: “Those four add up to four and a half minutes against a loss of thirteen.”
“A wheel lifted off the ground and spun by hand stops in two seconds, where a free wheel spins for forty.”
“A brake that never lets go is working against her for every metre of the ride, uphill, downhill and flat.”
clears: The lights: “cost her an average of forty seconds.”
The tyre: “about a minute over five kilometres.”
The detour: “which is two minutes at her speed.”
The wind: “worth perhaps a minute on an exposed road.”
cases.explain: Four honest delays, four and a half minutes between them. The brake is different in kind as well as in size, because the others take their toll at one place or in one condition and the brake takes its toll continuously. The spin test turns that into a number anybody can check in ten seconds.

cases.title: The Case of the Nine Missing Litres
cases.story: The ninety-litre class tank drops nine litres a week, and the log carries four suggestions from four different weeks. Every one of them loses some water. An open bowl of the same surface area was left beside the tank as a test and evaporated one point two litres in seven days. The filter outlet does splash, but the shelf and the floor under it were dry every morning for a fortnight. Gravel and ornaments were topped up in September and hold water, though a one-off absorption cannot repeat itself every week. The fish were blamed in October, and eleven small fish displace water rather than consuming it. Together those come to under two litres, and seven are unaccounted for. The hose from the external filter weeps where it joins the canister inside the cabinet. The towel under that joint weighs one point one kilograms dry and two point four when it is changed each morning. That is one point three litres a day, which is nine litres a week. The cabinet was not opened at all between September and the week the towel was found.
cases.question: Where are the nine litres going?

suspects.why: the hose from the external filter weeps where it joins the canister inside the cabinet
an open bowl of the same surface area evaporated one point two litres in seven days
the filter outlet does splash, but the shelf and the floor under it were dry every morning for a fortnight
a one-off absorption cannot repeat itself every week
eleven small fish displace water rather than consuming it

cases.answer: A weeping hose joint inside the cabinet loses over a litre a day.
proof: “Together those come to under two litres, and seven are unaccounted for.”
“The towel under that joint weighs one point one kilograms dry and two point four when it is changed each morning.”
“That is one point three litres a day, which is nine litres a week.”
clears: Evaporation: “evaporated one point two litres in seven days.”
Splashing: “the shelf and the floor under it were dry every morning for a fortnight.”
The gravel: “a one-off absorption cannot repeat itself every week.”
The fish: “displace water rather than consuming it.”
cases.explain: Evaporation is real and it is one and a bit litres. Everything else on the list is either zero or cannot happen twice. The towel is the whole case: weigh it wet, weigh it dry, and the difference is a measurement of the leak rather than an opinion about it.

cases.title: The Case of the Hall That Got Twelve Decibels Louder
cases.story: Assembly measured sixty-six decibels last year and seventy-eight this year, and four changes have been offered to explain it. All four happened. Thirty more children come to assembly, and sound adds on a scale where doubling a crowd buys you three decibels, so thirty more on three hundred is under half of one. The new public address system was measured at seventy decibels a metre from the speaker, which is what the old one gave. The ceiling fan was tested alone in an empty hall and read fifty-one, which is below the level of the room before anybody speaks. The chairs were replaced with plastic ones that squeak, and a squeak is brief and sharp rather than a rise in the whole level. The refit took out the full-length curtains and the carpet at the back and put down a hard floor. Reverberation time in the empty hall has gone from nought point nine seconds to two point six. In a room that holds its sound for nearly three seconds, every voice is still arriving while the next one starts. Nothing in the hall is making more noise than it did; the hall has stopped absorbing it.
cases.question: Why is assembly twelve decibels louder?

suspects.who: 🎭 The curtains and carpet taken out
suspects.why: the refit took out the full-length curtains and the carpet at the back and put down a hard floor
doubling a crowd buys you three decibels, so thirty more on three hundred is under half of one
the new system was measured at seventy decibels a metre from the speaker, which is what the old one gave
the fan was tested alone in an empty hall and read fifty-one, which is below the level of the room before anybody speaks
a squeak is brief and sharp rather than a rise in the whole level

cases.answer: The refit stripped out everything in the hall that absorbed sound.
proof: “Reverberation time in the empty hall has gone from nought point nine seconds to two point six.”
“In a room that holds its sound for nearly three seconds, every voice is still arriving while the next one starts.”
“Nothing in the hall is making more noise than it did; the hall has stopped absorbing it.”
clears: More children: “thirty more on three hundred is under half of one.”
The PA: “which is what the old one gave.”
The fan: “read fifty-one, which is below the level of the room before anybody speaks.”
The chairs: “a squeak is brief and sharp rather than a rise in the whole level.”
cases.explain: The crowd is the instinctive answer and the arithmetic kills it: decibels add logarithmically, so you would need six hundred extra children for three. The only change big enough is the one that altered what happens to sound after it is made, and the reverberation figure measures exactly that.

cases.title: The Case of the Drain That Everyone Blamed on Leaves
cases.story: The yard floods to a depth of ten centimetres in any heavy rain, and leaves have been blamed for three autumns. The gully was rodded and cleared the morning before the last storm and the yard flooded anyway. The gutter guards were fitted in September and the gutters were found clear afterwards. The sycamores do drop about twenty-five kilograms of litter each, which is a genuine nuisance and a slow one. The drain itself is a hundred millimetre pipe, and the manufacturer rates it at two thousand litres an hour. Thirty millimetres of rain fell in that hour onto the original roof, which measures three hundred square metres. Three hundred square metres taking thirty millimetres is nine thousand litres in one hour. The new sports hall roof was finished in July and plumbed into the same downpipe. It adds a hundred and eighty square metres, which is another five thousand four hundred litres in the same hour. A pipe rated for two thousand litres is being asked to take fourteen thousand. Clearing leaves out of a pipe does not make the pipe any wider.
cases.question: Why does the yard flood?

suspects.who: 🏗️ The new roof on the same downpipe
suspects.why: the new sports hall roof adds a hundred and eighty square metres, which is another five thousand four hundred litres in the same hour
the gully was rodded and cleared the morning before the last storm and the yard flooded anyway
the sycamores do drop about twenty-five kilograms of litter each, which is a genuine nuisance and a slow one
the gutter guards were fitted in September and the gutters were found clear afterwards
thirty millimetres of rain fell in that hour onto the original roof, which measures three hundred square metres

cases.answer: A second roof was plumbed into a downpipe already at its limit.
proof: “The drain itself is a hundred millimetre pipe, and the manufacturer rates it at two thousand litres an hour.”
“A pipe rated for two thousand litres is being asked to take fourteen thousand.”
“Clearing leaves out of a pipe does not make the pipe any wider.”
clears: Leaves in the gully: “the gully was rodded and cleared the morning before the last storm and the yard flooded anyway.”
The sycamores: “a genuine nuisance and a slow one.”
The gutter guards: “the gutters were found clear afterwards.”
The storm: “thirty millimetres of rain fell in that hour onto the original roof, which measures three hundred square metres.”
cases.explain: Three autumns of blaming leaves, and the clearing test settles it in one morning: cleared pipe, same flood. The storm is real and the old roof alone already overran the pipe by four and a half times. The extra roof is what turned an occasional overflow into every heavy rain, and no amount of sweeping addresses it.

cases.title: The Case of the Pumpkin That Stopped Growing
cases.story: The competition pumpkin reached sixty kilograms when the seed packet promises two hundred, and four growers have offered four reasons. None of them is nonsense. It was given ninety litres of water a day against a recommended eighty, and too much water swells a fruit rather than starving it. A soil test in June came back normal for nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium. It was pollinated on the eleventh of June, which is four days later than ideal and costs perhaps a week of growing. The patch gets six hours of direct sun where the guide asks for eight, which is a real shortfall of a quarter. Taken together those might take fifty kilograms off a record, and a hundred and forty are missing. The main vine was cut through by a mower on the twenty-ninth of July, forty days in. A pumpkin is fed by its leaves and everything they make travels to the fruit along that one vine. Before the cut it was drawing on about four hundred leaves and afterwards on the six beyond the break. The fruit measured eleven kilograms a day in July and under one kilogram a day in August.
cases.question: Why did the pumpkin stop at sixty kilograms?

suspects.why: the main vine was cut through by a mower on the twenty-ninth of July, forty days in
it was given ninety litres a day against a recommended eighty, and too much water swells a fruit rather than starving it
a soil test in June came back normal for nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium
it was pollinated four days later than ideal, which costs perhaps a week of growing
the patch gets six hours of direct sun where the guide asks for eight, which is a real shortfall of a quarter

cases.answer: A mower cut the vine and left the fruit with six leaves instead of four hundred.
proof: “Taken together those might take fifty kilograms off a record, and a hundred and forty are missing.”
“Before the cut it was drawing on about four hundred leaves and afterwards on the six beyond the break.”
“The fruit measured eleven kilograms a day in July and under one kilogram a day in August.”
clears: Too much water: “swells a fruit rather than starving it.”
The soil: “came back normal for nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium.”
Late pollination: “costs perhaps a week of growing.”
Too little sun: “a real shortfall of a quarter.”
cases.explain: Water, soil, timing and sun are the four things a grower controls, and three of them were slightly wrong in ways worth fifty kilograms. The mower is worth a hundred and forty because it did not reduce the supply, it cut it off. The daily weights show the exact day the factory closed.

cases.title: The Case of the Four Kilograms of Mud
cases.story: The cleaners weigh what they sweep off the main corridor and it runs at four kilograms of dried mud a day. Four sources have been named and every one of them does bring mud in. The football pitch is the obvious culprit, except that boots are changed in the boot room and the mat there was weighed at four hundred grams a day. Six builders sign in through the side door, and six pairs of boots on a scraper mat cannot carry four kilograms between them. The gravel path from the gate is dry and loose, and what comes off it is dust rather than mud. The reception children's garden is wet, but reception has its own door at the far end and its own corridor. Those four together were measured over a week at under seven hundred grams a day. In October a shortcut appeared across the field, and the grass along it is worn to bare soil for forty metres. A count on three mornings found a hundred and eighty children using it. Twenty grams on a shoe is a smear nobody would notice, and a hundred and eighty of them is three point six kilograms.
cases.question: Where is four kilograms of mud a day coming from?

suspects.who: 🥾 The worn shortcut across the field
suspects.why: a shortcut appeared across the field, and the grass along it is worn to bare soil for forty metres
boots are changed in the boot room and the mat there was weighed at four hundred grams a day
six pairs of boots on a scraper mat cannot carry four kilograms between them
the gravel path from the gate is dry and loose, and what comes off it is dust rather than mud
reception has its own door at the far end and its own corridor

cases.answer: A hundred and eighty children are crossing bare soil on the shortcut.
proof: “Those four together were measured over a week at under seven hundred grams a day.”
“A count on three mornings found a hundred and eighty children using it.”
“Twenty grams on a shoe is a smear nobody would notice, and a hundred and eighty of them is three point six kilograms.”
clears: The pitch: “the mat there was weighed at four hundred grams a day.”
The builders: “six pairs of boots on a scraper mat cannot carry four kilograms between them.”
The gravel: “what comes off it is dust rather than mud.”
Reception: “reception has its own door at the far end and its own corridor.”
cases.explain: Everybody looks for the muddiest feet, and the muddiest feet are a handful of pairs. The answer is the cleanest feet multiplied by a hundred and eighty. A source too small to see on any single shoe is the largest source in the building, which is what a count is for.

cases.title: The Case of the Fuel Bill That Rose a Third
cases.story: The minibus burned two thousand six hundred litres last spring and three thousand four hundred this spring, and four reasons have been put forward by the office. Each describes something that really changed. Fuel went up nine percent a litre in October, which raises the bill and leaves the litres exactly where they were. The route was altered in November and the new one is one point two kilometres longer on twenty-six, which is five percent. The driver's log shows an average of twelve minutes idling at the depot each day, worth about three percent of the fuel. The tyres were found twenty percent under pressure in February, which the manufacturer puts at three percent on consumption. Added together those changes account for eleven percent, and the rise is thirty-one. The second minibus failed its test in September and has been off the road since. This bus has covered the other route as well on Tuesdays, Thursdays and Fridays. The odometer reads nine thousand four hundred kilometres last spring and twelve thousand two hundred this spring. Thirty percent more distance in a vehicle that has not otherwise changed burns thirty percent more fuel.
cases.question: Why has the fuel use risen by a third?

suspects.why: the second minibus failed its test in September, and this bus has covered the other route on Tuesdays, Thursdays and Fridays
fuel went up nine percent a litre in October, which raises the bill and leaves the litres exactly where they were
the new route is one point two kilometres longer on twenty-six, which is five percent
an average of twelve minutes idling each day is worth about three percent of the fuel
the tyres were twenty percent under pressure, which the manufacturer puts at three percent on consumption

cases.answer: The bus is covering two routes because the other minibus is off the road.
proof: “Added together those changes account for eleven percent, and the rise is thirty-one.”
“The odometer reads nine thousand four hundred kilometres last spring and twelve thousand two hundred this spring.”
“Thirty percent more distance in a vehicle that has not otherwise changed burns thirty percent more fuel.”
clears: The price: “raises the bill and leaves the litres exactly where they were.”
The route: “one point two kilometres longer on twenty-six, which is five percent.”
Idling: “worth about three percent of the fuel.”
The tyres: “three percent on consumption.”
cases.explain: The price of fuel is the loudest change of the year and it cannot move a count of litres at all. The other three are real and come to eleven percent between them. The odometer settles it without any argument about efficiency: the bus went thirty percent further.

cases.title: The Case of the Sports Fund That Was Eighteen Hundred Short
cases.story: The sports fund should hold two thousand four hundred pounds and the statement shows five hundred and sixty. Four explanations are on the table and each one is a genuine outgoing. The engraving on the county trophy cost a hundred and ten pounds, and the invoice is in the folder. Unpaid subscriptions come to ninety-five pounds, which is money that never arrived rather than money that left. Bank charges run at three pounds a month, which is thirty-six pounds across the year. The cash tin float was raised from twenty pounds to fifty in September, moving thirty pounds rather than spending it. Those four come to two hundred and seventy-one pounds at the very most, and the hole is eighteen hundred and forty. The kit order was placed by the office in June and placed again by the coach in July. Both orders were paid, and the supplier's statement shows two payments of nine hundred and twenty pounds eleven days apart. One delivery was signed for and the second was never chased, because nobody knew to expect it. Eighteen hundred and forty pounds is exactly two times nine hundred and twenty.
cases.question: Where did the money go?

suspects.why: the supplier's statement shows two payments of nine hundred and twenty pounds eleven days apart
the engraving on the county trophy cost a hundred and ten pounds, and the invoice is in the folder
unpaid subscriptions come to ninety-five pounds, which is money that never arrived rather than money that left
bank charges run at three pounds a month, which is thirty-six pounds across the year
the float was raised from twenty pounds to fifty, moving thirty pounds rather than spending it

cases.answer: The kit order was placed and paid for twice.
proof: “Those four come to two hundred and seventy-one pounds at the very most, and the hole is eighteen hundred and forty.”
“The kit order was placed by the office in June and placed again by the coach in July.”
“Eighteen hundred and forty pounds is exactly two times nine hundred and twenty.”
clears: The engraving: “cost a hundred and ten pounds, and the invoice is in the folder.”
Subscriptions: “money that never arrived rather than money that left.”
Bank charges: “thirty-six pounds across the year.”
The float: “moving thirty pounds rather than spending it.”
cases.explain: Two of these are spending, one is income that failed to arrive, and one is money that only changed pockets. Telling those apart matters, and even so they come to two hundred and seventy-one pounds. The missing figure is not approximately the kit order. It is exactly twice it, and a number that exact is a duplicate.

cases.title: The Case of the Turkey That Took Seven Hours
cases.story: The turkey needed seven hours when the recipe allowed four and a half, and four reasons have been offered around the table. Every one of them does slow a roast. The bird came in half a kilogram over the weight planned for, and the recipe gives forty minutes a kilogram, so that is twenty minutes. The oven door was opened six times, and each opening costs about five minutes of recovery, which is half an hour. The bird was covered in foil for the first three hours, which the recipe expects and allows for. It went in straight from the fridge rather than standing out, and that is worth perhaps fifteen minutes on a bird this size. Those four come to an hour and five minutes against a delay of two and a half hours. A probe thermometer left in the oven read a hundred and twenty degrees all afternoon. The dial had been turned to the setting marked with a snowflake, which is the slow defrost programme. Cooking at a hundred and twenty instead of a hundred and eighty is not a delay of minutes but a different rate altogether. Nothing else on the list changes the temperature the meat is sitting in.
cases.question: Why did the turkey take seven hours?

suspects.who: 🌡️ The oven on the defrost setting
suspects.why: a probe thermometer left in the oven read a hundred and twenty degrees all afternoon
half a kilogram over at forty minutes a kilogram is twenty minutes
the door was opened six times, and each opening costs about five minutes of recovery
the bird was covered in foil for the first three hours, which the recipe expects and allows for
going in straight from the fridge is worth perhaps fifteen minutes on a bird this size

cases.answer: The oven was running at a hundred and twenty degrees all afternoon.
proof: “Those four come to an hour and five minutes against a delay of two and a half hours.”
“The dial had been turned to the setting marked with a snowflake, which is the slow defrost programme.”
“Cooking at a hundred and twenty instead of a hundred and eighty is not a delay of minutes but a different rate altogether.”
clears: The heavier bird: “the recipe gives forty minutes a kilogram, so that is twenty minutes.”
The door: “each opening costs about five minutes of recovery, which is half an hour.”
The foil: “which the recipe expects and allows for.”
The fridge: “worth perhaps fifteen minutes on a bird this size.”
cases.explain: Four honest delays, an hour and five minutes between them, and every one of them adds a fixed lump of time. The oven setting is not a lump, it is a rate, and a rate applies to every minute of the cook. That is why a sixty-degree error outweighs everything else put together.

cases.title: The Case of the Bake Sale That Made Sixty-Two Pounds
cases.story: The bake sale took two hundred and forty pounds at the table and handed sixty-two pounds to the fund. Four losses have been offered to explain the difference and all four happened. Eleven cupcakes were dropped or crushed before the sale opened, which at a pound and twenty is thirteen pounds of stock that was never sold. Fourteen were given free to helpers, worth sixteen pounds eighty. The last thirty were cut to sixty pence at half past three, which gave away eighteen pounds against the full price. The float of twenty pounds was counted into the takings by mistake and taken out again, so it changes nothing. Those real losses come to forty-eight pounds, and a hundred and seventy-eight pounds are missing. The ingredients were bought at the corner shop on the morning of the sale. Butter, eggs and ground almonds for two hundred cakes cost a hundred and sixty-one pounds there. The same list at the supermarket two streets away comes to forty-three pounds. Nobody in the planning meeting ever subtracted the ingredients from the takings at all.
cases.question: Why did a two hundred pound sale raise sixty-two?

suspects.why: butter, eggs and ground almonds for two hundred cakes cost a hundred and sixty-one pounds at the corner shop
eleven cupcakes were crushed before the sale opened, which at a pound and twenty is thirteen pounds
fourteen were given free to helpers, worth sixteen pounds eighty
the last thirty were cut to sixty pence, which gave away eighteen pounds against the full price
the float of twenty pounds was counted into the takings by mistake and taken out again, so it changes nothing

cases.answer: The ingredients cost a hundred and sixty-one pounds at the corner shop.
proof: “Those real losses come to forty-eight pounds, and a hundred and seventy-eight pounds are missing.”
“The same list at the supermarket two streets away comes to forty-three pounds.”
“Nobody in the planning meeting ever subtracted the ingredients from the takings at all.”
clears: Crushed cakes: “which at a pound and twenty is thirteen pounds of stock that was never sold.”
Free cakes: “worth sixteen pounds eighty.”
The price cut: “which gave away eighteen pounds against the full price.”
The float: “so it changes nothing.”
cases.explain: Three small losses and one that is not a loss at all. The meeting spent its time on the forty-eight pounds it could see at the table, because that is where the cakes were. The hundred and sixty-one pounds left the fund at eight in the morning, before a single cake was baked.

cases.title: The Case of the Mittens That Only Failed in the Wind
cases.story: The knitted mittens keep hands warm on the playground and the bought ones do not, and four differences have been suggested. All four are real differences between the two pairs. The knitted ones measure four millimetres thick and the bought ones three, which the textile table puts at about one degree of difference. The knitted ones are wool and the bought ones acrylic, worth roughly another degree when dry. The knitted cuff is six centimetres longer, which keeps the wrist covered and is worth about half a degree. The bought pair is black and the knitted pair cream, and colour does nothing at all on a cloudy day. Measured indoors in still air, hands in the two pairs finished within one degree of each other. Held in front of a fan at twenty kilometres an hour, the bought pair dropped eleven degrees and the knitted pair dropped two. The bought knit has visible holes between the stitches that air passes straight through. The knitted pair was made on small needles at a tension that leaves no gaps. Still air trapped in a fabric is what keeps a hand warm, and wind takes that air away.
cases.question: Why do the bought mittens fail?

suspects.who: 🌬️ The loose knit the wind blows through
suspects.why: the bought knit has visible holes between the stitches that air passes straight through
four millimetres against three is about one degree of difference in the textile table
wool against acrylic is worth roughly another degree when dry
the knitted cuff is six centimetres longer, which is worth about half a degree
the bought pair is black and the knitted pair cream, and colour does nothing at all on a cloudy day

cases.answer: Wind goes straight through the gaps in the bought knit.
proof: “Measured indoors in still air, hands in the two pairs finished within one degree of each other.”
“Held in front of a fan at twenty kilometres an hour, the bought pair dropped eleven degrees and the knitted pair dropped two.”
“Still air trapped in a fabric is what keeps a hand warm, and wind takes that air away.”
clears: Thickness: “which the textile table puts at about one degree of difference.”
The fibre: “worth roughly another degree when dry.”
The cuff: “which keeps the wrist covered and is worth about half a degree.”
The colour: “colour does nothing at all on a cloudy day.”
cases.explain: Indoors the two pairs are the same, which means none of the four differences amounts to much on its own. Put them in wind and one of them becomes nine degrees. A property that is worth nothing in one condition and everything in another is still the answer, and the playground is the condition that counts.

cases.title: The Case of the House That Would Not Stand Up
cases.story: The gingerbread house fell in on itself twice, and four reasons were offered by four bakers. All four are genuine weaknesses in that build. The kitchen was humid from the oven, and damp softens royal icing by about a tenth of its strength. The sweets stuck to the walls weigh forty-six grams altogether, against roof panels of a hundred and eighty grams each. The baking board flexes if you lift it from one corner, and it was carried flat on a tray both times. The panels came out two millimetres thinner than the pattern asks for, which weakens the gingerbread itself and not the joints. Those four between them change the load by well under a tenth. A royal icing joint cured for twelve hours holds about nine hundred grams before it gives way. The same joint after forty minutes holds about sixty grams. Each wall is carrying two hundred and forty grams of roof once the panels are on. The house was assembled forty minutes after the icing was piped, because the class ends at three.
cases.question: Why did the house collapse?

suspects.who: ⏱️ Icing given forty minutes to cure
suspects.why: the house was assembled forty minutes after the icing was piped, because the class ends at three
damp softens royal icing by about a tenth of its strength
the sweets weigh forty-six grams altogether, against roof panels of a hundred and eighty grams each
the baking board flexes if you lift it from one corner, and it was carried flat on a tray both times
the panels came out two millimetres thinner than the pattern asks, which weakens the gingerbread and not the joints

cases.answer: The icing had forty minutes to set when it needed twelve hours.
proof: “A royal icing joint cured for twelve hours holds about nine hundred grams before it gives way.”
“The same joint after forty minutes holds about sixty grams.”
“Each wall is carrying two hundred and forty grams of roof once the panels are on.”
clears: The humidity: “damp softens royal icing by about a tenth of its strength.”
The sweets: “weigh forty-six grams altogether, against roof panels of a hundred and eighty grams each.”
The board: “it was carried flat on a tray both times.”
The thin panels: “which weakens the gingerbread itself and not the joints.”
cases.explain: Three of the suspects adjust the load by a few percent and one weakens the wrong part. The cure time is not a few percent. Sixty grams of strength under two hundred and forty grams of roof is a house that was going to fall whatever else was true of it.

cases.title: The Case of the Lights That Never Went Off
cases.story: The hall's lighting cost forty pounds a month last year and three hundred and ten this year. Four changes have been blamed and each of them really did happen in that hall. The thirty-six new panels draw eighteen watts each, where the old fittings drew fifty-eight, so the new ones use less. The string of festive lights draws a hundred and twenty watts for six hours a day, which is about six pounds a month. The unit price of electricity rose nine percent in October, which is three pounds sixty on last year's bill. The hall is booked for twelve more hours a month than it was, which at the panels' draw is under three pounds. Those changes cannot account for more than a tenth of the rise. The movement sensor fitted in September was wired to the wrong terminal and holds the lights on permanently. Thirty-six panels at eighteen watts is six hundred and forty-eight watts, and the hall was lit for ninety hours a month before. It is now lit for all seven hundred and twenty hours in a month, including every night and every weekend. Eight times the hours on the same fittings is eight times the bill.
cases.question: Why did the lighting bill rise eightfold?

suspects.why: the movement sensor fitted in September was wired to the wrong terminal and holds the lights on permanently
the new panels draw eighteen watts each, where the old fittings drew fifty-eight, so the new ones use less
a hundred and twenty watts for six hours a day is about six pounds a month
the unit price rose nine percent in October, which is three pounds sixty on last year's bill
twelve more hours a month at the panels' draw is under three pounds

cases.answer: A miswired sensor has kept the hall lit twenty-four hours a day.
proof: “Those changes cannot account for more than a tenth of the rise.”
“The hall was lit for ninety hours a month before.”
“It is now lit for all seven hundred and twenty hours in a month, including every night and every weekend.”
clears: The panels: “so the new ones use less.”
The festive lights: “about six pounds a month.”
The unit price: “which is three pounds sixty on last year's bill.”
Extra bookings: “under three pounds.”
cases.explain: The new panels are the first thing anyone blames and they cut the draw by two thirds. Nothing on the list changes the wattage enough to matter. What changed is the hours, from ninety to seven hundred and twenty, and a bill is watts multiplied by hours whichever of the two you move.

cases.title: The Case of the Bell That Drifted Ninety Seconds
cases.story: The end-of-day bell rings ninety seconds late by Friday and on time again on Monday, and four causes have been suggested. All four are real sources of error in that system. The bell timer's own quartz is specified to drift two seconds a month, which is less than half a second across a week. The relay that fires the bell was measured with a stopwatch and lags four tenths of a second. There was one power cut in October, and a power cut stops the clock rather than slowing it, and it would show as a jump on one day. The timer is reset by hand each half term, which corrects the error rather than creating it. Those four cannot produce more than a second or two across five days. The caretaker synchronises the bell timer to the office clock every morning. The office clock is itself set each morning against the deputy head's watch. That watch was checked against the speaking clock and gains eighteen seconds a day. Eighteen seconds carried forward five mornings in a row is ninety seconds by Friday, and Monday starts again from zero.
cases.question: Why does the bell drift by ninety seconds?

suspects.who: ⌚ The watch the office clock is set by
suspects.why: the watch was checked against the speaking clock and gains eighteen seconds a day
the timer's quartz is specified to drift two seconds a month, which is less than half a second across a week
the relay was measured with a stopwatch and lags four tenths of a second
a power cut stops the clock rather than slowing it, and it would show as a jump on one day
the timer is reset by hand each half term, which corrects the error rather than creating it

cases.answer: The watch the whole chain is set from gains eighteen seconds a day.
proof: “Those four cannot produce more than a second or two across five days.”
“The caretaker synchronises the bell timer to the office clock every morning.”
“Eighteen seconds carried forward five mornings in a row is ninety seconds by Friday, and Monday starts again from zero.”
clears: The quartz: “less than half a second across a week.”
The relay: “lags four tenths of a second.”
The power cut: “it would show as a jump on one day.”
The reset: “which corrects the error rather than creating it.”
cases.explain: Every component in the bell system is accurate to within a second or two a week, and the system is ninety seconds out. The error is not in any component. It is in the daily habit of copying a time from a watch nobody ever checked, and copying it again the next morning on top of yesterday's copy.

cases.title: The Case of the Eight Degrees Lost Overnight
cases.story: The school was nineteen degrees at six on Thursday evening and eleven degrees at six on Friday morning. Four causes have been offered for the drop and every one of them does lose heat from that building. The fire door at the end of the science block was propped open, and a gap that size is worth about a degree over a night. The single-glazed windows along the north side were measured by the surveyor at roughly one and a half degrees across a cold night. The loft hatch above the stairs was left open, which the same survey put at half a degree. The thermostat is set back to twelve overnight, which is where the heating stops helping rather than a thing that takes heat away. Those four together come to about three degrees against a fall of eight. The boiler fault log shows a lockout at ten past eleven and no firing at all until the caretaker reset it at half past six. A building with the heating off does not lose heat faster, it simply stops being given any. The surveyor's own figure for this building unheated on a night below zero is seven to nine degrees.
cases.question: Why did the school lose eight degrees?

suspects.why: the fault log shows a lockout at ten past eleven and no firing at all until half past six
a gap that size is worth about a degree over a night
the surveyor measured the north windows at roughly one and a half degrees across a cold night
the same survey put the open hatch at half a degree
the setback is where the heating stops helping rather than a thing that takes heat away

cases.answer: The boiler locked out at eleven and did not fire again until morning.
proof: “Those four together come to about three degrees against a fall of eight.”
“A building with the heating off does not lose heat faster, it simply stops being given any.”
“The surveyor's own figure for this building unheated on a night below zero is seven to nine degrees.”
clears: The fire door: “a gap that size is worth about a degree over a night.”
The windows: “roughly one and a half degrees across a cold night.”
The loft hatch: “which the same survey put at half a degree.”
The setback: “which is where the heating stops helping rather than a thing that takes heat away.”
cases.explain: Three real draughts and one thing that is not a draught at all. Added at their worst they are three degrees. The building is designed to lose seven to nine with nothing coming in, which is a figure that was already written down, and the fault log says nothing came in from ten past eleven.

cases.title: The Case of the Two Kilograms of Seed a Day
cases.story: The feeders on the field are emptying two kilograms of seed a day, and four eaters have been blamed by the four people who watch them. All four are genuinely eating from them. The sparrows are the birds everyone sees, and a count at nine in the morning found about twenty on the feeders at once. A sparrow eats around five grams of seed in a day, so twenty sparrows is a hundred grams. Two squirrels have been photographed on the poles, and a grey squirrel takes perhaps eighty grams a day each. The catch tray underneath was emptied and weighed for a week and held sixty grams of spilled seed a day. The finches come in ones and twos and eat about the same as a sparrow. Those four together are under four hundred grams of the two thousand. The pigeons arrive at half past three, after the watchers have gone home, and the caretaker counted forty on and under the feeders. A woodpigeon eats about forty grams of grain a day, and forty of them is sixteen hundred grams. The birds that are seen all day are the ones that eat least.
cases.question: What is eating two kilograms a day?

suspects.who: 🕊️ The pigeons after half past three
suspects.why: the caretaker counted forty on and under the feeders, and a woodpigeon eats about forty grams of grain a day
a count found about twenty at once, and a sparrow eats around five grams in a day
two squirrels have been photographed, and a grey squirrel takes perhaps eighty grams a day each
the catch tray was emptied and weighed for a week and held sixty grams of spilled seed a day
the finches come in ones and twos and eat about the same as a sparrow

proof: “Those four together are under four hundred grams of the two thousand.”
“A woodpigeon eats about forty grams of grain a day, and forty of them is sixteen hundred grams.”
“The birds that are seen all day are the ones that eat least.”
clears: The sparrows: “twenty sparrows is a hundred grams.”
The squirrels: “a grey squirrel takes perhaps eighty grams a day each.”
Spillage: “held sixty grams of spilled seed a day.”
The finches: “eat about the same as a sparrow.”
cases.explain: Two numbers decide this and only one of them is about appetite. A pigeon eats eight times what a sparrow eats, and there are twice as many of them, which is sixteen times the total from a bird nobody counted. The watching was done at nine in the morning, and the eating is done at half past three.

cases.title: The Case of the Urn That Took Forty Minutes
cases.story: The staff room urn used to boil in twelve minutes and now takes forty, and four explanations have been offered. Each one slows a boil. It is filled to eighteen litres now rather than seventeen, which is six percent more water and about forty seconds. The staff room has been two degrees colder since the radiator valve stuck, which costs under a minute from a cold start. The lid is often left off, and a test with the lid on and off put the difference at six minutes. There is about a millimetre of limescale on the elements, which the manual says adds roughly five percent to a boiling time. Those four together account for eight minutes of the twenty-eight that have been added. The urn has three heating elements and an engineer measured the resistance across all three in February. Two of them are open circuit and have been since the power surge in January. One element doing the work of three takes three times as long to deliver the same heat. Twelve minutes multiplied by three is thirty-six, and the other faults account for the rest.
cases.question: Why does the urn take forty minutes?

suspects.why: an engineer measured the resistance and two of the three elements are open circuit
eighteen litres rather than seventeen is six percent more water and about forty seconds
two degrees colder costs under a minute from a cold start
a test with the lid on and off put the difference at six minutes
about a millimetre of limescale adds roughly five percent to a boiling time

cases.answer: Two of the three elements are dead, so one is doing all the work.
proof: “Those four together account for eight minutes of the twenty-eight that have been added.”
“One element doing the work of three takes three times as long to deliver the same heat.”
“Twelve minutes multiplied by three is thirty-six, and the other faults account for the rest.”
clears: The extra litre: “six percent more water and about forty seconds.”
The cold room: “costs under a minute from a cold start.”
The lid: “put the difference at six minutes.”
Limescale: “adds roughly five percent to a boiling time.”
cases.explain: Three of these add minutes and one adds a percentage, and the lid is the biggest of them at six. The elements do not add anything. They multiply, and losing two thirds of the power triples the time whatever else is going on. The resistance test is the only measurement here that looks inside the urn.

cases.title: The Case of the Hundred Cards That Never Arrived
cases.story: Three hundred and ten cards went into the school post and a hundred and ninety came out, and four losses have been accounted for. Each is a real card that genuinely failed to arrive. Fourteen were addressed to names that match nobody on the roll and came back to the office. Nine had no name on them at all and are in a box behind the desk. Six were handed straight to the person rather than posted, which means they arrived without passing through the system. Four were found torn in the sorting tray and could not be read. Those four groups come to thirty-three cards, and a hundred and twenty are missing. A second post box was put in the junior corridor on the Monday and nobody was told to empty it. It was opened on the following Friday and a hundred and three cards were taken out of it. Nobody ever counted a card into the system twice, so every card posted is somewhere. A hundred and three plus thirty-three is a hundred and thirty-six, and the rest turned up loose in the sorting tray.
cases.question: Where did the missing cards go?

suspects.why: a second post box was put in the junior corridor and nobody was told to empty it
fourteen were addressed to names that match nobody on the roll and came back to the office
nine had no name on them at all and are in a box behind the desk
six were handed straight to the person, which means they arrived without passing through the system
four were found torn in the sorting tray and could not be read

proof: “Those four groups come to thirty-three cards, and a hundred and twenty are missing.”
“It was opened on the following Friday and a hundred and three cards were taken out of it.”
“Nobody ever counted a card into the system twice, so every card posted is somewhere.”

No name: “are in a box behind the desk.”

Torn cards: “could not be read.”
