cases.title: The Case of the Eruption That Reached Thirty Centimetres
cases.story: The model volcano threw its foam thirty centimetres and the club record is two metres, and four differences have been proposed. All four are real differences from the record attempt. The bottle neck is thirty-five millimetres across where the record used twenty, and a wider neck does let the foam out more slowly. Forty grams of bicarbonate was used against the record's sixty, which is a third less gas. The vinegar is five percent acid and the record used eight, which is another real shortfall. The room was four degrees cooler, which slows a reaction a little without changing how much gas it makes. Those four might halve a height between them, and this one is down by six sevenths. The record attempt adds ten millilitres of washing-up liquid and this one used none. Gas on its own rises through the liquid and bursts at the surface, so most of it never lifts anything. Soap traps that gas as foam, and foam is what climbs the neck and keeps climbing. The same mixture with soap added was run afterwards and reached one metre seventy.
cases.question: Why did the eruption only reach thirty centimetres?

suspects.why: the record attempt adds ten millilitres of washing-up liquid and this one used none
the bottle neck is thirty-five millimetres across where the record used twenty
forty grams against the record's sixty, which is a third less gas
the vinegar is five percent acid and the record used eight, which is another real shortfall
four degrees cooler slows a reaction a little without changing how much gas it makes

cases.answer: There was no soap, so the gas escaped instead of becoming foam.
proof: “Those four might halve a height between them, and this one is down by six sevenths.”
“Gas on its own rises through the liquid and bursts at the surface, so most of it never lifts anything.”
“The same mixture with soap added was run afterwards and reached one metre seventy.”
clears: The neck: “a wider neck does let the foam out more slowly.”
Less bicarbonate: “which is a third less gas.”
Weaker vinegar: “which is another real shortfall.”
The cool room: “slows a reaction a little without changing how much gas it makes.”
cases.explain: Three suspects reduce the gas and one slows it down, and together they are worth about half the height. The soap does not make gas at all. It changes what happens to the gas that is made, and the rerun settles it: same weak vinegar, same forty grams, ten millilitres of soap, one metre seventy.

cases.title: The Case of the Jewels That Fell Off the Crown
cases.story: Thirty-eight of the forty stones on the play's crown were on the floor by the end of the first rehearsal, and four reasons have been offered. All four are true of that crown. The stones weigh one point four grams each, which is a real load on a vertical surface. The card base flexes when the crown is put on, and flexing does work at a glued joint. A coat of varnish was sprayed over the finished crown, and solvent in a varnish can soften some glues. The hall was warm under the lights, and warmth softens glue a little. The glue itself is rated at two kilograms per square centimetre, which is more than a thousand times the weight of a stone. The crown was sprayed with glitter spray before the stones went on. A pull test on a stone glued to bare card needed six hundred grams to shift it. The same glue on the glittered surface let go at four grams. The glue is holding perfectly well to a layer of loose glitter that is holding on to nothing.
cases.question: Why did the stones fall off?

suspects.who: ✨ The glitter spray under the glue
suspects.why: the crown was sprayed with glitter spray before the stones went on, and the glue is holding to a layer of loose glitter
the stones weigh one point four grams each, which is a real load on a vertical surface
the card base flexes when the crown is put on, and flexing does work at a glued joint
solvent in a varnish can soften some glues
the hall was warm under the lights, and warmth softens glue a little

cases.answer: The glue was stuck to loose glitter instead of to the card.
proof: “The glue itself is rated at two kilograms per square centimetre, which is more than a thousand times the weight of a stone.”
“A pull test on a stone glued to bare card needed six hundred grams to shift it.”
“The same glue on the glittered surface let go at four grams.”
clears: The stones: “weigh one point four grams each, which is a real load on a vertical surface.”
The flexing base: “flexing does work at a glued joint.”
The varnish: “solvent in a varnish can soften some glues.”
The warm hall: “warmth softens glue a little.”
cases.explain: Weight, flexing, solvent and warmth all eat into a glued joint, and the joint was rated a thousand times stronger than it needed to be, so none of them should have mattered. The pull test is the whole case: six hundred grams on card, four grams on glitter. The glue never failed. It was never stuck to the crown.

cases.title: The Case of the Stage That Sagged Eleven Millimetres
cases.story: The stage floor dips eleven millimetres under the piano and the builder's limit is three. Four loads have been blamed and every one of them is really up there. The piano weighs four hundred and eighty kilograms on four castors, which is a heavy point load and the obvious suspect. The choir of forty stands on the same stage, and forty people at sixty kilograms is two thousand four hundred kilograms. The staging blocks at the back add another hundred and ten. The lighting bar is hung from the ceiling and carries none of its weight on the floor at all. The stage was built for a distributed load four times what it now carries, and it did not sag last year under the same choir. A cable run was cut through the main joist in two thousand and nineteen, taking its depth from two hundred and twenty millimetres to ninety. The stiffness of a joist goes with the cube of its depth, not with the depth itself. Ninety cubed against two hundred and twenty cubed leaves about seven percent of the original stiffness. A beam with a fourteenth of its stiffness bends fourteen times as far under exactly the load it always carried.
cases.question: Why does the stage sag?

suspects.who: 🪚 The joist cut for the cable run
suspects.why: a cable run was cut through the main joist, taking its depth from two hundred and twenty millimetres to ninety
the piano weighs four hundred and eighty kilograms on four castors, which is a heavy point load
forty people at sixty kilograms is two thousand four hundred kilograms
the staging blocks at the back add another hundred and ten
the lighting bar is hung from the ceiling and carries none of its weight on the floor at all

cases.answer: A joist cut for cables has about seven percent of its stiffness left.
proof: “The stage was built for a distributed load four times what it now carries, and it did not sag last year under the same choir.”
“The stiffness of a joist goes with the cube of its depth, not with the depth itself.”
“A beam with a fourteenth of its stiffness bends fourteen times as far under exactly the load it always carried.”
clears: The piano: “a heavy point load and the obvious suspect.”
The choir: “forty people at sixty kilograms is two thousand four hundred kilograms.”
The blocks: “add another hundred and ten.”
The lighting bar: “carries none of its weight on the floor at all.”
cases.explain: Everyone argues about the load and the load has not changed, which the stage proved last year by carrying it. What changed is the beam. Cutting six tenths of the depth out of a joist does not take six tenths of its strength, it takes ninety-three percent, because stiffness answers to the cube.

cases.title: The Case of the String That Weighed More Than the Kite
cases.story: The kite flew well on the first day and will not leave the ground now, and four additions have been blamed. Every one of them is extra weight that was not there on the first day. The longer tail adds fourteen grams to a kite that weighs ninety. The paper took up damp overnight and a careful weighing put that at six grams. The plastic winder was clipped to the bridle to stop it rolling away, which is twenty grams. Extra tape along the spars adds four grams. Those four come to forty-four grams, which is a real handicap and not an impossible one. The string was changed after the first day from the thin nylon to the builder's line from the shed. Sixty metres of that line weighs two point one grams a metre. The thin nylon it replaced weighs a third of a gram a metre, or twenty grams over the same sixty. A hundred and twenty-six grams of line is more than the kite itself weighs. A kite does not only lift itself, it lifts every metre of string between it and the hand.
cases.question: Why will the kite not fly?

suspects.why: sixty metres of builder's line weighs two point one grams a metre
the longer tail adds fourteen grams to a kite that weighs ninety
a careful weighing put the damp at six grams
the plastic winder was clipped to the bridle to stop it rolling away, which is twenty grams
extra tape along the spars adds four grams

cases.answer: The new line weighs more than the kite it is attached to.
proof: “Those four come to forty-four grams, which is a real handicap and not an impossible one.”
“A hundred and twenty-six grams of line is more than the kite itself weighs.”
“A kite does not only lift itself, it lifts every metre of string between it and the hand.”
clears: The tail: “adds fourteen grams to a kite that weighs ninety.”
The damp: “put that at six grams.”
The winder: “which is twenty grams.”
The tape: “adds four grams.”
cases.explain: Four people weighed four things on the kite and nobody weighed the string, because the string is not on the kite. It is on the kite the moment the kite leaves the ground. Sixty metres of line at two grams a metre is the heaviest single component in the whole arrangement.

cases.title: The Case of the Seeds That Did Not Come Up
cases.story: Eleven seedlings came up from a tray of two hundred seeds and four reasons have been given, all of them genuine faults in the sowing. The packet is dated last March, and the seed house puts the fall in germination at about ten percent a year. The compost was the cheap bag left over from last summer, which the trial tray showed is worth perhaps another ten percent. The windowsill held at fourteen degrees where the packet asks for eighteen, which slows germination and does not stop it. The tray was watered once a week rather than kept damp, which the same trial put at fifteen percent. Those four at their worst would still leave well over a hundred seedlings. The seed was pressed in with a thumb to a depth of about two centimetres. The packet asks for five millimetres and says in bold that the seed needs light to germinate. A seed buried four times too deep in the dark never starts at all, whatever the compost or the temperature. A second tray from the same packet, sown at five millimetres into the same cheap compost, gave a hundred and sixty-eight.
cases.question: Why did only eleven seeds come up?

suspects.why: the seed was pressed in to about two centimetres where the packet asks for five millimetres
the seed house puts the fall in germination at about ten percent a year
the trial tray showed the cheap compost is worth perhaps another ten percent
fourteen degrees where the packet asks for eighteen slows germination and does not stop it
watering once a week rather than keeping the tray damp was worth fifteen percent in the trial

cases.answer: The seed was buried two centimetres deep when it needs light.
proof: “Those four at their worst would still leave well over a hundred seedlings.”
“A seed buried four times too deep in the dark never starts at all, whatever the compost or the temperature.”
“A second tray from the same packet, sown at five millimetres into the same cheap compost, gave a hundred and sixty-eight.”
clears: Old seed: “about ten percent a year.”
The compost: “worth perhaps another ten percent.”
The windowsill: “slows germination and does not stop it.”
The watering: “which the same trial put at fifteen percent.”
cases.explain: Four faults that each take ten or fifteen percent off a tray, and the tray lost ninety-five. Percentages multiply down slowly and this failure is nearly total, which points at something that works as an on and off switch rather than a discount. The second tray is that switch thrown the other way.

cases.title: The Case of the Water Bill That Tripled
cases.story: The meter read sixty cubic metres a quarter last year and a hundred and eighty-nine this quarter. Four causes have been put forward and each of them does use water. Forty more pupils joined, which at the published figure of four litres a head a day is about six cubic metres a quarter. The kitchen's new dishwasher is rated by its maker at four cubic metres a quarter. The hosepipe for the garden was metered separately through a trial fortnight and came to three. The new hand dryers replaced paper towels, and a hand dryer uses no water at all. Those four add nine cubic metres to a rise of a hundred and twenty-nine. The cistern in the disabled toilet has been overflowing quietly into the pan since the handle was changed in January. The flow was caught in a jug and timed at nine hundred millilitres a minute. Nine hundred millilitres a minute is one and three tenths of a cubic metre a day, or a hundred and sixteen across a quarter. A trickle nobody can hear is using nearly twice what the whole school used last year.
cases.question: Where is the water going?

suspects.why: the flow was caught in a jug and timed at nine hundred millilitres a minute
four litres a head a day is about six cubic metres a quarter
the dishwasher is rated by its maker at four cubic metres a quarter
the hosepipe was metered separately through a trial fortnight and came to three
the new hand dryers replaced paper towels, and a hand dryer uses no water at all

cases.answer: A cistern has been trickling into the pan since January.
proof: “Those four add nine cubic metres to a rise of a hundred and twenty-nine.”
“Nine hundred millilitres a minute is one and three tenths of a cubic metre a day, or a hundred and sixteen across a quarter.”
“A trickle nobody can hear is using nearly twice what the whole school used last year.”
clears: More pupils: “about six cubic metres a quarter.”
The dishwasher: “rated by its maker at four cubic metres a quarter.”
The hose: “came to three.”
The dryers: “a hand dryer uses no water at all.”
cases.explain: Every suspect here is an event that happens and then stops, and the one that matters never stops. Nine hundred millilitres sounds like nothing because it is measured in a jug. Multiply it by the minutes in a quarter and it is twice the school's entire annual usage, which is what continuous means.

cases.title: The Case of the Sunflowers That Stopped at Waist Height
cases.story: The sunflowers reached one metre twenty where the packet promises three metres, and four causes have been named. Each is a genuine shortfall in that bed. The bed gets four hours of direct sun against the eight the packet asks for, which the trial bed suggests costs about a third of the height. The compost was not fed after June, worth perhaps fifteen centimetres on the trial plants. Watering was weekly rather than daily in the hot fortnight, which showed as twenty centimetres in the trial. Slug damage was counted on every stem and found on nine of the hundred and four plants. Those four together could not take more than half the height, and five sixths is missing. The seed was sown along the row at ten centimetres apart where the packet asks for forty-five. A hundred and four plants are growing in a bed laid out for twelve. Each one has about a twentieth of the root space and the leaf room the spacing assumes. Three plants left at the end of the row, forty-five centimetres clear of their neighbours, are two metres eighty.
cases.question: Why are the sunflowers so short?

suspects.why: the seed was sown along the row at ten centimetres apart where the packet asks for forty-five
four hours against eight costs about a third of the height in the trial bed
not feeding after June was worth perhaps fifteen centimetres on the trial plants
weekly rather than daily watering in the hot fortnight showed as twenty centimetres in the trial
slug damage was counted on every stem and found on nine of the hundred and four plants

cases.answer: A hundred and four plants are crowded into a bed meant for twelve.
proof: “Those four together could not take more than half the height, and five sixths is missing.”
“Each one has about a twentieth of the root space and the leaf room the spacing assumes.”
“Three plants left at the end of the row, forty-five centimetres clear of their neighbours, are two metres eighty.”
clears: The sun: “costs about a third of the height.”
Feeding: “worth perhaps fifteen centimetres on the trial plants.”
Watering: “which showed as twenty centimetres in the trial.”
Slugs: “found on nine of the hundred and four plants.”
cases.explain: Sun, food, water and slugs take their toll in centimetres and percentages, and together they are worth about half. Spacing is worth a factor of twenty because every plant is taking what the others need. The three at the end of the row got the same sun and the same neglect and stand at two metres eighty.

cases.title: The Case of the Eggs That Stopped in October
cases.story: The six hens laid twenty-eight eggs a week in July and nine a week in late October, and four causes have been suggested. All four are at work in that run. Two of the hens are moulting, and a moulting hen stops laying for a few weeks, which accounts for perhaps eight eggs. The nights have turned cold, and the poultry guide puts a modest drop on cold without calling it a main cause. A fox got into the garden in September and frightened the birds, which costs a few days of laying rather than a season. The feed was changed in August to a brand with the same protein figure printed on the sack. Those four together might explain ten or eleven of the nineteen eggs that have gone. Daylight in the run has fallen from sixteen hours in July to nine hours now. The guide is blunt about it: laying falls away sharply below twelve hours and stops near nine. Light reaching the eye is what tells a hen the season, and nothing about the sack of feed changes that. The neighbour's flock under a lamp on a timer is still laying at July's rate.
cases.question: Why have the eggs stopped?

suspects.why: daylight in the run has fallen from sixteen hours in July to nine hours now
a moulting hen stops laying for a few weeks, which accounts for perhaps eight eggs
the poultry guide puts a modest drop on cold without calling it a main cause
a fox frightened the birds, which costs a few days of laying rather than a season
the feed was changed to a brand with the same protein figure printed on the sack

cases.answer: Day length has fallen from sixteen hours to nine.
proof: “Those four together might explain ten or eleven of the nineteen eggs that have gone.”
“The guide is blunt about it: laying falls away sharply below twelve hours and stops near nine.”
“The neighbour's flock under a lamp on a timer is still laying at July's rate.”
clears: The moult: “which accounts for perhaps eight eggs.”
The cold: “a modest drop on cold without calling it a main cause.”
The fox: “costs a few days of laying rather than a season.”
The feed: “the same protein figure printed on the sack.”
cases.explain: The moult is real and it is worth eight eggs, which is why it is believed. Everything else is worth two or three. The one change nobody made and nobody can see is the length of the day, and the neighbour's flock is the experiment: same weather, same month, a lamp, and July's rate.

cases.title: The Case of the Bins That Went From Six to Fourteen
cases.story: General waste has gone from six bins a week to fourteen and four causes are being argued over. Every one of them really is putting rubbish in those bins. Forty more pupils is a seven percent rise on a roll of six hundred, which is under half a bin. The refit produced rubble, and rubble went into a hired skip and never touched the bins at all. The paper recycling has been refused three weeks running, and a refused load is tipped into general waste, which is a real transfer of about one and a half bins a week. Grounds waste from the hedge cutting filled two bins, once, in September. Those four account for two bins at the very most. The canteen changed in September from washable trays to single-use boxes, cups and cutlery. Twelve hundred meals a day now leave four disposable items each behind them. Forty-eight hundred items a day is twenty-four thousand a week, and the bin measurements put that at six bins. Nothing else on the list produces rubbish every single day the school is open.
cases.question: Why has the waste more than doubled?

suspects.why: twelve hundred meals a day now leave four disposable items each behind them
a seven percent rise on a roll of six hundred is under half a bin
rubble went into a hired skip and never touched the bins at all
a refused load is tipped into general waste, which is a real transfer of about one and a half bins a week
grounds waste from the hedge cutting filled two bins, once, in September

cases.answer: The canteen switched to disposables and now throws away forty-eight hundred items a day.
proof: “Those four account for two bins at the very most.”
“Forty-eight hundred items a day is twenty-four thousand a week, and the bin measurements put that at six bins.”
“Nothing else on the list produces rubbish every single day the school is open.”
clears: More pupils: “under half a bin.”
The rubble: “went into a hired skip and never touched the bins at all.”
The recycling: “a real transfer of about one and a half bins a week.”
Hedge cuttings: “filled two bins, once, in September.”
cases.explain: Two of these are one-off events and one is a transfer rather than an increase. The refused recycling is a genuine weekly cost and it is a bin and a half. The canteen change is six bins a week because it multiplies a small object by twelve hundred people and then by five days.

cases.title: The Case of the Battery That Lasted Forty Shots
cases.story: The camera is rated at four hundred shots a charge and managed forty on the trip, and four drains have been blamed. All four really do take power. It was minus two degrees all day, and the maker puts cold below five degrees at about thirty percent of capacity. The screen was left on maximum brightness, which the same table puts at fifteen percent. The battery is three years old, and a pack of that age holds roughly eighty percent of what it did. The flash fired on twelve of the forty shots, which the table rates at a few percent across a day. Those four together would take four hundred shots down to about two hundred, not to forty. The wireless was switched on in September and has been hunting for a network ever since. The manual says a camera searching for a network with nothing to join drains a full pack in ninety minutes. It does that whether the camera is taking photographs or sitting in a bag. The trip lasted six hours, and the shots were simply what happened to be taken while the pack emptied.
cases.question: Why did the battery only last forty shots?

suspects.who: 📡 The wireless hunting for a network
suspects.why: the manual says a camera searching for a network with nothing to join drains a full pack in ninety minutes
the maker puts cold below five degrees at about thirty percent of capacity
the screen on maximum brightness is fifteen percent in the same table
a pack of that age holds roughly eighty percent of what it did
the flash fired on twelve of the forty shots, which the table rates at a few percent across a day

cases.answer: The wireless has been searching for a network all day, every day.
proof: “Those four together would take four hundred shots down to about two hundred, not to forty.”
“It does that whether the camera is taking photographs or sitting in a bag.”
“The trip lasted six hours, and the shots were simply what happened to be taken while the pack emptied.”
clears: The cold: “about thirty percent of capacity.”
The screen: “which the same table puts at fifteen percent.”
The old battery: “holds roughly eighty percent of what it did.”
The flash: “which the table rates at a few percent across a day.”
cases.explain: Four drains that are all tied to taking photographs, and between them they halve the count. The radio is not tied to taking photographs at all, which is why counting shots never found it. The camera was emptying its battery in the bag between every picture.

cases.title: The Case of the Beans That Died in the Experiment
cases.story: All twenty-four bean plants in the growth experiment died in eleven days and four causes have been written up. Each is a real departure from the method. The bench ran at twenty-six degrees where the method asks for twenty-two, which the control group shows costs growth and does not kill. The pots are seven centimetres where the method specifies nine, which crowds a root system at four weeks and not at eleven days. They were watered on alternate days rather than daily, and the control tray on the same watering is alive. The lamp sat fifty centimetres above the plants rather than thirty, which weakens a seedling over weeks. Those four together describe a slow decline and not a total loss inside a fortnight. The liquid feed was made up at five millilitres into five hundred millilitres of water. The label says five millilitres into five litres, so the solution is ten times the strength intended. A feed at ten times strength pulls water back out of the roots instead of giving anything to them. The control tray, fed from a bottle mixed by the technician, is forty centimetres tall.
cases.question: What killed the beans?

suspects.why: the feed was made up at five millilitres into five hundred millilitres where the label says five litres
twenty-six degrees where the method asks for twenty-two costs growth and does not kill
seven centimetre pots crowd a root system at four weeks and not at eleven days
the control tray on the same watering is alive
the lamp at fifty centimetres rather than thirty weakens a seedling over weeks

cases.answer: The feed was mixed ten times too strong.
proof: “Those four together describe a slow decline and not a total loss inside a fortnight.”
“A feed at ten times strength pulls water back out of the roots instead of giving anything to them.”
“The control tray, fed from a bottle mixed by the technician, is forty centimetres tall.”
clears: The bench: “costs growth and does not kill.”
The pots: “which crowds a root system at four weeks and not at eleven days.”
The watering: “the control tray on the same watering is alive.”
The lamp: “weakens a seedling over weeks.”
cases.explain: Four errors that each cost a plant some growth over weeks, against twenty-four deaths in eleven days. The timescales do not match, which is the first clue. The feed is the only error measured in multiples rather than in degrees or centimetres, and at ten times strength it works the wrong way round entirely.

cases.title: The Case of the Ice Cream That Served Fourteen
cases.story: Two kilograms of ice cream was bought to give forty servings and it ran out after fourteen. Four losses have been offered and all four happened on the day. The drip tray under the tub was weighed at the end and held sixty grams. Six free tastings were given to the helpers, which at the planned fifty grams is three hundred grams. A little was lost to the tub walls and the scoop, which a careful scrape put at forty grams. The tub was too hard at first and the server dug out chunks, which changes the shape of a serving and not its weight. Those four come to four hundred grams of the two thousand. The recipe sheet assumes a number twenty scoop, which holds forty-five millilitres. The scoop in the kitchen drawer is a number eight, which holds a hundred and twenty. Every serving went out at nearly three times the size the plan was written for. Two thousand grams divided by three times fifty is thirteen servings, and the fourteenth was the scrapings.
cases.question: Why did it only serve fourteen?

suspects.why: the recipe sheet assumes a number twenty scoop at forty-five millilitres and the drawer holds a number eight at a hundred and twenty
the drip tray under the tub was weighed at the end and held sixty grams
six free tastings at the planned fifty grams is three hundred grams
a careful scrape put the loss on the walls and the scoop at forty grams
digging out chunks changes the shape of a serving and not its weight

cases.answer: The scoop in the drawer holds nearly three times what the plan assumed.
proof: “Those four come to four hundred grams of the two thousand.”
“Every serving went out at nearly three times the size the plan was written for.”
“Two thousand grams divided by three times fifty is thirteen servings, and the fourteenth was the scrapings.”
clears: The drip tray: “held sixty grams.”
Tastings: “which at the planned fifty grams is three hundred grams.”
The tub walls: “which a careful scrape put at forty grams.”
The hard tub: “changes the shape of a serving and not its weight.”
cases.explain: Four hundred grams were genuinely lost and they would have cost eight servings, not twenty-six. The rest was served, correctly and cheerfully, to the first fourteen people in the queue. Nobody lost any ice cream. The unit the plan was written in and the unit in the drawer were different.

cases.title: The Case of the Appeal That Raised Four Hundred
cases.story: A thousand ribbons went out with a suggested donation of a pound fifty and the appeal raised four hundred and ten pounds. Four reasons have been given for the shortfall against fifteen hundred. All four are true. A hundred and eighty ribbons came back unsold, which at the suggested figure is two hundred and seventy pounds. The ribbons themselves cost a hundred and twenty pounds, which comes off the total and was never in it. Forty were given free to the helpers and the governors, worth sixty pounds. Nine pounds in foreign coins went into the tin and could not be banked. Those four come to about four hundred and sixty pounds of the eleven hundred that are missing. A count of a hundred consecutive donations gave an average of forty-two pence. Eight hundred and twenty ribbons at forty-two pence is three hundred and forty-four pounds. A suggested donation is a suggestion, and the arithmetic treated it as a price. Nobody did anything wrong, and the plan was built on a number that was never going to be collected.
cases.question: Why did the appeal raise four hundred pounds?

suspects.why: a count of a hundred consecutive donations gave an average of forty-two pence against a suggested pound fifty
a hundred and eighty came back unsold, which at the suggested figure is two hundred and seventy pounds
the ribbons cost a hundred and twenty pounds, which comes off the total and was never in it
forty were given free to the helpers and the governors, worth sixty pounds
nine pounds in foreign coins went into the tin and could not be banked

cases.answer: People gave an average of forty-two pence, not a pound fifty.
proof: “Those four come to about four hundred and sixty pounds of the eleven hundred that are missing.”
“Eight hundred and twenty ribbons at forty-two pence is three hundred and forty-four pounds.”
“A suggested donation is a suggestion, and the arithmetic treated it as a price.”
clears: Unsold ribbons: “which at the suggested figure is two hundred and seventy pounds.”
The cost: “which comes off the total and was never in it.”
Free ribbons: “worth sixty pounds.”
Foreign coins: “could not be banked.”
cases.explain: Three of these are real losses and one was never income at all. They come to four hundred and sixty pounds of an eleven hundred pound gap. The rest of the gap was in the forecast rather than in the tin, because a pound fifty was what the school hoped for and forty-two pence is what people gave.

cases.title: The Case of the Cylinder That Filled Ninety Balloons
cases.story: The helium cylinder is labelled for four hundred and fifty balloons and it filled ninety. Four causes have been suggested and each wastes some gas. The nozzle hisses when the balloon is pulled off, and a timed test put that at about two percent of the cylinder. The hall was cold, and a cold gas takes up less room, which affects the reading on the gauge rather than the number of balloons. The cylinder was second hand and the gauge started at ninety-five percent rather than full. Three balloons burst during filling. Those four together waste under a tenth of the gas. The label's figure assumes a balloon blown to twenty-three centimetres across, which is the size printed on the packet. The ones filled on the day measured thirty-eight centimetres, because a bigger balloon looked better. Volume goes with the cube of the width, and thirty-eight divided by twenty-three, cubed, is about four and a half. Four hundred and fifty divided by four and a half is a hundred, and the wasted gas accounts for the last ten.
cases.question: Why did the cylinder only fill ninety?

suspects.why: the label assumes twenty-three centimetres and the ones filled measured thirty-eight
a timed test put the nozzle leak at about two percent of the cylinder
a cold gas takes up less room, which affects the reading on the gauge rather than the number of balloons
the cylinder was second hand and the gauge started at ninety-five percent rather than full
three balloons burst during filling

cases.answer: Every balloon was blown to four and a half times the volume assumed.
proof: “Those four together waste under a tenth of the gas.”
“Volume goes with the cube of the width, and thirty-eight divided by twenty-three, cubed, is about four and a half.”
“Four hundred and fifty divided by four and a half is a hundred, and the wasted gas accounts for the last ten.”
clears: The nozzle: “about two percent of the cylinder.”
The cold: “affects the reading on the gauge rather than the number of balloons.”
The part-used cylinder: “the gauge started at ninety-five percent rather than full.”
Burst balloons: “three balloons burst during filling.”
cases.explain: Fifteen centimetres looks like a small overfill, which is exactly why nobody suspected it. Width is not volume. Going from twenty-three to thirty-eight centimetres is four and a half times the gas in every single balloon, and that one decision is worth more than every leak and burst put together.

cases.title: The Case of the Books Nobody Wanted
cases.story: The library's weeding list is built from loan counts and it names four hundred books that have not gone out once in two years. Every one of them is on the top two shelves. Four explanations have been offered and each describes a real effect. Old books do go out less, and the sample is older than the collection average by about six years. Dull covers are a real deterrent, and the list is heavy with plain cloth bindings. Subject matters, and poetry and reference always lend less than fiction. The catalogue mislabels some of these books, and a book nobody can find is a book nobody borrows. Those four together might explain a lower rate, and the figure here is not lower but zero. The top shelf is two metres and ten centimetres from the floor. The step stool was taken away in September two years ago after a pupil fell from it. Ninety-four percent of all loans since then have come from below one metre fifty. A librarian ran a different measurement last month and counted the dust-free tops of the pages. The high shelves show sixty-one books with worn page edges and broken spines, all borrowed heavily before the stool went. A loan count does not measure what people want to read. It measures what people can reach.
cases.question: Why have four hundred books never been borrowed?

suspects.who: 📏 The height the books sit at
suspects.why: the top shelf is two metres and ten centimetres from the floor and the step stool was taken away two years ago
old books do go out less, and the sample is older than the collection average by about six years
dull covers are a real deterrent, and the list is heavy with plain cloth bindings
poetry and reference always lend less than fiction
the catalogue mislabels some of these books, and a book nobody can find is a book nobody borrows

cases.answer: The books are on shelves nobody has been able to reach since the stool went.
proof: “Ninety-four percent of all loans since then have come from below one metre fifty.”
“The high shelves show sixty-one books with worn page edges and broken spines, all borrowed heavily before the stool went.”
“A loan count does not measure what people want to read.”
clears: Age: “older than the collection average by about six years.”
Covers: “the list is heavy with plain cloth bindings.”
Subject: “poetry and reference always lend less than fiction.”
The catalogue: “a book nobody can find is a book nobody borrows.”
cases.explain: Four real reasons a book lends less, and the list is not of books that lend less but of books that never lend at all. Nothing about a cloth binding produces a clean zero. The wear on the page edges is a second measurement of the same question, taken a different way, and it says these books were loved until the day the stool was removed.

cases.title: The Case of the Salad Nobody Chose
cases.story: The kitchen's uptake count says eleven pupils out of six hundred take the salad option, and the governors want it dropped. Four reasons have been given for the figure and each of them is a genuine problem with that salad. It costs twenty pence more than the pasta, which the kitchen's own pricing trial showed matters. It is served in a plain white bowl at the cold end of the counter, which is bad presentation by anybody's standard. The portion is smaller than the hot options by weight. And teenagers do pick hot food over cold in winter, which the county survey confirms. Those four would depress a figure and they would not flatten it to eleven. The salad is made in a single tray of about forty portions. The kitchen serves from half past eleven, and the tray is empty by seven minutes past twelve. The uptake count is taken from the till report at the end of service at twenty to one. Every pupil who wanted salad after seven minutes past was served something else and counted as something else. A tally kept at the counter for one week found a hundred and ninety pupils who asked for salad and were told it had gone.
cases.question: Why does the count say eleven?

suspects.who: ⏰ The count taken after the salad ran out
suspects.why: the tray is empty by seven minutes past twelve and the count is taken at twenty to one
it costs twenty pence more than the pasta, which the kitchen's own pricing trial showed matters
it is served in a plain white bowl at the cold end of the counter
the portion is smaller than the hot options by weight
teenagers do pick hot food over cold in winter, which the county survey confirms

cases.answer: The salad sells out long before the count that says nobody wants it.
proof: “The salad is made in a single tray of about forty portions.”
“Every pupil who wanted salad after seven minutes past was served something else and counted as something else.”
“A tally kept at the counter for one week found a hundred and ninety pupils who asked for salad and were told it had gone.”
clears: The price: “which the kitchen's own pricing trial showed matters.”
The presentation: “it is served in a plain white bowl at the cold end of the counter, which is bad presentation by anybody's standard.”
The portion: “smaller than the hot options by weight.”
The season: “teenagers do pick hot food over cold in winter, which the county survey confirms.”
cases.explain: The figure of eleven is wrong in a way no arithmetic catches, because eleven really is what the till recorded. The till can only record what the kitchen had to sell. A tray of forty cannot produce a number above forty however many people want one, and the counter tally found a hundred and ninety of them.

cases.title: The Case of the Brand That Snapped Most
cases.story: The breakage book says Haleby pencils break four times as often as Corwin pencils, and the school is about to stop buying Haleby. Four differences between the brands are offered and all four are real. Haleby leads test softer on the laboratory scale, and a softer lead does break more readily. Haleby barrels are round and Corwin barrels hexagonal, and a round pencil rolls off a desk. The Haleby batch was delivered in August and stored in the damp cupboard, which weakens the glue along the seam. And Haleby pencils are two centimetres shorter, which changes how hard a hand can press before the lead gives. Those four together might account for a difference of a third, not of four times. Haleby pencils are issued to Years Seven and Eight and Corwin pencils to the sixth form. The breakage book is filled in by the stock cupboard when a class asks for replacements. Sixth formers buy their own replacements from the shop rather than asking. A fortnight of marked pencils, fifty of each brand given to the same Year Eight class, ended with nine Haleby and seven Corwin broken. The book never compared two brands. It compared two age groups and one habit of asking.
cases.question: Do Haleby pencils really break more?

suspects.who: 🧑‍🎓 Who each brand was given to
suspects.why: Haleby pencils are issued to Years Seven and Eight and Corwin pencils to the sixth form
Haleby leads test softer on the laboratory scale, and a softer lead does break more readily
Haleby barrels are round and Corwin barrels hexagonal, and a round pencil rolls off a desk
the Haleby batch was stored in the damp cupboard, which weakens the glue along the seam
Haleby pencils are two centimetres shorter, which changes how hard a hand can press

cases.answer: The two brands went to different year groups with different habits.
proof: “The breakage book is filled in by the stock cupboard when a class asks for replacements.”
“Sixth formers buy their own replacements from the shop rather than asking.”
“A fortnight of marked pencils, fifty of each brand given to the same Year Eight class, ended with nine Haleby and seven Corwin broken.”
clears: The lead: “a softer lead does break more readily.”
The barrel: “a round pencil rolls off a desk.”
The cupboard: “which weakens the glue along the seam.”
The length: “which changes how hard a hand can press before the lead gives.”
cases.explain: Haleby pencils are genuinely the weaker pencil, by about a third, which the marked fortnight shows. The book says four times because it counts requests rather than breakages, and the group that never requests anything is the group holding the other brand. Put both brands in the same hands and the gap shrinks to almost nothing.

cases.title: The Case of the Row That Cropped Best
cases.story: The orchard record shows the north row yielding ninety kilograms a tree and the other four rows about thirty. The north row is to be propagated and the rest replaced. Four advantages of that row have been named and each is real. It faces south over open ground and gets about an hour more sun a day. It sits above the old stable yard, where the soil tests richer in nitrogen. It was planted three years earlier, so those trees are larger. And it is the only row on free-draining gravel rather than clay. Those four between them might be worth half as much again, not three times. The north row is picked by the head gardener with the orchard ladder. The other four rows are picked by classes on a Friday afternoon, without the ladder, for safety. A count made from the ground in October found fruit still hanging above two metres on every tree in rows two to five. Nine trees were picked properly by the gardener afterwards as a test, and they gave between seventy and eighty-eight kilograms. The record is not a measurement of what the trees grew. It is a measurement of what somebody could get down.
cases.question: Is the north row really the best?

suspects.why: the north row is picked by the head gardener with the orchard ladder and the others by classes without it
it faces south over open ground and gets about an hour more sun a day
it sits above the old stable yard, where the soil tests richer in nitrogen
it was planted three years earlier, so those trees are larger
it is the only row on free-draining gravel rather than clay

cases.answer: Only the north row is picked with a ladder.
proof: “A count made from the ground in October found fruit still hanging above two metres on every tree in rows two to five.”
“Nine trees were picked properly by the gardener afterwards as a test, and they gave between seventy and eighty-eight kilograms.”
“The record is not a measurement of what the trees grew.”
clears: The sun: “about an hour more sun a day.”
The soil: “the soil tests richer in nitrogen.”
The older trees: “those trees are larger.”
The drainage: “free-draining gravel rather than clay.”
cases.explain: Four genuine advantages, worth perhaps half as much again, against a record that says three times. The ladder is not an advantage of the trees at all, and the fruit left hanging above two metres is the missing two thirds. Replacing those rows would have destroyed four healthy rows on the strength of a safety rule.

cases.title: The Case of the Shed Where Nothing Was Stolen
cases.story: The bike shed log records two thefts in three years and the school is citing it to refuse a request for cameras. Four reasons for the low figure have been offered and every one of them is true of that shed. It is overlooked by the staff room window for most of the day. The frame is bolted into concrete and the hoops are the sort a cutter struggles with. The gate is locked from nine until three. And most pupils use a good lock, which a spot survey put at seventy-one percent. Those four would lower a theft rate, and they would not take it to two. The log is written up from forms handed in at the school office. The office closes at four o'clock and the shed empties between half past three and six. A pupil who finds a bike gone at half past five comes back the next morning to an office with a queue, and most do not bother. The local police were asked for their own figures last month. They hold nineteen reports of bicycles taken from that address in the same three years. Seventeen of the nineteen are timed after four o'clock.
cases.question: Why does the log show only two thefts?

suspects.why: the office closes at four o'clock and the shed empties between half past three and six
the shed is overlooked by the staff room window for most of the day
the frame is bolted into concrete and the hoops are the sort a cutter struggles with
the gate is locked from nine until three
most pupils use a good lock, which a spot survey put at seventy-one percent

cases.answer: Thefts happen after the only place that records them has shut.
proof: “The log is written up from forms handed in at the school office.”
“They hold nineteen reports of bicycles taken from that address in the same three years.”
“Seventeen of the nineteen are timed after four o'clock.”
clears: The window: “overlooked by the staff room window for most of the day.”
The frame: “the hoops are the sort a cutter struggles with.”
The gate: “the gate is locked from nine until three.”
Locks: “which a spot survey put at seventy-one percent.”
cases.explain: Every protection named here works during the day, and the log only exists during the day, so the log is a record of the hours the shed is safe. The police figures cover the same address and the same three years and are nearly ten times higher. Two is not a theft rate. It is an opening time.

cases.title: The Case of the Tank That Killed Fish
cases.story: Tank B has lost thirty-one fish in two years and tank A has lost four, and the club wants tank B stripped down. Four faults in tank B have been named and every one is real. Its heater runs a degree and a half warm, which the thermometer confirms. Its filter is the older model and turns the water over more slowly. It stands near the door and gets a draught whenever the room is used. And its gravel has never been replaced, so it holds more waste than tank A's. Those four would raise a death rate and they would not multiply it by eight. Tank B is the quarantine tank, and every fish bought for the club spends its first three weeks in it. Tank A receives only fish that have already survived those three weeks. A newly bought fish carries the stress of transport and whatever it arrived with, and the trade's own figure for first-month losses is about a quarter. Two hundred and ten fish have passed through tank B and sixty-eight through tank A. Thirty-one of two hundred and ten is fifteen percent, and four of sixty-eight is six. The gap is real and it is a third of the size the raw counts suggest.
cases.question: Why does tank B lose so many fish?

suspects.who: 🚪 Tank B being the quarantine tank
suspects.why: every fish bought for the club spends its first three weeks in tank B, and tank A receives only survivors
its heater runs a degree and a half warm, which the thermometer confirms
its filter is the older model and turns the water over more slowly
it stands near the door and gets a draught whenever the room is used
its gravel has never been replaced, so it holds more waste than tank A's

cases.answer: Tank B holds every new fish and tank A holds only the ones that lived.
proof: “Tank A receives only fish that have already survived those three weeks.”
“Two hundred and ten fish have passed through tank B and sixty-eight through tank A.”
“Thirty-one of two hundred and ten is fifteen percent, and four of sixty-eight is six.”
clears: The heater: “its heater runs a degree and a half warm, which the thermometer confirms.”
The filter: “turns the water over more slowly.”
The draught: “gets a draught whenever the room is used.”
The gravel: “holds more waste than tank A's.”
cases.explain: Counting deaths without counting fish is the first error, and it accounts for most of the gap. The second is deeper: tank A's fish were selected by tank B. Every weak fish died before it could be an A statistic, which is why the healthiest tank in the room is the one that never meets a new arrival.

cases.title: The Case of the Loudest Day of the Week
cases.story: The noise file says Wednesday is the loudest day in the building by eleven decibels, and the timetable is about to be rewritten around it. Four reasons have been put forward and each is genuinely true of Wednesdays. The whole school eats in two sittings rather than three, so the hall holds more people at once. Band practice runs at lunchtime in the room above the office. The corridor by the gym is used as a through route while the yard is resurfaced. And Wednesday afternoon is the only games session that starts indoors. Those four could add two or three decibels between them. The sound meter is not left running. It is fetched from the cupboard and switched on when somebody complains at the office. The office is staffed on Wednesdays and on no other day, because the administrator works one day a week. Forty-one of the forty-four readings in the file were taken on a Wednesday. A borrowed meter was left recording for a fortnight last term with nobody attending it. It found Thursday the loudest day of the five by four decibels, and Wednesday the third of the five.
cases.question: Is Wednesday really the loudest day?

suspects.who: 📋 The day the meter is switched on
suspects.why: the office is staffed on Wednesdays and on no other day, because the administrator works one day a week
the whole school eats in two sittings rather than three, so the hall holds more people at once
band practice runs at lunchtime in the room above the office
the corridor by the gym is used as a through route while the yard is resurfaced
Wednesday afternoon is the only games session that starts indoors

cases.answer: The meter is only ever switched on when the office is staffed.
proof: “Forty-one of the forty-four readings in the file were taken on a Wednesday.”
“A borrowed meter was left recording for a fortnight last term with nobody attending it.”
“It found Thursday the loudest day of the five by four decibels, and Wednesday the third of the five.”
clears: The sittings: “so the hall holds more people at once.”
The band: “band practice runs at lunchtime in the room above the office.”
The corridor: “used as a through route while the yard is resurfaced.”
Indoor games: “the only games session that starts indoors.”
cases.explain: Wednesday is genuinely two or three decibels louder and the file says eleven, because the file is forty-one Wednesdays and three of everything else. A measurement that is only taken when somebody is there to take it describes the observer's week. The unattended meter had no opinion about which day mattered, and it chose Thursday.

cases.title: The Case of the Tree That Dropped Everything
cases.story: The grounds record blames the big sycamore for eighty-one percent of the leaf litter cleared each autumn, and a felling notice has been drafted. Four points in its favour are made and all of them are true. It is the largest tree on the site by crown spread. Sycamore leaves are broad and heavy and do not blow away. It holds its leaves late, so it drops into the weeks when clearing is logged. And it stands at the top of the slope, so its leaves travel down across the whole site. Those four make it a genuine nuisance and a leading contributor. The record is compiled from the sweeping sheets, which are filled in for paths, steps and the yard. The sycamore is the only mature tree on the site standing over a path. The eleven limes, the beech and the two horse chestnuts all stand on grass, where leaves are mown in and nothing is swept. A netting trial last October caught fall over measured squares under every tree. The sycamore produced nineteen percent of the leaf mass on the site. The sweeping sheets never measured what fell. They measured what landed somewhere a broom was going to be used.
cases.question: Does the sycamore really drop four fifths of the leaves?

suspects.why: the record is compiled from sweeping sheets for paths, steps and the yard, and the sycamore is the only mature tree over a path
it is the largest tree on the site by crown spread
sycamore leaves are broad and heavy and do not blow away
it holds its leaves late, so it drops into the weeks when clearing is logged
it stands at the top of the slope, so its leaves travel down across the whole site

cases.answer: It is the only big tree standing over a surface anybody sweeps.
proof: “The eleven limes, the beech and the two horse chestnuts all stand on grass, where leaves are mown in and nothing is swept.”
“A netting trial last October caught fall over measured squares under every tree.”
“The sycamore produced nineteen percent of the leaf mass on the site.”
clears: Its size: “the largest tree on the site by crown spread.”
Its leaves: “broad and heavy and do not blow away.”
Its late fall: “it drops into the weeks when clearing is logged.”
Its position: “its leaves travel down across the whole site.”
cases.explain: Everything said about the sycamore is accurate, and it is the largest single producer on the site at nineteen percent. Eighty-one is the share of the swept leaves rather than the fallen ones. Fourteen other trees drop onto grass and vanish into the mower, which is a leaf nobody counts rather than a leaf that was never there.

cases.title: The Case of the Variety That Grew Giants
cases.story: The growers' table shows Hallow King averaging two hundred and forty kilograms and every other variety under ninety, and the club has voted to grow nothing else. Four strengths of the variety are listed and all four are genuine. Its vines run longer, which gives more leaf to feed one fruit. Its skin is thicker, so fewer entries split before the weigh-in. It sets fruit about nine days earlier. And its seed is sold by a single supplier with good stock records. Those four are worth real weight and the gap in the table is nearly three to one. The table is compiled from weigh-in results at the county show. The show charges four pounds an entry and will not accept a pumpkin under a hundred kilograms. Hallow King seed costs eleven pounds a packet and is bought by growers who intend to compete. The club's own patch records, kept for every fruit whether entered or not, tell a different story. Hallow King averages a hundred and six kilograms across all its fruit, and the next variety averages ninety-four. Every pumpkin under a hundred kilograms is missing from the table, and most pumpkins are under a hundred kilograms.
cases.question: Is Hallow King really three times better?

suspects.why: the show will not accept a pumpkin under a hundred kilograms, and most pumpkins are under a hundred kilograms
its vines run longer, which gives more leaf to feed one fruit
its skin is thicker, so fewer entries split before the weigh-in
it sets fruit about nine days earlier
its seed is sold by a single supplier with good stock records

cases.answer: The table only contains pumpkins heavy enough to be allowed in.
proof: “The table is compiled from weigh-in results at the county show.”
“The club's own patch records, kept for every fruit whether entered or not, tell a different story.”
“Hallow King averages a hundred and six kilograms across all its fruit, and the next variety averages ninety-four.”
clears: The vines: “which gives more leaf to feed one fruit.”
The skin: “fewer entries split before the weigh-in.”
The fruit set: “it sets fruit about nine days earlier.”
The supplier: “a single supplier with good stock records.”
cases.explain: Hallow King is the better variety, by about twelve percent, which the patch records show. The table says three to one because a cut-off at a hundred kilograms throws away the whole lower half of every variety, and it throws away more of the varieties that do worse. A rule about entries became a claim about plants.

cases.title: The Case of the Visitors Who All Came From the East
cases.story: The signing-in book shows eighty-four percent of visitors arriving from the east of the town, and the governors are planning the new car park on that side. Four reasons have been given and each is genuinely true of the east. The bus from the east stops at the gate and the western route stops four hundred metres away. The two nearest primary schools, which send most of the parents, are both east of the site. The eastern housing is denser, with about nine hundred more households inside a mile. And the eastern approach has a pavement the whole way, where the west has three hundred metres without one. Those four would make an eastern majority a fair expectation of perhaps sixty percent. The signing-in book lives on the desk in the east lobby, because that is where reception is. The west entrance has a buzzer, a door release and no book at all. A counter on the west door was read for a fortnight in March and logged two hundred and twelve people. The east lobby book recorded two hundred and sixty-one in the same fortnight. The book is not a record of where visitors come from. It is a record of which door has a pen on it.
cases.question: Do most visitors really come from the east?

suspects.who: 🖊️ The door the book sits on
suspects.why: the signing-in book lives on the desk in the east lobby and the west entrance has no book at all
the bus from the east stops at the gate and the western route stops four hundred metres away
the two nearest primary schools, which send most of the parents, are both east of the site
the eastern housing is denser, with about nine hundred more households inside a mile
the eastern approach has a pavement the whole way, where the west has three hundred metres without one

cases.answer: Only the east door has a book to sign.
proof: “The west entrance has a buzzer, a door release and no book at all.”
“A counter on the west door was read for a fortnight in March and logged two hundred and twelve people.”
“The east lobby book recorded two hundred and sixty-one in the same fortnight.”
clears: The bus: “the western route stops four hundred metres away.”
The primaries: “both east of the site.”
The housing: “about nine hundred more households inside a mile.”
The pavement: “the west has three hundred metres without one.”
cases.explain: Four honest reasons to expect an eastern majority, and a figure of eighty-four percent that no combination of them reaches. The west door counter turns the eighty-four into fifty-five in a fortnight. A car park built on the strength of that book would have been built on the position of a pen.

cases.title: The Case of the Service That Was Ninety-Seven Percent Punctual
cases.story: The bus company's figures show ninety-seven percent of journeys on the school route arriving within five minutes of the timetable, and the complaints are being dismissed. Four reasons for genuine good performance have been offered and all four hold up. The route avoids the town centre entirely. The timetable was rewritten in September with four extra minutes of slack at the midpoint. The same two drivers work it, both of whom know the road. And a bus lane was opened on the longest straight in October. Those four would produce a strong punctuality figure and nobody disputes that they help. The company's measure is taken from journeys that were operated. A journey that is cancelled generates no arrival time, so it enters neither the top nor the bottom of the fraction. The operations log shows forty-one cancellations on this route in the same term, out of four hundred and six scheduled journeys. Three hundred and fifty-four of the three hundred and sixty-five operated journeys ran on time, which is ninety-seven percent. Three hundred and fifty-four of the four hundred and six scheduled journeys is eighty-seven percent. A pupil standing at a stop does not care which of the two numbers the company prefers.
cases.question: Is the route really ninety-seven percent punctual?

suspects.why: a journey that is cancelled generates no arrival time, so it enters neither the top nor the bottom of the fraction
the route avoids the town centre entirely
the timetable was rewritten in September with four extra minutes of slack at the midpoint
the same two drivers work it, both of whom know the road
a bus lane was opened on the longest straight in October

cases.answer: The forty-one cancelled journeys are not counted at all.
proof: “The operations log shows forty-one cancellations on this route in the same term, out of four hundred and six scheduled journeys.”
“Three hundred and fifty-four of the three hundred and sixty-five operated journeys ran on time, which is ninety-seven percent.”
“Three hundred and fifty-four of the four hundred and six scheduled journeys is eighty-seven percent.”
clears: The route: “the route avoids the town centre entirely.”
The slack: “four extra minutes of slack at the midpoint.”
The drivers: “both of whom know the road.”
The bus lane: “a bus lane was opened on the longest straight in October.”
cases.explain: Nothing in the ninety-seven percent is false. Every journey it counts really did arrive on time, and the four improvements really did help. The worst outcome a passenger can meet, a bus that never comes, is the one outcome the measure cannot see, because a bus that never comes has no arrival time to be late.

cases.title: The Case of the Team That Only Won at Home
cases.story: The record book shows nineteen home wins and three away wins, and the coach is being asked to explain a collapse on the road. Four causes have been offered and each is a real effect in school sport. The home pitch is grass and most away fixtures are played on an artificial surface the team rarely trains on. The coach is present at every home game and misses about a third of away games. Travel takes an hour and the team plays within twenty minutes of arriving. And the home crowd is worth something that every player will swear to. Those four would produce a real home advantage, which the county average puts at about fifteen percent. The record book is kept by the fixtures secretary from the league return sheets. League returns are only submitted for competitive league fixtures. Friendlies are not returned, and the school plays almost all of its friendlies away because it cannot spare the pitch. The coach's own notebook lists forty-one away fixtures in the same period, of which the team won twenty-two. The book did not record a team that loses away. It recorded the fixtures that come with paperwork.
cases.question: Does the team really collapse away from home?

suspects.who: 📄 Which fixtures generate a return sheet
suspects.why: league returns are only submitted for competitive league fixtures, and the school plays almost all of its friendlies away
the home pitch is grass and most away fixtures are played on an artificial surface the team rarely trains on
the coach is present at every home game and misses about a third of away games
travel takes an hour and the team plays within twenty minutes of arriving
the home crowd is worth something that every player will swear to

cases.answer: Only league fixtures reach the book, and the friendlies are all away.
proof: “The record book is kept by the fixtures secretary from the league return sheets.”
“The coach's own notebook lists forty-one away fixtures in the same period, of which the team won twenty-two.”
“The book did not record a team that loses away.”
clears: The surface: “an artificial surface the team rarely trains on.”
The coach: “misses about a third of away games.”
The travel: “the team plays within twenty minutes of arriving.”
The crowd: “worth something that every player will swear to.”
cases.explain: A home advantage is real and worth about fifteen percent. The book shows something far stronger because it is not a list of matches but a list of matches that generated a form. Twenty-two away wins exist in a notebook nobody thought to add, and they are the fixtures the league never asked about.

cases.title: The Case of the Dinner Everyone Enjoyed
cases.story: The feedback cards from the Christmas dinner came back at an average of four point seven out of five, and the kitchen is repeating the menu unchanged. Four reasons for genuine satisfaction have been put forward and each is fair. The turkey was carved at the tables rather than plated in advance. The kitchen bought better potatoes this year, which the staff noticed independently. The hall was decorated by the art department and looked remarkable. And a free pudding was added at the last minute. Those four would lift a score and they would not lift it to four point seven. The cards were left face down on the tables and collected by the staff at two o'clock. Service began at half past twelve and the hall was timetabled to clear by half past one. A head count at twenty past one recorded a hundred and ninety pupils still seated out of four hundred and twenty served. Ninety-one cards were returned, all of them from tables still occupied at two. The pupils who left early include everybody who did not want a second helping, everybody waiting for a bus, and everybody who did not like the food. The score measures the people who stayed.
cases.question: Did everyone really enjoy the dinner?

suspects.who: 🪑 Who was still in the hall at two
suspects.why: the cards were collected at two o'clock and all ninety-one came from tables still occupied then
the turkey was carved at the tables rather than plated in advance
the kitchen bought better potatoes this year, which the staff noticed independently
the hall was decorated by the art department and looked remarkable
a free pudding was added at the last minute

cases.answer: Only the people still sitting there at two o'clock filled in a card.
proof: “A head count at twenty past one recorded a hundred and ninety pupils still seated out of four hundred and twenty served.”
“The pupils who left early include everybody who did not want a second helping, everybody waiting for a bus, and everybody who did not like the food.”
“The score measures the people who stayed.”
clears: The carving: “carved at the tables rather than plated in advance.”
The potatoes: “which the staff noticed independently.”
The decorations: “looked remarkable.”
The pudding: “a free pudding was added at the last minute.”
cases.explain: Four hundred and twenty people ate and ninety-one scored it. The ninety-one are not a sample of the four hundred and twenty, because staying in a hall for ninety minutes after your dinner is itself a sign of having enjoyed it. The people whose opinion would move the average are the people who had already gone.

cases.title: The Case of the Flavour That Outsold the Rest
cases.story: The bake sale's sheet shows chocolate selling two hundred and ten cakes against lemon's forty, and next term's baking rota has been rewritten around chocolate. Four reasons have been offered and each is real. Chocolate was on the front table where the queue forms. The chocolate cakes were iced and the lemon ones were plain. Chocolate is the flavour most people name when asked in the abstract. And the chocolate cakes were a few grams larger. Those four give chocolate a genuine edge and the sheet shows a ratio of more than five to one. The rota tells the bakers how many of each to make, and it asked for two hundred and forty chocolate and forty-five lemon. Two hundred and ten of two hundred and forty chocolate cakes sold, which is eighty-eight percent. Forty of forty-five lemon cakes sold, which is eighty-nine percent. The lemon table was cleared and packed away forty minutes before the sale ended. Twenty-two people were turned away from the lemon table in that forty minutes, which a helper counted on the back of a receipt. A count of what sold cannot tell you what would have sold, unless you also know what there was.
cases.question: Does chocolate really outsell lemon five to one?

suspects.who: 📝 How many of each were made

cases.title: The Case of the Mittens That Were Always Wool
cases.story: The lost property audit lists ninety-four wool mittens and six acrylic, and a letter is being drafted advising parents against wool. Four reasons have been given and each is a real property of wool. Wool mittens are more often knitted by hand and so have no maker's label or name tape. They are warmer, so children take them off indoors, which is where mittens are abandoned. They are bulkier and less likely to fit in a coat pocket. And they are more often handed down, so they are older and their elastic is looser. Those four would skew a lost property box towards wool and they would not produce a ratio of sixteen to one. The lost property box is emptied every Friday by the site team. Anything judged to have no value is bagged for the textile bank and not entered in the audit. The site team's standing instruction, written in two thousand and nine, treats synthetic gloves as having no resale value. A fortnight of logging everything that entered the box, with nothing discarded, recorded fifty-one wool and thirty-eight acrylic. The audit was never a list of what was lost. It was a list of what was kept.
cases.question: Are wool mittens really lost sixteen times as often?

suspects.who: 🗑️ What the site team throws away
suspects.why: anything judged to have no value is bagged for the textile bank and not entered in the audit
wool mittens are more often knitted by hand and so have no maker's label or name tape
they are warmer, so children take them off indoors, which is where mittens are abandoned
they are bulkier and less likely to fit in a coat pocket
they are more often handed down, so they are older and their elastic is looser

cases.answer: Acrylic mittens are binned before the audit ever sees them.
proof: “The site team's standing instruction, written in two thousand and nine, treats synthetic gloves as having no resale value.”
“A fortnight of logging everything that entered the box, with nothing discarded, recorded fifty-one wool and thirty-eight acrylic.”
“The audit was never a list of what was lost.”
clears: Name tapes: “so have no maker's label or name tape.”
Warmth: “which is where mittens are abandoned.”
Bulk: “less likely to fit in a coat pocket.”
Handing down: “their elastic is looser.”
cases.explain: Wool really is lost more, by about four to three, which the unfiltered fortnight shows. The audit says sixteen to one because a rule written fifteen years ago removes most of the acrylic before anybody counts. A letter telling parents to avoid wool would have been sound advice drawn from a sorting policy.

cases.title: The Case of the Recipe That Never Failed
cases.story: The gingerbread house recipe carries two hundred and eleven reviews online at an average of four point eight stars, and the class is using it unchanged. Four reasons for genuine quality have been offered and each stands up. The dough includes an extra egg yolk, which does make a firmer panel. The template is printed to scale rather than described in words. The method gives a weight for the icing sugar rather than a cup measure. And the author answers questions underneath, which catches mistakes early. Those four make it a better than average recipe and nobody is arguing otherwise. A review can only be left by somebody who has made the house and photographed it. The site requires a photograph of the finished build before a review will post. A house that collapsed cannot be photographed finished, and its baker has nothing to upload. The author's own question thread, where no photograph is required, carries four hundred and six questions. A hundred and seventy of them describe a wall that slid or a roof that came down. The stars are not a measure of how often the recipe works. They are a measure of how it went for the people whose houses stood up.
cases.question: Is the recipe really that reliable?

suspects.why: the site requires a photograph of the finished build before a review will post
the dough includes an extra egg yolk, which does make a firmer panel
the template is printed to scale rather than described in words
the method gives a weight for the icing sugar rather than a cup measure
the author answers questions underneath, which catches mistakes early

cases.answer: Only people whose houses stood up are able to leave a review.
proof: “A house that collapsed cannot be photographed finished, and its baker has nothing to upload.”
“The author's own question thread, where no photograph is required, carries four hundred and six questions.”
“A hundred and seventy of them describe a wall that slid or a roof that came down.”
clears: The egg yolk: “which does make a firmer panel.”
The template: “printed to scale rather than described in words.”
The icing sugar: “a weight for the icing sugar rather than a cup measure.”
The author's answers: “which catches mistakes early.”
cases.explain: The four point eight is honest and every star was given by somebody who built the house. The rule that produced it also removed every failure from the record, which is why the comments underneath and the stars above describe two different recipes. The question thread has no photograph rule and no average above four.

cases.title: The Case of the Bulbs That Failed Too Often
cases.story: The maintenance file records sixty-one LED failures and nine filament failures this year, and the school is reverting to filament bulbs. Four reasons have been offered and each is a real weakness of the LEDs that were fitted. They were the cheapest fitting on the framework and their drivers are the known weak point. They were installed in enclosed fittings the maker warns against. The corridor circuit they sit on has a voltage spike logged twice a week. And they run hotter in those fittings than the specification allows. Those four make the LED failure rate genuinely poor, which nobody disputes. A failure is recorded when a bulb is brought to the caretaker's office and a form filled in. An LED fitting costs eighteen pounds and is replaced under warranty, which requires the form. A filament bulb costs forty pence and the cleaners change them from the trolley without telling anybody. The stores ledger shows eight hundred and ninety filament bulbs issued this year against ninety LED units. There are two hundred and ten filament fittings in the building and three hundred and forty LED ones. The file records warranty claims. It was never a count of failures.
cases.question: Do the LEDs really fail seven times as often?

suspects.why: an LED is replaced under warranty, which requires the form, and the cleaners change filament bulbs without telling anybody
