they were installed in enclosed fittings the maker warns against
the corridor circuit they sit on has a voltage spike logged twice a week
they run hotter in those fittings than the specification allows

cases.answer: Only LED failures generate paperwork, so only LED failures get counted.
proof: “The stores ledger shows eight hundred and ninety filament bulbs issued this year against ninety LED units.”
“There are two hundred and ten filament fittings in the building and three hundred and forty LED ones.”
“The file records warranty claims.”
clears: The cheap fittings: “their drivers are the known weak point.”
The enclosed fittings: “the maker warns against.”
The spikes: “a voltage spike logged twice a week.”
Running hot: “they run hotter in those fittings than the specification allows.”
cases.explain: These LEDs really are bad, for four separate and documented reasons. The ledger still settles it: eight hundred and ninety filament bulbs into two hundred and ten fittings is more than four replacements each, against ninety units into three hundred and forty. Reverting to filament would be a decision taken from the one record that cannot see a filament bulb fail.

cases.title: The Case of the Clock That Was Never Wrong
cases.story: The checking book for the tower clock carries eleven years of weekly entries and not one records an error above thirty seconds. The clock is being left out of the restoration on the strength of it. Four reasons for genuine accuracy have been offered and each is fair. It was rebuilt in nineteen ninety-eight with a new escapement. Its pendulum hangs in a sealed case, which keeps the dust and most of the damp off it. The tower holds a steady temperature because of the stone. And it is wound every Sunday by the same person, which keeps the drive even. Those four would make it a good clock, and eleven years without a single entry over thirty seconds is better than a good clock. The book is filled in by the winder on Sunday mornings. The entry is made by comparing the tower clock against the winder's own wristwatch. The wristwatch is set each Sunday from the tower clock before the climb, because the kitchen radio is unreliable. A phone set by the national time signal was carried up in October and found the clock four minutes and twenty seconds slow. The book has been comparing the clock with itself for eleven years.
cases.question: Has the clock really never been wrong?

suspects.who: 🔁 The watch set from the clock
suspects.why: the wristwatch is set each Sunday from the tower clock before the climb
it was rebuilt in nineteen ninety-eight with a new escapement
its pendulum hangs in a sealed case, which keeps the dust and most of the damp off it
the tower holds a steady temperature because of the stone
it is wound every Sunday by the same person, which keeps the drive even

cases.answer: The watch it is checked against is set from the clock itself.
proof: “The entry is made by comparing the tower clock against the winder's own wristwatch.”
“A phone set by the national time signal was carried up in October and found the clock four minutes and twenty seconds slow.”
“The book has been comparing the clock with itself for eleven years.”
clears: The rebuild: “a new escapement.”
The pendulum case: “which keeps the dust and most of the damp off it.”
The tower: “the tower holds a steady temperature because of the stone.”
The winding: “which keeps the drive even.”
cases.explain: A record of eleven years without an error is not strong evidence, it is impossible evidence, and that is the tell. No mechanical clock does that. The book is not lying and the winder is not careless. The comparison simply has no outside reference in it, so it could only ever return the answer it did.

cases.title: The Case of the Field That Got Twice the Snow
cases.story: Eleven years of readings show the field taking twice the snow depth of the car park, and the grounds plan treats the two as different microclimates. Four reasons have been offered and each is physically sound. Grass insulates what falls on it, where tarmac holds warmth from the day and melts the first centimetre. The car park is gritted, and grit lowers the freezing point of what lands on it. The field is four metres higher and a little colder. And the car park is sheltered by the sports hall on its windward side. Those four would give the field a genuine edge of perhaps a third. The field reading is taken at the marker post, which was driven in beside the hedge in two thousand and twelve. The car park reading is taken in the open, in the middle of the hardstanding. Wind-blown snow piles against a hedge and scours the open ground beside it. A set of five measured stakes was put across the field last January at ten-metre spacings. The marker post read twenty-six centimetres and the open stakes read between nine and thirteen. The post was not placed to measure snowfall. It was placed where the hedge was, because a post needs something to be driven in beside.
cases.question: Does the field really get twice the snow?

suspects.why: the field reading is taken at the marker post beside the hedge, and wind-blown snow piles against a hedge
grass insulates what falls on it, where tarmac holds warmth from the day and melts the first centimetre
the car park is gritted, and grit lowers the freezing point of what lands on it
the field is four metres higher and a little colder
the car park is sheltered by the sports hall on its windward side

cases.answer: The field is measured in a drift against a hedge.
proof: “Wind-blown snow piles against a hedge and scours the open ground beside it.”
“The marker post read twenty-six centimetres and the open stakes read between nine and thirteen.”
“The post was not placed to measure snowfall.”
clears: The grass: “tarmac holds warmth from the day and melts the first centimetre.”
The grit: “grit lowers the freezing point of what lands on it.”
The height: “the field is four metres higher and a little colder.”
The shelter: “the car park is sheltered by the sports hall on its windward side.”
cases.explain: Four real differences worth about a third, and a record that says double. The five stakes show the field itself disagreeing with its own post by a factor of two, which means the difference is not between the field and the car park at all. It is between a hedge and open ground, measured eleven years running because that is where the post went in.

cases.title: The Case of the Garden Full of Robins
cases.story: The nature club's three-year record names the robin the commonest bird in the school grounds, ahead of every other species. Four reasons have been given and each is a true fact about robins. They hold a territory all year, so the same bird is reliably present. They are bold and will feed with people nearby. They are brightly marked and easy to identify with no doubt. And they sing through the winter, which draws attention. Those four make a robin far more noticeable than most birds in the garden. The record is kept as sightings, with one mark made each time a species is seen. A robin alone on a post is one mark, and a flock of thirty starlings arriving together is also one mark. The club meets at lunchtime, and the counts are made between half past twelve and one. A ringing session run by the county trust at dawn last March caught and counted individual birds instead. It recorded four robins, sixty-one starlings, fifty-three house sparrows and thirty-eight goldfinches. The record did not count birds. It counted the times somebody noticed a kind of bird, at the one hour of the day the club is free.
cases.question: Is the robin really the commonest bird?

suspects.why: a robin alone is one mark and a flock of thirty starlings arriving together is also one mark
they hold a territory all year, so the same bird is reliably present
they are bold and will feed with people nearby
they are brightly marked and easy to identify with no doubt
they sing through the winter, which draws attention

cases.answer: The record counts sightings, so one robin outscores a flock of thirty.
proof: “The record is kept as sightings, with one mark made each time a species is seen.”
“A ringing session run by the county trust at dawn last March caught and counted individual birds instead.”
“It recorded four robins, sixty-one starlings, fifty-three house sparrows and thirty-eight goldfinches.”
clears: Their territory: “the same bird is reliably present.”
Their boldness: “they are bold and will feed with people nearby.”
Their markings: “easy to identify with no doubt.”
Their song: “which draws attention.”
cases.explain: Everything the club says about robins is true, which is why the answer felt obvious. A sighting is an event in the observer's day, not a bird in the garden, and a species that flocks can never win a contest scored that way. The ringing session counted birds and found four robins to a hundred and fifty of everything else.

cases.title: The Case of the Machine Only Staff Used
cases.story: The usage report for the drinks machine shows ninety-six percent of cups taken by staff, and the machine is being moved into the staff room. Four reasons have been offered and all four are genuine. Staff have longer breaks and more of them across a day. The machine stands in the corridor outside the staff room. Pupils are not allowed hot drinks in lessons, which rules out most of their day. And staff drink more hot drinks per head than teenagers do by any national measure. Those four would give staff a clear majority and would not give them ninety-six percent. The report is generated from the staff key fobs, which log every cup against a name for the billing. A pupil pays with a coin, and the coin mechanism has no counter wired to the reporting board. The engineer's visit in February logged total cups dispensed from the flow meter instead. It recorded four thousand one hundred cups in a fortnight against the key fob total of one thousand six hundred. Two thousand five hundred cups in that fortnight were paid for in coins. The report was never a record of who used the machine. It was a record of who had to be billed for it.
cases.question: Do staff really take ninety-six percent of the cups?

suspects.why: the report is generated from the staff key fobs and the coin mechanism has no counter wired to the reporting board
staff have longer breaks and more of them across a day
the machine stands in the corridor outside the staff room
pupils are not allowed hot drinks in lessons, which rules out most of their day
staff drink more hot drinks per head than teenagers do by any national measure

cases.answer: The report counts billed cups, and pupils pay in coins.
proof: “The engineer's visit in February logged total cups dispensed from the flow meter instead.”
“It recorded four thousand one hundred cups in a fortnight against the key fob total of one thousand six hundred.”
“Two thousand five hundred cups in that fortnight were paid for in coins.”
clears: Break times: “longer breaks and more of them across a day.”
The position: “outside the staff room.”
The rule: “which rules out most of their day.”
Habits: “staff drink more hot drinks per head than teenagers do by any national measure.”
cases.explain: Ninety-six percent of the cups the system can see belong to staff, and that sentence is true. The flow meter counts water rather than names, and it finds pupils taking three cups in five. Moving the machine into the staff room would remove it from the people who use it most.

cases.title: The Case of the Year Group That Sent the Most Cards
cases.story: The post count shows Year Nine sending two hundred and twelve cards and no other year reaching sixty. The tutor team is being asked what makes that year group different. Four explanations have been put forward and each is plausible and partly true. Year Nine is the largest cohort by thirty-one pupils. It is the year the school runs its friendship and relationships unit, which raises the subject in February. Its form rooms are next to the art rooms, where the card-making club meets. And its tutors ran a charity link, giving twenty pence a card to the hospice. Those four would lift one year group's total and would not quadruple it. The single post box stands in the Year Nine corridor, outside room fourteen. Every other year group reaches it by crossing the quad or going up two flights. A second box was put in the Year Eleven corridor for three days as a trial this year. It took ninety-one cards in three days, against the main box's hundred and four over the same three days. A count of cards posted is a count of cards posted somewhere convenient.
cases.question: Does Year Nine really send four times as many cards?

suspects.who: 📮 Where the only post box stands
suspects.why: the single post box stands in the Year Nine corridor and every other year group reaches it by crossing the quad
Year Nine is the largest cohort by thirty-one pupils
it is the year the school runs its friendship and relationships unit, which raises the subject in February
its form rooms are next to the art rooms, where the card-making club meets
its tutors ran a charity link, giving twenty pence a card to the hospice

cases.answer: The only post box is in the Year Nine corridor.
proof: “A second box was put in the Year Eleven corridor for three days as a trial this year.”
“It took ninety-one cards in three days, against the main box's hundred and four over the same three days.”
“A count of cards posted is a count of cards posted somewhere convenient.”
clears: Cohort size: “Year Nine is the largest cohort by thirty-one pupils.”
The unit: “which raises the subject in February.”
The art rooms: “where the card-making club meets.”
The charity link: “giving twenty pence a card to the hospice.”
cases.explain: Four reasons that would each add a few cards, against a total four times everybody else's. The three-day trial is decisive and cheap: a second box in another corridor nearly matched the first. The cards were always being written. They were not being carried across a quad to be counted.

cases.title: The Case of the Volcanoes That Won Every Prize
cases.story: Eleven of the last fourteen science fair prizes have gone to volcano projects, and the department is worried that judges are being won over by spectacle. Four reasons have been offered and each is reasonable. A volcano is visual, and a judge remembers what they saw. It has a clear result that needs no explanation. It can be built by one pupil without a technician. And it photographs well for the newsletter, which shapes what the next year attempts. Those four would favour volcanoes and would not deliver eleven prizes in fourteen. Judging runs between two o'clock and three o'clock on the Friday afternoon. A judge walks the hall and asks each entrant to show what their project does. A volcano can be made to erupt on request in forty seconds. The germination trial, the mould study, the rusting experiment and the yeast investigation all need between a day and three weeks to show anything. Those four entries can offer a judge a folder of results and nothing to watch. The prize does not reward the best science. It rewards the science that can be performed inside a one-hour window.
cases.question: Why do volcanoes win every prize?

suspects.why: a volcano can be made to erupt on request in forty seconds and the other projects need between a day and three weeks
a volcano is visual, and a judge remembers what they saw
it has a clear result that needs no explanation
it can be built by one pupil without a technician
it photographs well for the newsletter, which shapes what the next year attempts

cases.answer: Judging happens in an hour, and only a volcano can perform in an hour.
proof: “A judge walks the hall and asks each entrant to show what their project does.”
“Those four entries can offer a judge a folder of results and nothing to watch.”
“The prize does not reward the best science.”
clears: Being visual: “a judge remembers what they saw.”
The clear result: “a clear result that needs no explanation.”
No technician: “built by one pupil without a technician.”
The newsletter: “which shapes what the next year attempts.”
cases.explain: Spectacle is real and it is not the mechanism. The judging method asks every entrant to perform, and a question like that can only be answered by projects whose result arrives in under a minute. Everything with a timescale longer than the fair was ruled out before a judge formed an opinion about it.

cases.title: The Case of the Most Photographed Crown
cases.story: The museum's figures show the Tudor crown photographed eleven thousand times last year, more than the next four objects together, and the gallery is being rebuilt around it. Four reasons have been offered and each is genuine. It is the only object in the museum that most visitors have seen in a schoolbook. It sits at eye level in an open case rather than behind a rail. It is lit from four sides, which makes a photograph that works. And it is the last object before the shop, where people have their phones out already. Those four would make it the most photographed and they do not explain a figure larger than the next four combined. The count comes from the photography permission scheme, where a visitor taps a card to unlock the no-flash rule in that room. Rooms two through seven are marked no photography because of loan conditions on their contents. There is no way for a visitor to photograph the Anglo-Saxon hoard or the illuminated psalter at all. The count of eleven thousand is a count of the one room where photography is permitted and logged. Six objects were never in the competition.
cases.question: Is the crown really the most photographed object?

suspects.who: 🚫 The rooms where photography is banned
suspects.why: rooms two through seven are marked no photography because of loan conditions on their contents
it is the only object in the museum that most visitors have seen in a schoolbook
it sits at eye level in an open case rather than behind a rail
it is lit from four sides, which makes a photograph that works
it is the last object before the shop, where people have their phones out already

cases.answer: It is the only object visitors are allowed to photograph.
proof: “The count comes from the photography permission scheme, where a visitor taps a card to unlock the no-flash rule in that room.”
“There is no way for a visitor to photograph the Anglo-Saxon hoard or the illuminated psalter at all.”
“Six objects were never in the competition.”
clears: Its fame: “the only object in the museum that most visitors have seen in a schoolbook.”
Its case: “at eye level in an open case rather than behind a rail.”
Its lighting: “lit from four sides, which makes a photograph that works.”
The shop: “where people have their phones out already.”
cases.explain: A ranking needs the things being ranked to be able to score. Six of the museum's best objects cannot be photographed by anybody under any circumstances, so a photograph count puts them at zero and calls it unpopularity. Rebuilding the gallery around the crown would be rebuilding it around a loan condition.

cases.title: The Case of the Pianists Who Were Better at Maths
cases.story: The school's figures show pupils who learn the piano scoring eleven points above the year average in maths, and a bid is being written to fund piano lessons for everybody. Four mechanisms have been proposed and each has some research behind it. Reading two staves at once trains the handling of two streams of information. Rhythm is counted in fractions, and pupils who count them daily meet them early. Practice builds a habit of returning to something difficult. And performance teaches work under pressure. Those four are real and the published effect for each is small. Piano lessons at this school cost eighteen pounds a week and are arranged privately by families. Ninety-one percent of the pupils learning piano are not eligible for free school meals, against sixty-two percent of the year group. When the same figures are compared within the group that pays for lessons, the piano gap falls to two points. The county ran a funded scheme in two thousand and nineteen giving free lessons to a randomly chosen hundred pupils. That cohort finished one point above its control group. Learning the piano is mostly a measure of being able to afford to learn the piano.
cases.question: Does learning the piano raise maths scores?

suspects.why: piano lessons cost eighteen pounds a week and are arranged privately by families
reading two staves at once trains the handling of two streams of information
rhythm is counted in fractions, and pupils who count them daily meet them early
practice builds a habit of returning to something difficult
performance teaches work under pressure

cases.answer: The pupils who learn piano are the pupils whose families can pay for it.
proof: “Ninety-one percent of the pupils learning piano are not eligible for free school meals, against sixty-two percent of the year group.”
“When the same figures are compared within the group that pays for lessons, the piano gap falls to two points.”
“That cohort finished one point above its control group.”
clears: Two staves: “trains the handling of two streams of information.”
Rhythm: “pupils who count them daily meet them early.”
Practice: “a habit of returning to something difficult.”
Performing: “teaches work under pressure.”
cases.explain: All four mechanisms are real and together they are worth a point or two, which is what the funded scheme found. The eleven points belong to the thing that decides who sits at a piano in the first place. The bid is still worth writing, for music, as long as nobody promises it will move a maths grade.

cases.title: The Case of the Kites That Never Met Bad Weather
cases.story: Four years of club records show the field's wind running between eight and forty kilometres an hour and never outside it, and a member is writing that the site has unusually steady weather. Four reasons have been offered and each is physically real. The field sits in a shallow bowl with rising ground on three sides. The line of poplars along the western edge breaks the strongest gusts. The site is twelve kilometres inland, away from coastal extremes. And the valley runs across the prevailing wind rather than along it. Those four would narrow a range and they would not put a hard floor and a hard ceiling on it. The readings are taken by whoever turns up, from the handheld meter in the clubhouse. Nobody drives to a kite field on a still day, because there is nothing to do there. Nobody drives to a kite field in a gale either, because the club rules forbid flying above forty. The parish council's own weather station, four hundred metres away, logs every hour whether anybody is there or not. It records winds below eight on a hundred and ninety days a year and above forty on thirty-one. The club measured its own attendance rules.
cases.question: Is the field's wind really that steady?

suspects.why: nobody drives to a kite field on a still day and nobody drives to one in a gale either
the field sits in a shallow bowl with rising ground on three sides
the line of poplars along the western edge breaks the strongest gusts
the site is twelve kilometres inland, away from coastal extremes
the valley runs across the prevailing wind rather than along it

cases.answer: Nobody goes to the field on the days the wind is outside that range.
proof: “The readings are taken by whoever turns up, from the handheld meter in the clubhouse.”
“The parish council's own weather station, four hundred metres away, logs every hour whether anybody is there or not.”
“It records winds below eight on a hundred and ninety days a year and above forty on thirty-one.”
clears: The bowl: “rising ground on three sides.”
The poplars: “breaks the strongest gusts.”
Being inland: “away from coastal extremes.”
The valley: “runs across the prevailing wind rather than along it.”
cases.explain: Four years of readings and not one outside the range is the tell, because weather does not have edges that sharp. The forty is the club rule and the eight is the point below which the drive is not worth it. A dataset gathered by volunteers records the conditions under which volunteers volunteer.

cases.title: The Case of the Lucky Corner of the Field
cases.story: The club's find book records sixty-one four-leaf clovers from the top corner of the field and nine from everywhere else, and the corner is being fenced as a conservation plot. Four reasons have been offered and each is a real possibility. The corner is the only part of the field that was never ploughed. It is damper, lying at the foot of the slope where water collects. It is mown less often because the mower cannot turn there. And disturbance is known to raise the rate of the mutation that produces a fourth leaflet. Those four could raise the local rate, perhaps by half. The find book records clovers found and has no column for time spent looking. The corner is where the club meets, because it is the only shaded spot and the gate is there. A log kept last summer recorded searcher-hours as well as finds. The corner took a hundred and forty hours of searching and the rest of the field took eleven. Sixty-one finds in a hundred and forty hours is one every two and a quarter hours, and nine finds in eleven hours is one every one and a quarter. Measured by the hour, the corner is the worst ground on the field.
cases.question: Is the top corner really luckier?

suspects.why: the corner is where the club meets, and the find book has no column for time spent looking
the corner is the only part of the field that was never ploughed
it is damper, lying at the foot of the slope where water collects
it is mown less often because the mower cannot turn there
disturbance is known to raise the rate of the mutation that produces a fourth leaflet

cases.answer: Almost all the searching has been done in that one corner.
proof: “A log kept last summer recorded searcher-hours as well as finds.”
“The corner took a hundred and forty hours of searching and the rest of the field took eleven.”
“Measured by the hour, the corner is the worst ground on the field.”
clears: The ploughing: “the only part of the field that was never ploughed.”
The damp: “lying at the foot of the slope where water collects.”
The mowing: “the mower cannot turn there.”
Disturbance: “raise the rate of the mutation that produces a fourth leaflet.”
cases.explain: A count of finds without a count of looking is not a rate at all, and the whole case turns on supplying the missing denominator. Once the hours go in, the corner falls from seven times better to nearly half as good. The club would have fenced off its own meeting place and called it a discovery.

cases.title: The Case of the Flooding That Started in Two Thousand and Nineteen
cases.story: The site record shows four flooding incidents in the yard before two thousand and nineteen and seventy-one since, and a drainage contract worth ninety thousand pounds is being prepared. Four causes have been offered and each is real. The playground was resurfaced in two thousand and eighteen with a tighter asphalt that takes water less readily. The new bicycle store covers a hundred and ten square metres that used to be grass. Rainfall at the parish station has risen about eight percent across the same period. And a new kerb line directs water that used to run onto the verge back towards the yard. Those four would raise a flooding rate and nobody is arguing they have not. The online estates form was introduced in January two thousand and nineteen and can be filled in from a phone in two minutes. Before that, a flood had to be reported by telephone to a county office open between ten and three. The caretaker's own diary, kept continuously since two thousand and eleven, mentions standing water in the yard in every year of its record. The diary counts between nine and fourteen floods a year throughout, with no step in two thousand and nineteen. The site record changed in that year. The yard did not.
cases.question: Did the flooding really start in two thousand and nineteen?

suspects.why: the online estates form was introduced in January two thousand and nineteen and can be filled in from a phone in two minutes
the playground was resurfaced with a tighter asphalt that takes water less readily
the new bicycle store covers a hundred and ten square metres that used to be grass
rainfall at the parish station has risen about eight percent across the same period
a new kerb line directs water that used to run onto the verge back towards the yard

cases.answer: The form changed in two thousand and nineteen, not the yard.
proof: “Before that, a flood had to be reported by telephone to a county office open between ten and three.”
“The caretaker's own diary, kept continuously since two thousand and eleven, mentions standing water in the yard in every year of its record.”
“The diary counts between nine and fourteen floods a year throughout, with no step in two thousand and nineteen.”
clears: The resurfacing: “a tighter asphalt that takes water less readily.”
The bicycle store: “a hundred and ten square metres that used to be grass.”
More rain: “risen about eight percent across the same period.”
The kerb: “directs water that used to run onto the verge back towards the yard.”
cases.explain: The yard genuinely drains worse than it did, for four documented reasons. None of them arrives as a jump in a single January. A record that steps the moment the reporting method changes is describing the method, and the diary, which never changed, shows a flat line straight through the year everything supposedly began.

cases.title: The Case of the Bed That Grew Everything Best
cases.story: Bed four has produced the heaviest crop in each of six years and the garden club wants the other five beds rebuilt to match it. Four advantages have been named and each is genuine. It is the only raised bed, so its soil warms earlier in spring. It was filled with bought compost where the others use the school's own. It faces south-west and catches the afternoon sun. And its timber sides keep the rabbits out, which the chewed rows elsewhere confirm. Those four are worth real weight and the gap is more than two to one. Bed four stands beside the outside tap. The hose reaches bed four without being dragged and reaches bed five only if the coil is unwound across the path. The watering rota has one instruction on it, which is to water what needs it, and it is carried out by whoever is free at the time. A log kept last summer recorded eighty-one waterings for bed four and between nine and nineteen for the other five. Bed two was moved next to the tap in September as a test and grew the heaviest crop this year. Bed four was moved to the far end and came fourth.
cases.question: Is bed four really the best bed?

suspects.why: the hose reaches bed four without being dragged and reaches bed five only if the coil is unwound across the path
it is the only raised bed, so its soil warms earlier in spring
it was filled with bought compost where the others use the school's own
it faces south-west and catches the afternoon sun
its timber sides keep the rabbits out, which the chewed rows elsewhere confirm

cases.answer: Bed four is the bed the hose reaches, so it is the bed that gets watered.
proof: “A log kept last summer recorded eighty-one waterings for bed four and between nine and nineteen for the other five.”
“Bed two was moved next to the tap in September as a test and grew the heaviest crop this year.”
“Bed four was moved to the far end and came fourth.”
clears: Being raised: “its soil warms earlier in spring.”
The compost: “where the others use the school's own.”
The aspect: “catches the afternoon sun.”
The sides: “which the chewed rows elsewhere confirm.”
cases.explain: Four advantages that travel with the bed, and the club proved they were not the cause by moving the bed. Everything bed four was built with went to the far end and finished fourth. What stayed behind was the tap, and the rota's one instruction quietly turns convenience into a crop yield.

cases.title: The Case of the Hens That Came Already Proven
cases.story: The six brown hens have laid two thousand one hundred eggs between them and the six white hens nine hundred, and the school is about to buy only browns. Four reasons have been offered and each is a real difference between the two groups. The browns are a commercial laying strain bred for output over sixty years. They are heavier birds and eat about fifteen percent more feed. They came with a vaccination record and the whites did not. And they were six months older on arrival, so they began laying four months sooner. Those four are worth a genuine advantage of perhaps a quarter. The browns were bought from a commercial unit that sells its birds on at seventy-two weeks. That unit culls any bird falling below five eggs a week at the forty-week check. The whites came from a hatchery as day-old chicks, with no selection of any kind applied to them. Every brown hen in the run is a bird that had already proved itself before the school saw it. The three whites that lay best in the run average five point two eggs a week, which is the number the commercial unit uses as its cut.
cases.question: Are brown hens really better layers?

suspects.why: the unit culls any bird falling below five eggs a week at the forty-week check
the browns are a commercial laying strain bred for output over sixty years
they are heavier birds and eat about fifteen percent more feed
they came with a vaccination record and the whites did not
they were six months older on arrival, so they began laying four months sooner

cases.answer: Every brown hen had already passed a laying test before the school bought her.
proof: “The whites came from a hatchery as day-old chicks, with no selection of any kind applied to them.”
“Every brown hen in the run is a bird that had already proved itself before the school saw it.”
“The three whites that lay best in the run average five point two eggs a week, which is the number the commercial unit uses as its cut.”
clears: The strain: “bred for output over sixty years.”
Eating more: “about fifteen percent more feed.”
The vaccinations: “they came with a vaccination record and the whites did not.”
Being older: “they began laying four months sooner.”
cases.explain: The browns really are the better strain, by about a quarter. The rest of the gap was manufactured by a cull the school never saw, which removed every poor brown layer before the comparison began. The best three whites meet the commercial standard, and in a brown flock they would be the survivors too.

cases.title: The Case of the School Where Everybody Walked
cases.story: The eco club's survey reports ninety-one percent of pupils walking or cycling to school, and the travel plan has been signed off on that basis. Four reasons have been offered and each is real. The catchment is compact, with three quarters of pupils living inside a mile. There is a safe crossing on the main road and a marked cycle lane the length of the hill. The school has run a walking bus for eleven years. And parking at the gate was removed in September, which does change behaviour. Those four would give a high figure and they would not give ninety-one percent. The survey was handed out at the eco club's Thursday meeting and to the club's contacts in form time. It gathered a hundred and forty responses from a roll of eight hundred and ten. The club meets to campaign about transport, and joining it is a choice pupils make. A gate count run by the office for five mornings in November, which counts everybody arriving by any means, found three hundred and nine arrivals by car. Three hundred and nine of eight hundred and ten is thirty-eight percent. A survey of people who care about walking will find that people care about walking.
cases.question: Do ninety-one percent really walk?

suspects.why: the survey was handed out at the eco club's Thursday meeting, and joining the club is a choice pupils make
three quarters of pupils live inside a mile
there is a safe crossing on the main road and a marked cycle lane the length of the hill
the school has run a walking bus for eleven years
parking at the gate was removed in September, which does change behaviour

cases.answer: The survey was given to the people most likely to walk.
proof: “It gathered a hundred and forty responses from a roll of eight hundred and ten.”
“A gate count run by the office for five mornings in November, which counts everybody arriving by any means, found three hundred and nine arrivals by car.”
“Three hundred and nine of eight hundred and ten is thirty-eight percent.”
clears: The catchment: “three quarters of pupils living inside a mile.”
The crossing: “a marked cycle lane the length of the hill.”
The walking bus: “for eleven years.”
The parking: “which does change behaviour.”
cases.explain: Nobody lied on a form. A hundred and forty people who chose to join a transport campaign really do walk, at ninety-one percent. The other six hundred and seventy were never asked, and a gate count that cannot be opted out of puts more than a third of them in a car.

cases.title: The Case of the Camera That Was Brilliant in the Dark
cases.story: The club's portfolio holds forty low-light photographs, every one of them sharp, and the camera is being recommended for the trip on that evidence. Four reasons have been offered and each is a genuine strength of the body. Its sensor is physically large, which gathers more light per pixel. Its lens opens to one point four. Its stabiliser is rated at four stops. And its processor applies a noise reduction that the reviews praise. Those four make it a good low-light camera and nobody is disputing that. The portfolio is assembled each term from whatever members choose to submit. The card from the November evening shoot was still in the bag and held nine hundred and six frames. Two hundred and forty of them are low-light and fourteen were submitted. A count of the two hundred and forty found a hundred and ninety-one too blurred to use and thirty-five visibly noisy. The camera's hit rate in low light is about six percent, and the portfolio's hit rate is a hundred. Nobody deleted anything dishonestly, and the weak frames simply were not worth submitting to a portfolio. A folder of successes cannot tell you anything about a rate unless somebody kept the failures.
cases.question: Is the camera really that good in the dark?

suspects.who: 🗂️ A portfolio made only of successes
suspects.why: the portfolio is assembled each term from whatever members choose to submit
its sensor is physically large, which gathers more light per pixel
its lens opens to one point four
its stabiliser is rated at four stops
its processor applies a noise reduction that the reviews praise

cases.answer: The portfolio contains only the frames that came out.
proof: “Two hundred and forty of them are low-light and fourteen were submitted.”
“A count of the two hundred and forty found a hundred and ninety-one too blurred to use and thirty-five visibly noisy.”
“The camera's hit rate in low light is about six percent, and the portfolio's hit rate is a hundred.”
clears: The sensor: “gathers more light per pixel.”
The lens: “its lens opens to one point four.”
The stabiliser: “rated at four stops.”
The noise reduction: “that the reviews praise.”
cases.explain: Forty perfect photographs are forty pieces of evidence that the camera can do it, and none at all about how often. The card that nobody emptied is the control nobody meant to keep. Six percent is still a usable camera, as long as the trip is planned for two hundred frames rather than fourteen.

cases.title: The Case of the Compost That Grew Giants
cases.story: The compost trial reports tray C averaging thirty-one centimetres against tray A's nineteen, and the school is switching to the brand in tray C. Four advantages have been offered and each is real. Tray C's compost tests higher in nitrogen by a fifth. It holds water better on the laboratory's own measure. Its texture is finer, which suits a small seed. And it is pasteurised, so it carries fewer fungal spores. Those four would give a genuine advantage of perhaps a quarter. The method sheet says to thin each tray to the strongest twelve seedlings at two weeks. Tray C was thinned on the fourteenth day as written. Trays A, B and D were not thinned, because the pupil responsible was away and nobody picked it up. Thinning also leaves the plants that remain with more root room and more light. Tray C's average is the average of twelve chosen plants and tray A's is the average of all forty-one that came up. The twelve tallest plants in tray A average twenty-nine centimetres. Thinning a tray does not make plants grow. It changes which plants are in the number at the end.
cases.question: Is tray C's compost really better?

suspects.why: tray C was thinned to the strongest twelve on the fourteenth day and the others were not thinned at all
tray C's compost tests higher in nitrogen by a fifth
it holds water better on the laboratory's own measure
its texture is finer, which suits a small seed
it is pasteurised, so it carries fewer fungal spores

cases.answer: Tray C's average is of twelve chosen plants and the others are of everything.
proof: “Tray C's average is the average of twelve chosen plants and tray A's is the average of all forty-one that came up.”
“The twelve tallest plants in tray A average twenty-nine centimetres.”
“Thinning a tray does not make plants grow.”
clears: The nitrogen: “higher in nitrogen by a fifth.”
Water: “holds water better on the laboratory's own measure.”
The texture: “which suits a small seed.”
Pasteurising: “it carries fewer fungal spores.”
cases.explain: Tray C's compost is better, by about two centimetres, which is what the matched comparison gives. The other ten came from a step in the method that was carried out in one tray and missed in three. An average over a group that has had its weakest members removed is not comparable to an average over a group that has not.

cases.title: The Case of the Flavour That Was Always Vanilla
cases.story: Three years of till data put vanilla at sixty-one percent of ice cream sales, and the kitchen is cutting the other flavours. Four reasons have been offered and each is fair. Vanilla goes with the puddings the kitchen serves, which the others do not. It is the flavour least likely to be refused by anybody. It is priced ten pence lower because it is bought in larger tubs. And it is the flavour most often chosen by the youngest pupils, who are the largest group of buyers. Those four would give vanilla a lead and would not give it sixty-one percent. The freezer in the servery holds two tubs. One is permanently vanilla by standing instruction, because it is the safe choice. The second rotates through chocolate, strawberry, mint and toffee, one at a time. A flavour that is not in the freezer cannot be chosen by anybody, however much they want it. A stock audit shows vanilla available on every one of the five hundred and seventy serving days. Each of the other four flavours was available on between a hundred and ten and a hundred and thirty days. Measured per day available, vanilla sells eighty-one portions and toffee sells ninety-four.
cases.question: Is vanilla really the most popular flavour?

suspects.who: 🧊 The standing instruction on the freezer
suspects.why: one tub is permanently vanilla by standing instruction and the second rotates through four flavours one at a time
vanilla goes with the puddings the kitchen serves, which the others do not
it is the flavour least likely to be refused by anybody
it is priced ten pence lower because it is bought in larger tubs
it is the flavour most often chosen by the youngest pupils, who are the largest group of buyers

cases.answer: Vanilla is on sale every day and the others about one day in five.
proof: “A stock audit shows vanilla available on every one of the five hundred and seventy serving days.”
“Each of the other four flavours was available on between a hundred and ten and a hundred and thirty days.”
“Measured per day available, vanilla sells eighty-one portions and toffee sells ninety-four.”
clears: The puddings: “which the others do not.”
Not being refused: “least likely to be refused by anybody.”
The price: “priced ten pence lower because it is bought in larger tubs.”
The young buyers: “the largest group of buyers.”
cases.explain: Sixty-one percent of sales is exactly what vanilla took, and five times the opportunity is why. Once the days available go into the denominator, vanilla is not even first. Cutting the other flavours would remove the best seller in the freezer on the strength of a rota.

cases.title: The Case of the Year Group That Gave Most
cases.story: The appeal's figures show Year Eleven giving four hundred and ten pounds and no other year reaching ninety, and Year Eleven is to be held up as an example in assembly. Four reasons have been offered and each is plausible. Year Eleven has the oldest pupils, who are likelier to carry money. It ran a cake stall alongside the ribbons. Two of its tutors have a long connection with the charity. And leavers' years do give more to school appeals, which the office has noticed before. Those four would lift one year group and would not multiply it by five. Ribbons were offered to Year Eleven in form time, at the desk, by a tutor, with a tin passed along the row. Every other year group was told in assembly that ribbons could be collected from the office at break. A trial this year took the tin into four Year Eight forms in exactly the Year Eleven way. Those four forms gave a hundred and sixty-eight pounds in a week, from a year group that gave sixty-one pounds in the whole of last year's appeal. Asking somebody directly and asking them to walk to an office are not the same question.
cases.question: Is Year Eleven really the most generous?

suspects.who: 🙋 How each year group was asked
suspects.why: Year Eleven was asked in form time with a tin passed along the row and everyone else was told to collect ribbons from the office
Year Eleven has the oldest pupils, who are likelier to carry money
it ran a cake stall alongside the ribbons
two of its tutors have a long connection with the charity
leavers' years do give more to school appeals, which the office has noticed before

cases.answer: Year Eleven is the only year group that was actually asked.
proof: “A trial this year took the tin into four Year Eight forms in exactly the Year Eleven way.”
“Those four forms gave a hundred and sixty-eight pounds in a week, from a year group that gave sixty-one pounds in the whole of last year's appeal.”
“Asking somebody directly and asking them to walk to an office are not the same question.”
clears: Older pupils: “likelier to carry money.”
The cake stall: “it ran a cake stall alongside the ribbons.”
The tutors: “a long connection with the charity.”
The leavers: “which the office has noticed before.”
cases.explain: Four real reasons to expect Year Eleven to lead, and a gap of five to one that none of them reaches. The difference is in the asking. Four Year Eight forms, given the same tin in the same room, beat their own year's entire previous appeal in a week, and nothing about those pupils had changed.

cases.title: The Case of the Balloons That All Landed in Towns
cases.story: Two hundred balloons were released with reply cards and sixty-three came back. Fifty-eight of the sixty-three were found in towns and villages, and the report concludes that the prevailing wind carries balloons towards settlements. Four reasons have been offered and each sounds sensible. Towns sit in valleys, and the valley wind does funnel along them. Buildings and street trees catch a descending balloon where open ground lets it skip. The town lies downwind of the launch field on most days. And warm air rising over a town is known to affect how a light object descends. Those four might tilt a distribution a little. A card can only come back if a person finds the balloon, reads the card, and posts it. Towns hold most of the people, so towns are where found balloons are found. The moorland downwind of the launch field holds four houses in eleven kilometres. The club walked a measured transect across eleven kilometres of moorland downwind three days after the launch. It recovered twenty-nine balloons, none of which had been reported by anybody. A hundred and thirty-seven balloons were never heard of again, and the moor is the only place anyone has looked for them.
cases.question: Do balloons really land in towns?

suspects.who: 📬 Only found balloons send a card
suspects.why: a card can only come back if a person finds the balloon, reads the card, and posts it
towns sit in valleys, and the valley wind does funnel along them
buildings and street trees catch a descending balloon where open ground lets it skip
the town lies downwind of the launch field on most days
warm air rising over a town is known to affect how a light object descends

cases.answer: A balloon that lands where nobody lives never sends a card back.
proof: “Towns hold most of the people, so towns are where found balloons are found.”
“It recovered twenty-nine balloons, none of which had been reported by anybody.”
“A hundred and thirty-seven balloons were never heard of again, and the moor is the only place anyone has looked for them.”
clears: The valley wind: “the valley wind does funnel along them.”
Buildings: “catch a descending balloon where open ground lets it skip.”
Being downwind: “the town lies downwind of the launch field on most days.”
Warm air: “known to affect how a light object descends.”
cases.explain: Sixty-three cards and every one of them true. The conclusion is still backwards, because the data was collected by the very thing it claims to measure: a balloon reports its landing place only if it lands near somebody. One walk across the moor turned up twenty-nine balloons that the study would have counted as never having come down.
